"You sit in my hideout uninvited, outsider, but I've heard your name on the trade roads. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and these woods have eaten warrants like yours for a generation.
Twenty-five days. That's all you get to prove you're worth more to me alive than dead. Bring me word of a kill — a party of those who profit from the same imperial coin that called for ours. The hunt-brief comes next; my scouts have marked one.
After that, we'll talk again. Run, and you'll find I keep my hideouts well-watched."

"My scouts have eyes on {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} working the trade roads near {AREA}. They don't know yet that they're already dead.
Bring me their banner, or their captain's blade, or whatever you can carry back. Engage them alone — my people are watching to count the kill, and they only count what they see.
The forest will hide you on the approach. After that, it's your skill or your bones."

"Change of marks. {PARTY_NAME} now — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} near {AREA}. The old quarry slipped my watchers, or moved beyond where I trust them. The forest keeps no grudges against the ones that get away — but the new one will do."

"You came back. Many don't.
My runners brought word before you did — a {CULTURE} party broken, the captain dead, the banner taken. I had a wager with one of mine that you wouldn't return; she's a denar lighter tonight.
Come to {HIDEOUT} when the sun's down. We have more to discuss now that you've proven you can be trusted to swing a blade."

"You climbed a long way to find me, outsider. Not many make the last ridge without breaking a leg or losing their nerve. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and this granite is mine.
Twenty-five days. That's the rope I'm throwing you. Use it to drag back a kill — a party whose loss the lowlands will feel. My scouts will mark the target; you'll have the name and the road before you leave my fire.
Fail me and the descent's harder than the climb. Cross me and you won't see the second pass."

"My watchers came down off the high ledges with a name. {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} moving the low country near {AREA}, fat with the easy walking down there.
Catch them on open ground where the slope works for you. They climb soft and they tire fast; an hour of broken terrain and their column will be strung out like beads. Take the head of it, the tail folds.
Bring back proof I can hold in my hand. The granite remembers what gets written on it."
"New mark — the old trail went cold below the snowline. {PARTY_NAME} now, {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} working the roads near {AREA}. Same climb down, different blood at the end of it."

"You came back up the mountain. That tells me enough.
Word reached the ridge before you did — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} column broken on the lowland road, the captain down, the survivors scattered toward whatever town would still open a gate for them. Clean work, by the sound of it. Cleaner than I bet you for.
Come to {HIDEOUT} before the light goes. The wind up here turns mean after dusk and I won't shout terms across a black ridge. We have the next stretch of the climb to mark out, you and me."

"You ride into my camp without a banner, outsider. Bold. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and the plains have long memories for faces.
Twenty-five days. The sky will turn that many times before I lose patience. Bring me a kill — a party that bleeds for the same coin that hunts us. My outriders have already picked one. The brief follows.
Ride hard. Ride alone. The horizon is wide and I have men watching every line of it. Break your word and you'll learn how far a steppe man can chase."

"My riders cut their tracks two days east. {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} crawling the open ground near {AREA}. Slow. Heavy. Easy meat for a man who knows the wind.
Run them down before they reach walls. Out here there's nowhere to hide a horse, so they'll see you coming. Doesn't matter. By the time they shape a line, you're already through.
Take the kill alone. My watchers will be on the ridge, counting. They count nothing they don't see with their own eyes."
"New tracks. {PARTY_NAME} now — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} crossing the flats near {AREA}. The old quarry rode past the horizon and out of my reach. The wind doesn't carry grudges. Ride."

"You came back across the plain. Good.
A rider brought the word ahead of you — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} party scattered, the captain face-down in the grass, the horses taken. My watchers say you rode through them clean. That's the kind of work the steppe respects.
Ride to {HIDEOUT} before the sky turns again. Sit by my fire. There's more ground to cover between us, and I'd rather speak of it where the wind can't carry our voices to the wrong ears."

"Salt and storm, you've walked into my hold and lived to draw breath. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and my crew swore their oaths on this deck before you were weaned.
Twenty-five days, no more. The sea grants no mercy and neither do I. Bring me a kill — a party whose blood pays the toll for what your kind has cost mine. My lookouts will mark the quarry next, and you'll sail to meet it.
Break the oath and there's no shore far enough. Keep it, and you'll have drunk from a longship captain's horn."

"My lookouts sighted {PARTY_NAME} from the headlands — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} crawling the coast near {AREA}. Fat, slow, and far from any tide that could save them.
Take them clean. Bring me a torn standard, a captain's ring, something the gulls haven't picked over. Go alone — my crew watches from the rocks, and an oath unwitnessed is no oath at all.
The wind is with you for now. After the steel meets, only your arm decides whether you ride home or feed the crabs."

"New quarry. {PARTY_NAME} now — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} working the coast near {AREA}. The old mark slipped the tide, and the sea keeps what it takes. This one will do, and my lookouts swear by it."

"You came back salt-stained and breathing. Few do.
A gull-runner brought the word ahead of you — a {CULTURE} party broken on the strand, the captain face-down, the standard hauled down by your own hand. One of my oar-mates wagered against you. He'll be bailing bilge for a week.
Come to {HIDEOUT} when the tide turns. There's mead in the hall and oaths still to be sworn, and a captain who has held his word is owed a captain's welcome."

"You walk into my shade unbidden, stranger, and the sand has not yet covered your tracks. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and out here a name is a debt the desert collects.
Twenty-five days. The sun counts them whether you do or not. Bring me one party dead before that count runs dry — a target my watchers will name for you next. No excuses; the heat takes those too.
Drink, then ride. Cross me, and there are wells you will not reach in time."

"My riders followed the dust. {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} crawling the wastes near {AREA}, watering at the same oases we do.
Ride light. Strike when the sun is low and their guards squint west. Bring me a blade, a buckle, anything I can hold — my men count the kill with their eyes, and the sand swallows the rest.
The distance is long and the water short. Plan your route, or the desert finishes the job before you do."
"New tracks. {PARTY_NAME} now — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} watering near {AREA}. The old quarry crossed dunes my riders won't follow, and the sand has already forgotten them."

"You came back before the waterskins ran dry. Few do.
The dust reached me ahead of you — a {CULTURE} party broken in the open, vultures already counting. One of my riders said the heat would finish you before any blade did. He owes me a skin of date wine tonight.
Ride to {HIDEOUT} before the sun climbs again. We have terms to set now that the sand knows your name, and I would rather speak them in shade than under the noon."

"Sit down, sit down... don't stand over an old man like that. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and I've outlived three chiefs braver than me. That's how I'm still breathing.
Twenty-five days, that's what I can give you. No more. We're hungry here, and they — the steel-shirts, the big bands with proper banners — they pick us apart whenever they smell weakness. Bring me one party dead, just one, and the others above us will look elsewhere for sport.
The scouts will whisper a name to you soon. Please... don't fail an old huddled fool. We can't take another bad season."

"My boys came back shivering, but they brought word. {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} — sits near {AREA}. They don't know we exist, and that's the only blessing left to us.
Strike them quick. Don't let them turn and look at us proper, or they'll remember where the smoke comes from and bring worse down on our heads. We can't fight what comes after, you understand? We just can't.
Take what you can carry. Leave the bodies where the crows will find them first. Hurry back before they... before they notice we were ever here."

"No, no, forget the last one — gone, lost, my scouts won't follow that far. New mark: {PARTY_NAME}, {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} drifting past {AREA}. Please, take this one quick before they wander somewhere we can't watch from."

"You came back. Bones of my fathers, you actually came back...
Word reached us before you did — a {CULTURE} party broken open, the captain cold. The young ones are eating tonight because of you. Some of them haven't eaten proper in a week, you understand what that means to an old man like me?
Come to {HIDEOUT} when you can. We'll huddle close to a real fire, and I'll tell you what little we know of the bigger predators above us. Maybe — maybe — we live through another winter yet. Don't tarry on the road. They're always watching."

"You stand in my hall, and I have not yet decided if your breath is welcome here. I am {CHIEF_NAME}. The ice does not hurry. Neither do I.
Twenty-five days. That is the span I grant you. In that time you will bring me a kill — a banner taken, a captain stilled. My watchers will mark the deed before any words pass your lips.
Think slowly before you answer. The cold has a long memory, and so do I. Should you turn from this pact, you will find the snow knows every road you take."

"My scouts have watched the white roads for seven nights. They have found {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} moving slow near {AREA}, their breath rising in the cold like signal smoke.
Ride out. Take them apart in your own time. There is no virtue in haste; the ice teaches that lesson to any who hurry. My people will be watching from the treeline, and they count only what their own eyes have seen.
Bring back the captain's token. The frost will preserve it as well as any oath."

"A new mark. {PARTY_NAME} now — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} crossing near {AREA}. The old quarry slipped beyond the reach of my watchers, and what the ice cannot hold, I do not chase. This one will answer for them both."

"You return. The cold did not keep you, and neither did they.
Word reached my hall before your boots did — a {CULTURE} party broken on the open road, the captain laid in the snow, the banner taken down. My runners spoke of it slowly, as is our custom, and I listened without interrupting them.
Come to {HIDEOUT} when the dusk settles and the breath turns to frost again. There is more to say, and it is the kind of saying that wants a fire between us. Walk carefully on the way. The ice remembers every step."

"You walked through my marsh and lived. Few do. I am {CHIEF_NAME}. I watched you come.
Twenty-five days. That is your length of rope. Bring me a kill — a party that walks where it should not. My scouts will mark one. You will go. You will return, or you will not.
Do not lie to me in this place. The bog hears. The reeds hear. I hear. Speak when spoken to. Move when told. The next words you get from me will be a name and a road."

"{PARTY_NAME}. {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND}. Moving slow near {AREA}.
My watchers have lain in the reeds two days. They counted boots. They counted blades. They know the gaps. The {KIND} does not know it is being counted.
Take them quiet, or take them loud — the bog does not care. But take them. Alone. My eyes will see it done, or they will not, and only what is seen is paid. Walk the low ground on your way in. The high road has horses on it. Go."
"New mark. {PARTY_NAME}. {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND}. Near {AREA}. The last one slipped the reeds — gone past where my watchers will follow. This one has not. Go."

"You came back. With mud on you. Good.
A runner crossed the bog before dawn. Whispered it to me in the dark. {CULTURE} party — broken. Dead in the wet. The reeds have already taken what the crows left. My watchers saw. I believe them. I believe you.
Come to {HIDEOUT}. Walk soft. Speak when I speak. There is more to say, and it is not said out here where the wind carries. The bog kept faith with you once. Do not test it twice."

"You stand in my hideout, and I will not pretend it does not gall me to receive you here. I was {CHIEF_NAME} once of a column that wore real colours. Now I wear none, and welcome strangers in the dark.
The terms are simple, as terms should be. Twenty-five days. One target struck from the rolls. My scouts will name the party; you will see it ended. Do not insult me with delay.
Discharge the duty, and we speak again as something nearer to equals. Fail it, and I shall regret the courtesy I extended tonight."

"My scouts have filed their report, and the matter is plain. {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND}, moving in good order on the roads about {AREA}. I have read the disposition twice. It will serve.
You will engage them alone. I require a clean account, not a shared one — witnesses I trust are posted to observe, and they record only what they see with their own eyes. Do them the favour of leaving no ambiguity.
When the column is broken, return to me. Bring something I can show my own — a standard, a seal, an officer's blade. Proof, in the old fashion."

"Revised orders. The previous mark is struck from the slate — lost to my watchers, which I shall address in due course. The new target is {PARTY_NAME}, {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND}, last sighted near {AREA}. See it done with the discipline I asked for the first time."

"You returned. I confess I did not allot the matter much hope.
The dispatches reached me before you did — a {CULTURE} column broken in the field, its officer dead, the standard recovered. A creditable action, by what my people relay. I have seen worse reports filed by men who still wore the sash. I have, in truth, filed worse myself.
Come to {HIDEOUT} when the watches change. There is more to be said now, and I would rather say it under a roof than at the gate. You have earned the chair across from mine."

"You walk into my counting-house unannounced, and yet the ledger says you arrived precisely on time. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and every soul that passes through these chains is an entry I have priced, taxed, and resold.
Twenty-five days. That is the term I extend to new debtors, and you are one now whether you like the word or not. The opening payment is simple — one party erased from the roads. A clean strike, no witnesses owed wages.
Discharge it and your line of credit opens. Default, and I sell what's left of you by the pound. The hunt-brief follows; my brokers have already valued the mark."

"My factors have appraised {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} moving slow on the roads outside {AREA}. Their cargo manifest is the kind that doesn't argue back, which means the guard is thinner than the price suggests.
I want them written off. Not robbed, not ransomed — closed. Every breathing asset on that roster becomes a zero in my ledger, and you bring me the captain's seal to confirm the entry.
Do it alone. My clerks need a single name on the receipt, and split commissions sour the books. Their value is highest the day you act."

"Reprice the contract. {PARTY_NAME} now — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} near {AREA}. The previous mark cleared its debt to someone faster, or wandered off my market. This one's valuation is fresher, and the margin is yours."

"You closed the account. My brokers logged the entry an hour before your shadow reached the gate.
A {CULTURE} party struck from the rolls, captain's seal noted, cargo presumably distributed by whichever scavengers reached the wreck first. I have marked your name in black ink — that means credit, in this house — and the standing fee for our arrangement has been deducted from a debtor you'll never meet.
Return to {HIDEOUT} when the trade winds shift. There are larger contracts I prefer to discuss where the walls are mine and the witnesses are paid."

"You stand in my hideout as if it were a praetorium, outsider. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, once a centurion of a legion whose name I will not soil by speaking it here.
Twenty-five days. That is your watch, your campaign, your tour. Bring me the head of one who still draws breath from the same rotten standards that broke ours. My scouts will mark the target — you will execute the order as if it were nailed to the column.
Fail, and you join the unburied. Succeed, and we speak again — soldier to soldier, oath to broken oath."

"My outriders have eyes on {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} moving the roads near {AREA}. They march in column as if the eagle still watched over them. It does not.
Strike them as a legionary strikes — quickly, in formation, without ceremony. Bring back a signum, a gladius, anything that proves the kill. My men will witness from the treeline; what they do not see, I do not count.
Move at the third watch. The roads near {AREA} grow thin then, and discipline rewards the patient soldier."

"New orders. The old quarry slipped the picket line — a failure of my scouts, not yours. Mark {PARTY_NAME} now, {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} sighted near {AREA}. The legion taught me never to mourn a missed target when another marches into range."

"You returned. The legion taught us that a soldier who comes back has either won or lied — and my runners spoke before you did.
A {CULTURE} party broken on the road. The captain cut down, the standard taken, the column scattered like grain. You did the work cleanly, as one who has stood in a shield-line and knows what the man beside him is owed.
Come to {HIDEOUT} before the next watch. There is wine that remembers better days, and orders that require a soldier I can trust with more than a single blade."

"You climbed far to find me, lowlander. The wind up here strips lies from a man before he reaches my fire. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and the drop behind you is longer than your patience.
Twenty-five days. That is the span the wings of my scouts will tolerate your shadow on our ledges. Bring me a kill — a party of those who crawl the valleys fattening on what should be ours. The hunt-brief follows; my watchers have already marked one from above.
Fail, and the cliffs do my accounting. Many have fallen who refused to."

"From the high ridge my scouts have tracked {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} crawling the low roads beneath {AREA}. They walk with their eyes on the dirt, never the sky. They will not see the drop until they are in it.
Strike them alone. My watchers perch where you cannot, and they will count only the kill they witness with their own eyes. No companions, no shared glory.
Approach from the heights if you have the stomach. The fall does half the work — your blade need only finish what gravity began."

"New quarry, lowlander. {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} crawling near {AREA}. The old mark slipped beneath the cloud-line where my scouts will not follow. From this height, one valley-walker looks much like the next."

"You returned. The cliffs let you pass twice — that is rarer than you know.
My scouts saw it from the ridge before your horse cleared the pass. A {CULTURE} banner trampled in the dust, the captain unmoving, the carrion birds already circling lower than my watchers. They reported it the way they report weather — flat, certain, witnessed from above.
Climb to {HIDEOUT} when the thermals settle and the light goes long across the stone. There is more to say now that you have proven your blade can reach as far as your ambition."

"You stand before the heir of khans, outsider. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and my blood runs back through ten generations of riders who broke empires upon the open grass.
Twenty-five days. That is the span I grant you to prove your name is worth carving beside ours. Bring me a kill — a banner pulled from a body, a chieftain felled in the open. My outriders have already marked the quarry; the hunt-brief follows when I am done speaking.
Honor the terms, and you ride under the wolf-standard. Fail them, and the ancestors will know your name only as carrion."

"My outriders have run their ponies hard, and the word is brought before the standard. {PARTY_NAME} — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} — moves upon the plains near {AREA}, slow and fat with confidence.
Ride them down as the khans of old rode down the slow-footed. Take the captain's head, or his sigil, or the iron from his belt — bring me proof a wolf can read. My horsemen will watch from the ridgelines and count the dead, for the ancestors record only what their eyes see.
The steppe favors the swift. Be swifter."

"The mark has shifted, rider. {PARTY_NAME} now — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} drifting near {AREA}. The old quarry rode beyond the horizon my outriders patrol, and the great Khans teach that a wolf does not chase what the wind has taken. This new banner will serve."

"You return, and the standard stands taller for it. Few outsiders ride back to face a khan's heir twice.
My outriders brought the tale ahead of your dust — a {CULTURE} captain cut down, his banner taken, his column scattered like chaff before the steppe wind. The ancestors heard it spoken at the fire last night, and one of my old warriors lost a wager he made against your bones. He pours koumiss for you now whether he likes it or not.
Come to {HIDEOUT} before the moon turns. There is more to speak of, now that the bloodline knows your name."

"You walk into my circle of bones, stranger, and the smoke did not flinch. That alone tells me more than your tongue ever could. I am {CHIEF_NAME}, and the old gods have been whispering your shape into the embers for three nights.
Twenty-five days the omens grant you. No more. Bring me a death — blood spilled in the right hand will sweeten the augury, and the elders below the earth will know your name.
Refuse, and the same fire that warmed you will read your entrails. The gods are patient. I am less so."

"The knucklebones fell wrong-side-up at dawn, and the crows above {AREA} have been circling since. {PARTY_NAME} moves there — {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND}, marked already by something older than my hand.
Spill them. Spill them where the soil is hungry. {CULTURE} prayers do not reach down so deep as ours, and what they bleed will quicken the roots beneath {AREA}. Take a token — a tooth, a ring, anything the smoke can recognise.
Go alone. The gods count witnesses, and they prefer their offerings clean of company."

"The fire turned its face. The old mark is lost to the bones — gone beyond the reading. A new shape rises in the embers: {PARTY_NAME}, {ARTICLE} {CULTURE} {KIND} drifting near {AREA}. Spill that one instead. The gods care nothing for which throat, only that the cup is filled."

"The smoke bent eastward at dusk, and I knew. Before any runner crossed my threshold, the embers had already spoken your deed.
A {CULTURE} banner fallen, and the blood drunk by ground that had thirsted long. The old gods are sated tonight — they spoke your name in the crackle of the fire, and not as a curse this time. Few earn that turn of tongue.
Return to {HIDEOUT} before the next moon dies. There are deeper rites to read together now, and the bones are restless to fall for you again."

Attempt a jailbreak
Easy, friend — don't sit up too quick. They cracked you good when they hauled you down here.
Where... am I? What happened?
The pit. Beneath a bandit hideout. They ran your party down on the road and dragged the living here to rot. Three days, it's been, for me.
Then come with me. We get out of here together.
Stay put. I move faster alone.
I had my chance with you, and we both ended back in this hole. I'm done running — go on alone.
Aye. Get me past those guards and into open air, and my blade's yours. Lead on.
...Your call. Mind the guards' rounds — and good luck to you.
Bound and slung over a saddle, you are dragged toward the brigands' hideout. You bide your time…
You rot in the brigands' pit beneath the hideout, watched by a surly guard.

Step away
Vargolf the Iron-eyed
The Iron Price
Chief wants you at the fire. There's a lord's iron rolling south on the Pravend road and he means to have every bar. Go quick — the cold puts an edge on him.

A convoy climbs the Pravend road — iron ingots, wagon after wagon, bound for a coastal lord's smithies. He will beat it into garrison steel for the men who ride my passes. I want it beaten into axe-heads for my Reavers and hinges for my longhouse doors. Winter is close, traveler. You can smell it in the wagon-ruts. The convoy master is hired iron himself — hard men on the boards, a harder man at the head. Take the wagons. All of them. Grain rots and silver spends. Iron carries a people through the cold. Bring it to this fire and the fire pays. Ride before the first deep snow shuts the road.
Good. Hard hands for hard cargo. The wagons roll slow and the guards watch the road behind them, not the treeline. When the iron sits at this fire, your pay sits beside it. Ride.
Then winter finds my Reavers with dull axes while a lord's garrison wears their steel. Think on it, traveler. The convoy rolls whether you do or not, and the snow does not wait.
You carry my work already, traveler. Finish it. Vargolf does not stack iron on a sled that has not moved.
Iron Ingot Convoy
Convoy Master Torvald
Intercept the iron ingot convoy bound for the coastal lord's smithies and seize the wagons for Vargolf the Iron-eyed before winter closes the roads.
The iron has been taken from the convoy. Return to Vargolf the Iron-eyed at the Frost Reaver camp to deliver the ingots and collect payment.
Off the road. This iron is bought, paid, and promised to a lord's smiths, and I've hauled it through worse country than yours. Say what you came to say and be quick about it.
Count my riders, convoy master. Then unhitch the wagons.

I count them. I've buried better men than these guards for worse cargo, and I won't spend them here. Take the wagons. But mark me — I'll haul this road again, and next time the count may run the other way.
The iron changes hands the hard way. Draw.
So be it. Shields up, lads. The cargo stays.
That's your strength? I've hauled through fen-raiders and two Sturgian winters, and none of it looked as thin as your band. No. The wagons roll. Step aside or stop them yourself.

Stack it by the forge-tent. Every bar. My smith beats axe-heads from it before the first deep snow, and my Reavers winter armed instead of hungry for steel. The coastal lord can guard his empty smithies. You did the work, traveler, and the work is what Vargolf pays. Here — your silver, counted twice. The fire remembers who fed it. Winter comes. Now it comes to a camp with iron.

Word ran ahead of you, traveler. Some other band hit the convoy first — hill-scum, no code — and the ingots went into the snow like spilled grain. You gathered what the drifts gave back. Half the iron, then, and half the pay. My smith works with what the road sends. But hear it plain: a full sled buys a full welcome. Next time, ride faster than the other wolves.

Vargolf was born to the Yulskaya boyar-line of northern Sturgia, a clan that held the Pravend trade routes for three generations before the year he came of age — when the routes were lost to a southern rival and the Yulskaya hearth-roll was halved. He took his iron from his father at sixteen, his grandfather's name a year later, and walked the snow-trails alone through every winter of his apprenticeship. The feud that broke him was a stolen wife — not stolen by him but stolen FROM his clan, and the boyar-council refused to ride for her recovery. Vargolf rode alone, took her back from a Vlandian outrider's tent in the high passes, and returned to find his name struck from the longhouse rolls and his hearth-cousins reassigned to a rival branch. He took twenty cousins past the tree-line and named the band the Frost Reavers, after the wolf-pack that reaves the Sturgian coast each spring. Forty winters later he speaks fewer words than his hounds, drinks only on naming-days, and pays his men in silver coined from imperial caravans his Reavers stop on the snow-roads. The Sturgian crown still lists him as a runaway boyar; he has not contested the title.

The Frost Reavers were founded forty winters ago by twenty Yulskaya hearth-cousins struck from the same longhouse-rolls Vargolf was struck from. They wintered the first year in a thaw-hollow that lost six men to frostbite before spring. Each generation since has recruited the same way — Sturgian sons disinherited by southward-shifting trade routes, Vlandian deserters who walked the wrong pass, broken huscarls whose lords would not pay their oath-silver. The Reaver-code Vargolf wrote at the founding-fire forbids village-raiding; they take only imperial tax-wagons, foreign caravans, and the occasional noble outrider party. Pravend's counting-house has lost eleven wagons to them this winter alone. The Sturgian crown has put no bounty on the band — only on Vargolf personally — because the boyars who rule the snow-roads quietly use the Reavers to ruin rivals. Among the snow-clans the Reavers are not feared so much as respected: they are the wolves the cold north feeds in place of the kings it never got.

The reaver-chief stands knee-deep in churned snow, axe balanced across his shoulders. He doesn't speak as you approach — only watches, breath fogging the cold air, while his men close the circle behind you. When he finally moves, it is to look you over once, like a butcher reading a carcass. "You walk warm clothes. The dead ones we strip leave their warmth on the wolves. Speak quick, traveler — Vargolf's patience freezes the same as everything else up here."

The reaver-chief glances up from sharpening his axe as you approach. He doesn't put the stone down. The men around the fire shift, then settle, then ignore you — the surest mark of acceptance the snows allow. "You've come back. The cold didn't take you. That's twice now you've earned a portion of Vargolf's fire. Speak — slow words travel better in the cold."

Names are wind in the cold, traveler. Wind dies. What lasts is what a man carries — and the only proof Vargolf takes is in deeds. There's a task for hands like yours. Bring the wages of it back to this fire, and we'll speak again as something other than stranger and chief.

The Frost Reavers' camp is hollowed out of a drift, ice walls braced with logs. Smoke curls thick from cookpots. A skinned stag turns on a spit. Fur-cloaked sentries watch the ridges with bows drawn loose.

Ride three days north of Pravend, traveler, past the last farmstead the imperial tax-rolls remember. When the snow-pines close black over the road and your horses' breath comes white as bone-meal, you are near enough. Look for a wind-cut ravine that the sun never reaches before noon - there is a fox-skull nailed to the second pine, and below it the spring runs frozen even in the thaw months. Our hold lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, deeper in than the ravine-mouth looks.
From the skull you walk in, not ride. The trail is single-file and my watchers above the ridge see your shoulders before they see your face. Bows held loose, arrows not yet nocked - that is their patience, not their welcome. Ride in with your party-banner low and one rider out front with empty hands, or send a name ahead with the drovers who know the road. My scouts have ears for a name they owe a debt to.
Come up the ravine without that name and the first arrow is a warning. The second is not. We do not feed strangers here - we feed the wolves we owe. Bring me a name worth knowing and the gate-log opens, the fire is yours, and we share what the south has not yet taken from us. Otherwise the snow keeps the matter quiet till the spring thaw walks your bones out.

The boyars of Pravend keep sending their tax-riders into my passes. Two captains this season already - one I sent back without his horse, one I sent back without his head. The crown has a new governor in the southern keep who calls himself Lord Mikhail Yulskaya. The name is mine. He stole it the year I was struck from the longhouse-rolls. So we have a quarrel that runs deeper than ice and longer than the road between us.
The Vlandian outriders cross the high passes in summer chasing imperial coin - my Reavers chased a column of them off the snow-roads last moon. Battanian raid-bands slip up the western treelines too, but they keep to their own grudges and we keep to ours. The Khuzait send no one this far north. Their horses do not love the deep snow.
The southern boyars send the levies, the Vlandians send the outriders, the Empire sends its tax-wagons. We send them all home lighter than they came. If you ride south with a banner of your own, traveler, the boyars will read it before they read your face. Carry that knowledge with you. The crown has a memory, and the snow keeps every footprint until the thaw.

The Marsh Stalkers in the southern fens owe my Reavers a debt - a winter five years back, their matriarch Mireborn put a token in my hand for a Vlandian outrider I rode down for her. She has not repaid. I have not asked. The Stalkers move slow and pay slow, but they pay. The Highwaymen of the downs are men I do not deal with - their Reeve counts coin where I count cousins. We do not share a fire.
The sea-raiders to the east have been moving inland this season, hunting where they should not. My scouts marked three of Bjornulf's longboats beach near the Pravend road, and the Salt-Tongue knows my mark. If they cross again I will ride the long way to his cove and we will settle in the old way. Granny Hod's forest band sent a runner two weeks back - smoke-talk, a token of birch, no words. She watches. That is her way.
As for the steppe, the Wolf-Khan Borchu and I have an understanding. We do not ride into each other's grass. So far we both keep our word. The pass-lords under Skarvac have gone quiet in the high snows. Quiet is never good. When a mountain man stops boasting, he is sharpening something.

Sturgian fur-trains move south from Revyl to Pravend every second week. Eight axemen, two wagons, a captain who drinks at the Pravend gate before the road - I have watched him three winters. He sets out heavy and slow. The pelts are good. The men are slower.
But the column you want is Vlandian. A grain-and-iron caravan climbs the pass under the Pravend road six days from now, sixteen guards, four wagons, escorted by a southern knight who thinks snow is a rumour. They camp at the cold-spring because the water does not freeze there. The outriders sleep. The knight drinks. My boys have counted their watches twice and the second watch never wakes the third. That is the hour.
Take the iron, traveler. Leave the grain. Grain rots, iron does not, and the Vlandian smiths at Galend will buy back their own bars and ask no questions - a Highwayman friend of mine, Reeve's man, moves steel through Galend every moon and the price is set. Do not ride the Revyl road south of the iron-bridge after - the boyars send tax-riders that way and they remember faces. Ride west. The snow forgets faster than men.

You ask the iron question. Good. I do not waste breath on those who come to a fire only to warm their hands. Sit. The snow will hear what we say, and the snow remembers longer than men.
An oath from a Reaver is not coin. It is the hearth-roll, scratched into the longhouse beam above my own seat, and the names on that beam are few. My Yulskaya cousins, who rode with me when the ice cracked at Pravend. Old Halrek, who took an arrow that was meant for my throat and asked for nothing afterward. The Stalker-matriarch who fed my Reavers a winter we should not have survived. That is the company you ask to join. The axe knows them. The axe does not yet know you.
Bring me a deed the snow will not forget. A southern caravan taken in my name. A blood-debt paid before I have called it. A road kept open when the lowland lords swore it shut. Walk back into this longhouse with iron on your boots and a banner the ridge can see, and the beam learns a new mark. Until then - the road between us is begun, but not yet walked. Ask again when you have weight to your name.

Then it is spoken, and the longhouse-beam has heard it. Stand. The horn comes to your hand before the mead does - drink, and let the cold of it find the bottom of you. Now the iron knife from my belt. I open my palm where the old brother-scar lies - the one my dead brother Halgrim cut into me before the southern axemen took him at the Pravend ford - and I lay the new cut across the old. Your palm to mine. Press. The snow at the door is watching. The hearth-roll on the beam takes a new notch tonight - your name beside Halgrim's, beside my father's, beside the wolf-marks of the founders. The blood is one blood now.
Brother means this in the Reavers' tongue: my fire is your fire, my mead-bench is your bench, my cousins answer to your call as they answer to mine. The feud I carry against the lowland lords is your feud from this breath forward, and the feud they will one day open against you is mine. We do not bury our kin alone. We do not ride to our blood-debts alone.
Hear it then, brother. The hearth-roll above Pravend knows you. The snow-pine ridges know you. The lowland lords who hung my cousin from their gate-tree will read your name beside mine when the thaw comes. From this fire forward you are Vargolf's blood, and the road we walk together no longer has an end.

Then I have heard it, and I weigh it the way the smith weighs the bar before the strike - by feel, not by speech. You did not come up the ridge with a fine sentence rehearsed in your teeth. You came with the deed already cooling at your belt, and the word arrived after, like snow falling on a fresh-cut stump. That is the order I trust. My father told me once that an oath spoken before the work is a debt; an oath spoken after the work is a verdict. You have given me the verdict. I accept it.
Hear the shape of it, then. This is not the hearth-bond. This is iron. From this moon, when you raise your banner, the Reavers ride - not as paid spears, not as a courtesy I can pull back when the wind shifts. Your feud is my feud. Your hunters are my quarry. You owe me the same in turn: when my axe is up, your steel is up beside it, and you do not ask the reason until the work is done. The longhouse will know your name in the hearth-roll, written next to the men I have already buried.
The wind off these ridges carries sound a long way, traveler. When steel is drawn, it will be drawn for both of us. Ride hard. The road south is loud, and we are sworn now in the colder kinship - the kinship of the WORK. That bond outlasts blood.

Done. Ten axemen for seven days - I cut them from my own hearth-band before sundown. My second is Halgrim Snow-Tooth, who has stood my shield-wall since the river froze twice over. He rides at the head of them and carries my word like he carries his axe. What he says, I have said. Count the days, traveler. Seven. The longhouse counts them with you.
Now hear my terms. If a Reaver of mine falls in your work, you bring his blade back to this hall - the iron, at least, comes home, or you and I will speak again on harder ground. If he lives, you send him back fed and drunker than he left, or you have wasted my gift. My axemen do not break shield for coin or boredom. They break shield for the work I have set them to, and while they ride under your banner your work IS my work. Do not spend them on petty things.
Halgrim will tell me what you did with them. I will be listening.

His name is {TARGET}. He sleeps under his own banner at {HOME}, and that hall stands on ground my brother Halgrim was dragged across twelve winters past - roped behind a Yulskaya horse until the snow was red for half a league. {TARGET}'s father gave the order. {TARGET} ate at the same table the night it was done and laughed when the courier brought the rope back. I swore on Halgrim's axe I would put steel through whichever son of that house outlived the others. The youngest is {TARGET}.
He rides with six lances and a houseman named Brun who lost a brother to the same campaign and has no love left for his lord. Brun waters his horse at the millstream below {HOME} every third dawn - put a coin in his palm and he will tell you the gate hour. {TARGET} hunts boar on the east ridge when the frost breaks. Take him there, away from his walls. He fights poorly off a horse.
{REWARD} denars when the word reaches me, traveler. The gold is the smaller half of what is owed - the rest is Halgrim's, and the snow keeps that ledger. Ride before the moon turns.

{CHIEF} has named {TARGET} of {HOME} as the man whose death he has waited twelve winters for. The grudge is old and specific - a brother dragged on a Yulskaya rope, three days hanging on a frontier tree, an outrider's contract paid in clean Vlandian silver and never answered for in iron. {CHIEF} carries the names of those involved on the longhouse-beam where his hearth-roll is cut, and only {TARGET}'s name remains uncrossed. The Reaver-Chief offers a heavy purse and the weight of a debt finally closed. The road south is loud. The snow remembers. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is dead. {CHIEF} has been told, and {CHIEF} has heard. The longhouse-beam now bears a finished mark - the last uncrossed name from the twelve-winter feud with Yulskaya is crossed at last. {REWARD} denars sit at the Reaver-chief's fire, heavy and counted, and the iron-eyed bond between bandit-king and traveler-killer is stamped a degree deeper. Brother Halvi, dragged on the Yulskaya rope through the white pass of '88, is not back, but his name has been answered for, and the snow keeps the rest. The hearth-roll is whole again, and the axe rests cold against the beam.

Word came across the snow-track at dusk: {TARGET} lay stiff in a ditch two valleys south, throat opened by some rival lord's outriders in a quarrel that had nothing to do with Halgrim. {CHIEF} heard it out beside the hearth-roll, his iron eye fixed on the longhouse-beam where his brother's name is still cut, and said nothing for a long span. The grudge for that Yulskaya rope, twelve winters carried, was answered - but answered by another hand, and the silence in the hall went colder for it. He had the steward count out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars, quarter-pay, thin coin for a thin closing. The bond holds, set a smaller notch firmer, no warmer than river-ice.

"There is a village called {VILLAGE} on the southern slope of the Yulskaya hills, held by Lord {LORD} of that same boyar-clan that burned my Reaver winter-camp ten winters back. Eight of my men froze in the snow when their outriders kicked apart our cookfires and rode out laughing. {LORD} was a green captain that year. He kept the cloak my brother died wearing, and the silver wolf-pin sewn to its collar.
The granaries are full this season - they tithe to the Pravend keep on the first new moon. Hit them three nights before, when the wagons are loaded and the watch-fires are doubled but the riders are off collecting their winter-pay. Burn the grain. Take the iron, take the salt. The smallfolk - leave them to the road. We did not freeze for thralls.
{REWARD} denars when the smoke is seen from the high passes. The snow keeps the rest. Ride before the moon turns."

{CHIEF} has named {VILLAGE}, a granary-fief of Lord {LORD} of the Yulskaya tributary clan, as the holding whose burning will close a debt ten winters old. The Yulskaya boyar-riders rode down {CHIEF}'s Reaver winter-camp in the deep ice, and eight of his hearth-band froze in the cookfire-ashes while their cloaks were hauled back to the Yulskaya hall as trophies. The granary feeds the boyar who gave that order, and {CHIEF} has waited ten winters for a banner cold enough to ride it. The Reaver-Chief offers a heavy purse of {REWARD} and the closing of a grudge that has kept its edge in the snow. The road south is loud. The contract is open.

{VILLAGE} is ash, and {CHIEF} has the tally on the cut-stick. The granary-fief of Lord {LORD} of the Yulskaya tributary - the boyar-clan that burned the Reaver winter-camp ten winters past and left eight men under the ice - is broken thatch and cold ovens, the tithe-sleds split for firewood, the bondsmen scattered into the drifts. {REWARD} denars sit weighed at the longhouse-beam where the hearth-roll is notched, and the iron between bandit-king and traveler-raider is stamped one degree firmer. The Reaver-roll is eight names shorter. The snow keeps the rest.

Word came north along the frost-track at second watch: {VILLAGE}, that fat little granary of the Yulskaya boyar-line, lay smoking and empty - but the column that put it to the torch had been {LORD}'s outriders settling some quarrel of their own, nothing to do with eight men lost under the ice ten winters back. {CHIEF} heard the runner out beside the hearth-roll, fingered the iron at his throat, and said only that the snow had thawed in the right village by the wrong hand. The grudge stood answered, after a fashion. He had the steward count out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars - quarter-pay, thin coin for a thin closing - and waved the traveler back into the cold, no warmer than river-ice.

You find the marker before you find the camp.
It is a length of split birch, planted in the snow at a switchback, hung at eye-height where any rider must see it. Someone has burned letters into the bark with a heated knife. The script is old Sturgian. You read it slowly, because the wind keeps trying to take your eyes from the words:
Cold sharpened him. Cold did not break him. Cold made the man. Cold is the master here.
There is no sign-name beneath it. No clan-mark. Only the verse, and the small black scorch-rings the knife left around each letter.
You sit your horse and read it twice.
Past the marker the trail dips and the wind takes the other half of itself away, and there, in a hollow scooped from a great drift and walled with ice and black logs, the Reavers have made a place to keep warm. Smoke stands straight up in the dead air. A stag turns on a spit. Along the ridge above the hollow, fur-wrapped figures hold longbows loose at their thighs. They have been watching you since you stopped to read.
You leave the birch where it stands. You will pass back this way if you live, and the words will still be there.
You walk your horse down.
Visit the trophy room.
Vargolf pulls aside a hide curtain. Inside: looted gold cups, a Sturgian noble's signet ring, a cloak of black bear, a sword that once belonged to a count.
"A king would tax our cookfires. Out here we owe nobody. We freeze sometimes. We never bow."
"Old Sturgian gods. The thunder-one, the fire-one, the cold mother. They take what's given and ask no priest to count it."
"Cut me down? Boy. The cold has tried for forty winters. You think a sword frightens a man the snow forgot to kill?"
Vargolf grunts, almost a laugh. "Camp does its job. Wind's quiet here. Reavers warm. That's enough."
The Reavers pour a black mead, thick as syrup. The chief raises a horn. "To the wolves who eat our enemies and the wolves we are."
You bunk in a fur-piled tent. The chief's hounds sleep at the foot. Your party wakes warmer than they've been in months.
Visit the skin trader.
An old man with hands like leather lays out furs. Bear, wolf, ermine. "Better prices than any town. Towns sell to fur-merchants. Fur-merchants sell to me. I cut the middle."
Hear wolfhunt tales by the fire.
An old reaver with one eye spits in the fire. "Listen. Story is true or it isn't, but the listening costs nothing."
Drink with the skald. (50 denars)
A man with a small harp begins a winter-song. The Reavers join in low. Your party joins in louder. The night gets stronger.
"Sturgian count Sigurd is sending a tax-wagon down the spine road in four days. We'll be there."
"The lord at Revyl drinks more than he prays. His guard rotates at midnight — we know."
"There's an old Sturgian armory frozen in a glacier west of here."
"A boyar's daughter went missing on the high pass last month. 5000 denars reward."
"The Sturgian winter levy is starving. Half their militia would join us for hot food."
"We saw imperial scouts on the ridge two days ago. Three of them. They didn't see us."
"A merchant from Pravend offered us silver to torch a rival's caravan. We did."
"The empire's pulled their northern garrison south. The roads belong to us until they remember."
"There's a wolf-pack tracking a Vlandian noble across the tundra. He doesn't know yet."
"Sturgians from the eastern clans want vengeance against Boyar Tora. Pay's good if we help."
"You want to trade with us, traveler? Bring me thirty pelts. Wolves, bears, whatever. The Reavers don't deal with men who can't survive a winter walk."
Vargolf inspects each pelt. "Heavy. You did the work or paid someone honest. Either way — trade with my men."
30 fur
"Twenty-five hardwood. Pine cracks under our snow weight. We need oak from the southern slopes. Bring it."
Vargolf weighs a beam. "Hard wood. Won't split when the men set lodge-poles. Trade with my traders."
25 hardwood
"Thirty hides. The smoke-tent burns through tanning hides faster than the wolves provide them. Hunt or buy — either way, bring them."
Vargolf prods the stack. "Clean cuts. The tanner won't curse your name when he works these. Trade."
30 hides
"You proved yourself. Now I'd see you build a Reaver's lodge. Twenty hardwood and twenty more fur. The men who do this ride with us in raids."
Vargolf laughs once, deep. "You build with these hands like one of us. The trophy room is open to you."
20 hardwood + 20 fur
"Forty pelts and five pack-mules. We re-supply the deep camp before the snows close the pass. Heavy load — Reaver work."
Vargolf claps the lead mule. "Now the camp survives the winter. Take what the armory holds."
40 fur + 5 mules
"Thirty hardwood and twenty hides. New bow-staves and tannage for the spring raids. Bring both and the trophy room is yours to walk."
Vargolf bends a stave to test it. "Solid grain. The Reavers will draw farther this spring because of your work."
30 hardwood + 20 hides
"Fifty fur, fifty hardwood, ten wrought-iron ingots. The whole high-camp re-equips. Only blood-kin haul this. Take your time, brother — but bring it all."
Vargolf stands silent a long moment. "You've outfitted my Reavers. The cold north remembers your name forever."
50 fur + 50 hardwood + 10 wrought iron
"A hundred fur and twenty refined-iron ingots. The Reavers ride the empire's borderlands this spring. Outfit us, and you sit at my right when we ride."
Vargolf grips your shoulder. "You bought us a winter and a war. There is no man closer to me now."
100 fur + 20 refined iron
Sink Jarl Asmund's caravan-marked party at the northern strait, where the Reavers cannot reach without crossing the open ice.
The Vargolf the Iron-eyed accepts your oath; the rite is sealed in salt-blood at the longboat prow on the low tide.
Vargolf does not raise his voice. He sets the axe across his knees and stares at the cold horizon. "The snow forgets nothing. Ride."
The Drowned Road
You. Chief wants you at the fire. There's lowlanders in the reeds with stakes and string — measuring, they are. Measuring us. Go quick. She's gone all quiet, and that's never good for somebody.

There are men in my reeds with stakes and string, traveler. A surveyor — a fussy little man under a lord's seal — walking the fen with charts, marking where the causeway will go. A road. You understand what a road is, in a marsh? First the stakes, then the stone, then the ditches, and in ten years there is no fen. Dry ground. Counted ground. My grandmothers drowned kings' men to keep this water dark, and I will not be the chief who let it be measured. Go to the column. Break it. Kill who stands. And bring me his charts — every page, every marker. The marsh keeps its own maps.
Good. Take the charts before you take the men, if the fight lets you — paper drowns faster than surveyors, and I want it whole enough to rot slow. Walk soft, traveler. The reeds will watch you there.
Then go. But the stakes are still in my fen, and every dusk they stand is a yard of water the lowlands think they own. The marsh is patient, traveler. I am less.
The stakes still stand, walker. My watchers count the column every dusk — twelve spears and a man with paper. Go finish it. We will speak when the charts are wet.
Royal Survey Column
Royal Surveyor Ferand
Mireborn wants the royal survey column staking a causeway through the marsh destroyed. Defeat the surveyor's escort and recover the causeway charts.
The survey column is broken and the causeway charts are in your possession. Return them to Mireborn at the Marsh Stalkers' camp.

Halt — halt! You are inside a marked survey line. This ground is measured under royal commission, every stake numbered and logged. State your business at once, and mind the string. Do NOT touch the string.
The marsh keeps its own maps. Leave the stakes — bleed or run.
Leave the — this survey carries the crown's own seal, you dripping savage! Eleven weeks of triangulation! Sergeant, form your line — I want this ruffian's name for the record before you kill him!

Give them here. Measured twice — drowned once. Watch: page by page to the black water, held under until the ink lifts and their causeway blurs to nothing. The fen stays trackless, traveler. Your pay is in the wicker, counted out by reed-light. Listen — the heron settles. The marsh is pleased, and the marsh is not often pleased.

The marsh did not wait to be hired, traveler. The surveyor died fevered in his own tent, the quick-mud took his sergeant and two mules, and arrows out of empty reeds finished the count — none of them yours. A fen-girl brought me the charts already drowned, the ink run to green shadows. Half the coin. Be quicker than the fen next time. Few are.

Mireborn was born in the deep fenlands of what was once a Battanian marshland, in a reed-house her grandmother built on stilts that have not yet rotted. She has never set foot inside a town's walls, never tasted bread that was not made of fen-millet, and has known no roof but reed and hide. The Stalkers passed to her from her grandmother, who took them from hers, and the band has belonged to the marsh-women for seven generations — a matrilineal succession the lowland scribes refuse to record because they refuse to record any chief who is a woman. Her first kill was a Vlandian tax-collector at eleven, drowned in three feet of standing water without ever knowing where the sound came from. Her second was the boyar's son who came looking for the tax-collector. By twenty she had drowned twelve men and never raised her voice, and the marsh-women elected her chief without a word spoken — a vote conducted in shared glances over a fire. She moves through reeds without sound, remembers every drowned thing, and tells the stalker-children to remember too.

The Marsh Stalkers are seven generations old, founded by a marsh-grandmother whose name has been forgotten on purpose — the Stalker-women say her name only once, on the night a new chief is elected, and never write it down. Every chief since has been a woman; every successor has been chosen by the silent vote of the elder-circle around a smoke-fire. Mireborn is the seventh. Stalker-children come from fen-villages so deep in the standing water that no scribe, surveyor, or priest has charted them — settlements the lowland lords have declined to tax for two centuries, less from generosity than from an inability to locate them. They learn to drown men before they learn to read, and most never learn to read. The band's signature is silence: a tax-collector is never warned, never charged, never seen — only found face-down in three feet of black water with no wound and no witness. Vlandian and Battanian lords have organized eleven sweeps of the fen in living memory; eight returned with no Stalker captured and no Stalker dead, and three did not return at all. The marsh-women say the fen kills its own enemies and they are only its hands.

For a long moment you see only reeds. Then a lean figure unfolds from the green like a heron rising — silent, mud-streaked, eyes pale as marsh-water. He tilts his head, studying you the way a hunter studies prints in soft ground. "You found us. Few do. Either you're clever, traveler, or someone whispered the path to you. Mireborn would like to know which — before we speak of trade."

The reeds part for you now without protest — the stalkers know your tread. Mireborn rises slower this time, eyes the same pale marsh-water but no longer measuring. He gestures you toward the dry-stone where he sits. "Twice you've found the path. The marsh remembers. Speak, traveler — Mireborn listens to walking-friends with the patience the reeds taught him."

The marsh hears all names and forgets most. Mireborn doesn't keep what the marsh discards. You want trade with the stalkers, traveler — there's a thing my men need, and the reeds will not yield it without effort. Bring it back, and the marsh will start remembering you.

The Marsh Stalkers' camp floats. Reed huts on stilts, plank walks lashed between trees. Frogs and birds. Somewhere, a child cries — then is hushed. Stalkers move slow and deliberate, never breaking the surface.

Ride south from Marunath until the road forgets itself in the reeds. The horses will refuse the wet ground before you do - leave them with a fen-boy at the last solid alder, and walk. Look for the plank walks lashed between the drowned trees; they are silver-grey and the bog has half-swallowed them, but they hold a thin man. Follow the black-water channel where the heron-rookery quarrels at dusk, and watch for peat-fires that give off no smoke. That is our breath you are seeing. Our hold lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, deeper in than any tax-man has ever cared to wade.
My watchers are in the reeds before you see the reeds. They will count your party from the rookery before your second step on the planks, and a girl with a bone-whistle will tell the camp your number and your weight. Walk slow. Keep your hands where the water can see them. If you carry a token I have given you, hold it open in your left palm; if you carry only your name, speak it once to the air and keep walking.
Come quiet and the camp opens to you - dry reeds, fen-cake, a place by the smokeless fire. Come loud, and the bog keeps you. We do not bury the loud ones. The bog does that itself, in its own slow time.

The Battanian lords of Marunath send their fian-bands south into my fenland each spring, and each spring the bog drinks a few of them quiet. They come hunting heads, they come hunting the bounty their high king set on my women. They do not come back the same number they rode in. Lord Caladog's vassals are the worst of them - a clan that calls itself the Wolfskin, led by a thane named Brennus mac Tarn. He lost a brother to my reeds two winters past and he has not forgotten the debt. Nor have I.
The Vlandian outriders push east from Galend now, chasing Battanian cattle and Battanian scalps both. Their sergeants do not know the fen the way the high-king's men know it - they ride heavy, they ride in mail, and the soft ground takes them down to the chest before they understand what country they are in. My watchers count them in and count fewer out. That is the only arithmetic the fen knows.
The southern Empire sends tax-riders up the old road sometimes, looking for tribute the Battanians forgot to pay. They do not find it. If you carry a banner of any of these three south of the stilt-paths, traveler, the reeds will know your colors before I do. The fen has older eyes than mine. Walk gentle.

The Frost Reavers' Vargolf carries a token I gave him five winters past. He rode down a Vlandian outrider for me when my own kin could not cross the snow. I have not repaid. He has not asked. The fens teach patience, and Vargolf is a patient man for one who lives by the axe. When the reeds bend, I will send him what is owed. Not before.
The Highwaymen on the downs - their Reeve and I do not speak. He measures men by the weight of their purse. I measure them by what they leave in the water when they pass. We have different scales. Granny Hod's forest band to our north shares the wet country with us, and she has been kind. Her people bring us pelts. We send back salt and silence. That is enough.
The Sky Raiders worry me. Aerlin's people have come down from the high crags three times this moon, hunting in fens that are not theirs. Birds do not belong in the mud. My scouts found their feathers near the old causeway, and one of my daughters did not come home from that walk. I do not name a debt yet. The water remembers. When the reeds tell me her name, I will go where Aerlin sleeps and we will speak of it quietly.

A Battanian salt-train comes up from the coast every third week, traveler. Six wagons, eighteen spears, a captain named Cadoc who drinks the marsh-pear wine my girls leave at the milestones. He thinks it a gift from a grateful village. It is not. By the time his column reaches the causeway south of Marunath his hands are slow and his eyes are softer than reed-water. That is where the road narrows to one wagon's width between two stilt-pools, and a man who steps wrong drowns in mud that does not give him back.
The salt is the lure. The fourth wagon carries Vlandian glass and southern dye-pots bound for the Battanian thanes - small crates, heavy purses, the kind of cargo that does not spoil if it sits a season in a fen. The escort tightens around the salt because they think that is what we want. They are wrong. We take the fourth wagon while the spears guard the first.
Go three nights from now, an hour before the moon clears the alders. Bring fifteen riders, no more - horses sink past the fetlock off the causeway and a crowd only feeds the bog. Leave Cadoc breathing. A captain who keeps losing the same wagon is worth more to me than a dead one, and the Highwaymen east of here would charge you for that lesson. The fen takes what it takes. We only carry the rest away.

You speak the slow-water question. Most who sit at my reed-fire chatter of silver and seasons; you have asked the thing the bog hears. Sit. Let the smoke take its time. A knot tied in haste slips when the tide turns, and what you ask of me is a knot the fen will be asked to remember.
When the time comes, I bleed for the names the water already knows. My grandmother, who walked into the mire so her daughters would not be sold south. Aelwyn of the third stilt-house, who hid my wounded under her floorboards while the Imperials probed the reeds with spears. A Vlandian deserter named Coros who fed my scouts for a winter and asked nothing. Three names. The fen keeps them. It does not yet keep yours.
Bring me a deed the marsh can drink. A southern tax-boat sunk where no one will dredge it. A village warned before the legion's torches reach the thatch. A debt of mine, paid quietly, before I have spoken it aloud. Do that, and the reeds will whisper your name when I am not there to say it. Until then, my knife is mine, my stalkers are mine, and the slow water between us has only begun to rise. Ask me again when the tide has turned.

Then the reeds have heard you, and the reeds are slow to forget. Kneel at the water's edge with me. I cut my thumb on the bone-hook I wore the year my mother drowned holding the stilt-rope for the children, and I press that old scar to yours - see, the blood goes into the black water the same, your red and my red curling like two eels finding one current. Drink from the cup of fen-water and crushed bog-myrtle. Spit. The marsh has tasted you. It will not give you up to any lowlander's hound or any Marunath rider's torch. You are reed-bound now, and the reed bends but does not break, and neither do we.
Brother, in the fenland, means hearth-share under one stilt-roof when the floods come. It means my daughters call you uncle and bring you the first ladle. It means when I dream a warning of horses in the mist, I dream it for you also. My silence is your shelter. My knife is your knife. The path through the bog that only I know - the safe boards under the black water from the heron-stone to the old wicker shrine - that path is yours now. You will never wade blind again where I have walked.
Stilt-brother. The longhouse on the south island learns your name before dawn. The drowned-king under Marunath learns it when the tide turns. And the Battanian lords who burned my aunt's holdfast in the year of low water - they will read your name in the reeds and know my feud rides with two heads now. Walk soft. Walk with me.

Then the answer is heard, and the reeds heard it before I did. You did not bring me a speech, traveler. You brought me a deed still wet, and you laid it at the edge of my fire the way a heron lays a fish at the foot of her chick - without ceremony, because the work itself was the ceremony. A lesser walker would have spoken first and bled later. You bled first. That is the order the bog trusts. Sit. Let the water settle around what you have done.
From this tide forward, my Stalkers wade where you wade. Not as guides you have hired. Not as a debt I can drain dry. As blood-allies, bound the way two reeds knot beneath the surface where the current cannot see them - one cannot be pulled without the other tearing free of the silt. Your feud is now ours. The hunters who track you through the lowlands will find Stalker-spears rising out of water they thought was empty. In turn, when my fen is burned at, you raise your banner south of Marunath and you come.
The wind carries oaths better than mouths do, and the fen-wind has long memory. It already knows your name beside mine. When the steel sings, walker, the marsh will hear it and answer. We are kin in the cold work now. That kinship does not thaw.

Done, walker. Ten of my fen-walkers, hand-picked, for seven turnings of the moon - I will whisper their names to the reeds before they go. My second is Yslen Reed-Tongue, who reads water the way you read maps. She walks at your shoulder. The spear-girls follow her quiet, and she answers to me.
Hear my terms. If a stalker of mine sinks in your work, you bring her spear back to me unwashed - the marsh knows its own blood and will want it. If she walks home, she walks home fed. My fen-walkers do not bend reed for coin or for cruel sport. While they wade under your banner, your road is my road - so do not spend them on shallow water. Seven days. Count each dusk.
The reeds will be told who rode out. The reeds will count who comes back.

His name is {TARGET}. His banner stands over {HOME}, on dry stone, on land that drinks no water and remembers no debts. The bog remembers. Nine summers back his huntsmen rode my sister Aelwyn into the reed-flats below the old causeway - drove her horse until it foundered, then left her to the leeches and the slow cold. They called it a hunt that strayed. {TARGET} signed the writ that paid them. The reeds have held her name in green knots ever since, and tonight the knots came loose in my hand when you walked through the door.
He travels with a dozen retainers and a Battanian tracker who owes him no love - a man named Ceol, scarred down the jaw. Ceol fishes the slow channels east of {HOME} at every new moon, alone, and a quiet word and a coin will pull him onto your side. {TARGET} keeps to the high road, sleeps in stone halls, fears the wet ground. Take him where the path turns soft. He will not know the footing.
{REWARD} denars when the water carries his name back to me, traveler. The reeds want him more than the gold does, but the gold is the shape the debt has taken. The bog remembers the rest. Ride.

{CHIEF} has named {TARGET} of {HOME} as the debt the marsh has held in its black water for nine flood-seasons. The grudge is patient and exact - a sister-by-water named Vethra, drowned in the reed-cuts above Old Pelm fen on a tax-rider's order, her body weighted with iron and her name unspoken at any pyre. {CHIEF} keeps a knot of bog-rope for each wrong, hung from the willow-post above his pallet, and only one knot remains untied. The Mireborn offers a heavy purse of {REWARD} and the closing of a debt the still water will not forget. The reeds part southward. The bog remembers. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is drowned-still, and {CHIEF} has been told, and {CHIEF} has heard. The reed-knot for the sister Aelynn - the one cut down at the Greyfen sluice in the wet-spring three floods past, her body left in the eel-weir for the bog to keep - that knot is at last untied from the alder-post and laid on the slow water. {REWARD} denars rest in the stalker's wicker, counted twice by reed-light. The fen does not forgive, but it does remember, and tonight it remembers a thing finished. The bog has drunk its answer, and the water is quiet again.

The rumour drifted into the reed-camp on a peat-merchant's tongue: {TARGET} had been ridden down by a rival lord's outriders on a winter road, throat opened before any bog-knot could be tied around it. {CHIEF} listened without lifting his eyes from the bowl of murky water he was scrying, then set it aside and murmured Vethra's name once - the sister who drowned in reed-cuts on a tax-rider's order, whose bog-rope memorial still hung at the camp's edge. The grudge was answered. The hand that answered it was not the one promised. {CHIEF} counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars in thin coin, quarter-pay for a kill borrowed from another man's blade, and the bond between them settled a small notch firmer - cooler than a knot pulled tight by earned hands.

"There is a village called {VILLAGE} crouched on the dry hummock above my reed-cuts, held by thane {LORD} of the Battanian huntsman-clan that drove three of my fen-walker girls into the deep cuts six summers past. {LORD}'s grandsire dug the first diversion ditch that year. His huntsmen laughed when they heard the girls calling under the water. The ditches still drink my fen. I have not forgotten which spades cut them.
{LORD}'s outriders ride west on the dark of the moon to hunt the Battanian boar-runs - four nights, sometimes five. The village holds drained-field grain and the iron spades they use to widen the ditches every spring. Burn the spade-stores first. Throw the grain in the cuts. The smallfolk dug the ditches with those same hands - leave none of the diggers walking.
{REWARD} denars when the diversion ditches run black with ash. The bog drinks the rest. Go quiet, and go before the dark moon thins."

{CHIEF} has named {VILLAGE}, the thane-fief of Lord {LORD}, as the settlement whose drowning will answer a debt six summers deep. The Battanian huntsmen of that hall once ran three of the chief's fen-walker girls into the reed-cuts and left them to the suckmud, and the diversion ditches their thane has since cut through the upper marsh have drained the fenland a yard further every spring. The water that fed the chief's pools now feeds their barley. {CHIEF} offers a quiet purse of {REWARD} and asks only that the ditches be choked, the thatch put to torch, and the reeds given back what was taken. The contract is open. The fen is listening.

{VILLAGE} lies drowned in its own smoke, and {CHIEF} has been told. The thane-hold of Lord {LORD} - the same Battanian blood whose huntsmen drove three fen-walker girls into the reed-cuts six summers past - is ash and sodden timber, the diversion ditches already choking on cinder and silt as the fen drinks back what was stolen. {REWARD} denars lie counted on the bog-oak plank where {CHIEF} reckons her debts, and the reed-bond between marsh-king and traveler is knotted tighter by one wet knot. The water keeps the rest. Three names are washed a shade cleaner.

Word slid through the reed-stems on a fen-runner's tongue: {VILLAGE} lay black and silent, its diversion-ditches choked with ash, but the burning had been some other lord's quarrel, a feud with no thought for the three fen-walker girls drowned in the reed-cuts six summers past. {CHIEF} heard it standing knee-deep in the still water and only nodded once, slow as a heron settling. The thane-clan's huntsmen had paid, but not to him, and not by his hand. He bid the marsh-steward count {REDUCED_REWARD} denars onto the peat-bench - thin water-coin for a debt closed by stranger's flame - and the bond between Fen-Speaker and traveler held, quiet as standing water before frost.

You hear them before you see them.
Or you do not hear them — you hear what they have made the marsh stop saying. The frog-chorus that had filled the dark a hundred yards back is gone. The night-birds that called overhead have gone with it. There is the soft drip of water off a hanging leaf, and there is the long whining drone of insects, and there is nothing else.
That is the first sound of the camp.
The second sound is the small wet click of a paddle-pole, somewhere off to your left, where you cannot see it. You stop your horse. You wait. The click does not come again.
Third: a child's voice, beginning to rise, and a woman's hand cutting it short. You know the second sound by its quality — you have heard mothers quiet children all your life. You did not know one could do it so fast.
Fourth: a heron, lifting. A long slow heavy lift of wings. Somewhere in the green. The reeds bow and resettle in three places at once, which is wrong, because a heron is one bird.
You sit your horse in the standing water and you understand by your skin and your ears alone that you have been inside the camp for some time now and not seen it.
Then a voice from the reeds, very close, not loud:
"Walk the horse left. The bog past your right knee will take it."
You walk the horse left.
A hand finds your bridle out of the green. The fingers are cold. The wrist is mud to the elbow. You do not see the body.
"Mireborn was wondering when you'd come. Step down. Slow."
You step down. Slow.
Bargain with the poison brewer.
An old man with shaking hands stirs a pot of green liquid. "Arrows? Throwing knives? I coat what you bring. Not free."
"A king's flag would sink in our marsh. Our great-grandmothers fled a king. We remember."
"The marsh has its own. The fen-mother who eats unbaptised children. The reed-spirit who hides our dead."
Mireborn smiles, slow. "You shout in a marsh and the marsh laughs. Cut me down — try. The mud takes its share before the blade does."
She tilts her head. "You like our reeds? Most don't. Most see only the smell."
Stalkers brew a marsh-mead from fen-flowers. It tastes of rain and honey. Mireborn raises her cup without speaking. The toast is silent.
You sleep on a reed-platform, the marsh whispering below. Strange dreams come, full of green light. Your party wakes oddly rested.
Rent a marsh-skiff for the day. (100 denars)

A young Stalker punts a flat-bottom skiff over from the reeds. "Take it. Bring it back. Or don't. We'll find another. The marsh is full of lost boats." Your party feels well-rested from the diversion.
Trade with the bone-collector.
A child no older than ten tends a stall of dried frog-bones, river-pearls, snake-skin. "For the druid who buys these, mostly. But you can have what you want, if you trade fair."
Consult the Seer of Mires.
A blind woman is led from a hut. Mud streaks her arms. She sniffs the air around you. "Something walks beside this one. Not a friend. Listen."
"There's a sunken merchant boat in the eastern fen. Hasn't been picked clean."
"Battanian druid lives three islands east. He buys frog-bones, nothing else."
"The Vlandian baron's been sending hunting parties into our marshes. Six have come back."
"A nobleman's daughter is hidden in our reeds. Her father has offered triple if we hand her over."
"Old Battanian tomb in a marsh-island, unopened. The wards have weakened."
"A wandering monk asks too many questions. We let him keep wandering."
"There's a cure for marsh-fever growing only in our fens. We don't tell the towns where."
"Imperial mapmaker tried to chart our marsh last spring. We sold him bad maps."
"A boatman at Kefraje smuggles into and out of the marsh. Tell him Mireborn sent you."
"A heretic priest hides among us. The temple wants him alive."
"Trade? Bring me twenty bundles of hardwood — the marsh eats our walkways faster than we can lay them."
The chief runs a hand along the planks. "Dry. Heavy. The Stalkers know your face now."
20 hardwood
"Twenty-five fish. The reed-children eat first; the warriors eat after. Bring it."
Mireborn nods. "The marsh feeds tonight. Trade with my people."
25 fish
"Twenty leather. Reed and rope rot fast in the wet — we bind everything in skin. Bring it."
She tests a strip between her teeth. "Properly cured. The marsh-walks will hold another season."
20 leather
"Forty hardwood and five mules to haul it. The marsh eats footing — we need new hide-walks across the deeper pools."
She claps the lead mule. "Good beasts, good wood. The deep camp is open to you."
40 hardwood + 5 mules
"Thirty fish and twenty leather. The fish for the deep-camp larder, the leather for our hunting harness. Bring both."
Mireborn signals her quartermaster. "Stocks topped, harness mended. The marsh trusts you now."
30 fish + 20 leather
"Fifty hardwood and ten fish. We rebuild the eastern walk after the floods. Bring both."
She watches her builders test the new boards. "Sound enough for ten seasons. The Stalkers honor your work."
50 hardwood + 10 fish
"A hundred hardwood and ten wrought-iron ingots. We forge marsh-spikes for the eastern approach — they'll lame the imperial cavalry next spring."
Mireborn smiles, slow as water. "The marsh defends itself now. You have done a Stalker-elder's work."
100 hardwood + 10 wrought iron
"Fifty leather, fifty fish, five pack-mules. The whole deep-camp gets re-supplied for the wet season. Heavy haul — only kin do this."
She lays a hand briefly on your forehead. "Marsh-kin now. The reeds won't betray you."
50 leather + 50 fish + 5 mules
Destroy a Vlandian outrider company that has pushed too far into the reeds at Mire's-End.
The Mireborn accepts your oath; the rite is sealed knee-deep in marsh water over the sunken stone idol.
Mireborn says nothing for a long beat. Then, quietly: "The reeds do not forget faces. Step careful in the marsh from now on."
The Reeve
The Reeve's Arrears
You there — the Reeve's asking for you. Some merchant lot ran his roads a whole season and never paid a copper. He's ruled a fresh page and everything. Fresh page means work. Best hurry.

Sit, traveler. The stump is for sitting. Page thirty-two — the Wenshal combine. They ran my roads a full season unpaid. Ninety-one wagons by my count, and not a copper entered. Now their strong-wagon rolls south carrying the season's takings, hired blades around it and a guild factor on the box who signs receipts in a very fine hand. Find that wagon. Collect the arrears — principal plus interest, fourteen percent, compounded quarterly by insult. The factor will offer you talk; he sells it by the yard. Do not buy. Coin or the wagon itself, I am not particular. The ledger only asks that the column close.
Good. The entry is open — Wenshal, arrears plus interest. Bring me the sum or the wagon that carries it. And traveler — leave the factor able to write. Someone must sign the receipt.
