As you please. But one unpaid toll teaches every merchant on the road the same arithmetic. The column stays open. Interest accrues. Come back before it compounds into something bloodier.
You carry an open contract already, traveler — I can read an unclosed column off a man's shoulders. Settle your own page first. Then we will talk about Wenshal's.
Wenshal Strong-Wagon
Guild Factor Hamon

Find the Wenshal Strong-Wagon on the western roads and collect the Reeve's arrears. The merchant combine ran his tolled roads unpaid for a full season, and the wagon carries the season's takings under hired guard.
The Wenshal account is settled. Return to the Reeve at his camp to enter the sum in his ledger and collect your share.

Ah. The Reeve's collector — he does keep punctual staff. Let us not waste the light. I am authorized to discuss figures, and my blades are authorized to discuss everything else. Which conversation are we having?
You know my name. Pay the full arrears, with interest.
I do know it. Everyone on this road does, more's the pity. Very well — the full sum, and the Reeve's usury on top. Open the box. Note, please, that I was courteous.
Half the arrears now, and your wagon rolls on.
Half. Yes. A sensible figure — the figure I was authorized to reach, as it happens. The combine will be pleased. Do give the Reeve my compliments on his flexible arithmetic.
No figures. The Reeve sent me for everything.
Pity. Blades — earn your wages. Hold the wagon, no quarter, and someone mark the time for my report.

Forgive me. I keep the combine's correspondence for three kingdoms, and I pride myself on names — yours has never crossed my desk. Not once, in any hand. So we return to figures, and the figure, respectfully, is no.

Full weight. I have counted it twice and the second count flattered the first. A season of arrears, the interest to the copper, and a receipt signed by their own factor — that last is worth more than the coin. Every combine from Pravend to Galend will read this column by market-day and pay at the milestone like honest men. Your share, weighed fair. The road keeps its law, traveler, and today you were the law's handwriting.

Half. Mm. Half settles the principal and leaves the insult drawing interest. I will take it — coin refused is coin wasted — but the column does not close. It carries forward to a new page with Wenshal's name at the head, and next season their toll doubles until the balance clears. Your share, counted to the copper. Adequate work earns an adequate entry, traveler. The full-weight column would have earned you a better one.

A war-party out of the south broke the wagon before you reached it — I had the dispatch at second bell. The takings went into the ditches and the pockets of men who keep no books. My riders recovered perhaps half; the rest is scattered arithmetic. The column closes at half-weight, marked as act of lords — the one entry no clerk can prevent. Half fee, counted clean. You rode in good faith, and the ledger records faith even when it cannot record delivery.

Before he was a bandit he was a clerk — third son of an Imperial border-lord's secretary, sent to the road-courts at fourteen to learn the trade his elder brothers were too well-connected to bother with. He rode the south-eastern circuits for twenty years with a strongbox and two armed escorts, collected the road-tolls for a different lord every five seasons, and never once short-changed an account. The trouble began when the lord he served stopped opening the books — the man's wife had taken to gambling and his stewards to drink, and the strongbox was no longer being audited at all. The Reeve discovered, one quiet autumn, that the lord's records were lazier than his own counting; coin could disappear and bandits would be blamed because there were always bandits to blame. He arranged the first false robbery himself, walked away with a year's salary, and reported it stolen with two genuine tears. By spring he had a band of twelve, all former soldiers the lord had cashiered for petty offences. The Reeve has been a bandit for fifteen years now; the books he keeps in his saddlebag still balance to the copper, and he files his year-end accounts with a forger in Praven who passes them up the line as if nothing has changed.

The Highwaymen are the youngest of the great bandit bands and the only one organized like a magistracy. The Reeve founded them eighteen years ago with seven other dismissed Imperial road-clerks — men who knew the toll-tables and patrol-rotations of every road between Pravend and Lageta because they had written them. The pool they draw from is not peasants or veterans but clerks, accountants, and literate sons of small-merchants who lost positions in the imperial reorganization — men whose hands could hold a quill and whose standing could not survive a clerk's dismissal-notice. The band keeps a real ledger: every taken purse entered, every share calculated, every captain audited at the end of each season. They never burn what they take; they negotiate ransoms in writing, on parchment, with imperial seal. Three Imperial circuit-judges have been Highwayman captives — two paid in silver, one in grain — and all three were released on the same road they were taken from with their robes brushed clean. The Empire still has not declared the band outlaw because it does not yet know how to outlaw an institution more orderly than its own road-courts.

A clean-shaven man in stolen Vlandian leathers does not look up from his ledger as you approach. He finishes his column, sets the quill down, and only then meets your eyes — calmly, almost professionally. "Welcome. The stump is for sitting. We do business by the page here, traveler — every coin recorded, every favor inked. So tell me your name, your purpose, and what page of mine you'd like to be written on."

The Reeve has your name in his ledger now. He nods you toward the stump without looking up, finishes a notation, and only then sets the quill aside. "Welcome back. Page seven, line eleven — I keep all repeat business in the same column. What entry are we adding today, traveler?"

Names go on page one, traveler. Page two is where I record what's been done for the company — that's the column that matters to me. There's an entry waiting for you there. Earn it, and we'll talk business proper. Until then, you're a heading without a story.
The Highwaymen camp is orderly — almost like an army camp. Tents in rows, watch-fires at four corners, a cook-tent with a real pot. The Reeve runs it like a counting-house.

Take the post-road south from Charas, traveler, and keep the milestones on your right hand until you count the seventh. There you will find a cairn the locals stack higher each summer - my men add a stone for every purse the road owes us. From the cairn, follow the cart-ruts west to the old toll-house, the one the crown burned in the famine year and never rebuilt. Past its broken chimney the stake-fence begins, and each post is numbered in tar like a clerk's ledger. Our hold lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, at the end of that counting.
The watch-tower on the rise sees you long before you see it. My scouts will mark your party, count your spears, weigh your saddlebags by the set of your horse's gait - we keep a running tally the same as any honest house of business. Ride slow, hands open on the reins, and when you reach the third numbered post, halt and let them read you. A man who hurries past the count is a man who means to cheat the count.
Come correct and the gate opens to tents in proper rows, watch-fires at four corners, and a cup of decent wine while we settle accounts. Come crooked and you join the ledger on the wrong side of the page - we balance the books before the moon turns, and the downs are wide enough to bury what does not balance.

The Reeve: "Vlandia owns these downs on parchment, traveler, and parchment is what I read. The crown sends its tax-riders down the Charas-Galend road four times a season - I have the dates ruled in my ledger, ink still wet on the last column. Lord Derthert's bannermen pass through in spring chasing tournament purses, the lesser knights in autumn chasing imperial mercenary contracts. Both pay my toll. Neither knows they paid it.
The house I watch closest is Clan Caraveer. Their seneschal raised my toll by three denars last Praven assize and called it a road-tax. I have raised his caravan-losses by three hundred. We are square now, by my count, but he does not yet know we are keeping the same book. There is also a Vlandian outrider captain - Sir Almund of the southern marches - who has burnt two of my watch-posts this year. His head is worth eighty denars on my ledger and I will pay it to the man who brings it.
The Battanian raiders cross the western tree-line whenever Marais sleeps, and the imperial cataphracts come north when the Khuzaits press them. Both ride through my country without paying. I do not forget a crossing, traveler. If you carry a kingdom's banner one day, ride the long way around the junction at Galend. The Reeve's ledger has a column for friends and a column for tolls, and I will know which side to write you under."

Let me reckon the ledger. The Reavers up north - Vargolf's lot - I do not share fire with, as he no doubt told you. He counts cousins. I count coin. A man who weeps over kin will burn a profitable bridge to prove a point, and I have crossings to keep open. We have an arrangement of distance, which is the cheapest kind of peace. Owes me nothing. I owe him nothing. Long may that column balance.
Skarvac's pass-lords in the mountains owe me four hundred and twenty denars from the spring caravan we routed onto their road for a cut. They have paid one ninety. I am patient. Interest accrues at a denar a week in goodwill, and I will collect in salt or in throats, whichever moves first. Granny Hod's forest band south of Galend is the trouble this season - she has taken to charging her own toll on MY road, the stretch between the two mileposts past the ford. That is a debt of blood and copper both, and I am tallying it.
The Stalkers in the fens have gone quiet these six weeks. No runners, no token-trade, no smoke from the marsh-fires. That is never good news. Either the Mireborn is dead, or she is moving men somewhere she does not want counted. I have a boy watching the causeway. When he comes back I will know the price.

Three columns matter on these downs, and I have them all in the ledger. The Charas-to-Galend wool train rolls every eighth day - four wagons, eight crossbow levies, a Vlandian sergeant who counts heads at every milestone but never looks up the bank. He thinks the road is the danger. The road is never the danger. The bank above the third ford is the danger. We have lifted his rear wagon twice and he still writes the same route in the same hand to the same boyar.
The second column is the salt-cart out of the Pravend mines - two wagons, six guards, but the captain is a sober man named Otric and I will not waste men on him. Mark him off. The third is the prize: a Vlandian merchant-banker's strongbox-wagon that rides hidden inside a grain convoy on the new-moon week. Twelve outriders, but only four know what they guard. The rest think they are minding oats.
If you want clean coin, traveler, take the wool train at the third ford on the eighth day. Bring twelve horse, hit from the upper bank, leave the sergeant alive so he writes the same report and the boyar sends the same caravan again. That wagon has paid my winter for three years. I will charge you nothing for the route - I have already taxed it. Just do not break the pattern. A broken pattern is a closed purse.

You ask a ledger-question, and you ask it sober, which is more than most. Sit on the bench across from me. I keep two books at this junction - the day-book, where every wagon and every toll is entered fresh, and the red-book, where the debts that outlive coin are signed in a hand that does not smudge. You are asking after the red-book. Few travelers know it exists.
The red-book is short. There is the smith at Galend who shod my horse the winter the road froze and would not take silver for it - his name is in red. There is the Charas notary who burned a writ of seizure rather than serve it on my mother's house - his name is in red. There is a captain of the southern road, dead now, who rode against four men so I could finish counting a tithe-chest - his name is in red. When their kin come to this junction, the toll is a smile and a cup. When their enemies come, the toll is something else.
You are entered in the day-book, traveler, in a careful column. Bring me a deed I can write in red - a debt collected that the law would not collect, a wagon turned my way when the south leaned on you, a column closed in MY favor - and the red-book learns your name. The contract is open. It is not yet signed. Come back when the entry is ready.

Then the entry is made. Sit. The red book opens between us - here, on the left page where my own mark was cut when old Halbrec the Counter put a knife to my thumb on the Charas road thirty winters back. Press your thumb to the wax. There. The ledger takes the print. Now the quill, now the line beneath: paid in full, no balance, no lien, no further reckoning. I sign as witness. The book signs as oath. Drink the small beer from the clerk's cup - it is sour and it is honest, the way every true entry is. The red wax cools. The seal holds. We are written.
Brother, in my trade, is the one line the ledger cannot strike. Coin can be returned. Tolls can be refunded. A debt of silver settles and the page closes. But a brother-entry runs forever in the margin, carried forward year on year, paid in kind and never in coin. My cousins at the Galend weigh-station become your cousins. My ink is your ink. What is owed to me is owed to you, and what wounds you wounds the book itself - and the book does not forget. From this hour my reeves call you kin.
The Charas toll-house learns your name tonight. The downs-clerks of Galend learn it by morning rider. Count Derthert's tax-men will read it next time they audit our road - and they will know the second name on the seal is no longer alone. Brother. The ledger is one.

So. The ledger answers itself. I asked you a question on the Charas road - whether you would bleed for me when the column came - and you have not answered it in words. You have answered it in a margin entry, paid in full, dated before I knew to ask. That is the order I keep. Deed first, word after, signature optional. A lesser hand would have ridden in with a speech and a thin purse. You rode in with the purse heavy and the speech almost forgotten. Sit. The ink of what you have done is still wet, and I am the man who reads it.
From this audit forward, the Reeve's books carry your name in the red column - not as debtor, not as patron, but as co-signatory. When you raise your banner against a house, my toll-riders ride against that house, no fee, no question, no separate reckoning. The downs between Charas and Galend are your passage now, road-tax waived, gate-coin returned. In exchange, when my collectors are run down by some baron's hounds, your sword answers the summons. This is not the hearth-bond. This is the war-bond. Costlier. Plainer. Older.
My old reeve was killed for a ledger he would not surrender. I have kept it since, and now your name is in it, in the same red ink, on the same page. The wind off the downs carries the sound of drawn steel a long way. Let it carry ours together. We are bound in the WORK now - and the work has never released a man yet.

Marked in the red book. Ten collectors, seven days - I have already drawn the tally line beside their names. My under-reeve goes with them: Vellic of the Short Quill, who keeps the count when I cannot. He carries my seal. What he says on the road is what I would say. The collectors answer to him, and he answers to me.
Now the terms, traveler, and I will speak them plain so the ledger is clean. If a road-man of mine falls in your work, you bring me his tally-stick and the coin he was carrying - both, not one. If he lives, you return him on the seventh day with his boots still on his feet. My reeves do not break shield for petty road-work. They break shield for tolls owed and debts collected. While they ride your road, your road is on my ledger - so do not spend them on errands a farmboy could run.
Seven days. I will mark the date their tally reopens. The red book remembers what men forget.

The name is {TARGET}. Banner over {HOME}, signet in red wax, and a debt in my ledger eleven years old. Page forty-one, third column - one hundred and twenty wagons of southern grain, paid for in good Vlandian silver, signed for by his factor at the Helmsford crossing, and never delivered. His men took the silver, burned the wagons, and called it a road tax. My uncle Aldric kept that ledger. They hanged him for the loss when the merchants came for their bond.
He travels with six riders and a notary who carries his seal. The notary lodges at the Greysend tollhouse on market-eves and drinks with the weighmaster - put a denar in the right cup and you will have his master's road, his bedchamber, his morning ride. {TARGET} is fat at the table and thin in the saddle. Take him at first light, before the column counts itself.
{REWARD} denars on delivery of his seal-ring, weighed and tallied against the page. The debt is older than the gold, but the gold settles the line. The red book waits. Ride.

{CHIEF} has entered {TARGET} of {HOME} into the red book under the heading of unpaid debts, and the column has been open for nine years. The entry runs to three lines: one strongbox of tithe-silver lifted from the Bramblegate toll-house on the eve of Saint Arwa's feast, one factor named Olen of Pellic strangled in the counting-room and left across his own ledger, and one writ of immunity signed by {TARGET}'s seneschal that closed the matter before the assizes could open it. The Reeve carries a purse and the figure {REWARD} written in clean hand. The contract is logged. The column waits to be ruled across.

{TARGET} is dead. {CHIEF} has been told, and the red ledger is opened to the page where the Westbridge column has stood unbalanced for nine years. The eighty-four wagons of taxed Battanian wool, the burned tally-house at Coppersmoor, the strangled clerk Aelwin found face-down in his own ink - all of it draws a single ruled line across the foot of the column. {REWARD} denars are counted in, recounted, and entered on the credit side in {CHIEF}'s own small precise hand. The Westbridge account is closed. The book is shut and the wax pressed warm.

Word reached {CHIEF} by a wool-carter out of the eastern passes: {TARGET} had been cut down in a roadside ambush by a rival lord's outriders, the body stripped and left for the crows before any hand of ours could close the account. {CHIEF} heard it out, opened the red book, and inked the line against uncle Aldric's name and the forty-one wagons of grain with the same patient stroke he gave any closed column - though the nib lingered a breath longer than it ought. The grudge stood answered on the page; it did not stand answered in the room. He counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars in thin coin, slid them across the trestle, and ruled the ledger shut. The bond held, set a smaller notch firmer, but the warmth of an earned kill was not in it.

"Open the red book to the page marked {VILLAGE}. It is a hamlet on the cart-road south of the Vlandian marches, entered under the seal of Lord {LORD} - the same house whose seneschal struck my collector Adelaine across the face at the last assize and whose villages have refused my road-tax for two ledgers running. Two years of dust on that column. The ink remembers what the lash forgot.
The outriders ride to the assize on the fifteenth to swear loyalty over wine; the village will be three swords and a sleeping reeve. The tithe-barn is stacked with the grain they would not weigh for my men, and the chapel-loft holds the silver candlesticks Adelaine was sent to count. Burn the barn. Take the silver. The smallfolk pay no tax to me - leave them their hands and their doors.
{REWARD} denars on delivery, struck against the column and the column closed. The ledger waits. Ride."

{CHIEF} has entered {VILLAGE} into the red book as the chattel of Lord {LORD}, a Vlandian house whose holdings have refused the road-tax for two ledgers running. The arrears are itemised: caravan tolls unpaid, bridge-pence withheld, the wintering-fee struck through with a seneschal's mark. At the last assize the same seneschal laid an open hand across the face of the collector Adelaine, and the matter was carried back to {CHIEF} in three lines of small script. The Reeve has assessed the principal, the interest, and the dishonour, and posts the burning of {VILLAGE} as the settlement. A purse of {REWARD} is held in escrow against delivery. The account stands open.

{VILLAGE} burns, and {CHIEF} has been told. The tithe-village of Lord {LORD} - of the same Vlandian house whose seneschal struck Adelaine across the face at the last assize, the same villages that withheld two ledgers of road-tax - is ash and broken thatch, the tax-rolls scattered in the trampled rye. The red book is opened on the trestle, the column ruled, the entry inked in {CHIEF}'s own hand. {REWARD} denars are weighed against the standing arrears and the balance noted as part-settled, no more. The collector's bruise is paid in coin and cinder. Two ledgers stand. The third will be called in turn.

Word reached the toll-house at second bell: {VILLAGE} had been put to torch and the ledgers of that Vlandian house were burning with it, but the hand that struck was {LORD}'s war-column, not a collector of ours. The Reeve received the dispatch standing, read it twice, and set it aside without remark. Two ledgers of refused road-tax stood closed. The mark across Adelaine's face stood unanswered by the right hand. The red book would note the entry settled at half-measure, the column "satisfaction" left blank. He had the steward count out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars - a clerk's quarter-fee for intelligence delivered, not collection performed - and signed the chit with the smaller seal.

Of this stretch of road they tell this.
A wool-merchant from Pravend rides it once a season, with two armed boys and a strongbox he never lets out of his sight. Twice in seven years he has been stopped on it. Twice he has been received with the courtesy due his trade. Twice he has continued, lightened only by the standard toll — which is, as everyone south of Lageta knows, fourteen percent of the cargo's declared value, payable in coin or in kind, with a receipt issued under a forged Imperial seal that is, the merchant has more than once observed, a better seal than the one his last legitimate factor used.
They say a circuit-judge passed this way three winters back and did not return for ninety-one days. They say his robes came back to Lageta brushed clean. They say the family paid the ransom in grain, not silver, and that the Reeve credited them for the grain at market rate, not at the discount usually applied to such captives, and that the judge himself was not displeased with the transaction once he had recovered the use of his hands.
They say no body has been left on this road in eight years. They say this is policy.
They say the Reeve was once a clerk himself. They say his ledger balances. They say a clerk in Praven still files his year-end accounts.
They say a great deal about this road. Some of it is true.
And then you came up it.
The night is orderly. Too orderly — the verges swept, the milestones standing straight, the silence behaving as though it had been issued instructions. Past the rise where the beeches crowd the road, the small dry sound of someone keeping a tally by lamplight: coin counted, names counted, the road's takings reckoned out.
You sit your horse at the top of the rise and decide what page of theirs you would like to be written on.
Buy information from the Reeve. (200 denars)
The Reeve flips through his ledger. "Two camps of our cousins. I'll mark them on your map."
"A kingdom's a business with worse margins. We tax the same caravans, but we keep the profit."
"Gods of the road. The Quiet Saint who watches caravans. The Ledger-Keeper who tallies what's owed. Practical faiths."
The Reeve sets his pen down carefully. "That kind of talk gets transcribed in my ledger, friend. Under the column 'unfortunate accidents.'"
He inclines his head. "Disciplined men are productive men. Tell that to the next merchant who calls us savages."
The Reeve produces a flask of imported wine — Vlandian, by the seal. "The merchant who carried it never reached his customer. We toast his memory."
Your party gets a real cot, in a real tent, with a real cookfire. The Reeve runs the camp like a captain runs a barracks.
Browse the highwayman's ledger. (100 denars)
The Reeve flips a few pages. "One nearby cousin we'd missed. Pleasure doing business."
Hire a sword arm. (200 denars)
A scarred veteran nods at you. "Two weeks of bodyguarding. I drink, but I don't drink before fighting. Take it or leave it." Your party's morale rises.
Visit the document forger. (300 denars)
An old scribe hunches over parchment. "What you need? A passport, a writ, a letter from a noble? I do them all. I do them well. Twice this town's price, half the wait." Your morale rises a touch.
"Caravan from Pravend, six wagons, escorted by mercenaries. Departs in three days."
"Vlandian baron's tax-collector takes the south road on the first of every month."
"There's a secret cache of imperial dispatches buried under a roadside shrine."
"The merchant Eustace pays bandits to attack his rivals' caravans."
"A guard captain at Charas takes bribes. Half the smuggled goods in town pass under his nose."
"The Empress is sending a private courier westward — ungentlemanly business, no escort."
"A priest at Marunath has been embezzling temple gold."
"Sturgian mead caravan rolls through the pass tomorrow night."
"There's a bounty on a Battanian rebel — 800 denars, dead or alive."
"The arena fighter Hokkar throws fights for coin."
"Five hundred denars. Up front. Call it your toll, call it what you like. No coin, no business."
He counts the coin twice, smirks. "You learn fast. The roads are ours now, and so are you — within reason."
500 denars
"Fifty leather. Saddle-bags, harness, gear-straps. The road eats our kit faster than we can pay for it. Bring leather, save us the trip."
He weighs the stack, slings a bundle over his shoulder. "Honest hide. The road is friendly to you now."
50 leather
"Thirty amphorae of wine. Imperial vintage if you can find it. The boys ride harder when the night warms."
He pulls a cork. "Imperial. You've got connections we'd want. Trade with us."
30 wine
"Two thousand denars. That's a real toll. Hand me that, and you're not a customer of the road — you're a partner."
He weighs the bag. "Heavy enough. The road is yours when you ride it. Take what you need."
2000 denars
"Eighty leather and thirty wine. We're outfitting two new gangs for the southern road. Bring both."
He nods once. "Two more gangs ride this week thanks to you. The boys salute."
80 leather + 30 wine
"Fifteen hundred denars and we forget the last three caravans you didn't pay tax on. Coin solves problems faster than anything."
He pockets the coin without counting. "Books are clean. The boys have your back on the road."
1500 denars
"Five thousand denars. The road-network is opening to you — every gang from here to the southern marches takes orders from a man who walked in with this kind of money."
He weighs the chest, then locks it without counting. "You don't pay this kind of money to be a customer. You pay it to be a king of roads. Welcome."
5000 denars
"Fifty velvet and a hundred leather. We're fitting out a noble-looking caravan to ambush a real noble-caravan. Bring the disguise."
He laughs at the velvet bolt. "This is the kind of audacity that makes legends. The southern road is ours together now."
50 velvet + 100 leather
Escort a stolen-goods caravan from the Reeve's hideout to a fence town within three days, no losses.
The The Reeve accepts your oath; the rite is sealed in wax-stamped ledger ink, signed by candlelight at the wayhouse table.
The Reeve closes the ledger and slides it under the stump. "Your account is settled. Don't come up this road again expecting credit."
Khalid the Chain
Break the Rival's Chain
Oi — the master wants you at the receiving-stump. Somebody's been selling on our roads. Cheap. Khalid don't shout when he's angry, and he ain't shouted in three days. Go quick.

Sit, traveler. Drink. This is a small matter of bookkeeping. Faruk drove for me six years — knew my wells, knew my buyers. Now he runs his own string on my roads and sells at seven denars a head against my nine. Understand me: I do not begrudge a man ambition. I begrudge him my routes taken without purchase. The ledger calls that theft, however politely it is done. Find his column, break it. His men trained at my fires, so they will fight well — and Faruk will talk before he fights, because talk was always his best-selling item. Do not buy. There is silver in this, weighed fair.
Good. A clean entry. Break the column, scatter what he drives, and bring me word — or better, bring me his stock. The ledger pays by weight, traveler, and Faruk weighs heavy on it.
As you like. But roads that carry cut-rate flesh soon carry cut-rate everything — your contracts included. Think on it over the wine. The entry stays open a while yet.
You carry unfinished business, traveler — I can smell an open contract the way a camel smells water. Close your ledger first. Then we will speak of Faruk.
Faruk's Cut-Rate Column
Find Faruk's Cut-Rate Column on the desert roads and destroy it. A splinter ring of slavers is poaching Khalid the Chain's routes and undercutting his prices.
Faruk's ring is broken. Return to Khalid the Chain at his camp to settle the contract.

Khalid's new errand-rider — right on schedule. The old man keeps punctual help. Before anyone draws, hear a number: three thousand denars, yours tonight, and all you tell him is the roads were empty. Empty roads are the cheapest goods I sell. Well?
Three thousand, counted now. The roads were empty.
Counted and yours. A pleasure doing honest business, friend — Khalid taught us both that lie. Ride slow and tell it plain. The desert's roads have never been emptier.
Keep your denars. Khalid paid for a breaking.
Shame. You'd have made a fine partner. Instead you'll make nine denars a head — whatever's left of you sells somewhere. Chains up, boys. Close this one's ledger.

So Faruk's chain is off my roads. Good. Sit, drink — and answer the one question the ledger cares about: he was driving stock when you took him. Forty head, by my factors' count. Where do they walk now, traveler?
Driven to your pens. Count them yourself.

Already counted — my tally-boys had them at the gate before you sat down. Sound stock, delivered at fair weight without a single loss. That is how an entry should close, traveler. Full price, weighed while you watch.
I struck the chains. They scattered into the dunes.
Forty head, walking free in my desert. You cost me their price and told me to my face. Most men would have lied. I dock the loss and note the spine — the ledger has a column for both.

The account closes clean, then. Faruk's column broken, his string driven whole to my pens, his buyers already writing to me at the old price — nine denars a head, as the desert intended. Here is your silver, weighed against the full delivery, no skim, no haggling. You do tidy work, traveler. Men who deliver what they contract are rarer on these roads than sweet water. When the ledger next opens a page worth your while, I will send for you.

Faruk is broken and his prices with him, so the contract stands — half of it. The other half walked into the dunes when you struck their chains, and I do not pay for stock I cannot sell. Here is your silver, lighter than it might have been. And yet — forty head chose the desert over the block, and you stood there and watched them go. Curious economics, traveler. I have known one other man who kept books that way. Drink before you ride.

You come to sell me news I bought yesterday, traveler. A desert emir's lancers caught Faruk's column at a dry well and did my breaking for me — loudly, and free of charge. So the roads are mine again, and your contract died of another man's blade. Still. You rode out in good faith, and a merchant who stiffs honest effort teaches his partners to stiff him back. Half-weight, counted clean. Faster hooves next time.

You told me the roads were empty. Faruk sold at seven denars in Quyaz within the week — my factors count better than you lie. What he paid you is entered under your name; that page does not reopen. No wine. No trade. Speak standing.

Khalid was born free in a Nahasawi desert village his grandfathers helped found three centuries ago — a small settlement on the rim of the deep dunes, watered by a spring that has never failed. He grew up tending camels, learning the dune-paths from his father, and would have inherited the village's tenuous chieftaincy had the slavers not come the autumn he turned nineteen. They took thirty of his kin in a single dawn raid; Khalid escaped because he was sleeping under a date-palm and the slavers did not check beneath the trees. He spent four years tracking them, learning their routes, and finally — when he could find no other way to learn the inner workings of their network — he sold himself to a slaver-captain on a forged contract, riding chained for nine days through the dunes. He freed the men he was chained to on the seventh night using a bone-pick he had hidden in his cheek; they killed three guards, took the lead-camel, and rode south. The freed slaves became his first crew, and he has been freeing slaves and selling false-papered shipments to corrupt sultans ever since. Khalid the Chain runs the desert routes from the other end now — buying the men he was once chained beside, freeing them, and selling the bills of sale to lords who collect such things.

The Slaver Caravans are not new — they are the surviving fragment of an old Aserai chain-trade the early sultans tolerated and the later sultans forbade. When the trade was outlawed two generations ago, most chain-merchants converted to spice or wool; a small core of Nahasawi families refused, retreated into the deep dunes, and kept moving. Khalid's grandfather was one of them. Desert-villagers whose wells have failed, Aserai sons disinherited by imperial-leaning fathers, and southern men who have learned the trade-tongues of three nations and found no honest employer for the skill — these are the people the Nahasawi families take on. Their caravans never stop in a town; they trade at well-heads, at oasis-edges, at half-stripped sultanate forts the maps have forgotten. The Aserai sultanate has placed a standing bounty on every Slaver chief for forty years and has never collected it. Among the southern lords the band is half-rumor, half-trade-partner — lords who would never speak Khalid's name in court still buy his stock through a cousin's cousin, and Khalid has noted every name in a coded book he keeps under his receiving-stump.

The caravan-master does not rise. He sits cushioned and content, a cup of date-wine in one ringed hand, while behind him manacled figures stand in absolute, practiced silence. He watches you a long beat, weighing — the way a merchant weighs a stranger's purse without touching it. "Coin or chains, traveler. Khalid the Chain finds most who come to his fires bring one or wear the other. Which are you?"

Khalid does not gesture for you to sit, but he no longer signals his bodyguards either. The date-wine cup is offered without a word — a courtesy he extends only to those he has decided not to chain. "Back to my fires, traveler. Khalid finds you've a useful habit of arriving without dragging trouble behind you. Drink. Speak. Trade."

Khalid has heard the name. Heard hundreds. Most arrive expecting trade and leave wearing their welcome instead of their armor. The Chain's measure of a man is what he hauls home from the first errand. There is an errand. Complete it, and Khalid will pour you the wine he reserves for partners — not the wine he serves to fools.
The Slaver Caravans' camp is a maze of pens and tents, ringed by armed guards. Children in chains haul water. Khalid sits like a magistrate at his receiving-stump.

Ride east out of Quyaz one full day, until the city's perfume of myrrh and rotting fruit gives way to the clean stink of camels. You will strike a dry wadi running south like a knife-cut in the sand - follow it. When the wadi forks, take the right hand, and you will see slave-pens of mud-brick rising before you like teeth in a broken jaw. Behind them stands a single deep well, the only sweet water for twenty leagues. Our hold lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, and the well is the heart of it.
My drover-boys watch the dune-ridges from before the sun is up. They will mark your party from a league out and count your spears before you count your own waterskins. Ride beneath a banner of honest colors - white and rust like ours, or any merchant's stripe - and keep your hands open on the reins. If you arrive at noon, water your horses at the trough outside the gate; that is the sign of a man who knows the courtesy of the road.
Come correct and I will receive you at the receiving-stump like any other ledger-business: a cup of date-wine, a fair price on flesh or steel, my word on a contract. Come wrong, with hidden weapons or an empty purse and a loud mouth, and my guards will add you to the chains hauling the water. I sell what walks into my camp, traveler. Walk in carefully.

The Aserai sultan's tax-collectors ride out from Quyaz with twenty spears at their back, and they think the dune-fringe is a column in their ledger. I have taught three of them, this season, to read a different column. One paid in silver. One paid in horseflesh. The third signed his name in the sand with what was left of him. The sultanate keeps sending replacements because the sultanate keeps having sons it does not want at court.
There is a desert emir - Mubarak of the Banu Hilal, a clan-name you will hear in the south markets - who has sworn to my ruin in three separate audiences. He says I sold his cousin to a Vlandian count. He is correct. The count paid in good northern gold, and the cousin sang on the road, so the bargain was clean on both ledgers but his. Mubarak rides with forty lancers and a grudge older than his beard.
The Vlandian outriders cross the deep desert in late summer chasing slave-coin and Aserai horseflesh - rich fools, badly watered, easy ledger-work. Khuzait raiders push west when the steppe-grass burns. If you carry an Aserai banner south through my country, traveler, the emir will read your colors before he reads your purpose. The desert remembers debts. So do I.

The desert is a ledger, friend, and every chief upon it owes someone. Hakkun's dune-band runs the southern wells - small men, small contracts, but they sell me captives at fair weight and ask no questions about destination. I respect a man who delivers clean goods on time. Boll's outcasts I would not buy from if they paid me. Diseased stock, broken limbs, half of them dead before Quyaz. The Crone Vael's cult sends emissaries every other moon asking for "tribute in flesh" - I send them polite refusals and double my outriders for a week.
The blood-debt I carry sits with Aurelius and his Fallen Legionaries. Two seasons back his column took a caravan of mine on the Empire road - thirty head of stock, four guards, my second cousin running the manifest. He claims he did not know the mark. I claim the interest compounds. We have not met across a fire since. One day we will, and the account will close.
The quiet that troubles me is Bjornulf Salt-Tongue. His longboats have not raided the Aserai coast in three months, and silence from a sea-raider means he is counting something he does not want counted aloud. My scouts on the Pravend road brought back tongue-chatter of his men buying horses inland. A sea-raider who buys horses is a sea-raider who means to ride. Mark the name.

A spice-train leaves Quyaz every eighth dawn for the Vlandian ports - four wagons, eighteen guards, an Aserai captain named Mufaddal who drinks date-wine from a copper flask he thinks no one sees. He sees nothing past the third cup, and the third cup arrives at the dune-fringe waystone where the well-road bends north. My ledger has him crossing my reach in six days. The lead wagon carries saffron and cardamom for the boyars who pay in silver they minted from Sturgian mines - the second wagon is bolts of southern silk, the third is the only one that matters: bonded servants for the slave-blocks at Sanala. The escort doubles around that wagon and thins everywhere else.
If you ride with fifteen lances, traveler, take the front two wagons at the bend and let me have the third. That is a clean trade. I will pay you in silver weighed against the saffron, no haggling, no skim. The bonded servants are my ledger entries already - the buyers in Sanala have been promised, and a Slaver who breaks a delivery does not get a second contract.
Do not touch the rear-wagon. It carries a Vlandian factor's son riding back to his father, and the Highwaymen tried that game last spring. Reeve still owes me eighty dinars for the column I rerouted to bury his mistake. The desert remembers who collects, and who pays.

You ask the ledger-question, southerner. Most who sit at my fire ask for water, for safe passage, for a cut of the salt-road. You ask to be written into the book of binding. That is not a thing whispered between sips of tea. Sit. Hold your tongue while I read what is already inked under your name.
When Khalid the Chain bleeds for a man, it is because that man is sealed in salt and sworn in the ledger of flesh. I have three such names. Tariq, who broke his thumb-bone over my wrist when the Banu Hilal would have sold us both. Old Rashida, who covered my caravan-debt in Quyaz before the qadi knew my face. A bondsman whose chains I struck off in the dunes, who now wears them by choice, around his neck, as my mark. These are my chains. These are my bound.
Bring me the deed of a bondsman, not a buyer. A rival caravan turned to my profit. A debt I did not know I was owed, paid. A road east of Quyaz held open while the wells went dry. Do that, and the ledger learns your name in salt. Ask me again when the ink is wet, and not before.

Then it is written. Kneel at the ledger - rise as a name within it. I take the salt-jar from the lead camel's pack, the same jar my father pressed to my tongue when I was eight and screaming, and I press a pinch to your tongue now. Taste it. That is the dune east of Quyaz, where I cut my first thumb-bond at twelve over a stolen girl and a stolen mule. I draw the curved knife - the one that opened the Quyaz factor who tried to short the manifest - and I score your palm beside the brand on mine. Press. The salt finds the cut. The cut remembers the salt. The ledger has tasted you now, brother, and the ledger does not forget what it tastes.
You are kin-of-the-chain from this hour. Not chattel - kinsman. My camels are your camels. My drivers bow to you as they bow to me. The slave-girl who pours my coffee pours yours first now, because the elder brother drinks last in the caravan-master's tent. My debts are your debts. My salt-stores in Quyaz, in Iqbayl, in the deep-desert caches no factor knows - yours to draw upon as breath.
Let the dune-fringe witness. Let the Quyaz emirs who paid me in clipped dinars witness, for they will learn this name when their warehouses next burn. You are Khalid's brother now - chained to me by the salt and the ledger and the scar. The road from here is long, brother, and we walk it weighing every soul we pass.

Then the ledger is read, and the entry stands. You did not come to my tent with a merchant's speech, with terms and clauses and a hand half-extended for the seal. You came with the work already finished and the salt of it still on your boots. I asked once if you would bleed for me when the time came, and you answered not with breath but with iron. That is the only currency I weigh. Sit. Let the chain settle on the post while I name what you have bought.
From this hour my caravans are your road, and your enemies are my freight. When you raise your banner against a lord, my outriders sweep his villages before his couriers reach him. When you ride into the deep dunes, my water-stations open to you as they open to no other rider south of Quyaz. In return you owe me this and only this: when I send word that a debtor has run, you bring him back, alive or in pieces, and we split the ledger clean. Not brothers. Not hearth-kin. Blood-allies, the way a man and his chain are allies - one cannot move without the other, and both leave a mark.
The salt-seal on my tent flap was set in the year my first caravan-master broke his word and I broke his neck. It has held every oath since. It holds yours now. Ride out, ally. When my men hear hooves at the dune-crest, they will not draw steel - they will count your numbers and add them to ours.

Done, and the salt-seal closes it. Ten chain-riders for seven days - I count them out myself, by name, by collar, by the brand on their forearm. My second is Qadir Salt-Tongue, who has driven caravans from the desert to the wet coast and knows which of my outriders ride straight and which ride for themselves. He goes with you. The chain leaves my post at dawn.
Hear my terms, buyer. A man of mine is not a coin you spend - he is a coin I loaned. If one falls in your work, you bring me his collar and the name of the blade that took him, and I will set the price of that name later. My caravan-guards do not break shield for petty work. They break shield for cargo that pays, for roads that need clearing. While they wear my mark under your banner, do not waste them on errands a stableboy could finish.
Seven days. I have already written it in the ledger. When the moon turns, I expect ten men back at my gate - or nine men and one good story, told by Qadir himself.

His name is {TARGET}. He keeps his banner over {HOME}, and his father bought my sister Aluneh from a Geroia broker nineteen summers past - bought her with my own coin, traveler, coin he owed me for a salt-shipment he never paid. She died scrubbing his floors in {HOME} the winter before last. I have her tally-mark cut into the wood of this counting-desk. {TARGET} signed her death-warrant when he refused to ransom her back to me at three times her weight.
He rides a tall grey and travels with twelve riders, but four of them are sons of men who owe me chain-money - they will not draw fast. He counts his coffers in {HOME} on the first morning of each moon. Take him on the road home from his accountant, when his purse is heavy and his guard is drunk on the count.
{REWARD} denars when his seal-ring reaches my desk. The ledger of flesh remembers what gold cannot wash clean. The salt-seal waits. Ride.

{CHIEF} has set {TARGET} of {HOME} upon the open page of his salt-ledger, and the entry is older than any living factor remembers. Seven seasons past, a slaver-caravan out of Iskon-Drabh was broken on the coast road, its iron struck off and its cargo scattered into the brush; among the lost was a chained woman called Suren who had served the Chain as steward and counter, and who carried in her head the names of every buyer from Quyaz to the Kanikat strait. {TARGET} kept her ransom and burned the manifest. The Chain pays a heavy purse in clean coin. The seal of salt waits. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is dead. {CHIEF} has been told, and the ledger of flesh is opened to the page that has waited eleven seasons for closing. The Razih entry - the salt-caravan of forty-three souls broken on a hill outside Quyaz, the iron neck-ring of his sister Amineh struck off and lost in the dust - is now scored through with the long red mark of debt-paid. {REWARD} denars are weighed on the salt-stone and folded into the chain-master's coffer, heavy as a closed contract. The salt-seal is pressed once, and the name is taken off the chain. The ledger is shut.

Word reached {CHIEF} by a salt-runner out of the southern passes: {TARGET} had been cut down in a rival lord's ambush along a coast road, throat opened before the slaver's own blade ever found the mark. The chief took the news at his ledger, the same ledger where Aluneh's name still stood unpaid - the sister he had once seen bought, worked, and buried by the very chain that traded her flesh. He weighed the report against that older debt and judged it answered, though not cleanly. The grudge was closed; the salt-seal pressed; yet the killing had not been earned. Quarter-pay was counted out in thin coin, {REDUCED_REWARD} denars stacked without flourish, and the bond between them set a smaller notch firmer - acknowledged, ledgered, but cooler than a kill delivered by hand.

"There is a village called {VILLAGE} in the red dunes south of the salt-road, held by Lord {LORD} of the emir-clan that refused my salt-toll nine seasons running. Nine seasons, scribe. I counted each one in a ledger bound with goat-hide. Their elders snapped the iron neck-chain my brother Tariq forged with his own hands - snapped it across a well-stone and laughed while the slaves walked free. Tariq does not laugh anymore. He does not speak.
{LORD} keeps his outriders close to the wells through the dry month, but the grain-fields ripen now and his men sleep through the noon-heat under the date-palms. Burn the threshing floors. Take the brass scale-weights from the headman's house - they are mine by salt-right. The smallfolk you may chain or leave; I have buyers in Quyaz either way, but the chained ones pay better.
{REWARD} denars in struck silver when the smoke rises over the dunes. The ledger waits, and Tariq's hand grows colder. Ride."

{CHIEF} has named {VILLAGE}, the grain-fief of Lord {LORD} of an Aserai emir-clan, as the ledger to be closed in fire. Nine seasons running, this village refused the salt-toll the caravan-master sets on every loaf of bread that crosses his road, and nine seasons the chain-master has marked them in the iron book his brother Tariq kept before the elders broke the chain Tariq forged with his own hands. Tariq is gone. The chain is broken. The grain-fields ripen now, and {CHIEF} will see them harvested by other hands. A purse of {REWARD} is offered to the rider who will bring the torch. The salt-toll falls due. The contract is open.

{VILLAGE} smolders, and {CHIEF} the Chain has weighed the news. The emir-fief of Lord {LORD} of the Aserai - the salt-debtors of nine seasons, the elders who shattered the chain Tariq forged - lies opened to the wind, its ripened grain trampled into the dust, its wells fouled, its men roped in coffles bound for the southern blocks. {REWARD} denars are counted out on the merchant's scale where Khalid keeps his ledger of unpaid tolls, and a fresh link is hammered shut in Tariq's memory. The salt-toll is collected at last. One debtor-clan answers no more.

Word reached the caravan-pavilion at the second muezzin-call: {VILLAGE} lay scorched, the granaries cracked open, the elders scattered - but the torch had been {LORD}'s, carried for some border quarrel that had nothing to do with nine seasons of unpaid salt-toll, nothing to do with the chain my brother Tariq forged that those elders broke across their threshing-stone. {CHIEF} heard the runner out, folded the ledger, and smiled the smile that does not warm the eyes. "The grain is burned," he said, "but the debt was not collected. A creditor takes no satisfaction from a fire he did not light." He counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars himself - half-weight, paid clean - and waved the matter closed.

Khalid's last manifest, recovered from a clerk's saddle outside Quyaz two months ago, read as follows:
Cargo, southbound from Razih: Adult males, sound, age 16–35: forty-two head Adult males, lamed, age 35–50: nine head Adult females, sound, age 14–30: thirty-one head Children, both sexes, age 6–12: twenty-two head Infants (with mothers): four Loss in transit (heat, attempted escape, illness): seven Net delivered, payable to Chain of Quyaz: 101 head Per head, gross: 12 dinar Less feed, water, guard wages, road-tolls: 3 dinar/head Net to seller: 9 dinar/head Total: 909 dinar Signed in good faith, K., for the Chain
It was a clean ledger. The hand was educated. There were no marks in the margin for the seven losses, no notes on why they were lost, no entry at all for the four infants except the line that bracketed them in with their mothers as one figure each. The bookkeeping was as good as any imperial counting-house. That was the part that turned the stomach.
You read it twice on the road and could not stop reading it.
Now you sit your horse at the top of the dune-track and you can hear, in the lee of the rocks below, the small even sounds that book becomes when a book is what is happening: iron link against iron link, a cough swallowed, the murmur of a great many people being quiet in a way that has stopped being fear and become a habit.
A heavy man sits on a cut stump at the camp's heart as though it were a magistrate's bench, and a line waits on his judgment.
Khalid is doing his accounts.
You take the manifest out of your saddle-bag and look at it once more in the torchlight. You fold it. You put it back.
You ride down to add a line of your own to the book.
Browse the slave market.
Khalid claps. Two figures are dragged forward. "Strong backs, weak wills. Pick what you can use."
"A king would outlaw our trade in public and buy from us in private. The arrangement we have is more honest."
"We pray to Tariq, who blesses the bargain. Coin doesn't care which god is invoked over it."
Khalid laughs without moving his face. "Bold for a man my guards outnumber four-to-one. Shall I add your name to my inventory?"
He shrugs. "Fine? It's a market. The merchandise complains, the buyers complain. Normal day."
Khalid pours a clear spirit from the south. The captives watch in silence. "Drink, friend. Business is better when the partners are loose-tongued."
You sleep in a guarded tent. The chains clink all night. Your party rises tense, but better-rested than the road allows.
Visit the auction hall.
Khalid leads you to a tent where finery is laid out — looted dresses, jeweled rings, a noble's writing-set. "What we strip from the merchandise. Premium prices, but prime quality."
Tap the whisper network. (200 denars)
Khalid lights a long pipe. "My chains travel everywhere. So do my eyes. Two camps marked. Tonight you don't even pay full price."
Hire a whip-trainer. (500 denars)
A scarred man with a whip walks past you. "He'll train your soldiers in cruelty. Useful when the world is cruel." Your party's morale shifts uneasily, but they march harder.
"There's a market for noble captives in the Aserai south. Triple the price."
"Imperial law forbids slavery, so the imperial nobles use middlemen. We are middlemen."
"The Khanate has a labor camp in the eastern steppe. They've paid us twice for new bodies."
"A Vlandian lord's son was captured by us last month. We sold him to a rival house."
"Galleys along the southern coast need rowers. They pay in advance, no questions about accent."
"There's a tunnel under Husn Fulq used for moving captives."
"A noble's daughter ran away to marry a smith. The father's hired us to find her."
"The desert sultan buys eunuchs at any price."
"A merchant prince in Quyaz is collecting captive scholars. 5000 denars per."
"Imperial galleys lost a slave shipment to pirates. They want them back."
"Bring me ten loads of iron. We need it for shackles, for chain. The trade we run isn't pretty."
He weighs the ore in one hand. "Clean. You don't ask what I do with it. The caravan trades with you now."
10 iron
"Five mules. The caravan moves bodies, and bodies need beasts to carry them. Bring sound stock."
He inspects each animal's teeth. "Strong-backed. The caravan rolls with you now."
5 mules
"Fifteen leather. Restraints, harness, hood-bags. We don't pretend our trade is otherwise."
He runs a strap between his fingers. "Properly cured. Trade with us."
15 leather
"Ten mules and ten iron. Pack animals and shackles. You bring this, you sit at our table."
He runs a chain through his fingers. "Iron and beasts. The caravan opens its rolls to you."
10 mules + 10 iron
"Twenty iron and twenty leather. The next caravan moves doubles. We need restraint-kit for forty."
He nods grimly at the stack. "Now we move forty. The caravan owes you a share."
20 iron + 20 leather
"Eight mules and thirty leather. We're swapping out our string and re-harnessing the lot. Heavy haul — caravan-rider work."
He claps the lead mule's flank. "Fresh stock, fresh harness. The desert's ours together."
8 mules + 30 leather
"Thirty pack-mules and fifty iron. We're moving the largest single caravan our crew has ever run — three hundred bodies south. Don't ask, just bring."
He doesn't smile. "Three hundred souls move because of your work. The caravan owes you a debt of blood. Don't think on it too long."
30 mules + 50 iron
"A hundred iron and twenty wrought-iron ingots. Heavy chains for a hundred captives. The crew's biggest take of the year hangs on this."
He locks the chest of finished chain. "That's a southern fortune in steel. The caravan rides with you on the rest."
100 iron + 20 wrought iron
Intercept a rival slave caravan being escorted to a foreign faction and seize the cargo before it crosses the border.
The Khalid the Chain accepts your oath; the rite is sealed with the brief click of a chain linking your wrist to the chief's for one heartbeat.
Khalid pours wine and does not offer the cup. "You came to my fires under truce. The truce is ended. Walk out before the chains find you."
Centurion Aurelius
The Lost Standard

You there. The old man's been at the whetstone since the pickets came in — imperial column on the road, carrying something that's ours. He wants you at the standard-stone. Quick-march, he said. He never says quick-march to outsiders.

Stand straight and listen once. My pickets marked an imperial column on the post-road — a wagon under canvas, an escort, and a captain young enough to still believe in the Senate. Under that canvas rides the eagle of the Twelfth. My eagle. The one they stripped from us the afternoon they struck our numerals from the rolls. Some clerk has decided it will decorate a garrison shrine. It will not. Twenty years I have drilled boys under an empty pole. Bring it home. Buy it or take it — the method I leave to the field commander. But it comes back whole, and it comes back to me. Questions? No. Then move.

Good. That word was given like a soldier gives it. The column halts at the milestones to water — catch them strung out on the road, not camped. Bring my eagle home and the cohort counts you one of ours.

As you were, then. But mark this: every dawn count, ninety men salute an empty pole. The offer stands until that column reaches its garrison. After that the eagle goes behind walls, and the ledger stays open another twenty years.

You have standing orders already, soldier. One duty at a time — that is how a cohort stays a cohort. Finish what you carry, then report back. The eagle will keep a little longer. It has kept twenty years.
Cassius' Eagle Column
Captain Cassius
Find Cassius' Eagle Column on the imperial roads and recover the eagle standard of the Twelfth Legion for Centurion Aurelius.
Return the recovered eagle standard to Centurion Aurelius at the Fallen Legionaries' camp.

Halt there. This column marches under imperial writ — the standard of the disbanded Twelfth, bound for the shrine at Lycaron. I know what you are. State your business and clear the road, or my escort will clear it for you.
You know my name. Count my spears, then hand down that eagle.

I know it. So do my men — I can hear them knowing it behind me. Sergeant, uncrate the standard. Present it properly; we will not be shamed twice in one hour. Take your eagle. The report I write tonight will flatter neither of us.
Fifteen hundred denars for the eagle. No blood, no report.

Put it away — no. Give it here, quickly, before I think. The men are owed three months' pay and the Senate is owed nothing by me. Sergeant, the crate. It fell from a wagon at the ford. That is what happened. Go.
The eagle stays on this road. Draw.
Escort — form line! Shields front, dress on me! You want a legion's eagle, brigand? Then meet a legion's drill. It was carried by better men than either of us. Come and take it.
Your name. I have read every dispatch out of Lycaron this season and it appears in none of them. No. The eagle rides with me, and if you want it you may try steel — my escort could use the drill.

Hand it up. Slowly. There. Twenty years since this weight was in my hands, and my hands remember it to the ounce. Look — the crown is nicked where the Dasalir arrow struck. I was standing under it. Sound the muster. The cohort makes the dawn count under a full pole for the first time since our numerals were struck from the rolls. You did this, soldier. Stand at my right for the count. That post has been empty a long time.

So this is how it comes home. Pulled out of a ditch by whoever got there first, mud in the wing-feathers, crown stove in. Give it to me. An eagle is not disgraced by mud, soldier — only by the men under it, and the men under it now are mine. The smith will hammer out the dent. The rest we leave. It should look like what it has been through. Half-honors on the ledger. Full place on the pole. Dismissed.
Disowned Centurion

Aurelius enlisted in the Northern Empire's Twelfth at fifteen, the youngest son of a smallholder family in Praven who had no inheritance to look forward to and no land to farm. He served with distinction in the Khuzait wars of his youth, was promoted to optio at twenty-two, and made centurion at twenty-eight after his predecessor was killed at the Battle of the Dasalir Crossing. The trouble began the year the imperial succession fractured into three claimants — pay-shipments stopped arriving, requisitions went unanswered, and the cohort was left to forage on the imperial highways for three full winters with no word from the capital. Aurelius held the line at Pravend through all three winters, refused to disband his men or surrender the standards to opportunistic lords, and waited for relief that never came. When the cohort's water-stores ran out for the second time he made the decision: he marched the legion off the imperial roster with the eagles and the pay-chests they had captured from a corrupt prefect. Twenty years on, the cohort still drills at dawn, still wears the imperial purple, and still numbers in the hundreds — pension-veterans, deserters, and second-generation children born inside the cohort's marching-camp. The empire has issued three separate edicts demanding the return of the eagles; Aurelius has filed three separate counter-petitions demanding the back-pay he is still owed.

The Fallen Legionaries are exactly what they appear to be — what is left of the Northern Empire's Twelfth, after the cohort was disbanded without back-pay in the second imperial reorganization and twenty years of accrued pay-claims written off the rolls in a single afternoon. Aurelius held the cohort together for the first march east, then the first winter, then the first refusal of an imperial decree. The original survivors numbered ninety-one. Only veterans of imperial service are admitted, and only those who can produce proof of the rolls they were dropped from. The camp is laid as a cohort-camp — palisade, ditch, regular tents, dawn-drill, evening watch-rotation — because that is what it remains, and the inverted eagle in front of Aurelius's tent has not been touched in twelve years. The Empire treats them as an embarrassment more than a threat: the Senate has tried twice to amnesty them in exchange for surrender of arms, and both delegations went home empty-handed. The Legionaries take only imperial wagons, only imperial revenue-trains, only imperial granary-shipments — never private merchants, never peasants, never anyone the cohort would once have been sworn to defend.

The grey-haired man straightens as you approach, snapping his hand up in a salute that is older than the empire he no longer serves. His eyes scan you head to foot the way a centurion still does — armor, posture, weapon-hand, the small tells. "Eyes front, soldier. Aurelius doesn't ask twice. State your business in two sentences and stand straight while you do it — I have buried better men for taking three."

Aurelius's salute is curter this time — the kind a centurion gives to a soldier who has earned the omission of formality. His eyes still scan you, but they no longer linger. "At ease, soldier. The watch reports you've held discipline on every visit since the first. Make your report. Aurelius will hear it through this time."

Name noted, soldier. The roster wants more than a name. Aurelius has command of men who survived three campaigns the Empire forgot they were sent on — they don't take new comrades on names alone. There is a duty waiting for you. Carry it through, and the cohort will know your name like its own.
The Fallen Legionaries' camp is laid out like an imperial cohort camp — palisade, ditch, regular tents. Aurelius drills the boys at dawn. The eagle banner hangs upside down.

Ride the old imperial post-road west out of Lycaron until the paving stones break apart and the weeds take them. You will pass a collapsed milestone leaning in the grass - the numeral is half-gone but the eagle is still cut clean on the upper face. From that stone, turn south into the sentinel-hill country and keep the highest hill on your right shoulder. When you see the inverted eagle on a pole above a proper palisade and ditch - dug to the book, not scratched out by goat-herds - you have found {HIDEOUT_NAME}.
My pickets hold the ridgelines a full mile out. They are old legionaries and they will mark your column before you mark them. Ride at a walk, banners shown, hands off the hilt. If you have a centurion's vinestaff or a broken eagle of your own, raise it. We were soldiers once and we still answer the old signs. A man who comes in at the trot with weapons bared earns the response his manners deserve.
Come in proper order and you will eat what we eat - black bread, stale wine, iron discipline. Come in like brigands and my line will form on the drilling-yard and you will learn what a cohort still remembers. The Empire disowned us. We did not forget the drill. Keep that in your head before you cross my ditch, traveler.

The Empire has not forgotten us, traveler. Three cohorts they have rotated through the sentinel-hill country this season - imperial outriders, the kind I once commanded, riding the old frontier road west of Lycaron like they own the milestones. They do not. The milestones were cut by men whose grandsons I drilled. I gut their picket-riders when they stray, and I leave the bodies sitting upright against the ruin-walls so the next column reads the message.
There is a tribune called Lucius Varro who hunts me by name. He was a junior officer under my command at the Lycaron muster, and now he wears the eagle I was stripped of. He sends his scouts in pairs, never threes - he was always cheap with rations. I have killed four of his pairs this season. Sooner or later he will come himself, and then we will settle the ledger the legion never let me close.
The Vlandians push their outriders into the western passes when the snow breaks, chasing imperial bounties on my head - a tidy sum, I am told. The Battanians stay clear; they remember the punitive expedition my old cohort ran through their hills, and they have long memories for grudges. If you ride my country under an imperial banner, soldier, my pickets will read the colors before they read your intent. Carry that knowledge. The frontier still belongs to me.

My pickets keep a roster, same as any cohort - know your neighbors, know who holds the next hill. The Sky Raiders nest above the sentinel ridges north of us. Aerlin and I have a treaty signed in nothing but silence: her hawks do not stoop on my picket fires, and my crossbows stay capped when her riders pass the ridgeline. We were both legion-broken in our own ways. That is enough.
The Highwaymen of the downs are another matter. Their Reeve sold a tally of my supply caches to a Vlandian tax-rider two winters back. Three of my men bled out in a ditch for that ledger. I owe him a debt paid in iron, and one day my second cohort will ride the down-road and collect it in full. Granny Hod's forest band to our west I leave alone - she trades honest, keeps her snares off my ration runs, and her boys have warned my scouts twice when imperial outriders came hunting.
The quiet one is Khalid's slaver caravan. My scouts have not crossed his column in six weeks. A slaver does not go silent because he is resting. He is moving cargo somewhere he does not want witnessed, and when a man like that vanishes from the road, somebody downwind is about to find chains on their wrists.

My pickets have been counting wheels on the Lycaron post-road for six weeks running. There is an Imperial grain-column that moves east on the kalends of each month - eight wagons of milled flour and salted pork bound for the garrison at the old sentinel-hill forts. The escort is sixteen legionary-pattern spears and four crossbows, which sounds like a cohort until you watch them eat. They halt at the third milestone west of the ruined Aurelian bridge, unbuckle their helms, and pass a wine-skin the quartermaster pretends not to see. That hour, traveler, is when the column is a sleeping dog.
The captain is one Tribune Marcellinus - a sharp man on parade, a drunk man after noon. Bribe his outrider sergeant for twenty denars and the pickets will face the wrong way. We have done it. The third wagon carries the pay-chest disguised under flour-sacks; the lead two are honest grain. Hit the rear, not the front, and the spears in front will keep marching half a furlong before they notice their tail is gone.
There is also a Vlandian silk-train that cuts north through my hills on the dark of each moon, running pepper and dyed cloth up to the Sturgian boyars. Smaller escort, ten riders, but they march at night and they do not sleep. Leave that one to my cohort. The grain-column is yours if you want it. A soldier should eat well before he fights.

You ask the sacramentum, stranger. The oath-question. In the cohort we did not speak it twice, and we did not speak it at all to men who had not earned the standing. Sit. The fire is mine, and so is the silence that follows what you have just asked.
I have sworn the blood-oath twice in this life. Once to the Eagle, before the Senate sold it for grain prices and frontier maps. Once to Decimus, my optio, who took a Khuzait arrow in the throat at the Lycaron crossing because I had broken formation to drag a recruit from the river. I bled for him before he bled for me, and the ledger between us closed only when he stopped breathing in my arms. That is what an oath from a centurion costs. Not coin. Not a season's loyalty. The drill, until the drill ends you.
Bring me a frontier held against orders. A column kept in line when the line should have broken. One deed done in the discipline of the old standards, not the mercenary rabble of this age, and I will read your name into the roll where Decimus is written. Speak the question again when you have stood the watch.

Then the sacramentum is spoken twice in one life, and the second time the gods of the legion did not flinch. Stand at attention. No - stand easy. I have not given that word to a man in nine years. Draw your gladius. Lay it across mine on the stone where the cohort's eagle used to rest before the Senate struck our numerals from the rolls. Now the cut. Forearm, soldier's cut, the one the drill-master opens on the first day so you learn what your own blood smells like. Press it to mine. There. The iron drinks. The eagle that was taken from us still sees, and tonight it counts one more.
From this watch forward you are my brother under the old oath, the one they could not unmake when they unmade us. My cohort is your cohort. My wound at Lycaron - the one the tribune called desertion and the surgeon called bone-deep - is your wound now, and the answer we owe for it is your debt as it is mine. You sleep inside my watch-line. You eat from my mess. When I drill at dawn you drill beside me at my right hand, where the signifer used to stand before they hanged him.
Brother. The frontier west of Lycaron knows your name tonight. The ruined castra knows it. The legate who disowned us will hear it when our shields come over his wall. Fall in.

Then it is heard, and it is enough. You did not come back with a speech rehearsed on the road. You came back with the deed already cold on your blade and the word offered after, as a soldier offers his report - flat, factual, finished. That is the order I was taught before they stripped the eagle from our standard. The sacramentum was never the words. The sacramentum was what a man had already done by the time the centurion called the roll.
So hear the terms as a soldier hears them. When you raise your banner, my cohort forms on your flank. Not as auxiliaries the Senate can recall by edict - that lie I have already outlived once. As sworn shields, bound by the same iron oath we swore to a legion that disowned us. Your enemies inherit my grudge-list. The lords who paid the bounty on my head will find my men in their grain-stores and at their gate-hinges. In return you give me what the Empire withheld: the right to be SPENT for a cause that meant it.
The drill carries this now. Every dawn count, every cadence-step my legionaries take, your name marches in the line. When steel is drawn, the eagle - mine, broken though it is - rises beside your standard. We are not kin. We are something the legions understood better. We are sworn, and the sworn do not break ranks until the field is ours or we are under it.

Granted. Ten line-men, seven days, counted from the next dawn watch. I will draw them from the second file - they still remember the drill, which is more than I can say for the rest of this pit. My optio, Brennus Quintus, rides at their head. He took an oath on my standard the day the eagle fell, and he has not broken it since. He answers to you as he answers to me. No further.
Now my terms, traveler. The sacramentum binds them to the work, not to your purse - so the work had better be worth a legionary's sweat. If one of mine falls in your line, you bring me his gladius and the name of who put him down. I will see to the rest. If he lives, you return him fed, watered, and with his kit intact. I count blades when they march back through this gate.
Seven days. The cohort expects them at the seventh dawn, formed up and accounted for. Do not be late.

His name is {TARGET}. He sleeps under his own banner at {HOME}, fed and warm, and that is the wound. Nine years ago I held the Third Cohort's left flank at the Drava ford under our sacramentum to the old eagle. {TARGET} commanded the relief column. He turned south. Forty-two of my men were ridden down in the shallows while he wintered his horses at a wine-merchant's villa. The legion called it lost dispatches. I called it what it was. He has lived nine years on that lie.
He rides with twelve in his household guard, but only four are veterans, and the veterans hate him for the same reason I do. His captain is a man called Brennus who lost a brother at the ford - find him at the smithy in {HOME} on market days, stand him a drink, and he will speak. {TARGET} hunts boar in the woods west of the keep every third dawn. He goes with two outriders. Take him on the trail.
{REWARD} denars when the eagle is paid back in full. The cohort keeps the rest. Now move.

{CHIEF} has named {TARGET} of {HOME} as the magistrate whose ledger must be closed in blood. Eleven years past, on the Veranda road south of Lycaron, the Tenth Cohort marched on stale bread and forged orders - a quartermaster's contract sold for clean denarii to a man wearing a senator's ring. Forty-two legionaries fell to a Khuzait ambush that was never supposed to happen, the eagle taken, the standard-bearer's hands struck from his wrists before he died. {CHIEF} carries the cohort-roll on a strip of tanned hide beneath his lorica, and {TARGET}'s name is the last unblotted line. The drill demands answer. A heavy purse of {REWARD} denarii is offered, and the sacramentum waits to be honoured in iron.

{TARGET} is dead, and {CHIEF} has been told. The name of the magistrate who signed the disbandment order at Lavium in the ninth year - the man whose seal scattered the Tenth Cohort and left Quintus rotting in a ditch outside the gate - has been struck from the long bronze tally nailed above the cohort's fire. {REWARD} denars sit counted in the strongbox beside the broken eagle, and the relation between centurion and sword-for-hire is set one notch deeper into the wax. Quintus does not march again. But the sacramentum has been honoured. The drill is kept. The ledger of Lavium is shut.

Word reached {CHIEF} at second watch: {TARGET} was dead, bled out in a ditch off the post road, cut down by some rival baron's outriders over a tax quarrel that had nothing to do with the eagle, nothing to do with Lavium, nothing to do with Decimus face-down in the Drava silt. The centurion received the news standing, the way he had received the disbandment order years ago, and said little. The grudge was answered on paper. The ledger of the optio's drowning was closed by another man's blade, in another man's quarrel, and that sat in him like cold iron. He counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars - quarter-pay, the price of a result without the doing of it - and set the bond a notch firmer, though no warmer. The broken eagle stayed broken.

"There is a village called {VILLAGE} on the {LORD} clan's eastern revenue list. They sent seventy modii of wheat to the column that betrayed us at Lavium - and the forged marching orders that put my cohort on the wrong road were sealed in {LORD}'s grandfather's hall. Twelve years on, that village still grinds the bread the traitor-column ate while my centuria bled in the river-fords. The debt is grain, and grain it shall be paid in.
Their militia rides patrol on market-days and returns at dusk drunk on the lord's wine. Strike at the third watch when the bread-ovens are cold and the granary stewards are counting tally-sticks by lamplight. Burn the wheat first, then the tally-house, then the millstones. Spare the field-hands and the bondswomen - they grind for whichever banner stands over them. Kill any man wearing {LORD}'s sash.
{REWARD} denars when the granaries are ash and the modii are settled. Discipline first, then the burning. The legion's ledger does not forget."

{CHIEF} has named {VILLAGE}, the holding of Lord {LORD}, as the field where the cohort's ledger will be balanced in fire. The granary there fed the column that turned on the Lavium oath, and the orders forged in that village's scriptorium moved the betraying standards into position before dawn.
