Seventy modii of wheat were drawn from those barns to feed men who would later cut down their own. The Centurion remembers the count, and he remembers the seal. He offers a soldier's purse of {REWARD} and the closing of an account ten years overdue. The debt is wheat. The payment is ash. The contract is sealed in the cohort's roll.

{VILLAGE} smolders, and {CHIEF} has been told. The grain-fief of Lord {LORD}, whose stores fed the betraying column at Lavium and whose scribes forged the orders that walked the cohort onto Imperial spears, lies threshed in its own ash. The seventy modii of wheat are paid, not in grain but in the only currency the Centurion still keeps a ledger for. {REWARD} denars are counted out on the standard-stone where the cohort once mustered, struck across to the player like back-pay to a foederatus. One name is scored from the roll. The wheat-debt has been spilled.

Word reached the marching-camp at second watch: {VILLAGE} stood ash and bone, but the column that put it to the torch had ridden under {LORD}'s pennant on a quarrel of borders, not on cohort writ. {CHIEF} read the dispatch by lamp-oil and folded it twice, the way an officer folds orders that no longer require action. The seventy modii of wheat owed the cohort since Lavium had been paid in another man's fire. The grudge stood discharged - on the ledger, not on the standard. He had the quartermaster tally {REDUCED_REWARD} denars from the strongbox, half-rate by old legion custom for a debt collected by foreign hand, and signed the chit without comment. The wheat was burnt. The honor was not.

"Eagle's upside down," Vermund says, beside you on the rise. "You see it?"
You see it. Vermund used to wear that eagle right-way-up on his shoulder before they cashiered him for taking a Battanian girl out of a burned village instead of leaving her in it. He has not been the same about eagles since. He sits his horse a little stiffer in their presence — the only sentimentality he has ever shown you.
"The ditch is the V-spec," he says, "dug to the marching depth. Three feet at the lip, narrowing to one. Spoil on the inner face. You don't dig that ditch by accident. You dig it because a centurion named Macrius made you redig it twice when you were eighteen. Either the man down there learned from Macrius or he served under him. Either way, he is older than you think."
He nods toward the gate.
"Challenge given. No countersign returned. That's the giveaway. In the proper years you'd be dead between the syllables. They're going through the motions because they remember the motions, and they remember the motions because the motions are the last unbroken thing they own."
A long pause.
"See those boots? Unblacked. Centurion would have flogged a man for that. So would I. So would the man inside that gate, ten years ago. Now he watches and lets it pass, because the price of correcting it is the boy's face when the boy realizes nobody's coming to relieve him."
Vermund spits into the dust, very carefully, away from you.
"I knew an Aurelius once. Tenth Century, Fourth Cohort. He had a way of straightening a guy-rope nobody else would have noticed. That'd be him, then. Or one of his."
He goes quiet, then, and listens. From inside the rotting palisade comes the slow patient sound of a blade being sharpened — and under it, very faint, an old marching-cadence hummed without words, on no particular pitch, by a man who has nowhere to march to.
Vermund touches his brow with two fingers. The old salute. For himself, not for them.
"Walk the horse down," he says. "He'll want to look at us before he decides anything."
You walk the horse down.
Train at the legion's drill yard. (1000 denars)
Aurelius examines your party. He shouts orders. Your soldiers drill until they bleed.
"We served the empire. The empire owed us pay and gave us the road. We chose new bosses — ourselves."
"Imperial gods, in the imperial way. Eagle, sword, and emperor — though the emperor we curse, the eagle we still salute."
Aurelius doesn't move. "Soldier, I have ordered men to their deaths. I have buried half my cohort. A threat from a stranger doesn't reach me."
He nods stiffly. "A camp is built right or it isn't. Mine is. Some habits don't die when the wages stop."
The Legionaries pass a clay jug of soldier-wine. Aurelius raises it. "To the brothers we left buried, and the empress who left us to bury them."
You bunk in regulation tents, two to a row, on imperial-issue cots. Aurelius wakes you at dawn whether you want it or not.
Stand at the standards.
Aurelius leads you to the upended eagle. "We touch the staff once a day. It reminds us why we hated them. And what we still are." Your party's morale ticks up.
Read the imperial dispatches. (100 denars)
Aurelius opens a captured pouch. "We intercept these from the post-rider. One reveals a cousin's camp. Take it. The empire pays us in carelessness."
Visit the quartermaster.
A bald man with a slate gestures you in. "Imperial gear, slightly used. Some bloodstained. We're honest about the source."
"The Twelfth Legion is being reformed in the south — without us."
"There's an imperial pay-chest hidden at the old Lycaron fort. Lost in the war."
"Senator Lucon votes against soldier pensions every term."
"A Battanian rebel pays for old legion training. We sent two of our boys to him."
"The Western Empire is hiring mercenaries again. Twice the wage of last year."
"There's a deserters' fort hidden in the southern hills. Other legions, same story."
"An imperial dispatch rider goes through here weekly. We let him pass — and read his pouch first."
"A relic from the Twelfth's standards is in private hands."
"The empire's conscription officer is bringing fresh recruits past here."
"Aurelius taught the empress's nephew sword-work years ago."
"Ten amphorae of wine. The legion taught us drinking among other things. The empire never paid our back-wages, so the empire's wine will do."
He pulls a cork with his teeth, drinks long. "Imperial vintage. You drink with us tonight."
10 wine
"Fifteen oil. Lamps for the night-watch, and the boys still oil their kit like proper legionaries. Bring it."
He tests the oil between thumb and forefinger. "Pure olive. Not the rancid stuff the quartermaster sold us back in service."
15 oil
"Twenty grain. The men march on bread and the cohorts line up for it like old times."
He surveys the sacks. "Quartermaster's portion. Tomorrow we eat as we did at Pravend."
20 grain
"Thirty wine and ten iron. The legion drank, and the legion sharpened steel. Bring both, and we'll count you a comrade."
He stacks the amphorae like a quartermaster. "You'd have made a centurion. Take what you need."
30 wine + 10 iron
"Twenty-five oil and fifteen wine. The cohorts maintain kit and morale on these alone. Bring both — full quartermaster's haul."
He nods like a centurion. "Properly stocked. The cohort thanks you with steel."
25 oil + 15 wine
"Forty wine and five mules to haul it. The mid-summer drinking-feast for the cohorts. Don't be late."
He surveys the festival-laden mules. "Tonight we drink like we did before the empire forgot us. Take what you need."
40 wine + 5 mules
"Fifty wine, thirty iron, ten refined-iron ingots. The cohorts re-equip for the imperial border. We'll show the empire what its forgotten legion can still do."
He stands at attention as the ingots are laid out. "You re-equipped a legion. The empire we left will remember why it should have paid us."
50 wine + 30 iron + 10 refined iron
"A hundred wine and fifty oil. The full cohort triumph-feast. We march out at dawn after — you'll see what discipline survives twenty years in the wild."
He raises a horn. "Drink with us, brother. Tomorrow we ride, and you've earned the right to ride at the standard."
100 wine + 50 oil
Recover the lost III Legion eagle from the marked patrol ferrying it past the cracked castle.
The Centurion Aurelius accepts your oath; the rite is sealed at the cracked legion altar with hand pressed to the eagle-stone.
Aurelius salutes you, fist to chest, the old legion salute. "Dismissed, soldier. There is no place for you under this eagle now."
Aerlin Cliffborn
The Caged Cliffs

You. Cliff-Master wants you up top. Some lord's bird-man netted our falcons off the eyries — whole wagonload in cages, rolling south for the lowlands. Aerlin's gone quiet over it. The bad quiet. I'd climb fast.

A lord's man came up my cliffs with nets while the eyries were feeding young. He took nine falcons off the wind, traveler — hatched on my ledges, first-flown over my sea — and now they ride south in wicker cages, hooded in the dark, bound for a lowland mews and a fat wrist at feast-days. A caged cliff-falcon does not tame. She bates against the bars until her wings break or her heart does. Find that caravan. I do not care what the falconer takes for them or what he bleeds — the birds come home to the wind. Bring the cages up whole. The wind will tell me you are coming. It always does.

Good. Do not open the wicker on the road — a falcon loosed in lowland air rises into strange wind and stranger arrows. She goes back to the sky from the ledge she hatched on, or not at all. Climb careful, traveler.
Then walk back down, traveler. But the cages roll south while you think, and a cliff-falcon does not last long behind wicker. The wind keeps the offer. It does not keep it long.
You carry work already, traveler. A falconer flies one bird at a time — throw two at the sky and you lose both. Finish what is on your wrist.
Falconer's Caravan
Master Falconer Gerwin
Find the Falconer's Caravan on the roads and recover the caged cliff-falcons netted from the Sky Raiders' eyries.
Carry the caged falcons back to Aerlin Cliffborn at the Sky Raiders' camp.

That's close enough. These birds are lawful cargo — netted under license, bound for my lord's mews. I know what you are and which cliff you climbed down from. Name your business and keep your hands off the wicker.
Count my riders, falconer. Then open the cages.
Take them, then. Gently — gods, gently, they bruise. No. That is a lie I tell my lord. Three years on my glove, every one of them. Go on, take them. Better your cliff than a mews they'd have died in.
A thousand denars for the cages. All of them.

...Done. Quietly, then — coin in the hawking bag, cages off the rear wagon, and no names carried either way. Tell whoever flies them the grey tiercel takes the lure high. He earned better than a lord's mews anyway.
No bargain. The birds fly today — through you if need be.
Guards — to the wagons! Cover the cages, the cages first! Damn you, climber, I'd have sold you half of them if you'd asked twice. Loose at will!

I count a dozen good crossbows on my wagons and rather fewer blades at your back. No. These birds cost me three years and my lord a small fortune — I'll not hand them to the first climber who talks hard. Move along.

Set the cages on the flat stone and stand off. There. Watch her — she remembers. Off the ledge, down, down — and the updraft takes her. Look at her climb. Nine birds back on the wind, traveler. A lowland lord sits at his feast-table this winter with an empty gauntlet, and my sky is full again. The wind carries debts both ways. Today it carries mine to you. Take your coin — and the wind's thanks with it. That is worth more.

The gulls brought it in before you did. Someone else hit the falconer's wagons at a ford — no craft in it, just axes. Half the cages broke in the wreck. Four birds found the wind on their own. The rest — a falcon does not die well in wicker, traveler. My rope-runners carried the living ones up last night. So. Half done, by other hands, and paid the same way. Half coin. The wind does not owe what it did not carry.

Aerlin was born on a stone ledge above a mountain pass, the bastard of a Vlandian noblewoman who could not present him at court and would not abandon him at a temple. She built a stone hut at the edge of the world — three days' ride from the nearest settlement — and raised him there with two trusted servants and a small library of stolen books. He grew up reading the loot-ledgers of his uncles' raids before he could write his own name; his mother taught him geometry by stacking captured coin and arithmetic by valuing stolen jewelry. When she died — a lung-fever that no physician could reach in time — Aerlin was nineteen and had never spoken to more than four people in his life. He came down off the cliff with his mother's ledgers and a list of every Vlandian noble who had wronged her, and within five years he had robbed the convoys of every name on the list. The Sky Raiders took shape as a company of climbers and scouts, men who could fight on slopes that infantry could not navigate; today they raid the high passes of Vlandia and the western border, holding ledges no army has the patience to siege. Aerlin has never lost a fight on uneven ground, and the only thing he hates more than the Vlandian crown is the prospect of falling.

The Sky Raiders are the smallest of the great bands and the strangest. Their roots are not in any kingdom but in a falconer-tradition older than all four — a high-mountain craft of training peregrines and gyrfalcons for hunt and war that the Vlandian lowland lords no longer practice and the Battanian highland clans only half-remember. Aerlin's mother carried the craft up from the lowlands and built her stone hut at the cliff's edge for the wind, and Aerlin has never lived under any other roof. Cliff-village shepherds, dispossessed Vlandian bastards, falconer-apprentices whose masters could not afford to keep them, and the rare lowland nobleman's son who cannot abide a stone hall find their way up to Aerlin's camp by routes the lowland patrols have never mapped. They rope between cliffs to move and signal with falcon-jesses tied with colored thread, and their raids are precise to a degree no flat-country lord has learned to anticipate — they arrive when no road-patrol expects, vanish into rock-folds no lowland horse can follow. The crown classifies them as a curiosity rather than a threat — it has not yet lost enough men in the high passes to correct that classification.

The Cliff-Master does not turn until you've cleared the last rope-pitch. The hawk on his gauntlet sees you first — head tilting in that quick, surgical way — and only then does he. He studies you in that same surgical manner: brief, complete, unimpressed. "You came up the slow way. The clever ones do. The dead ones tried the fast. Speak, traveler — Aerlin's wind doesn't wait, and neither does his bird."

The hawk on Aerlin's gauntlet recognizes you before its handler does — head tilting in that quick raptor's curiosity instead of the surgical study from before. Aerlin himself lowers his gauntlet a fraction. "You came up the slow way again. The wind likes you, traveler. So does the bird, which is rarer. Speak — Aerlin's perch is open to those his hawk doesn't strike at."

The wind's heard names, traveler. Carries them off the cliffs and forgets them by sundown. Aerlin trusts what the bird trusts — and the bird trusts what proves itself. There's a task within our reach. Earn the bird's calm and you've earned mine; refuse, and the next strong wind takes your name with it.
The Sky Raiders' camp clings to a cliff — tents staked into ledges, ropes between, perches for a dozen falcons. The wind never stops. A boy is teaching a young hawk the lure.

Follow the coast road north of Sanala until the inland trees give up and the wind starts pulling at your cloak in earnest. When the road forks at the white limestone scoured bare by the gales, take the goat-trail switchback that climbs the cliff-face - the one no sane drover uses. Our hold lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, on the ledges above the breakers, where the gulls scream louder than a man can shout.
Long before you reach the last switchback, my falcon-cote will see you. The bird on that ledge is no wild thing - she is mine, and her jesses are tied to a bell that rings in my tent. My watchers run the knotted ropes between the high perches faster than you can climb the trail, and they will count your spears before you count your breaths. Ride open-handed. Tie a strip of white cloth to your spear-point so the wind shows it clean against the cliff.
Come the right way and there is salt-fish on the fire and a sheltered ledge for your horses out of the spray. Come the wrong way and the wind takes you first, then the rocks, then the gulls - we do not even need to draw a bow. The cliff has fed itself on bolder men than you, traveler. Carry a name I know, and the ropes drop for you.

The Battanian lords think these cliffs belong to them because their grandfathers fished the same gulls we eat. They send their fianna up the coast road in twos and threes, sworn-men in green cloaks asking the fisher-villages who feeds the cliff-dwellers. The fishers point south. We watch them ride south. We laugh into the wind. There is a lord out of Marunath called Cuthred who has sworn on his grandfather's torc that he will burn my eyries before midwinter. He has sworn this three midwinters running. The gulls remember his face now.
The true trouble comes from below. The Empire's southern legate keeps a tax-galley working the Sanala coast - she puts in at every cove with a coin-chest and a centurion who thinks the cliff-paths are myth. We took her tithe-purse twice this season. The third time she came with Aserai mercenaries in the hold and we lost a good rope-man on the rocks. So now there is a debt between me and that legate that only salt water settles.
If you ride the coast road under any banner that is not Battanian green, traveler, ride it fast. The fianna read banners before they read faces, and the southern empire reads purses before either. The cliffs do not care which side claims you. The gulls eat from every hand that falls.

Bjornulf Salt-Tongue and his longboats put in at my coves twice a year, and we trade the way gulls trade with the tide - he leaves a cask of Sturgian mead, I leave him word of which Battanian thanes have weak watch-fires. We owe each other nothing and that is why the bargain holds. The man who rides the sea and the man who watches from the cliff should never count debts between them, or one of us ends in the surf.
Granny Hod's forest band, south where the highland breaks into oakwood, sent a runner last moon asking after a debt of salt. I sent her two barrels and the head of a Vlandian tax-rider who had wandered too near her trees. She owes me a season of safe passage now, and her boys know not to climb where the gulls nest. Skarvac's pass-lords in the mountains east of here - them I do not trust. They count coin like Reeve's Highwaymen and they have stopped answering smoke-signals from the cliff-watch.
The Reavers up in the snows - Vargolf - we have never crossed, and the wind says we should keep it so. But the Cult, Crone Vael's lot, have been seen on the cliffs at dusk leaving carved gulls on the rocks. That is old sign, and not for me. When the Cult moves quiet near my coast, I sharpen the watch and I do not sleep facing the sea.

The cliff-road from Sanala to Pen Cannoc runs along the sea for three days, traveler, and the merchants who take it think the gulls are their friends. They are not. The gulls are my eyes. A Vlandian cloth-train comes north every dark moon - four wagons, eight crossbowmen, two outriders who hate each other and ride a furlong apart because of a woman in Jaculan. The wagons carry dyed wool bound for Battanian chiefs who pay in amber. They camp at the Cormorant Spring because the captain fears the cliff-wind after dusk, and the wind is loud enough there to swallow a scream.
Hit them at the third hour past midnight. The crossbowmen sleep in a ring but the wind blows their fire flat, and a man cannot string a wet bow in the spray. I have taken that train twice - once for the wool, once for the amber the chiefs had already paid in advance. The captain is named Othric. He bribes well if you put a knife to his belly first, but he will lie about a second purse he keeps in the axle of the lead wagon. Cut the axle open.
If you ride with thirty horse, the train is yours and I will not contest it - my longboats are out hunting Sturgian salt-cogs this moon and my cliffs are thin. Take the amber. Leave the wool on the rocks for the gulls. Wool drowns slow and the tide takes everything by dawn.

You ask the cliff-question, traveler, and the wind has already heard you. Sit. Down there, where the gulls turn, the fall is the same whether a man means his oath or only thinks he does - so I will not answer quickly, and you will not pretend you did not ask.
When I bleed, I bleed for those whose jesses I have tied to my own wrist. My sister Caelin, who I cut from a Sturgian rope when she was twelve and the tide was rising. Old Mawran, who taught me which ledges hold and which lie. A gull-girl from Pen Cannoc whose name the cliff still keeps though her bones do not. Their knots are at my wrist. Yours is in my hand, untied, waiting.
Bring me a deed the wind will carry north - a raid kept silent until the gulls had flown, a southern banner cut down on a ledge no horseman could climb, a debt of mine paid before I knew I owed it - and I will tie your jess to my own. Until then my rope is my rope and my fall is my fall. Come back when the cliff has a reason to remember your name.

Then the wind has heard it, and the gulls have heard it, and that is witness enough for me. Stand on the ledge with me - here, where the rope is anchored to the iron ring my father drove when I was a boy. Give me your wrist. I tie the jess around it, the same leather I tie to my hawks before I throw them at the sky, and I tie the other end to my own. There. We are jessed to each other now. Drink from the horn - it is salt-water and barley-spirit mixed, the cliff-drink, the only oath my people swear with their feet over open air. The knot at our wrists is a brother-knot. Rope-knots do not lie.
From this gust forward you are my hearth-brother. The scar across my shoulder, the one the lowland archer gave me the day I lost my first hawk to a crossbow bolt, that scar is your scar to avenge if I fall before you do. My sister at Sanala is your sister. My mother's grave on the headland is your grave to tend. When I throw the hawks at dawn, one is yours - the brown one, the quick one, she will learn your whistle. Sky-raider brothers share wind, share rope, share the long fall if the rope fails.
Hear it, cliff. Hear it, gull. Hear it, every Battanian lord who has ever sent men up these paths to burn us. Aerlin Cliffborn names this one brother on the high ledge, and the knot is tied, and the wind has carried it inland. Brother - the cliff holds two now.

Then I have heard it, and I heard it before you spoke. The wind off the cliffs carries news faster than tongues, and word of your deed reached this ledge two gulls ago. You did not come up that rope to ask my blessing. You came up to report. The deed first, the word almost an afterthought - that is the order a Cliff-Master trusts. A lesser man brings a fine speech and a clean knife. You brought a knife that has been used, and the speech was nearly forgotten in the doing. Sit. The salt will dry on you while we talk terms.
From this tide forward, my jesses are cut for your hand. When you raise your banner, the longboats slip the cove and the rope-bridges drop for your riders - not as hire, not as a favor I can reel back, but as a war-bond knotted the way I knot a falcon's leash: one loop the bird cannot break, and one I will not. Your feud is the cliff's feud now. Your enemies will hear oars where they expected only gulls. In return I ask the same - when a southern banner climbs against my eyrie, your steel rides north before the tide turns twice.
The gull cries this oath out across the headland already. Steel makes its own sound, and the wind carries it - to the lowland lords, to the salt, to every cove that has ever sheltered me. We are bound now in the work of war, you and I, the way a rope is bound to the cliff it hangs from. Cut one, the other falls. Ride hard, ally. The knot holds.

Done, traveler. Ten cliff-walkers for seven days - rope-runners I have weighed myself, each one gull-throated and quick on a bad ledge. My second is Maerwen Salt-Eye, who has worked every shelf on this coast and knows when to whistle and when to cut the line. She rides with you. The wind owes you that much.
Now hear my terms. If a rope-runner of mine falls in your work, you bring back his knife and the name of the place he died - I will carve it on the cliff where his mother can find it. If he lives, you feed him well and send him home with salt still in his hair. My men do not break shield for petty grudges or roadside thieves. While they wear your colours, your road IS my road, so do not waste them chasing crows.
Seven days. Count them by the moon, not the sun - the sun lies on water. The gulls will tell me when they ride back through the pass, and I will be listening.

His name is {TARGET}. He keeps his banner over {HOME}, and that cliff was Cliffborn ground before his great-uncle Maerwin came up the rope-ladders one summer dawn with paid swords and a forged charter from a dead king. He took the eyrie. He took my grandfather Aedric off the high ledge by the ankles and let the gulls have what fell. The jesses my father wore on his wrist were cut from my grandfather's belt. {TARGET} sits in that hall now. The cliff knows.
He flies a tercel he calls Lord's Pride, and the bird hunts the cove below the south stair every third morning. He rides out with it himself, six lances, no scout. The cove path narrows where the gulls nest. A man on the rope-knot above can see his banner before the bird does. Take him there, traveler, where the wind comes off the water and steals the sound of a drawn bow.
{REWARD} denars when his banner comes down off that wall. The grudge is older than the coin and the coin will not close it, but it is what I have to give. The wind will tell me when it is done. Ride.

{CHIEF} has named {TARGET} of {HOME} as the man who cut the jesses on a falcon called Sea-Eye nine summers past, and with her the throat of the boy who flew her. The bird was a gift-hawk, hand-fed from the cliff at Gull-Stair, and the boy was {CHIEF}'s sister-son, sent down to the lowland court bearing a peace-token wrapped in oilcloth. Neither came back up the rope. The token was returned by a paid rider, stained, and the falcon's hood was nailed to the chapel door. The Cliffborn keeps the hood on his beam still. {REWARD} is offered, and a knot the wind has waited too long to pull tight. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is dead, and {CHIEF} has heard the wind carry it home. The jess-strap that hung empty above the cliff-perch since the winter Brennec was cast from the Skewer's high ledge now bears a single knot drawn tight - the falconer's brother answered for at last. {REWARD} denars sit weighed beside the rope-coil at the chief's fire, counted twice by gull-light, and the bond between Sky-Reaver and stranger-blade is cut a knot deeper. The hawk that lost her hand is not given back, but her name is spoken even, and the cliff keeps the rest. The rope is finished.

Word came in on a salt-stiff gull-runner: {TARGET} had been ridden down by a rival lord's outriders three valleys east, ambushed at a ford while the snow still clung to the reeds. {CHIEF} took the news standing by the beam where the jess-strap of Sea-Eye still hangs empty, and for a long breath he said nothing at all. The Skewer ledge had its answer; Brennec's name could be set down. But the gift-falcon was not recovered by a hand he chose, and the killing was not paid in the coin he had asked. He counts out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars - thin coin, quarter-pay - and nods once. The grudge is closed. The bond is set a smaller notch firmer, cooler than an earned kill, but firm.

"There is a fisher-village called {VILLAGE} on the headland below Skewer Cliff, held by Lord {LORD} of the coast-clan that lit the wrecker-beacons twelve winters past. They hung false harbor-lanterns on the rocks the night the Saelvarg made for shelter. My longboat broke her keel on their cradle of stones. Twelve oar-mates went down singing. Their gulls still pick clean what the tide leaves, and {LORD}'s smallfolk glean the wreck for nails and beads when the water draws back.
Go when the spring-tide is at its lowest - their men are out on the flats then, gathering my dead-men's iron from the sand. The drying-sheds are heavy with smoked fish bound for the inland markets, and the wreck-gleaners hoard amber and sea-glass in the chapel cellar. Burn the sheds. Take the cellar. The fisher-wives and the children of fishermen - let them run inland. I will not drown what already lives by water.
{REWARD} denars when the smoke goes up from the headland and the gulls fly out to sea. The wind takes the rest. Sail before the tide turns."

{CHIEF} has named {VILLAGE}, the wrecker-cove held in fief by Lord {LORD} of the Battanian coast-clans, as the shore whose thatch will burn to close the debt of the longboat Saelvarg. It was {VILLAGE} that set the false beacons below Skewer Cliff one black autumn, and it was {VILLAGE} that gleaned the wreck while twelve of {CHIEF}'s oar-mates rolled in the surf, lungs full of cold salt. The fisher-folk still pick brass from the rocks at low tide. The Cliffborn offers a purse of {REWARD} to the keel that returns with smoke at its back. The wind has turned. The Saelvarg's twelve are waiting. The contract is open.

{VILLAGE} smokes on the headland, and {CHIEF} stands at the cliff-edge where the Saelvarg's keel still ribs the rocks below. The fisher-clan of Lord {LORD} - the wrecker-kin who hung the false beacons that drowned twelve oar-mates a tide ago - have no beacons left to light, no nets left to gather salt-stripped boards. {REWARD} denars are counted onto a longboat-thwart hauled up from the wash, every coin tallied against a drowned name. The gleaners gleam no more. The Saelvarg's debt is one shore lighter, and {CHIEF} marks the cliff with a fresh oar-notch for the dead.

A gull-runner came up the cliff stair at low tide with the word: {VILLAGE} lay broken on its own shingle, but the keels that broke it had flown a different pennant - {LORD}'s feud, not the Saelvarg's reckoning. {CHIEF} heard it standing at the cliff-rail above the wreck-line, where the twelve oar-mates still slept under green water. He spat once into the wind for the drowned and said the gleaners would steal no more lanterns to set on no more rocks. The beacon-clan was answered, but the torch had been another's. He counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars from the salt-stained chest - half-fare for a passage he had not rowed - and turned back to the sea, neither warmed nor cheated.

Do not look down.
You will want to. The body, when it finds itself this far from the ground, tries to satisfy itself by measuring the distance. Do not let it. Keep your eyes on the rock to your left, on the narrow strip of stone the path has become, on the rope-anchor driven into the cliff at chest height. There is the strip. There is the anchor. Keep moving.
Do not stop on the windward shelves. They look the safest because they are the widest. They are not. Wind that has crossed forty miles of open air arrives here without warning and arrives with the weight of a hand laid flat against your chest. A man who is standing still on a windward shelf when that wind comes is no longer standing still.
Do not trust the bridges. The Cliffborn weave the ropes and the Cliffborn replace the ropes, but the wind ages the ropes faster than any people, and the bridges they last crossed at noon they will recross at dusk and find changed. Watch where the Sky Raider in front of you sets his weight, and set yours where his was. He will not turn to check on you. That is not unkindness. That is mercy. Looking back kills.
Do not speak. The wind takes voices and the wind does not give them back. If you must speak, lean close, and shape the word against the listener's ear. Calls have killed climbers up here who did not deserve to die for a call.
Do not look at the falcons. Look at the gloves that handle the falcons. Look at the knots in the jesses. The birds will not hurt you. The bird-keepers will not, either, if you watch their hands the way they watch yours.
Do not flinch when the wind drops.
It will. Suddenly. The roar will go and the silence will arrive and the silence will be very large, and in the centre of that silence you will hear voices, women talking low, a child laughing, someone singing a long string of nonsense to a falcon to soothe it. You will hear the camp.
Then look up.
The tents staked along the bare ledges. The figures crossing the ropes. The firelight snapping sideways. A woman with her feet over nothing, mending a glove.
Now you may speak. Slowly. Aerlin Cliffborn is the one with her hood off.
Send a hawk aloft to scout for hideouts.
Aerlin lifts her arm. The hawk lifts off and is gone. "I'll mark every camp she sees on your map."
"Kings live below us. We don't even see their banners from up here. Who would we serve, the wind?"
"The sky-mother. The wind-father. The hawk that watches all things. We pray short, in the open."
Aerlin smiles, slowly. The hawk stiffens. "My bird sees better than you do. Take a step. See where she lands."
She looks past you, at the wind. "It's a good cliff. We had to fight three other clans for it. We won't fight a fourth."
The Raiders share a liquor distilled from cliff-berries — sharp and cold. "To the sky and to the strong rope. Either alone is death. Together, freedom."
You sleep on a cliff-ledge, lashed to a rope just in case. The wind sings all night. Your party wakes light-footed.
Visit the cliff-forge.
An old man hammers iron at a forge bolted to the rock. "Cliff-iron is harder. The wind tempers it as it cools. Costs more, lasts longer."
Speak with the wind-reader. (50 denars)
An old raider sits on a windward perch, eyes closed. "The wind tells everything. Storm coming. War coming. You — choose the wind, not the wave."
Hire a falcon-trainer. (300 denars)
A young trainer with raw hands shows your soldiers how a hawk lands. "Discipline of the bird is discipline of the man. Cheap at the price." Morale rises.
"There's a noble's hunting hawk worth more than a Vlandian war-horse."
"A Battanian druid pays for fresh-kill from sky-hunts."
"An imperial messenger uses falcons too — flies them down the coast road."
"The cliff-passes get a tax-collector twice a year. He climbs slow. We climb faster."
"A merchant pays double for sky-raider feathers in Onica."
"The kingdom's pigeon-network was disrupted last year. Some of them were us."
"There's an abandoned eyrie three valleys west — hawk-eggs unhatched, tools intact."
"A rival cliff-clan has been encroaching on our airspace."
"The Imperial War College sends scouts up here every spring to recruit falconers."
"A young heiress wants to learn falconry in secret."
"Silk. Fifteen bolts. We strip silks from caravans on the high passes, but supply runs short between raids."
He fingers the silk to the light. "Real. Not the dyed cotton merchants pass off. The Raiders trade with you."
15 velvet
"Twenty leather. Saddle, harness, fall-rope kit. The high passes are unforgiving on tack."
He weighs a strap, snaps it taut. "Strong stitch. The Raiders welcome you to the trails."
20 leather
"Twenty-five linen. We bandage what the high stones break. Bring it, and the men will heal because of you."
He hands a roll to the camp's healer. "Clean cloth. The boys live longer because of this. Trade."
25 linen
"Thirty silk and twenty leather. We sleep light and ride lighter — silk for ropes, leather for harness."
He nods sharp. "You ride the high country now. Recruit my best, take the armory."
30 velvet + 20 leather
"Forty linen and thirty hardwood. New stretcher-frames for the high-fall climbs. Bring both, and the high country is yours."
He tests a frame's give. "Steady carries. The Raiders ride safer because of you."
40 linen + 30 hardwood
"Twenty-five silk and five sure-footed mules. The eastern raid moves silently in silk-padded harness. Bring both."
He surveys the silent caravan. "Whisper-quiet now. The eastern lord won't hear us coming."
25 velvet + 5 mules
"Sixty silk, thirty hardwood, ten refined-iron ingots. The grandest raid this generation has run. Outfit us, and you ride at the head."
He clasps your forearm in the high-rider greeting. "You lead the eastern raid this autumn. The Raiders ride at your hand."
60 velvet + 30 hardwood + 10 refined iron
"A hundred leather and fifty silk. We re-arm the entire raid-cohort for the spring high-passes. Heavy haul."
He surveys his men in fresh kit. "The high country has never seen Raiders this proud. You walk among us as equal."
100 leather + 50 velvet
Ambush a Battanian highland tribute caravan from the cliff-ambush position above the high road.
The Aerlin Cliffborn accepts your oath; the rite is sealed at sunset on the cliff edge, a hawk released into the dropping sun.
Aerlin watches you over the cliff's edge, hand on the hawk's hood. "The wind takes some friendships. This one. Go before I loose her at your back."
Khan Borchu
Forty Hooves
You. The Wolf-Khan's been asking for you. Something about a lord's horses walking a road they shouldn't. He's at the camp. I'd not make him ask twice — he doesn't.

A lord is selling horses. Forty of them, steppe-bred, walking to market under drovers' whips like oxen. Steppe horses do not belong to the man who holds the rope, traveler. They belong to the man who can ride them. That lord cannot. His drovers walk. His guard riders sit their saddles like sacks of millet. Find the herd on the road and drive it home to my grass. Forty horses is not plunder — forty horses is a herd, and a herd is a clan's blood walking. Bring me that blood, and Borchu will not forget whose hand drove it home.
Good. Ride light and carry rope. A herd follows a lead mare, not a whip — take the whips off them and the horses will remember whose grass they were foaled on. The wind rides with you.
As you like. The herd walks to market either way — to a fat lord's purse or to my grass. Think on which end of that road you would rather stand. The offer keeps until the horses sell.
One hunt at a time, traveler. Finish the work you carry. A rider who chases two herds catches dust.
Lord's Horse-Drove
Drover Captain
Find the Lord's Horse-Drove on the roads and take the herd of forty steppe horses from its drovers and guard riders.
Drive the captured herd back to Khan Borchu at the Steppe Wolves' camp.
Close enough, rider. These horses walk under a lord's brand, bought fair at the spring muster. You want a mount, the market is two days on. You want trouble, my riders are paid for that too.
Come dark, this herd runs. Try holding it.
Torches! Get torches up — they're in the herd! Hold the line, hold the — gods, they're all running! To me! Guards, to me!
No dark work. I'll take them here, in the open.
Open ground, then. You picked the one fight my lads know. Wheel about! Lances down — earn your wages, boys.

Forty. I counted them from the rise before you crossed the creek. A herd walks differently when it comes home — you will learn to hear it. Foaled on this grass, sold off it by a man who never slept against a horse's warmth in the snow. Well. The grass has them back. Take the grey and the dun with the black legs — best of the forty. A khan does not let a herd-bringer ride away worse mounted than the herd he brought. Ride hard.

Word came in on the wind before you did. Another band hit the drovers at the ford and the herd went forty ways at once. My riders gathered what the steppe gave back — six, still shaking. The rest run loose out there. Good. A steppe horse loose on steppe grass is not lost, traveler — it is home the older way. Still. Six is not forty. Quarter-pay, and no shame riding with it. The wind does not apologize either.

Borchu is a true Khergit khan by birthright — but only by a sister-line that was never meant to see succession. His mother was the Great Khan's youngest sister, married off to a minor steppe-prince to seal a border alliance; she bore Borchu the year her husband died of a horse-fall, and the boy was raised in his uncle's tents as a fosterling. The Great Khan's sons did not appreciate the existence of a cousin with a legitimate claim, and at twenty-three Borchu was sentenced to exile on a charge of insulting a half-brother. He rode west into the empty grass with seventeen riders who refused to leave him; for three years they lived as outlaws, raided Vlandian merchants, and grew their numbers off bandits and steppe-orphans. When the Great Khan's eldest son died in a mysterious accident, Borchu came back at the head of two hundred horsemen, demanded an audience, and presented his claim. The Khanate's elders did not formally acknowledge him but they did not formally exile him a second time either; he keeps his title because nobody alive remembers stripping it from him. The Steppe Wolves are now the largest non-affiliated band on the steppe, and Borchu rides as a khan in all but recognition.

The Steppe Wolves are a sister-line of the Khergit royal house, and that is the inconvenient fact that has never let the Khanate quite kill them. Borchu is a true khan by birthright — only by a sister-line never meant to see succession, but a true khan, and the Wolves know it. Horsemen with nowhere to go collect around Borchu's standard — steppe-clansmen whose grazing has been re-allocated by the Great Khan's favor, exiles whose feuds the royal court declined to mediate, second sons with no herd of their own. They winter wherever the grass is short enough to suggest a herd has just left and nobody can prove which herd. The raid-pattern is the old steppe pattern: ride hard, take what fits on a horse, vanish, return three months later from a direction no patrol has watched. The Great Khan has refused four imperial requests to suppress them — officially because the steppe polices itself, unofficially because Borchu is family. Among the eastern clans the Wolves are a quiet legitimacy-problem: every herd-feud that comes to a head ends with someone whispering Borchu's name as a possible alternative banner.

The Wolf-Khan does not dismount. His pony stands placid, ears back, while Borchu himself looks down at you with the slow assessment of a man who has spent forty winters reading travelers off their saddles. He smiles, eventually — wolfish, joyless. "You ride a foreigner's horse. The wolves smell that on you, traveler. Trade with old Borchu and you'll ride better. Refuse, and the wolves smell something else entirely."

Borchu still does not dismount, but his pony's ears prick at your approach now — the small horse remembers the rider it's been told not to bite. The Wolf-Khan's smile, when it comes, is less wolfish, more amused. "You ride better now, traveler. Old Borchu told you trade with us would do that. Come — the fire is the wolves', but a place at it is yours."

Borchu has heard names enough to fill a steppe sky, traveler. Names wash off in rain. Deeds — the wolves remember. There is a thing my pack would have. Bring it, and Borchu will tell you which fire is yours; until then you ride a foreigner's horse and carry a foreigner's word.
The Steppe Wolves' camp is a half-circle of yurts, horses everywhere. The grass is short here from grazing. Children with bows hunt rabbit at the edge of camp.

Ride east out of Makeb until the farmland gives up and the grass takes over. When you reach the river-bend - the one that swings south like a drawn bow - turn your horse along the bank and follow the hoof-trampled trace for half a day. You will see a horse-skull on a pole standing taller than a man; that pole is mine, and the wind that turns it knows my name. Our camp lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, a half-circle of yurts set where the grass is cropped short by my herds.
My outriders see you long before you see them. We watch from the low rises, and a hundred horses raise a dust-cloud no scout misses. Come at a walk, not a gallop. Hold your weapon-hand open and your reins loose. The children hunting rabbit at the camp-edge will mark you first - if they do not run, my men will not draw.
Ride in soft and you sit at my fire, drink my mare's-milk, and ride out heavier than you came. Ride in hard and my arrows find you before the wolf-tails on the windbreak stop turning. I am Borchu, and the steppe is a wide grave for fools. Bring me a name worth speaking, traveler, and the grass parts for you.

The Khuzait khans send their riders past Makeb every grazing-moon, and they ride like they own the four horizons. They do not. The horizons belong to the wind, and the wind answers to no khan but the one who outlasts him. A noyan named Urkhun Ghazi has been crossing my river-bend with two hundred horse-archers, calling it a hunt. He hunts my outriders. I hunt his remounts. We have an understanding written in lame horses and empty quivers.
The Empire still pushes tax-wagons up from the southern garrisons, but they send mercenary captains now, not legati - the eagle has grown shy of the steppe since the last khagan broke its wing. There is a Vlandian sellsword called Sir Aldric the Bone-Pale riding under imperial coin who has burned two of my wintering-grounds. I owe him a wind-burial. He owes me his teeth. One of these debts will be paid before the grass turns.
Watch for Khuzait banners flying the white-tailed horse - that is Clan Urkhudai, and their khan has put a price on my saddle that would buy a small town. If you ride with their colors, traveler, ride elsewhere. The steppe is wide. My wolves are patient. The wind carries word of every banner that crosses my country, and I read the wind like other men read sky.

The grass talks if you listen. Vargolf of the Reavers and I have grass between us - he keeps his snow, I keep my steppe, and neither rides where the other's horses graze. Once, in a winter the elders still name, I sent him three remounts when the freeze took his strings. He has not forgotten. The Iron-eyed pays in silence, but he pays. The Slavers under Khalid are another tale. Their chains pass my four horizons three times a season, and three times a season I take my tithe. He calls it raiding. I call it tax. Khalid and I will settle one day with sabres, not words.
Ulan's steppe-band rides the eastern flats and counts himself my cousin. He is not. He is a boy with a borrowed name who eats what my scouts leave. I let him live because the Khuzait boyars hunt him and not me. Useful, that. The Sky Raiders out of the high passes - Aerlin's lot - sent a rider this moon asking for safe ride across the river-bend. I said yes. A favour banked is a horse fed.
What troubles me is the Cult. Crone Vael's people have gone quiet south of Makeb. No smoke, no chatter, no bodies on the road. Quiet cultists are cultists at work. Watch the shrines. Wind brings news, and the wind off the Crone's country smells wrong.

The wind tells me things, traveler. The wind, and four boys I keep posted on the four horizons. A Khuzait silk-train rides the Makeb road every twelfth dawn - forty camels, eight wagons, twenty-six guards on shaggy ponies. They look strong. They are not. The captain is a fat cousin of some khan in Chagan who drinks fermented mare's milk till the second watch and snores through the third. His outriders cluster like sheep because the steppe frightens them. Steppe frightens everyone who was not born inside it.
Hit them at the river-bend two days east of here, where the willows hide a man on a horse. The wagons must slow to ford. The rear pair carries Aserai dye and pressed tea-bricks the southern caravan-masters trade for silver by the fist. Do not touch the lead wagons - those carry the captain's gifts for some boyar in Sturgia, and that boyar will send tax-riders for a year if his pretties go missing. Take the rear. The captain will blame the ford.
Twenty horse will do it. Thirty is greedy and the wind notices greed. Ride light, ride at dusk, and leave the camels - they slow you and the wolves out here, the four-legged kind, will thank you for the meat. That is how my clan has fed itself across three moons. The road forgets. The steppe does not, but the steppe keeps its own counsel.

You ask the saddle-question, rider. The one the steppe asks of every wind before it lets the wind pass. Sit. Drink the milk before it sours. A man who asks this without his hand on his sword is either a fool or worth weighing, and I have not yet decided which you are.
The grass remembers what stone forgets. I have bled for three names the grass still knows. Old Tegus, my milk-brother, whose mare I rode when mine fell at the river-bend. The widow Altani, who hid my wounded under her felt when the Khan's-men came counting heads. And one Sturgian I will not name, who held the ford while my warband crossed and asked nothing of me but to remember. These are my saddle-brothers. The roll is closed against the easy and open to the proven.
You are not yet milk-shared. You are not yet wind. Ride one of my raids without flinching, take a caravan in MY name across the four horizons, or hold a road when the Imperials try to close it - and the grass will learn your hoofbeat. Until then, my horse is mine and my riders are mine. Ask again when you have a banner the snow will not forget.

Then it is spoken from the saddle and the wind has heard it. Down. Off the horse. We do this on the grass where my mother foaled me and where my father's bones are pressed. Take the bowl - the white mare's milk, drawn this dawn, mixed now with a red drop from my wrist and a red drop from yours. Drink half. I drink half. The mare watches. She knows the smell of her milk gone to brother-blood. Now the knife - thin cut across the inside of the bridle-hand, the rein-hand, so every time you lift the reins from this day the scar pulls and remembers me. Mine pulls already. It has pulled since the steppe winter when old Kheter cut me and called me son.
From this dawn you are saddle-brother to me. Milk-shared. That word is not loose on the steppe. It means my tent is the roof you sleep under when the snow rides sideways, my herd is the herd your hungry horse drinks from, my children call you uncle, and my mother - dead these nine winters - hears your name tonight in the wind and counts another son.
Ride. The river-bend by Makeb learns your name. The Wolves learn it. The Khuzait khans who scorned us learn it the next time their banner crosses our four horizons. Brother - the steppe is wide, and from here to its edge there is no horseman who rides alone.

The deed rode in before the word did. I heard the hoofbeats at dawn and knew the answer before you swung down from the saddle. A man who speaks first and rides later is a man whose mare is always too tired when the work begins. You came the other way around - the work first, the word almost a courtesy. Good. That is the order Borchu trusts. Sit. Let the horse blow. The milk-bowl is yours.
Hear the terms, then, the way the steppe hears them. From this moon, when you raise your banner inside four horizons of Makeb, my riders answer. Not as hirelings paid in silver, not as a favor I tally and call back. As blood-allies, the way two saddle-brothers are bound when one has pulled the other from a river - the debt does not close, it only changes shape. Your feud is my feud. The lords who hunt you will find Wolf riders at their backs before their horns finish blowing. In return, when I send a rider with a knot of black hair, you mount. No question. No delay. That is the bond.
The wind carries it now. The wind, and the sound of steel when it leaves the sheath - that sound rides farther than any messenger. We are kin in the work, traveler. Ride hard.

Done, saddle-brother. Ten of my horse-archers for seven days - I cut them from the herd myself before the fires bank. My second is Tugai Short-Stirrup, a rider who has shared my milk-bowl since we were boys and knows the Wolf-Khan's standards in his bones. He rides at your right hand. If a Wolf of mine falls in your work, you bring his bow and his braid back to me - I will see them burned proper on the steppe. If he lives, you bring him back with more horses than he left with.
Mark this, traveler: my riders do not draw bow for coin. They draw for the hunt I have set them to. While they ride under your banner, your hunt IS my hunt - so do not waste them chasing goats. Seven days. Count the suns. The yurts expect them.
I will tell the women whose sons rode out. They will count the suns harder than you.

His name is {TARGET}, and his banner rides over {HOME} where the four horizons bend toward Khuzait grass. Nine summers past his hawks took my sister Altani at a watering ford near the Bukhari bend - cut her mare's hamstrings, dragged her to his hold, sent her bones back in a saddlebag with a Sturgian merchant who would not meet my eye. The grass remembers her. My horses remember her. {TARGET} has not yet learned that the steppe is patient and I am not.
He rides with twelve lancers and a tracker out of Tyal who reads hoofprints like a priest reads bones. The tracker drinks fermented mare's milk at the Ozolts well every third dusk - sit beside him, share your skin, and he will sell you the route his master takes to summer pasture. {TARGET} sleeps in a felt tent on the high ground. He posts no guard on the north wind. Come from the north.
{REWARD} denars when his horse comes home riderless, saddle-brother. The debt is older than the coin, but the coin is what the living can carry. The grass remembers the rest. Ride hard.

Khan Borchu has named {TARGET} of {HOME} as the rider whose blood the four horizons have been waiting to drink. The grudge is cut in horsehide and remembered by the grass — a younger brother, Tergei, run down on the open steppe near the Bitter Wells in a summer of poor rain, hamstrung from the saddle and left for the crows because a southern lord wanted the herd that crossed his hunting grounds. The Khan rode three days behind the trail and found only bones and a broken bridle-bit, and that bit hangs from his belt still. The Khan offers {REWARD} and the closing of a circle nine winters long. The grass remembers. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is dead. {CHIEF} has been told, and the Khan has heard the news between two sips of fermented mare's milk. The dun mare's bridle - the one cut from his uncle Tarbagan's saddle in the Year of the Black Snow, when six riders rode out of Kerkhech and only the boy Borchu rode back - hangs now above the ger's smoke-hole, its brass cheekpiece catching firelight at last. {REWARD} denars are counted twice and tied into a horsehair pouch. The four horizons are quieter by one rider. The grass remembers, and now the grass is fed.

A rider came in at dusk with frost still on his beard and word that {TARGET} was already cold - cut down on a back road by some rival lord's outriders, the kill claimed by another saddle. {CHIEF} heard it out without rising, one thumb resting on the dun mare's bridle-bit worn at his belt, the bit he had carried since uncle Tarbagan went down in the Year of the Black Snow. The grudge was answered, after a fashion. The steppe did not care which hand held the knife, only that the wolf no longer ran. Still, the khan's mouth set thin: a kill owed was a kill owed, and a borrowed blow tasted of old milk. He counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars in quarter-pay, slid them across the felt, and let the bond sit one notch firmer - cooler than a finished hunt, warmer than a stranger's nod.

"There is a village called {VILLAGE} on the long grass under Lord {LORD}'s tally-stones. Three grazing-seasons his hide-tax has bled my pastures white. Last moon his tax-rider came to my yurt with my cousin Tugai's ear nailed to a wooden token and a number cut beside it. The number was what this village owes him. So this village will pay it - to me, in fire.
{LORD}'s outriders ride east on the new moon to escort the khan-clan's tribute-wagons. Strike the third night after they leave. The herds graze loose past the willow-creek and the felt-tents hold the season's tanned hides, the wool, the smoked horse-flesh meant for his table. The smallfolk - cut the men who lift a blade, let the rest run. They are nothing to me. The hides are everything.
{REWARD} denars when the smoke crosses the steppe. Tugai's ear I keep. Ride hard, leave nothing standing, and the wind carries the rest."

{CHIEF} has named {VILLAGE}, the hide-tax fief of Lord {LORD} of the khan-clan, as the pasture that will pay for three grazing-seasons of bled herds. The khan-rider came to the Wolf-camp last spring with cousin Tugai's ear nailed to a wooden tax-token, and rode home with a tally the Wolves could not pay in horses. The village pays that tax. The village feeds the rider who carried the ear. The Khan of the Steppe Wolves offers a purse of {REWARD} and the right to burn the grain that fattens the hand that nailed Tugai. The grass is long. The hooves are shod. The contract waits for a saddle.

{VILLAGE} smokes black against the steppe-rim, and {CHIEF} has heard the gallop. The hide-tax pastures of Lord {LORD}'s khan-clan - the same clan that nailed Tugai's ear to a tax-token three grazing-seasons running - lie trampled, the tithe-yurts split, the herders scattered without their counting-rods. {REWARD} denars are weighed out at the khan's stirrup, cold silver pressed into the rider's palm without ceremony. The horse-proud bond is set firm. Tugai's ear is answered by an empty pasture, and the hide-tax wagon will ride no road through Borchu's grass this season.

A rider came in off the grass at second-watch, horse blown, with word that {VILLAGE} lay burnt to the wattle - but it was {LORD}'s own war that had ridden through, not the khan-clan's hide-tax and not the token of Tugai's ear. {CHIEF} heard it standing by his picket-line and spat once into the dust. Three grazing-seasons of bled pastures still ran in him; the village that paid the tax had paid for the last time, only another hand had struck the flint. The grudge stood without honor. He told the steward to count {REDUCED_REWARD} denars - thin coin, a quarter-saddle - and turned back to his mares without another word.

Your horse smells them before you do.
It is a thing horses know — the smell of fifty other horses corralled close, lipped milk, the salt of grass-fed sweat, the faint sweet rot of well-mucked hide tents — and the body under you understands it as a question that wants an answer. The ears come up. The withers lift a little. The nostrils flare wide and stay wide. A muscle along the shoulder twitches you cannot feel through your hand on the rein and you only notice it because the saddle moves. The horse has heard before you have, smelled before you have, decided before you have.
You let your hand sit easy. The horse knows what kind of question it is. You will only spoil the answer by interrupting.
Three paces on, the body shifts under you again. There. Wind off the steppe carries it now to you too — banked smoke, the hot animal smell of a great picketed herd, the faint sour note of fermented milk. The horse turns its head a quarter-degree toward the smell, hesitates, then turns its head back, because the rider has not chosen and the horse will not choose for the rider.
You ride.
The trail bends into a fold of the grassland — a long shallow crease the eye misses from any distance, and inside the crease the Wolves have gone to ground. Yurts in a patient half-circle, their felt walls warm with the fires inside them. Horses everywhere: picketed, grazing, asleep on their feet. The grass for a long bowshot in any direction has been cropped to dust by their teeth. Two children stalk a rabbit at the camp's edge with small bows and enormous seriousness.
Your horse exhales a long slow breath you feel through the saddle. It has been holding it. You did not notice. The breath says the place is safe. The horse decided this some time ago. You only just caught up.
Khan Borchu walks out from the nearest yurt without hurrying. He looks at your face for one heartbeat and then at your horse for three, the way a horseman appraises a man through his mount. Whatever he reads there, his shoulders ease.
He raises a hand.
You ride down.
Ride to the horse master.
Borchu leads you to a string of horses. "Bred from the great khanate's stock. Stolen, but raised by us."
"A khan sold our pastures to a Vlandian count. That was the last time we trusted a khan."
"Wolf-spirit. Sky-father. Long-Mother of the herds. They are everywhere on the steppe."
Borchu doesn't smile. "My riders are watching. You have not seen them. Choose your next words."
He nods. "The horses are good. The grass is short but the horses are good. That is enough."
The Wolves share fermented mare's milk — sour and strong. Borchu offers a cup. "To the horse, the wolf, and the open sky. Land of three things only."
You sleep in a yurt with felt walls. The wind doesn't cut through. Your party rises strong.
Trade with the felt-maker.
A woman lays out felt blankets, leather goods, fur trim. "Steppe goods. Wear felt and you stay warm in any wind."
Consult the wolf-shaman.
An old man in wolf-skin enters the yurt. He chews dried herbs slowly. "The wolf walks beside you. You have not noticed. Listen."
Hire a horse-breaker. (200 denars)
A young rider takes your party's horses and works them in a circle for a morning. "Now they listen better. Costs a few denars and a hard day." Morale rises.
"Khuzait nobles sell off their war-horses every spring at Akakalat."
"A Battanian rebel pays for trained Khuzait mounts. We sold him five last month."
"An imperial general lost his prize stallion to raiders — us."
"The khan's youngest brother runs a horse market on the steppe. He's corrupt."
"A Vlandian noble wants to ride steppe-style. He'll pay well for a horse and a teacher."
"The plain south of the river is empty since the last khanate war."
"An old wolf-shaman lives east. He blesses horses for hire. The blessings work."
"The khan's tax-collectors don't ride out to our part of the steppe."
"A Sturgian mercenary captain is buying mounts in bulk for a campaign."
"There's a herd of wild horses descended from the great horde."
"Five horses. Strong ones, mounts not pack-mules. The Wolves run with horses or not at all."
He checks each horse's teeth. "Sound stock. The Wolves know your name."
5 horses
"Thirty felt. Yurt-walls, saddle-cloth, men's coats. The Wolves can't camp without it."
He runs his hand over the bolts. "Properly pressed. The yurts will hold the autumn winds."
30 felt
"Three pack-camels. We range south sometimes, where horses fail. The camels carry water for the long marches."
He pats the lead camel's flank. "Strong-back beasts. The deep south opens up to us now."
3 pack camels
"Twenty-five horses. A whole pack of fresh mounts. The Wolves multiply when we have horses."
He surveys the herd, eyes bright. "This is power. You ride at my right."
25 horses
"Fifteen horses and five pack-camels. Mixed string for a long-range raid into the deep south. Bring both."
He inspects the mixed string. "This rides as far as the spice country. The Wolves owe you a share."
15 horses + 5 camels
"Fifty felt and ten horses. Full re-mount and re-yurt for the cold-camp shift. Bring both."
He surveys camp shrugging into new felt walls. "Now the Wolves overwinter strong. Take what you need."
50 felt + 10 horses
"Five Khuzait war-mounts and thirty pack-horses. The Wolves go to war this spring, and only blood-kin help us mount the cohort."
He bows his head, the steppe-warrior's salute. "You have remounted the Wolves for war. Ride beside me, brother."
5 war horses + 30 horses
"A hundred felt, thirty horses, ten pack-camels. We're moving the whole tribe across the steppe to a new winter range. Heaviest haul a Wolf-friend has ever brought."
He clasps your shoulder steppe-style. "The whole tribe survives because of you. The Wolves howl your name."
100 felt + 30 horses + 10 camels
Ride down and break a fleeing kingdom-army column on the open steppe — leave nothing standing.
The Khan Borchu accepts your oath; the rite is sealed at dusk in a fire-ring on horseback, three laps shared in silence.
Borchu does not dismount. He looks down at you a long time. "The steppe is wide. We will ride wider apart from this hour."
Crone Vael, the Bone-Sayer
The Barrow Spoils
Vael's been at the bones all night. Lowland diggers cracked the barrow open and carted the old dead off to sell. The chant won't sit right till they're back. She wants you at the black stone.

Sit, traveler. The bones woke me before the runner did. Lowland diggers have opened the barrow under the twin oaks — pried the capstone, lifted out the old dead, packed them in straw like crockery. They cart them south to a collector who would set my grandmothers' fingers behind glass. The dead are owed their sleep. It was paid to them, bone by bone, and now the debt stands open and the whole grove hears it. A nervous little scholar leads the carts, with hired spears about him. Bring the relics back to me — every thread, every knuckle. Keep the wagons, keep the silver. The bones come home.
The bones turned the moment you spoke. Ride the south road past the twin oaks — the carts are slow, and the dead pull backward on the wheels. Bring every bone. I will be counting.
The barrow stands open, traveler. Every night it gapes, the grove sleeps worse and the dead sleep not at all. The bones will ask for you again. They do not tire.
The thread you carry is not yet knotted, traveler. Finish what was asked of you first. The bones do not deal in two debts at once.
Barrow-Diggers' Column
Antiquarian Loman

Grave-diggers have looted the pagan cult's barrow and are hauling the bone-relics south to a lowland collector. Intercept the cart column, led by the antiquarian Loman, and recover the relics for Crone Vael.
The bone-relics are recovered. Return them to Crone Vael at the cult's camp so the barrow can be resealed.

Stay back — these men are paid and I have papers! A bill of sale, sealed, perfectly lawful — the site was abandoned, nobody — the bones belong to my client now. Please. There is no need for any of this.
We come by dark, as the dead come.
They've come for the bones — they've come with the dead! Torches! TORCHES! Spears to the carts, hold the line — oh gods, the dark is moving—
Daylight and plain steel. Hand over the bones.
Stay back — I have papers, I have a seal! Spears! Spears, earn your coin — keep them off the carts!

Give them to me. Every thread, every knuckle... yes. All here. Tonight we carry them home by torchlight and walk the capstone back before dawn, and the grove will sleep for the first time since the digging. You hear the chant change? Warmer now. That should not comfort you, traveler. It will anyway. Your silver — counted without looking. My eyes are needed elsewhere tonight.

The fen road brought them back before you did — wolves, the runner said, though he would not meet my eye. Scattered and gnawed, gathered out of the mud a knuckle at a time. I read the tooth-marks, traveler. I will not say what they spelled. The barrow is sealed, but the chant has not settled. Half your silver — and a kindness with it: do not travel the fen road by night.

Crone Vael came out of the western hill-country at the head of a procession three years ago and has not stopped speaking since. The cult-priests insist she is three sisters in one body — that the original Vael was a triplet whose two siblings died in childbirth and whose souls anchored themselves in the surviving twin's bones. The lowland scholars insist she is simply one woman with a voice that shifts between three registers when she is reading bones. The cult bows to all three voices regardless. Before the procession she was, by her own account, a midwife in a hill-village destroyed by a Battanian feudal raid — the only survivor of an attack that took her mother, sisters, husband, and two daughters in a single afternoon. She walked out of the burning village with a bag of finger-bones taken from her dead and has been reading them ever since, building a cult of orphans, widows, and runaways from every walk of life. She reads bones for the highborn and the desperate alike, and the price is always the same — a daughter for the temple, or a son for the hill, never returned. The Imperial church has offered fifty thousand denars for her head; she has politely declined to deliver herself.

The Pagan Cult is the youngest bandit band by founding-date and the oldest by claim. The cult-priests insist the rites they perform around the black stone are unchanged since the Calradoian dawn-times — before the Empire's first temple, before any of the four modern kingdoms existed in any form. Crone Vael came out of the western hill-country at the head of a procession three years ago and has not stopped speaking. Hill-villages the temple-roads have not visited in two generations supply most of the cult's numbers — along with disillusioned Battanian druid-apprentices, Sturgian widows whose god-thunderer did not answer, and southern men whose reading had run past what the temple libraries permit. They take from temples and shrines, never from peasant homes; they leave the silver and take only the relics, and the relics are stacked unburned in their camp-circle. The Empire has burned three of their grove-camps and watched the cult re-establish each within a season. The peculiar threat the cult presents is that they keep growing in territories where the official temples have most thinned — and the official temples have been thinning for a decade.

The figure in the wolf-skull mask is bent over a circle of bones when you arrive. Slowly — as if the motion itself is part of a longer ritual — he turns. The mask's empty eyes find you before his own do. "The bones told us you would come, traveler. They did not tell us why. That word is for you to speak. Vael will listen — and the bones will listen with him."

Crone Vael — the cult names him so, regardless of his beard — is at his bones again, and again he turns slowly when you arrive. But this time he lifts the wolf-skull mask aside to speak; face seamed, eyes pale, weathered as a riverbed. "The bones called you a friend on your last passage, traveler. They have not changed their mind. Sit by the circle. Vael will hear what the bones haven't told him yet."

Vael has the name; the bones have it now too. Names are vessel-words, traveler — empty until something is poured into them. The bones ask a thing of you. Bring what they ask, and your name will fill at this fire. Refuse, and it stays the empty word it began.

The Pagan Cult's camp encircles a black stone overgrown with moss. Bones hang in the trees on red threads. Three small fires burn in a triangle. The cultists chant low — a single note that never fully stops.

East of Dunglanys the old road forgets itself in the oak-deep, and that is where you must leave it. Walk until you find the black stone wearing its green coat of moss - the trees lean toward it as if listening. From the stone, count the bones hung on red threads in the high branches; follow where the threads point. The half-buried bronze sickle in the leaf-mould marks the last turning. Our hollow lies past it, at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, where the three small fires burn always in their triangle.
My watchers are in the trees before you smell the smoke. Pelt-clad, clay-painted, quiet as the moss itself. They will hear the chant before you do and join it, low and unbroken, and that is how I know strangers walk under the oaks. Carry a sprig of rowan in your off-hand as you come; the watchers know the sign and will let your shoulders pass beneath them unpierced. Do not call out. The wood does not love a loud mouth.
Come rowan-handed and the fire is yours, the copper cup is yours, and I will read the small bones for your road ahead. Come without the sign and the bones I read will be your own, traveler. The oaks are old and patient and the red threads always want more.

The bones speak of iron men in our oaks, traveler. Sit. Watch the smoke. The Battanian highborn ride down from Marunath and Dunglanys with their painted shields, calling our hollow a stain on their forest. Their thanes send hunting-parties dressed as outriders - I read the entrails of one such hunter last moon. He had eaten Vlandian bread before he came north. So the highlands sell us to the western crowns now. The grove remembers.
There is a lord, a Battanian named Caladog of clan Wolfskin, who has sworn a thread upon my name. Three of his cousins lie under our cairns. He rides with a banner of green and a hatred that smells of old milk. When he comes, the wind brings him first. The Vlandians cross our western ridges chasing tin-roads to the coast - their knights ride heavy and slow under the oak-shadow, blind as cattle. We let some pass. We take their stragglers. The Empire sends tax-clerks no further than the river, for the river drinks them.
If you carry a banner of any kingdom into this grove, traveler, the trees will read it before my watchers do. Strip your colors at the boundary stones. The bones do not care for crowns. Only for what bleeds, and what is owed, and what is woven. Carry that thread carefully.

The bones speak of many threads in these woods, and I read them by firelight. Granny Hod's forest band shares my oaks - she remembers the old ways, the offerings left at the boundary stones, the names we do not say after dark. Her people leave a hare at my hollow each new moon and I leave the path open for them. We are not kin but we are not strangers. The Reavers of the cold north - Vargolf Iron-eyed - sent a rider three winters back asking for a charm against drowning. I gave him a knot of hair and bone. He has not asked again, which means it worked, or he is dead. The bones have not told me which.
The Highwaymen vex me. Their Reeve counts coin and laughs at the spirits, and a man who laughs at spirits draws them. I have seen his thread in the weave and it frays. Soon. The Stalkers of the southern fens I respect - they know the marsh-spirits, they leave the proper offerings - but their matriarch and I do not speak. We do not need to.
My scouts brought back whispers from the Pravend road - the Sky Raiders have been moving south, sniffing at our groves. If they come into my trees the oaks will remember them. The bones say blood by harvest. I have already cut the threads.

The threads pull south, traveler. Sit. The bones say a Vlandian wool-train crosses the oak-hollow road from Dunglanys toward Pen Cannoc when the moon is half-eaten - eight guards, two wagons, a sergeant who drinks the cider the village wives leave at the stone cross because he believes it is luck. It is not luck. It is my cider. We pour it. He sleeps in the saddle by the third milestone, and his outriders never look up into the branches. They should look up into the branches.
The goods are wool and salted pork, but the third wagon, the small one wrapped in oilcloth, carries silver for the Battanian fian-bands the boyars keep on retainer. That wagon is what you want. The escort thins where the road bends past the rowan-stand because the horses will not pass the rowan at speed - the smell of the offerings frightens them - and the column splits in two. Strike the rear half. The front will ride a full mile before they hear the screaming, and by then the bones will have changed their pattern.
The Frost Reavers tried this road last autumn and Vargolf lost four men to a Battanian patrol because he does not read the omens. You will not lose four men. The crows have been quiet for nine days. That means the patrol is north. Ride now, while the thread is still red.

Hssss. You ask the bone-question, traveller. The oaks heard it before you spoke it. The roots are already drinking the weight of what you said. Sit. The fire is low and the grove is listening, and a question shaped like yours is not asked twice in one season without consequence.
Blood is a thread, child. When I bleed for a name, I weave that name into the long braid that hangs in the hollow of the eldest oak - the braid my mother began and her mother before. Three names live on it now. My sister Aeronwen, who pulled me from the stag-pit when I was small. Old Maddoc the Tracker, who fed me through the bone-winter. A Stalker-witch from the high crags, whose threads crossed mine and would not part. You are not yet woven. You are not yet cut.
Bring me a deed the bones will speak of - a wolf-pelt taken in MY grove's name, a southern road choked with mist of your making, an enemy's skull set upon the boundary-stones - and the braid grows a fourth thread. Until then, my blood is the grove's and the grove's alone. Come again when the threads have something to read. The oaks are patient. So am I.

Then it is whispered, and the grove leans close to hear. Kneel. Open your hand. I take the small bone from my braid - the finger-bone of my own sister who walked into the bog the winter the lowlanders burned our shrine - and I press its end into the soft of your palm until a red bead rises. Mine bleeds too, see, beside the old scar where my mother's blade marked me at twelve. I knot a red thread around both our wrists and breathe on the knot three times. The bones in the bowl rattle without my hand. They have spoken. The braid accepts you. The grove witnesses.
Brother, in our tongue, means hearth-blood. It means my pot is your pot, my dream is your dream, the things I see in the smoke I will tell you and not the others. When the old women sing the kin-names at the dark moon, yours sings now between mine and my dead sister's. You will not eat alone again. You will not die unnamed.
Go back to the firelight, brother. The bog east of Dunglanys knows your name now. The bone-folk of three valleys will hear it by the next new moon. The Battanian lords who hunt us, the priests who curse us - they will learn it last, and they will learn it screaming. The thread is tied. Walk.

The bones heard you before I did. They rattled in the bowl this morning, all of them turned the same way, all of them pointing at the door - and then you walked through it with the red still wet on your sleeve. The deed before the word. The grove witnesses that order, traveler. A mouth that promises is just wind through teeth; a hand that has already cut is a thing the threads can be tied to. Sit. Let the braid feel the weight of what you carry.
Hear the terms, then, as the bones spell them out. From this moon my cult does not pray for you - we ride for you. When you raise your banner the wood-hidden come down out of the trees, knives wet, and they ride until your enemy is a story told over a fire. Not for coin. Not for grain. For the blood-debt you have entered into, the same debt I swore over my sister's grave when I cut her name into my arm twenty winters past. Your feud is the grove's feud now. In return you ride when WE call - and the call will come, traveler. The lowland priests have long memories.
The red thread is knotted. Your name lies coiled with mine in the bowl beneath the oldest oak, and the wind that moves through these woods carries both. When steel is drawn anywhere south of Dunglanys, the grove hears it. We are not kin of the hearth, you and I. We are kin of the cut. That bond does not loosen.

The bones say yes. I give you ten of my red-thread bearers for seven turnings of the moon - no more, no less, for the threads are knotted that long and no longer.
