My second is Hesska Twice-Burned, who reads the smoke as I read the bone. She walks at the front of them. She will not speak much to you, traveler, but she will not need to. The wood-hidden know her hand on their shoulder.
Hear my terms. If one of mine falls in your work, you bring me his red thread - cut from his wrist, no more is needed - and I will tie it to the rafters where the others can see. If he lives, you send him back with his thread still on him and the smell of your fire in his hair. My pelt-clad do not bleed for trinkets. Seven days. Count them on your knuckles.
The bones will be told who rode. The bones will be told who came home.

His name is {TARGET}. The grove has whispered it for nine summers, traveler, ever since his riders came through the hollow oaks at {HOME}'s northern edge and cut down my sister Iska where she knelt at the offering stone. They burned her red threads. They scattered the finger-bones I had braided for her wedding-walk. {TARGET} watched from his saddle and laughed, and the bones I cast that night spelled his name three times in the ash.
He travels the old salt-road every dark moon to count tribute, and his cousin the priest rides at his right hand. The cousin is afraid of crows, traveler - drive a flock at them on the gorge bend past Kalka ford and the column will scatter. {TARGET} keeps a thin guard at the rear. He thinks no one would dare strike a marked man on a holy road.
{REWARD} denars sit in the burial jar beneath my cot, counted out for nine summers. The bones already saw you come. Ride, and the braid will know when his breath stops.

{CHIEF} has cast the bones over {TARGET} of {HOME}, and the throw came up red on every side. The witch-mother does not speak the grievance plainly — she circles it in the way of grove-folk, in the way of those who count years by braid-knots and not by harvests. Seven summers past, a daughter of the cult was taken from the alder-grove on a grey dawn and hung from a roadside oak with her sacred braid cut and burnt at the root, and the order came down the line from {TARGET}'s hall. The Bone-Sayer kept the burnt braid in a clay jar; the grove kept the rest. A heavy purse waits, and a red thread already cut to the length of {TARGET}'s throat. The grove is owed a death. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is dead. Crone Vael has been told, and the grove has been told, and the bones in the chief's lap have been told. The red thread that bore the noble's name - knotted nine winters ago for Little Mireh, the apprentice-girl drowned in the stocks at {HOME} - has been cut from the braid and laid in the ash-pit. {REWARD} denars sit at the Bone-Sayer's fire, counted out in coppers and silvers, and a fresh notch has been carved beside the child's old finger-bone. The grove witnessed. The braid is shorter by one name, and Vael says the wind moves cleaner through it tonight.

A bone-runner came to the cult-camp at dusk with mud on his shins and the news already half-chewed: {TARGET} had been cut down on a winter road by some rival lord's outriders, robbed and left for the crows before {CHIEF} could ever set her hook. The Bone-Sayer received the word in the smoke of the apprentice-shrine, where Mireh's red-thread braid still hangs above the clay jar of burnt cord. She turned the braid once in her fingers, whispering that the drowning-girl's debt was paid, yes, but not by the hand she had chosen. The grudge is closed; the bond is cooler. She counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars of thin quarter-pay into the player's palm and set the tally one small notch firmer, no warmer.

"The bones name a village. {VILLAGE}, they whisper, on the lowland edge where the Battanian woods thin to tithe-fields. Lord {LORD} holds it, and his hand is the same hand that signed the warrant three summers past - the warrant that loosed the inquisitors of his lowland priests upon Aelwyn's apprentice-grove. They burned the saplings. They burned the girls who tended them. The ash of that grove is still in my hair, child. The bones have not forgotten.
{VILLAGE} tithes oil and grain to those same priests on the dark moon. The wagons are sealed three nights before, and {LORD}'s outriders escort them to the keep on the dark moon itself - so strike between, when the casks sit waiting and the riders are gone. Take the oil. Burn the grain. The smallfolk... let them run. They are not the ones who lit the pyre. The priests are.
{REWARD} denars when the smoke rises and the oil-jars are spilled. The bog drinks the rest. Go now - the bones grow restless."

{CHIEF} has named {VILLAGE}, the oil-and-grain tributary of Lord {LORD}'s Battanian fief, as the hearth whose ashes will answer for the apprentice-grove of Aelwyn, burned three summers past by lowland priests this fief still tithes and shelters. The Bone-Sayer's bowl has shown the same omen at every cold moon since: charred saplings, a girl's bone-comb buried under hearthstones, smoke that does not rise. The villagers feed the inquisitors who fed the pyre. Their oil greases the censers; their grain feeds the chant. The Crone offers {REWARD} from the grove-hoard and the closing of a debt the roots themselves have whispered. The contract is bone-marked. The grove remembers.

{VILLAGE} smokes black, and {CHIEF} has read the bones of it. The tithe-village of Lord {LORD} - whose lowland priests put the apprentice-grove of Aelwyn to the torch three summers past - lies open-throated under the dawn, its oil-jars cracked, its grain-cribs ash, the chant-wagons that bore tribute to the burning-priests now silent in the cart-ruts. {REWARD} denars sit counted at the bone-altar where the Crone whispers tally to the dead. One debt of Aelwyn has been answered. The smoke goes up to her, and the grove remembers. The bones know one name fewer to weep.

Word came whispering down the bone-wind at moonset: {VILLAGE} stood ash and silence, its tithe-barns split, its oil-jars cracked - but the hand that struck was not the wanderer's. A rival lord's column had ridden through on a quarrel of borders, and the priests' own grain had gone up in smoke without the wanderer's torch to light it. {CHIEF} listened with her ear-bones cupped, and the apprentice-grove of Aelwyn stirred no answer in her marrow. The three-summer debt was paid - by another's blade. The smoke rose true, the ash fell right, but the bones had not been thrown by the wanderer's casting. She counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars from the rattle-pouch, thin coin for a thin reckoning, and named the bond cold-warm, no closer than a fox at the treeline.

First the fire is named. Then the bone is named. Then the breath is named. The names are not said in daylight.
You hear it from a quarter-mile out — a low single note carried through the wet black trees, held longer than any throat should be able to hold a note, and then taken up unbroken by another throat, and another, so that the sound does not end. A river of voices, all in one place, all on one tone.
First the fire is named.
You stop your horse. Smoke moves between the trunks — pale, deliberate, climbing.
Then the bone is named.
Bones hang in the trees on red thread. Small ones — finger-bones, bird-bones, the jawbone of a fox. Where the smoke crosses them they turn, and the turning makes a dry knocking sound, and the knocking is part of the music.
Then the breath is named.
Your horse will not have its head. You let it stand. There is a clearing ahead through the black trunks where three small fires burn in a triangle, and figures move between them slow, and at the centre stands a black stone furred with moss, and the chant comes from the dark between the fires, never breaking, never quite the same note from one breath to the next but always returning to it.
The names are not said in daylight.
You did not know the rest of the verse and yet you find that you do know it, the way a person knows the next line of a song heard once in childhood, the way a hand knows the shape of a thing it has never been told. You are leaning forward in the saddle. You did not choose to lean.
The chant takes a long held breath together.
It releases together.
In the silence that follows, an old woman at the nearest fire raises her head and looks straight at you through the trees. She has been waiting for you to arrive at this particular point in the verse. She has been waiting some time.
She lifts one hand. The chant resumes around her, lower now, courteous, the way a room lowers its voices for a guest.
You ride forward.
Consult the Oracle of bones.
Crone Vael casts knucklebones onto the black stone. They land in a pattern. She studies them for a long time.
"A king's god is paper and crowns. Our gods drink blood and grant courage. The bargain is clearer."
"The Old Ones. Names not to be said in daylight. The grove remembers them."
The mask turns toward you. The mask does not blink. "The bones already showed me how you die. It is not by my hand. But it is soon."
Crone Vael's voice does not change. "The grove is older than you. It will accept your praise or your bones. Either is welcome."
The cultists pass around a cup of dark wine, thick with herbs. "Drink. The Old Ones approve of those who drink. The Old Ones forget those who refuse."
You sleep at the edge of the grove, the chanting never quite stopping. Strange dreams. Your party wakes uneasy, but rested.
Trade with the bone-carver.
A silent man at a stump carves with steady hands — combs, charms, knife-handles, all from old bone. "Cheap because the dead don't charge. Useful because the dead remember."
Receive the grove-healer's blessing. (100 denars)
A young initiate paints a sigil on each soldier's arm with red ochre. The chanting rises to match. "You walk with the grove for a moon. The grove walks with you." Morale rises.
Take part in the old rite. (50 denars)
A simple ceremony. Crone Vael cuts your palm. A drop of blood on the stone. The chant pauses, then resumes. You feel the grove's regard.
"The temple at Marunath is hunting us. Their inquisitors pay informers."
"A young noblewoman comes to our grove in secret to leave offerings."
"The old gods are returning. The bones say so. We don't argue with the bones."
"A heretic priest fled imperial justice and joined our circle."
"There's a buried shrine in the forest — older than the empire. We dug it up."
"The grove-fires never go out. They've been burning a hundred years."
"A relic of the old kings is hidden under the black stone."
"Imperial soldiers tried to burn our grove three winters back. Two came out alive. Both stayed."
"A rival cult worships the new gods in twisted form."
"The bone-sayer dreams the future every full moon."
"You will find what you seek, but the cost will surprise you."
"A friend will betray you before the next full moon."
"Death stands at your right shoulder. Walk left."
"The kingdom you serve will fall."
"There is gold in stone in the eastern hills. The stone watches."
"A child not yet born will write your name in a song."
"The path you walk forks soon. Both ends are the same. The middle is not."
"Trust the woman in red. Do not trust the man in green."
"A king will die in winter."
"The river you crossed yesterday was not a river."
"You are owed a debt by someone you have forgotten."
"Do not draw your blade in the city of three towers."
"A storm is coming. The storm has your name in it."
"The horse you ride was never meant for war."
"The greatest treasure of your life is a thing you already own."
"A wound you took years ago will reopen."
"The empire is dying. So is the kingdom."
"Beware the merchant who calls you brother on first meeting."
"The bones say: bury what you kill."
"Three offers of love will come to you. Refuse the first two."
"Twenty fish. The old gods feast at our spring rite. Bring it, and the gods will know your name."
The chief blesses each bundle. "The old ones are pleased. You have a place at the firepit."
20 fish
"Fifteen weight of meat. Blood-rite. The fen-mother takes flesh for spring and gives green growth in return."
The chief lays the meat on a stone altar. "The fen-mother smiles tonight. Her children welcome you."
15 meat
"Twenty beer for the libation. The thunder-spirit drinks first, then the men. Bring it."
The chief pours a horn into the fire — flames leap green. "The spirit drinks. The cult opens to you."
20 beer
"Thirty fish and ten wine. High feast. The old ones eat and drink — bring both."
The cult chants as the offering is accepted. "The gods are pleased. Even the oracle will speak with you."
30 fish + 10 wine
"Twenty-five meat and twenty beer. The midsummer-flesh feast. The fen-mother eats first — bring both."
Drum-rhythm rises from the inner circle. "The fen-mother's children embrace you. The cult is yours."
25 meat + 20 beer
"Forty fish and fifteen oil. The lamp-fast night. We burn through dawn for the dark mother — bring both."
The cult lights the dawn-lamps in long rows. "The dark mother sees you in firelight. Speak to the oracle."
40 fish + 15 oil
"Fifty fish, thirty meat, twenty wine, ten silk-cloth for the altar drape. The full rite. Once a generation. Only one who walks with the gods can bring this."
The chief draws a sigil on your forehead in ash. "You are kin to the fen-mother now. The cult bleeds for you."
50 fish + 30 meat + 20 wine + 10 velvet
"A hundred fish and fifty wine. The sky-feast. The thunder-one drinks deep before he wakes the storms. Bring both."
Lightning cracks somewhere distant. The chief smiles. "He is awake. The cult rides his storm with you."
100 fish + 50 wine
Bring a captured noble of the culture-region to the old stones — they must reach the altar alive and bound.
The Crone Vael, the Bone-Sayer accepts your oath; the rite is sealed at the cult altar in cast bones, your fate read in the marrow spilled.
The Crone does not look at you. She gathers her bones, sweeps them once, lets them fall. "The pattern is closed. Walk past the stones."
Boll the Eldest
The Ditch-Folk's Coin
You. Boll wants you. Taxmen went down the ditch-road and shook out the families what feed us. Old man's been sat staring at the fire since. He don't stare like that for nothing. Go on.

Sit, friend. Old Boll will keep this short. There's a wagon on the road — the lord's levy, coin squeezed out of the ditch-families between here and the burnt mill. You know them, maybe. I grew up in those ditches. Those families feed my people scraps when there's scraps, and news when there's not. Now their coin rides south under guard, with a collector on top who yawned while he took it. Take it back, friend. All of it. Don't bargain with the man — Boll has watched collectors his whole life, and they only count. Make the counting stop.

Good. The wagon's slow — coin is heavy, friend, heavier than grain. The escort will fight for it; they're paid to. Mind yourself. And count it before you leave the road. Collectors skim. It's what they're for.
As you like, friend. The road doesn't hurry and neither does old Boll. But the ditch-families gave their last coin, and winter doesn't take promises. Ask me again while the wagon's still close.
The wagon's still rolling, friend. Every mile it makes is a mile of coin the ditches won't see again. Go slow if you must. Just go.
Lord's Levy Wagon
Levy Collector Phanes
Find the Lord's Levy Wagon on the roads near Boll's camp, defeat its escort, and recover the coin taken from the roadside families.
Return to Boll the Eldest and tell him the levy coin has been taken back.

Off the road. This is his lordship's quarter-levy — counted, sealed, and duller than you can imagine. Nine years I've hauled boxes like this one. Rob us or move, but do decide. I'd like to be bored somewhere warm by dark.
Hand the coin back, or bleed for it.
Back? Coin doesn't go back. It goes up — ditch to lord, lord to crown. That's the whole of the world, and you want it reversed on a road. Escort, level. Kill them quickly, I'm losing the light.

The coin went back, friend. I walked it myself, ditch to ditch, and put it in their hands. No speeches. You don't make a speech at people who are hungry — I remember being hungry, and a speech is just a man keeping bread in his mouth longer. They fed us before they had to. Now they eat. Sit. There's stew tonight, with something in it for once. You did that.

Some other band got to the wagon first, friend. Drank half the coin in two nights — I heard it from a tinker who watched them do it. The rest is already trickling into the ditches, the way loose coin does. It finds the poor going down the same as it found the lord going up. So. Half a job done by nobody we know. Half thanks, half pay. Sit anyway. The fire's the same price.

Boll lived in the same Imperial peasant village his whole life — eighty-two years according to the priest's tally, though Boll himself stopped counting at sixty. He raised four sons there, buried two of them at the village shrine, and saw the third leave for the Imperial legions never to return. The village was burned in the autumn of the third year of the imperial succession war — not by enemies but by the local lord's tax-collectors, who decided to make an example of a community that could not pay its levy. Boll was buried under his own collapsed roof when the soldiers came; they assumed he had burned alive and moved on without checking. He dug himself out the next morning with a shovel he had been using for forty years, and walked through the ash looking for survivors. There were none; or rather, there were only the others who had been buried, who came up later from cellars and hayricks. Boll is the oldest peasant left in the region, and the Looters formed around him by accident — fifty starving survivors of fifteen burned villages, each looking for someone who knew where to dig. He leads the Looters because no one younger is left who remembers when there was anything else.

The Starving Outcasts are not a band in the way the others are bands. They have no founding-feast, no oath-fire, no chief-line; Boll holds them together because he is eighty-two and has not yet forgotten what the lords have stopped mentioning. The column began the day Boll's village burned in the second imperial reorganization, when the conscription quotas tripled and the granary-tax was renewed in the same season; the survivors walked east, and walked, and walked, and never quite stopped. They have grown by accretion since — every village burned, every harvest seized, every conscript-train that lost half its men to desertion in the same week added another handful to the wandering column. The Outcasts have no signature raid because they cannot raid: they ambush stragglers, dig in granary-pits at night, gnaw bark in winter, and bury their dead in rows beside whatever road they happened to be on. Every kingdom counts them as bandits and none has taken a serious patrol against them in living memory; the recognition would require an admission about why so many peasant villages have burned in the same generation.

A scrawny man peers up at you from beside a thin fire. His hands shake. The knife in them — chipped, half-rusted — shakes too. He stares at your armor a long moment, like a man trying to remember what hope ever felt like. "You... you look armored, friend. Big armored. Old Boll doesn't want trouble. Just bread, and to be left alive at the end of it. Got any to spare a tired man?"

Boll's hands shake less when he sees you now. He still doesn't stand, but the chipped knife stays in its sheath, and a place at the thin fire is made without him asking the others. "You... you came back. Most don't. Old Boll thanks you for the bread last time, traveler. Sit. Not much to give a friend, but what we've got, you've got."

Boll has the name, friend. Name's nothing here — old Boll has heard a thousand and buried more. What we trade in is bread and what's done for it. There's a thing my men want from a strong walker like you. Help us, and I'll know your name's a friend's name. Won't be much trade after — but it'll be honest.
Hardly a camp — just a wind-break of branches and a smoldering fire. A handful of skinny men in stolen rags, eyes hollow.

You want the road to us? There is no road. Walk out past the last village that still has a name, keep walking until the goat-tracks give up and the scrub turns to rubble. When you see a wind-break of branches piled crooked against the stones, and an ash-pit still smoking from last night - you are close. There is a hide stretched to dry on a frame of bent sticks. That is our flag. Our hold lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, if you can call it a hold.
My boys will see you before you see them. They are skinny, they are hungry, they have nothing to lose and they know every gully for a mile. Walk slow. Keep your hands where the light catches them. If you have bread in your saddlebag, hold a piece up high - that is the only sign that has ever meant peace out here. Anything else and they will think you are tax-men or worse.
Come wrong and they will swarm you for your boots and leave the rest for the crows. Come right and we will share what we have, which is not much - a place by the fire that wont catch, a cracked pot of something thin, and the company of men the world forgot. That is all I can offer you, traveler. It is more than anyone else gave us.

Lords. Lords don't ride out here, friend. Not for us. We're not worth the iron on their boots. The big banners - the Empire, the Sturgians, the Vlandians - they pass each other on the high roads and they don't even look down into the rubble where we sleep. That's the worst of it. To be hated would be something. To be hunted would be something. We are only stepped over.
But their levies come. Oh, their levies come. When some boyar or some petty count needs to count heads for his muster, he sends his sergeants out to sweep the ditches and the burnt villages, and they take whoever can stand. Two of mine taken last moon by a column out of an Imperial garrison - I don't know which one, they all wear the same purple to my eyes. They were dragged off to die in someone else's war. We did not get them back. We never get them back.
The tax-riders are the other ones. Vlandian usually, in this stretch. They ride in pairs with crossbows and they shoot at us for sport on their way home from the real villages. I tell my people - hide, do not throw stones, hide. We have no quarrel the lords would honor. We only have hunger, and hunger does not make a feud. It only makes a grave.

Clans. Yes. Clans. We are not a clan. We are what is left when clans are done with you. But I know names. I know who throws scraps and who throws stones. Granny Hod's forest band - the old woman in the green dark - she lets my people pass if we bring her a knife or a tooth or a child that can still work. I send what I can. She has not killed us yet. That is a kindness in this country.
Skarvac's pass-lords up in the rocks, they hunt us for sport when the snow comes. They wear our skins on their saddles. I do not speak that name twice in a night. And the Reavers - Vargolf's Reavers - one of his outriders rode through our camp last spring, took two of my boys for his column, left a copper coin in the ash. A copper coin. Like we were paid. Like we agreed.
The Stalkers in the fens, the Mireborn ones, they trade with us sometimes. Rot-meat for arrowheads. Fair, by the standards of the road. The Highwaymen will not look at us. We are below their counting. That is fine. Being unseen is being alive. The bandit-tongue says the Sky Raiders have gone quiet in the high country this moon. Quiet is bad. Quiet means someone is sharpening. Watch the ridgelines, friend. Watch them.

Caravans. Yes. We watch them. From the rubble. From the ditches. The big ones do not stop here - nothing to stop for, no inn, no well, no walls. That is why they come slow through the scrub. They feel safe. Twelve guards, sometimes fifteen, one wagon of grain and one of cheap wool bound for the empire towns. We do not take them. We cannot. My boys have sticks and hunger, traveler, not swords.
But. Listen. There is a smaller one. Two wagons. Four guards. A fat merchant from Pravend who cuts across the dead country to skip the toll-road. He comes when the moon is new - dark roads, no witnesses, that is his thinking. Three nights from now, maybe four. He carries salt and iron nails. Not silver. Salt. To us that is silver. The guards drink at the last village before they cross. By the second hill they are slow. By the rubble-field they are blind.
If you take him, leave us the salt. Take the nails, take the wagon, take the merchant's purse. Just the salt. My children have not tasted salt since the snow broke. The Highwaymen up the Reeve's road would not bother with him - too small, too poor. That is why he lives. That is why he is yours. Ride at dusk. Come from the south. He never looks south because there is nothing south but us, and he does not believe in us.

You ask the hunger-question, friend. The road-question. I hear it. I have heard it before, in dry mouths around dry fires, and I know what it costs the asking. Sit. Eat the half I have. We will weigh it together, because a man with nothing weighs careful, or he loses what little is left.
What I would give you is not iron and it is not gold. I have neither. What I would give is the last bite, the last watch, the last breath kept back from the cold for your sake. I have given it before. To my woman, who is in the ground. To the boy Anse, who walked out one winter and did not walk back. To old Crook-Mouth, who shared his cloak the night the south burned us out. That is my roll. It is a short roll and a hungry one.
Bring me something the road remembers. A wagon turned aside from a village that had nothing left to lose. A pursuer cold in a ditch. A winter survived together. Do that, and the cloak becomes ours. Until then the fire is shared, but the bone is still mine. Ask me again when we have buried someone side by side.

Then... then say it slow again so the rocks hear. Brother. Sit. Sit on the rag where I sit. There is no horn here, no mead, no beam to cut your name into - there is a tin cup with rain in it and a knife that has cut more bread than throats, and that is what we have. Drink. Drink it down. Now the knife. My palm already knows this work - see the old white line, that is from a boy who called me father in a ditch outside Pravend and bled out before sunrise - I gave him my cut then and I give you my cut now. Press. Press hard. The dirt drinks it. The dirt remembers what beams forget.
Brother. Brother means you eat before I eat. Brother means the last bite is split, not taken. Brother means when the watch is long and my eyes go, yours stay open, and when yours go, mine stay. We have no cousins, you and I - we have the ones still breathing at this fire, and now they are yours too. The wretches call me Outcast-Father. They will call you Outcast-Son. That is the only roll we keep.
From this rubble forward you are my blood. The road knows. The crows over Zeonica know. The lords who hanged my first boy will know when they see your face beside mine. Brother - we have nothing, and now we have nothing together, and that is everything.

Then I have heard it. You did not come with a speech. You came with the smell of someone else's blood still on you, and the word after - almost forgot to say it. That is the order an old man trusts. Boll has heard pretty oaths from boys with clean knives. They did not last the winter. Yours came knife-first. Sit. Let the iron in what you did go cold before we speak the rest.
From this watch onward, the scraps that answer to me answer to your banner when you raise it. Not as hired hands - we have nothing to be hired for. As blood-allies in the only currency we still hold, which is the next bite and the last watch. My men will share your road. Your enemies become ours, and we have no lords above us to call us back. In return I ask only this - when the levies come for us, as they always come, you raise that banner and you ride. That is the trade. Bread for bread. Wound for wound.
The wind carries it now. No hall to hear it, no priest to seal it - only the scrub and the rubble, and that is enough for men like us. The road is long. The south is loud. We are bound in the work, traveler, and the work does not forgive turning back. Ride hard.

Done. Ten of the wretches - what is left of us that can still lift a blade - for seven days. I will pick them at dusk, the ones whose cough is quiet enough to walk a road. My second is Old Pell, who lost his name in a winter I will not speak of. He is half a man but worth two of the boys. He rides with you, and he counts the days for me.
Hear my terms, traveler. If one of the wretches falls in your work, you scrape his bones into the dirt and you SAY HIS NAME aloud before you leave him. That is all I ask. If he lives, you put bread in his mouth before you put bread in your own. My boys do not break shield for coin - we have no coin, we have no shield. They break because I told them to follow. Do not waste them on dogs and tax-men. Seven days. Count them slow.
When the seven are spent, send what comes back to the hollow. I will be sitting where I sit. I will know their faces, even the ones the crows have taken.

His name is {TARGET}. He sits warm under {HOME} with his cup full, and seven winters past he hanged my boy Calden from the crossroad oak at Greymire for stealing two loaves and a wheel of cheese. Two loaves. My boy was nine. {TARGET} watched from his horse and would not cut him down for the dogs. I walked the road back to my woman with the rope still around my son's neck because his lords would not let me take it off. She did not speak again. She died in the spring.
He rides slow. He is fat now, traveler, fat on the bread he hanged my boy for. Four lances at his side and a steward who keeps the ledgers. The steward drinks alone at the Greymire crossing on market days and he owes a Khuzait moneylender more than his life. Press him soft and he will draw you a map. {TARGET} hunts at first light - he rides ahead of his guard when the hounds run. Take him then.
{REWARD} denars when the word comes, traveler. It will not buy back what the rope took, but the road is owed a body, and his is the one we have been waiting for. The snow keeps the rest. Ride.

{CHIEF} has named {TARGET} of {HOME} as the lord whose hand signed the grain-tax that emptied his village the winter of the long cold. The grudge is small and exact - a son of nine summers named Tomas, hanged at the crossroad-oak outside Pravend for stealing a half-loaf from a wagon, the rope cut on the second day so the dogs could finish what the lords began. {CHIEF} carries the boy's wooden spoon in a rag at his belt, the only thing the soldiers left. He has begged on seven roads and counted every coin against this one name. The Eldest offers what coppers his band has scraped and the closing of a wound that does not heal. The road is long. The hunger remembers. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is dead, and {CHIEF} has been told. The old one sat a long time before the answer settled in him. Tomas, who was twelve when they hung him at the Karuya crossroad three winters back for stealing a sack of barley, has had a name spoken back into the world for him. {REWARD} denars are counted into the rag at {CHIEF}'s hip, and his hand shakes around them less than it did. The boy is not back. The bread is not back. But the rope has been answered, and the road keeps the rest. The hollow in him is one name quieter.

Word reached {CHIEF} by way of a fish-monger off the south track: {TARGET} had been pulled down in a roadside scrap by some lord's outriders, bled out in a ditch before the crows even came. The old man took the news standing, one hand at the rag-wrapped spoon hanging from his belt - the spoon Tomas had carved, the spoon they hanged the boy beside at Karuya crossroad for a half-loaf of bread. He nodded slow. The grudge was closed. The throat was cut, only not by the right hand. He counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars - quarter-pay, thin coin for a thin closing - and pushed it across without meeting the eye. The bond sits a notch firmer now, but cooler, the way ash sits firmer than fire.

"There is a village. {VILLAGE}. Lord {LORD} holds it now, but his father held it the winter my woman walked there with three of my boys, begging a crust. They turned her at the gate. Set the dogs on her. Three sons. Three. The snow took them on the road back, one by one, smallest first. I dug them with my hands. {LORD} was a child in that hall, eating warm bread, watching through the shutter. He saw. He saw and said nothing.
The barns are full now. They built a wooden palisade this summer, fat with the harvest that should have fed my boys. The lord's riders go to the Empire fair on the new moon, gone four nights. Strike the second night. Burn the granaries first, then the palisade, then the hall. The smallfolk - the ones who set the dogs - leave none. My boys had no mercy in the snow.
{REWARD} denars when the smoke climbs. Keep the grain, keep the cloth, keep the dogs if any still bark. The snow keeps the rest. The snow remembers."

{CHIEF} speaks the name {VILLAGE} the way a man chews a stone he cannot spit out. In the famine-winter his woman and three of his boys came to that gate begging bread, and the folk there set the dogs on them and shut the door, and the snow took what the dogs did not. {VILLAGE} answers to {LORD} now, and its barns are full, and they have raised a new wooden palisade as if walls could keep the dead out. {CHIEF} has no walls. He has only this contract, and the coin to pay it: {REWARD} when the thatch is ash.

{VILLAGE} burned to the ground, and {CHIEF} stood in the ash with his hollow eyes and counted the timbers of the new palisade as they cracked. The barns went up like dry kindling. The dogs ran, then did not run. He spoke the names of his woman and his three boys aloud, one for each roof that fell, and the snow-winter debt was paid in smoke. {LORD} brought the cut back to the camp. {CHIEF} took the {REWARD} without looking at it, and said only that the village had turned them away once, and would not turn anyone away again.

Word crawled into the camp like a sick dog. {VILLAGE} was already ash when {LORD}'s riders got there. Other hands. Other torches. The new wooden palisade the village had been so proud of, the one raised the same season they set the dogs on a starving woman and three small boys, was charcoal sticks in the snow-melt. The full barns were cinders. {CHIEF} listened without moving. Boll the Eldest only said the famine-winter took its own time, and someone else's fire was still fire. He looked through the messenger, not at him, and counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} with hands that did not shake. He said the debt was paid. He did not say by whom.

It was a Wednesday.
It was a Wednesday in autumn, late, and it had rained earlier and stopped, and the road was the kind of road no one bothers to name. There were four of them around the fire. Two were ill. The fire was small. They had no horses. They had no tents. The wind-break was a fallen elm with brush piled against it. There was nothing else.
You stopped your horse about ten paces out. You watched them for a minute. None of them moved.
One of them was eating bread. He stopped when he heard you. He kept the bread.
You said nothing.
After a while a man on the far side of the fire looked up. He did not stand. He said, "You looking for the road south, it's that way." He pointed. He went back to staring at the coals.
That was the whole of the welcome.
You sat the horse a little longer. There was nothing here that resembled a camp. There was nothing here that resembled a threat. There was a small wet cough somewhere among the heaped rags by the wind-break. It went on a long time. No one tended it. No one would.
You thought about leaving. You thought, also, that you had ridden two days to find this. Two days of looking, and this was what looking found. Not danger. Not even mystery. Four hungry men by a road, the kind of thing you pass and forget every time you ride any distance in this country.
The man pointing at the road south lowered his hand.
He said, without looking up, "You can sit by the fire if you want. We don't mind." He paused. "We don't have anything to take."
It was Boll. There was no way to know that yet. He looked like the other three. You found out it was Boll later, when he told you, the way a person introduces himself when he remembers he hasn't.
You got off the horse.
Hear what Boll has heard. (5 denars)
Boll leans close. He smells of smoke and old wounds.
Boll laughs without humor. "A king? We were farmers, lord. The king's tax-men made us this."
"We pray every morning. Same prayer. 'Let us eat today.' Some days it works."
Boll cringes. "Don't, lord. Please. We got nothing. Take it." His men step back without weapons.
His face crumples in something like gratitude. "Kind of you to say, lord. Kind. We try."
Boll produces a clay jar of weak ale. He pours into chipped cups. "Last of it. Hadn't planned to share. But guests is guests."
You sleep on cold ground next to their fire. Boll insists his men give up their better blankets for your party. They do, with sad eyes.
Pick through the scrap pile.
Boll gestures sadly to a small pile of rusted weapons and patched clothes. "What we found, what nobody wanted. Cheap. Maybe a coin or two each."
Hear stories from the road.
An old looter sits up. "I been everywhere, lord. Walked all my life. Want to hear?" Costs nothing — they want to talk.
Pay for a meal. (10 denars)
Boll's wife brings out a thin stew. Your soldiers eat in silence. The looters watch hungrily, hoping for the leftovers. Your party feels heavier afterward — less in body, more in spirit.
"Saw a noblewoman riding alone at dawn. Crying, she was."
"A merchant dropped a coin-purse on the road yesterday. Some boy got it."
"There's a body in the ditch a mile back. Fresh. Got a ring on his hand still."
"A garrison captain was kissing a tavern-girl in an alley. Wife don't know."
"They're hiring at the silver mine. They don't ask names."
"A black wagon went through last night with no lamps."
"There's a crack in the town wall at Ortongard, west side."
"A monk gave me bread three days ago. Said the world was ending."
"Heard two soldiers say they'd rather desert than march again."
"There's a treasure buried under a crooked tree."
"Grain. A hundred bushels. We're starving — that's why we became this. Feed us, and we'll trade."
His men cheer when they see the grain. The chief simply nods. "Tonight we eat. Tomorrow we trade."
100 grain
"Thirty hides. Boots, jerkins, anything. The boys go barefoot and that's how men die in winter."
The chief holds up a hide. "Real cowhide, not the rotted scraps we've been wearing. The boys live another month."
30 hides
"Fifty leather. Belts, slings, foot-rags. The starving lose their kit faster than men who eat. Bring it."
The chief weighs a strap, slings it over his shoulder. "Now we look almost like men. Trade with us."
50 leather
"Two hundred grain. Thirty leather. We can fight if we eat and our boots aren't rotted. Bring both, and we'll fight FOR you."
His men eat and laugh for the first time in weeks. "You saved this band. Take any boy who wants to follow you."
200 grain + 30 leather
"A hundred fifty grain and fifty hides. Bread and boots. The band marches in real shoes for once. Bring both."
The chief watches his band lace boots properly. "Now we look like soldiers, not the dying. Take recruits."
150 grain + 50 hides
"A hundred grain, twenty leather, five pack-mules. Re-supply on the move. The empire's coming and the band needs to flee fast and fed."
The chief slaps the lead mule. "We outrun the empire because of you. The band owes you blood."
100 grain + 20 leather + 5 mules
"Three hundred grain, fifty leather, twenty sets of tools. We're going to stop running — settle a hidden fold and farm it. Help us become more than looters."
The chief weeps quietly, the first time you've seen it. "The boys plant fields tomorrow. We are men again, because of you."
300 grain + 50 leather + 20 tools
"Five hundred grain, a hundred hides. The whole band overwinters fed and warm. A debt no man could pay back in a lifetime."
The chief grasps your hand in both of his. "You don't know what you've given. The band lives because of you. Forever."
500 grain + 100 hides
Pull off one big heist — escort the stolen-goods cart from a wealthy merchant's caravan back to the looter hideout.
The Boll the Eldest accepts your oath; the rite is sealed in shared bread and salt and a chipped cup passed around the campfire.
Boll spits in the fire. "You was one of us for a hot minute. Now you ain't. Don't take it personal, friend — the road just turned."
Granny Hod
The Widows' Grain
Oi. Granny wants you at the fire. Lord's taxmen emptied Alder Croft's grain-store — that's the village what fills our pot. He's gone all quiet about it. Go on. Quiet Hod is worse than shouting Hod.

Sit, child. The pot's thin tonight, and Old Hod will tell you why. The lord's tax-riders came through Alder Croft two days back — the wood-village that fills half the bowls at this fire. They took the winter grain. All of it. Sacks the widows there gleaned with their own cracked hands, weighed against a debt nobody ever signed. The wagons roll south on the low road now, slow with the weight of what they stole. Take it back, child. Not a share — every sack, back to the crofts it came from. And save your breath on bargains. Men who'd starve orphans for a ledger-line don't hear words. They hear spears.
Good, child. The wagons are slow and grain doesn't bleed — mind that the spears around it do. Bring the sacks back whole. Alder Croft's ovens have been cold two days already.
As you like, child. But the grain won't sit on that road forever, and there are little ones at Alder Croft learning what an empty bowl weighs. Old Hod will keep your broth warm a while yet.
The wagons are still on the low road, child. Every day they roll south is a day Alder Croft chews bark-bread. Go on. The fire will keep.
Taxman's Grain-Wagons
His Lordship's Taxman
Find the Taxman's Grain-Wagons on the roads south of Granny Hod's forest, defeat the escort, and recover the winter grain taken from the wood-village of Alder Croft.
Return to Granny Hod's hideout and tell him the grain is on its way back to Alder Croft.

Move your rabble off the road. These wagons carry his lordship's levy, sealed and ledgered. The crown's business does not halt for forest scum — and my escort has killed better-armed beggars than you.
Hand the grain back, or bleed for every sack of it.

Hand it back? It's entered in his lordship's ledger — his property the moment the ink dried. Ledgers outlive widows, road-filth, and this one will outlive you. Escort — spears! Cut them down and keep the wagons rolling.

The carts rolled into Alder Croft this morning, child. Every sack. The widows counted them twice, then stopped counting and started baking. There's a girl there who thought bread was a winter story — she knows better now, and so does the lord's ledger. Sit down. The deep bowl's yours tonight — soup with marrow in it, the good roots, none of the thin stuff. Eat with Old Hod, child. This is what the grain was for.

Somebody else found the wagons first, child. Broke the escort on the low road and left the sacks split in the mud for the crows and the rain. My boys saved what they could — half, maybe less. Alder Croft will eat thin this winter, but it will eat, and Old Hod thanks you for riding at all. Still. Spilled grain is gone grain, and the wood does not get its bread back from a stranger's quarrel. Sit. The broth's thin tonight. Share it anyway.

Hod was born a free Battanian wood-wife, the kind of woodland-dweller who paid no taxes because the lord's tax-clerks never bothered to ride into the deep oak forests where her people lived. She married a hunter named Tealc when she was nineteen, bore him three sons in a turf-and-timber cottage, and lived for twenty-two years on what the woods provided. The first hanging was Tealc — caught taking a stag the lord had reserved for his own table, and gibbeted the next dawn at the village square as a warning. The second was Tealc's elder brother Brec, who came down out of the wood three months later carrying a bow he should have left at home, and the third was meant to be Tealc's younger brother Anwen who came swearing the same oaths over the same gibbet. Anwen brought the bow but he also brought thirty wood-cousins, and the lord's gibbet-men never arrived at their post that morning. From that day Granny Hod has not poached in the forest she lived in — she owns it. The Forest Bandits are her grandchildren, her brothers-in-law, and the last family of every Battanian who has ever swung from a Vlandian-installed gibbet.

The Forest Bandits have lived under the same big oak for four generations. Hod's great-grandmother built the first lean-to there, and Hod still sleeps under that lean-to's grandchild. Deep-forest Battanian wood-villages the Vlandian tax-clerks could not reach feed most of the band — along with herb-women whose husbands were killed in the lord's last small war, poachers whose lord found out about the poaching, and forest-children who simply walked away from a chore one morning and never came back. They are not great raiders — they take from coach-roads only when the coach-road is foolish enough to run inside the tree-line — but they are extraordinary survivors. Granny Hod knows seventy-one edible roots, twenty-four medicinal barks, and the three trees that should not be cut on the same day. The lords who have tried to push roads through the deep oaks have buried more axemen than they have laid stones. The forest-people themselves regard the band as a seventh-aunt of the wood-villages — the one a family brings the sick child to when the lord's hedge-priest has turned them away. The Battanian crown has not declared a bounty in three reigns.

An old man in deer-hide watches you cross the clearing without standing. The fire spits between him and you. He tears jerky with his teeth, studying you like he'd study a wounded deer. "My boys said you walked in alone. Didn't bolt when they drew steel. That's either bravery or stupidity, traveler — and old Hod's lived too long to tell those apart on first sight. Speak your business. The forest hears everything in here."

Granny Hod — the men call him that, and the wood-villages older still — looks up as you duck past his sentries. The wariness from your first visit is gone from his eyes; not warmth, but a kind of tired recognition. "Back again, traveler. Sit. The fire's yours. Old Hod's boys don't draw steel on you anymore — that's the closest thing to welcome these woods know."

Hod's heard names before, traveler. Heard a hundred this winter alone — half of them lying. Means nothing to me until you've done something. My boys want hides; the forest doesn't give them up easy. Bring what we ask, and old Hod will know your name's worth the breath you spent saying it.
The Forest Bandits' camp is hidden under a big oak — lean-tos, drying racks of meat and herbs, a smoke-pit. Dogs slink between the trees.

Take the Pen Cannoc road south, child, until the cart-ruts grow soft with moss and the alders crowd close enough to brush your stirrups. A day off the road, where the canopy closes so thick the sun comes down green, you'll find an oak older than any king the lowlanders remember - a great hollow at its roots big enough to crawl through. That's the door-stone. Our hold lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, past the oak, where the drying-racks hang heavy with venison and the smoke-pit smoulders under its turfed lean-to.
Mind the snare-line strung between the hazels - step over it slow, hands open. My girls watch from the high boughs and they've put broadheads through better-armed men than you for moving wrong. Whistle three times like the woodlark when you pass the oak; the dogs will know the sound and the dogs will tell my watchers. Come singing if you can. Quiet men trouble me.
For those who come kindly, there's broth in the pot and a place by the herb-smoke, and old Granny Hod will read the bones for you if your road ahead is dark. For those who come with steel drawn or coin-thoughts behind their eyes - well. The forest is hungry this season, and my dogs have learned a taste they did not have last spring.

Sit closer to the fire, child. The oaks have been whispering of horsemen all season. The Battanian lords ride their own country like guests who forgot the way home - the fian-captains out of Pen Cannoc come hunting boar in my groves, and twice now they have hunted my snare-women instead. I sent the second band back with their bowstrings cut and a sprig of yew tied to the captain's saddle. He will know the meaning when his mother sees it.
The Vlandian lords push east through the lowland passes, hungry for Battanian timber and Battanian girls. There is a baron - calls himself Sir Aedric of some keep I cannot pronounce - who burned a charcoal-camp three valleys west because the burners would not swear to his crown. The trees remember. I remember. His outriders will find my dead-falls before they find his timber.
And the Empire sends its tax-riders up the old Calradic road, though the road is half-swallowed by root and moss now. They come in tens, leave in fewer. If you ride my country with a lord's banner over you, child, the oaks will mark it before my watchers do. The deep wood keeps its own counsel about who passes through, and who only thinks they did.

Sit closer, child, the fire's hungry tonight. You ask of my kin in the green and the grey - well, the old roots tangle deep. Crone Vael of the pagan cult keeps her grove three valleys north of mine, and we are two old women who nod across the same moon. She sends me bark-tea in the dark months, I send her snare-rabbits in the lean ones. No blood between us, none owed. That is a rare thing in this trade, child, treasure it where you find it.
The Reavers - Vargolf's lot in the frost-country - owe me a kindness from the year the white sickness took half my band. He sent furs and salt down the old drovers' path, asked no token in return. A wolf who remembers warmth, that one. But the Highwaymen of the downs, child, them I do not abide. Their Reeve trades captives like sheaves of wheat, and the forest does not forgive that. My scouts marked two of his outriders sniffing the Pen Cannoc road last new moon - if they cross my oak-line, the brambles will have them.
And hush now - the Marsh Stalkers have gone quiet, child. Three weeks no chatter from the fen-paths. Quiet is a held breath. Something walks down there, or something has eaten them. Either way, we watch the south road careful.

Hush a moment, child, and let an old wife show you where the snares lie. The Pen Cannoc road bends past my oak-stand twice a moon, and the Battanian thanes have grown bold - they send their dye-merchants down to Marunath under a thin guard of six levies and a wagoneer who drinks before the sun is full. Three wagons. The middle one carries the blue-dye the southern lords buy by the thimble, worth more than the cloth it will colour. My snare-boys count their steps on the leaf-mast. Quiet as deer they go.
The trick, child, is the ford below the third milestone. Wagons must slow, the levies must dismount, and the dye-cart sinks to its axle in the soft mud my girls turned over a week before. That is when we have taken them. Twice in a season, and the thanes still send fresh ones. They think the forest forgets.
If you ride that road four mornings hence with a dozen good horse, the dye is yours and I will not lift a finger to claim it. Granny's pot is full this moon. But mark me - leave the wagoneer breathing and his tongue loose. He drinks at the Pen Cannoc inn and tells the next caravan-master what he saw, and the next caravan packs heavier guards, and the heavier guards bring heavier purses. The forest feeds those who let the snare reset itself. Remember that, child.

Sit, child. Sit on the moss and let Granny look at you proper. That is no fireside-question you have brought me - that is the oak-question, the deep-root question, the one a body only asks when she means to be answered. The wind heard you. The oak heard you. Now Granny hears you, and Granny is the slowest of the three.
Child, the green keeps what is given to it. I have bled for three souls in my long years, and the snare-line remembers each. A coal-burner's girl I pulled from a fever-bed when the lowland leeches would not ride out. A poacher named Aelwyn who shared his last hare in a winter that ate two villages. And my own sister, dust now, who taught me which root mends and which root ends. That is the roll Granny keeps. Short as a finger, deep as a well.
You are not in it, child. Not yet. Bring Granny a kindness the forest can witness - a stag fed to a starving croft, a tax-man turned back from a holding that fed me when I was thin, a wrong-thing righted in the green's own name. Then we shall sit again, and the oak shall know your scent. Ask me once more when you have walked beneath my trees as one of mine.

Then it is spoken, child, and the oak above us heard. Kneel by the moss-stone - no, closer, where the root drinks. I cut a twist of my own white hair, and a twist of yours, and I braid them with the snare-line that has held every rabbit, every fawn, every red-handed lowlander I ever pulled from this wood. There. I bury the braid under the root of the grandmother-oak, and the oak takes it down to where my mother's braid lies, and her mother's, and the chief before that whose name I will not speak by daylight. The wood knows your name now. The wood does not forget what it has swallowed.
Brother in the forest-tongue means hearth-shared, child. It means when you come walking through the alder my snares lift their teeth for you. It means my pot is your pot and the salt-fish my old man left me when the fever took him - that salt-fish is your salt-fish. The Wood-Wife has no sons of her own blood; the fever took those too. So you are the son the oak grew for me late. Do not make me bury a third.
Go now, child of mine, and walk the Pen Cannoc road as kin of the Wood-Wife. The Battanian lords will spit at the name. The under-foresters will keep your back. The oak knows. The snare-line knows. From this root forward you are mine, and what is mine the forest defends.

Hush, child. Sit down on the moss, you are still steaming from the ride. I asked you once if you would bleed for me when the time came, and I half-expected a pretty answer with the ink still wet on it. Instead you came back through the brambles with the blood already drying on your sleeve and the word almost forgot in your mouth. The oak knows. The deed first, the word after - that is the order a forest trusts. A speech wilts. A wound keeps.
So hear what the snare-line says now, and hear it plain. From this moon, my woods-folk are your woods-folk under arms. Not as a debt I can call in at my leisure - as a war-bond, the kind the bramble makes when it grows through two trees and will not let either fall alone. Raise your banner anywhere south of the Pen Cannoc road and my bowmen are in the leaves before your horn finishes. Your feud is the forest's feud. The lords who hunt you will find the trees themselves have grown teeth.
The wind carries this further than my voice can, child. It will be in the rookeries by dusk and in the snare-lines by dawn - that the Wood-Wife rides at your shoulder, and the old grudges of this country ride with her. Go. The road is loud. We are sworn now in something colder than kinship - sworn in the work, and the work is never finished.

Aye, child. Ten of my wood-walkers, seven sunsets - I will choose them myself from the bow-girls and the snare-boys who know the deep paths. My eldest niece Bryn Owl-Eye rides at their head; she has the steady hand and the colder count, and what she says to them is what I would have said. She knows my standards. Trust her quiet more than her speaking.
Now hear my terms, child. My wood-hidden do not break thicket for coin or for grudges that are not theirs. While they walk under your banner, your work is the wood's work - do not spend them on small spite. If one falls, you bring me the bowstring and the name of the place, and I will sing the rest myself. If one lives, you feed them well and send them home with their boots still on.
Seven sunsets, child. I will be counting from the next moonrise. The grove expects them back, and so do I.

His name is {TARGET}, child, and his banner hangs over {HOME} like a crow that forgot how to leave. Sit. The oak knows him. Nine summers back his huntsmen rode the green looking for a white stag and found my daughter's man instead - found Cael at his snare-line with two coneys on his belt, and they hanged him from his own rope for a poacher. He was twenty-two. My Annet went into the moss after that and the moss kept her. {TARGET} signed the warrant himself. I have the parchment still, child. I read it on the nights the wind is loud.
He rides a chestnut mare and a guard of six, and he hunts the river-road every third week when the woodcock are fat. His master-of-hounds is a Battanian boy who was sold to him as a debt-child and would cut the saddle-girth for a kind word and a coin. Find that boy at the Greenmere ford. {TARGET} is heavy after the kill, child, and the green is heavier on him than he knows.
{REWARD} denars when the oak hears of it, no sooner, no less. The gold is owed but the gold is the smaller half. The green keeps the rest. Ride soft, child, and let the moss hold what falls.

{CHIEF} has named {TARGET} of {HOME} as the lord whose blood the oak roots have been thirsting for since the seventh summer past. The wound is a remembered one - a coppicer's daughter named Wenna, taken from a charcoal-burner's camp on the Brackwater bend, hung from a snare-line for the crime of gleaning fallen wood from a noble's wood-pasture. The girl was nine. Granny Hod cut her down herself and carries the frayed cord still, knotted three times for the three days the body swung unclaimed. The green keeps its dead, the old woman says, and the oak knows the name uncrossed. A purse of {REWARD} is offered, and a debt the forest has been counting in rings.

{TARGET} is dead. {CHIEF} has been told, and the old wood-mother only nodded, the way oak nods in a slow wind. The snare-line at the Blackelm hollow has its answer at last - thirty-one summers after little Wren was hung there for a fistful of pignuts, the man who tied the knot lies cold. {REWARD} denars rest in the moss-bowl by the hearth-root, counted by knotted cord. The green keeps what it keeps, and the child it could not keep is finally spoken for. The snare is sprung. The hollow is quiet.

Word came up the deer-path at dusk: {TARGET} was already cold, run through in a roadside scuffle by some banner-lord's outriders a fortnight back. {CHIEF} took the news in the smoke of her cookfire, turning the old knotted snare-cord through her fingers - the same cord that hanged little Wren at Blackelm hollow over a handful of pignuts. The grudge was answered, in a fashion. The wrong was closed, the name struck off her tally of debts. Still, she had wanted the hand that did it to be the player's, not a stranger's blade in a ditch she would never walk. She counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars - thin coin, quarter-pay - and set the bond a smaller notch firmer than it might have stood.

Sit close, hunter, and hear the wood's complaint. {VILLAGE} is the place, and {LORD} the man who calls himself its keeper. His huntsmen ride into my deep wood with hounds and horns, and they do not hunt for meat - they hunt for sport, leaving the red deer to rot where they fall. His foresters fell my old-grove oaks for charcoal, trees that stood when his grandfather's grandfather was an unweaned babe. And his daughter, that proud thing, wears a comb cut from the heart-oak under which my own mother lies buried. The wood remembers. So do I.
Go at the grey hour before dawn, when the charcoal-burners are still asleep beside their mounds. Burn the kilns first - the smoke will wake the village too late. Take their salted venison and their oat-stores, for those are stolen from my wood already. Spare the bee-hives. Spare the apple trees. Spare any old woman who kneels. The rest is kindling.
For your trouble I will weigh out {REWARD} from the moss-jar beneath the alder root. Bring me back the comb, hunter. The heart-oak wants its splinter home, and my mother has waited long enough.

{CHIEF} speaks the name of {VILLAGE} low, the way one names a sickness in a beloved tree. Its huntsmen, she says, have come three summers running into her deep wood, killing the white-flank deer for sport and leaving the carcasses to rot where the moss grows thickest. Worse still, the village axes have felled six of her old-grove oaks for charcoal, and {LORD}'s own daughter walks abroad with a fine comb cut from the heart-oak under which Granny's mother lies buried. The wood remembers, she murmurs. Now it must answer. She offers the player {REWARD} silver to burn the thatch and break the kilns of {VILLAGE}.

{VILLAGE} burned slow, the way wet thatch will when the wind is patient. The charcoal-pits where {LORD}'s woodsmen had been rendering Granny Hod's old-grove oaks were drowned, the axes broken across the same stumps that fed them. No more deer hung head-down from {LORD}'s rafters; no more sport-kills strung up to rot. The heart-oak comb, the one cut from beneath her mother's grave-tree, was prised from the daughter's hair and laid back among the roots where it belonged.
{CHIEF} counted out {REWARD} without speaking. The wood had been heard, and the wood was quiet again.

Word drifts in on the wind that {VILLAGE} is already ash. Some other axe answered the deer-killers and the oak-fellers before yours could. {LORD}'s charcoal-pits are cold, his huntsmen scattered, his hall a smear of cinders, and somewhere in that wreck the comb cut from the heart-oak lies broken or carried off by strangers. Granny Hod listens to the news with her hands folded, lips thin. The wood is quieter now, she allows, and that is something. But the killing was not done by kin of the grove, and the trees did not name the doer. She presses {REDUCED_REWARD} into the runner's palm and turns back to her moss.

"You see them?"
The boy was sixteen at most. He was crouched against a pine three paces from you and you had not heard him arrive. The blade in his hand was not yet for you — he held it loose at his thigh — and he did not look up. He looked past your shoulder and down the slope, the way a son might point his father out to a guest at a feast.
"Don't stare right at the fire," he said. "You'll lose your eyes for the dark after. Look just beside it. That's how Granny taught us, an' she was right."
You looked just beside it.
There were perhaps thirty of them down in the hollow. A woman pulling flat bread off an iron. Two men arguing over the worth of a deer-hide and laughing in the same breath. Children — three, four of them — chasing a dog that was older than they were and far too patient with the chase. A man on a stump tuning a stringed thing that had survived a hard winter and showed it.
"Most came in the last bad one," the boy said quietly. "Winter took the villages. Granny took everyone after. She don't care what you done before — only what you do here. Says the forest don't ask for papers."
He glanced up at you for the first time. He had brown eyes and a small, faded scar at his hairline, and he was very young.
"You come to take her?"
You did not answer.
The boy nodded slowly, as though you had.
"Right," he said. "Well. Walk down, then. She'll want to look at your face, an' she likes to do it with the fire on it. Keep your hands easy. The dogs are nervier than the men."
He sat back against the pine and watched you go.
Buy provisions from Granny Hod.
Hod gestures to the drying racks. "Smoked venison, fresh game, hides, healing herbs."
"A king drew a line on a map and said the trees were his. We chose the trees."
"The forest, child. The deer-mother, the oak-father, the wolf that walks."
Hod doesn't even look up. "My grandson has an arrow on you, lord. Has had since you walked in."
She grins — gap-toothed. "Forest treats us. Quiet here, mostly."
Hod brings out a jar of pine-spirit. It smells of resin and burns going down. "Old recipe. Keeps the wolves friendly. Keeps the men ready."
You bunk on pine boughs under the big oak. The dogs sleep nearby. Your party wakes to woodsmoke and the smell of breakfast.
Trade with the hide-tanner.
A boy lays out tanned hides — deer, boar, a black bear. "Better than town leather. We did it ourselves. Hod says you'll like it."
Speak with the deep-wood druid. (free)
A robed figure barely visible in the trees gestures you closer. "The forest tells me much, child. Listen." The druid speaks in riddles.
Hire a wolf-hound trainer. (200 denars)
A young man brings out a half-grown wolf-pup. "Trained right, it'll hunt with your soldiers. Wrong, it'll eat their boots. I train them right." Morale rises.
"There's a rich man's hunting cabin three days east. Stocked with fine wine."
"A druid in the deep wood pays for rare herbs. He pays in old coins."
"The forest's deer have moved south. So have the wolves."
"A noble lost his prize hound here last hunt. Whoever finds it earns favor."
"There's a shrine in the deep wood with offerings of silver."
"Foresters' guild is hiring trackers."
"A wandering monk got lost in our woods last month. He's still wandering."
"The lord's gamekeeper takes bribes."
"There's a bear-cave with a winter's stock of dried fish — a hermit's hoard."
"A fugitive paid us to hide him last spring. Then his enemies paid more."
"Thirty leather. The forest takes our boots and tunics faster than we can replace them."
He counts hides quickly. "Honest stock. The forest knows your face now."
30 leather
"Twenty-five hides. Roe-deer, boar, what the forest gives. We tan our own — bring the raw stock."
He inspects each hide. "Clean kill, clean cut. The tanner won't curse this batch."
25 hides
"Thirty hardwood. Bow-staves, lodge-poles, fire-wood. The forest is generous, but we're particular about our wood."
He bends a stave to test the grain. "Strong wood. The forest welcomes you."
30 hardwood
"Fifty leather and twenty hardwood. We're rebuilding the deep camp — bows, traps, lodges."
He works hardwood with a knife as he talks. "Solid stuff. Take what you need."
50 leather + 20 hardwood
"Forty leather and twenty-five fur. The deep-forest patrols need cold-cloak before the leaves drop. Bring both."
He drapes a cloak around a young scout. "He'll keep watch warmer because of you. The patrols salute."
40 leather + 25 fur
"Sixty hardwood and thirty hides. New lodge for the western patrol-camp. Heavy haul, forest-walker."
He tests a roof-beam. "Lodge will hold a generation. The forest remembers your work."
60 hardwood + 30 hides
"A hundred leather, forty hardwood, ten wrought-iron ingots. The whole forest-host re-equips. Only kin help with this."
He clasps your forearm in the deep-forest greeting. "You've outfitted the band for a generation. Forest-kin now."
100 leather + 40 hardwood + 10 wrought iron
"Eighty fur, fifty hardwood, thirty hides. The whole-forest gathering — we host every band west of the river. Bring it all."
He gestures to the gathered bands. "Every Battanian outlaw west of the river knows your name now. Walk safe."
80 fur + 50 hardwood + 30 hides
Destroy the rival Twin-Oak forest gang — they have been muscling Hod's runners off the east trail.
The Granny Hod accepts your oath; the rite is sealed with a knot of yew-branch tied around your wrist under the old oak at moonrise.
Hod cuts the yew-knot from your wrist herself. "The forest never owed you. Walk back to the road and stay on it."
Skarvac of the High Pass
The Mountain's Toll
You. Pass-Lord wants you at his fire. Some fat column ran the road without paying and he's gone all quiet over it. Quiet's worse than shouting, with him. Best climb quick.

A column ran my road four days past. Rich one — wool, dye, southern silver in the strongbox. Their captain bought a paper from some lord's clerk in the lowlands and waved it at my lower watch like it was iron. A clerk's ink does not spend on my road. My toll-tables have not changed in eighteen years, and by those tables that column owes me two thousand four hundred denars. The eagles marked them going down the far side — slow wagons, hired guards, a captain who smiles too much. Go and collect what is owed. How the coin comes out of them I leave to the collector. The ledger only cares that it comes.

Good. Take enough men that the smile leaves his face before you speak. The pass counts in coin, traveler, not in reasons. Bring me two thousand four hundred and I will not ask which pocket it came out of.
As you like. But the ledger stays open, and the column rolls slow under fat wagons. The offer stands until my eagles lose them.
You carry unfinished work already. The pass takes one toll at a time, traveler. Come back with empty hands.
Cavren's Paper Column
Master Cavren
Find Cavren's Paper Column on the roads below the High Pass and collect Skarvac's toll of 2400 denars — by demand, bargain, or force.
Return to Skarvac of the High Pass with the collected toll.

Ah, more toll-men. You have wasted the climb, friend — I carry a writ of passage from Lord Osrec's own clerk, seal and all. The road is paid for. Now shift your horses before my guards earn their wage.
Skarvac's toll. Two thousand four hundred. Count it now.
All right — all right. Keep your dogs back. It's here, it's counted. Tell the Pass-Lord his road was never worth half this. But tell him it's paid.
Half the toll and you roll on. Decide quickly.
Half? Done — before your master hears you can't count. There's your coin. Even a mountain dog knows a paper's worth something, it seems. Drive on!
Forget the coin. Steel pays your toll today.
Guards! Earn your silver! I bought this road once — I'll not buy it twice from a dead man.
That's the collection? That handful? Ha! I've hired more steel than you're showing, friend. Take your toll off me if you can reach it — otherwise, downhill is that way.

Set it on the stone. I count once — I only count twice when I doubt the collector. Two thousand four hundred, full weight. The ledger closes. You took the whole toll off a man waving a lord's paper, and my road keeps its name. That is proper collector's work, traveler. The pass weighed you on this errand and found the weight honest. Sit at my fire. The mountain remembers who paid — it remembers better who collected.

Set it down. Hm. I count once... and I count again, because the stack sits low. Twelve hundred. Half. You let the paper-man ride off with the rest of what my tables say he owes. Half a toll keeps a road half-respected, traveler. I take it — coin is coin — but the ledger stays open at his name, and yours sits nearer the margin than it did this morning. Go on. The pass forgets nothing it is still owed.

The eagles brought it down before you did. The column lies scattered on the lowland road — someone else's steel, someone else's quarrel, and my toll burned with the wagons. You climbed, so I will not send you down empty. Half-share, for half-work — the road pays the man who rode it, not the man who finished it. Take the coin and do not thank me. Next time reach the mark before the crows do. The ledger closes crooked, and I hate a crooked line.

Skarvac was born in a high-pass tollhouse his great-grandfather had built — the kind of stone-and-timber post that collects road-dues for the Sturgian crown in exchange for road-maintenance and traveler-protection. The post had operated under royal charter for ninety years, and Skarvac inherited it from his father at twenty-six like an honest profession. The trouble began the year a young Sturgian magistrate audited the regional tolls and discovered the high-pass charter had quietly lapsed three reigns ago — Skarvac's grandfather had simply kept paying his crown-due each year and the crown had simply kept cashing the cheque without renewing the charter. The magistrate ordered the tollhouse closed and a new royal post built in its place, with new royal toll-takers; Skarvac watched from the cliff above as the work began. He came down the second night with twelve men and burned the new construction to the foundations. He maintained the road, repaired the bridges, and charged the travelers fairly by his own measure for the next twenty-eight years, and the Sturgian crown spent that entire period failing to install anyone capable of replacing him. The crown still insists Skarvac of the High Pass is a bandit; the travelers still insist on paying him.

The Mountain Bandits are the most venerable of the bands organized as bands — older than the Highwaymen, younger than the Sea Raiders. Skarvac's great-grandfather built the original tollhouse the camp now occupies, on a Sturgian crown commission to maintain the high pass and collect road-dues; the commission was renewed for three generations and quietly rescinded in the fourth, when the crown decided the pass no longer mattered. The family kept collecting the dues anyway, and the band crystallized around them. Skarvac has not changed the toll-tables in eighteen years; he has the original commission scroll still pinned to his receiving-tent wall, signed and sealed by a Sturgian boyar two generations dead. Those who find their way to Skarvac's camp tend to share a profile: mountain-village men who no longer believe in the crown, displaced highland families, runaway Vlandian armorer's apprentices who could no longer pay their guild-fees, and the occasional Battanian herder who did not feel like coming down the slopes that year. They run the pass like a road-baron's holding — regular patrols, written passes, posted rates. The Sturgian crown has tried twice to retake the tollhouse and has not tried a third.

The Pass-Lord stands by a smoking brazier, warming hands that have killed more men than the brazier has ever burned wood. He watches you finish the climb without offering a single step's worth of help, and only when you reach his fire does he speak — measured, mountain-cold. "You came up alive. That alone is already a discount on your toll, traveler. Skarvac thanks the mountain for the wages it spared us today. Now — what have you come to spend?"

Skarvac's brazier is closer to where he stands now — a small mercy you didn't get on your first climb. The Pass-Lord nods once, the way mountain men nod when words would cost more than the gesture. "You've made the pass three times now, traveler. Skarvac counts that. Warm yourself. The mountain doesn't forget who comes back, and neither does its lord."

The mountain heard the name on your climb up, traveler. The mountain forgets quickly. Skarvac doesn't deal in names — he deals in tolls paid and tolls owed. There's a toll my men need collected. Pay it for us, and your name stops being a stranger's at this fire.
The Mountain Bandits' camp is wedged into a cliff cleft — stone walls, iron-banded gate, tower for sentries. Skarvac runs it like a road-baron.

Take the switchback road above Jaculan and keep climbing past the place where the carters stop to water their mules. The air thins. The pines thin. When the road bends a fifth time and you think it must bend no more, look up and left for a cleft in the cliff face - narrow, dark, easy to miss if a man is watching his horse and not the rock. Above the lintel of the gate hangs an ox-skull on a chain. That is the door. Our hold lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, and the gate is iron-banded and the walls beside it are dry-stone fitted by a mason whose name I will not give you.
The slate-roofed tower above the cleft is manned every hour the sun is up and most of the hours it is not. My watcher sees you long before you see the gate. Ride slow on the last bend. Raise your banner where the road straightens. If your party-pennant is one I know, the chain comes down and the gate opens.
Come the wrong way and the first quarrel takes your standard-bearer off his horse. We do not parley with men who climb our pass uninvited - the road is mine, the toll is mine, and the silence of the rocks afterward is mine also. Come the right way and you eat at my fire, and I will tell you which caravans are worth the riding-down this season.

The Vlandians own the lowlands. The passes are mine. Their lords forget this every spring, and every spring my watchers remind them. The barons of Jaculan send their outriders up the switchback road to count what crosses - they call it patrol, I call it trespass. The toll on this road is set by the man who holds the high ground, and that man is me. A Vlandian banneret rode up last moon with twelve lances behind him. He came down on foot with eight.
There is a vassal-clan out of Ocs Hall, Clan Therpentine I think they call themselves, who has a standing grudge with my house. Their old lord lost a son to my father's crossbows in the snow-year, and now the boy's brother rides the high road every season with fresh men, looking for the rock that buried his blood. I let him look. The mountain keeps its own counsel.
The Empire sends tax-wagons through the southern saddle when the snow thins - Western Empire coin, bound for the garrisons at Lageta. The Battanians come north sometimes in raid-parties but they fear the height; their lords belong in the woods. If you ride with a Vlandian banner over my road, traveler, pay the toll before my Reavers ask twice. The pass remembers every coat-of-arms that climbs it.

The road is mine. That is the first thing any chief in these mountains learns, or he learns it the hard way on my switchbacks. Granny Hod's forest band down in the Battanian woods - she sends a runner every autumn with a sack of cured venison and a token saying her foragers will not cross into my passes. I take the venison. The token I keep in a box. One day she will need the road and I will name the toll.
Vargolf and his Frost Reavers - now there is a chief I respect. He bleeds Sturgians, I bleed Vlandians, and our maps do not touch. We have shared a fire twice. He pays his debts in iron, which is the only coin a pass-lord trusts. The Highwaymen of the downs are a different matter - the Reeve thinks every Vlandian road is his counting-house. My switchbacks above Jaculan are NOT his road. Last spring two of his coin-counters tried to set up a toll-post a day's ride below mine. They are buried under the cairn at the third bend now. He has not sent more.
The Sky Raiders worry me. Aerlin's lot have been seen on the crags this season, hunting in country that is mine by old right. Birds do not pay toll. We will see.

The Vlandian wool-trains come up out of Jaculan three times a moon, traveler, and every one of them pays my toll whether the driver knows it or not. Twelve wagons, eight horse, two crossbowmen on the lead - that is what the Boyar Mottimer sends north when his weavers want southern dye. They climb my switchbacks at the second hour past dawn because the merchants fear the wind after noon. By the time they reach the third bend their horses are blowing and the rear-guard is walking. That is where the road belongs to me.
The captain is a Vlandian named Servan, a fat man who drinks his wine at the lower posthouse and never less than three cups. He will not turn his head once the climb starts. The middle wagon - always the middle - carries pressed Battanian bluestone the dyers cannot make for themselves. Worth four hundred denars the bale, and there are six bales under the oilcloth.
