If you take them, take them at the third bend before the snowmelt-ford, not after. After the ford a Vlandian outrider-patrol rides down from the watchtower at the eleventh hour. Hit them clean, ride east into my passes, and the patrol will find nothing but cart-tracks I have already brushed. The road pays its toll one way or another. Better it pays you and me than the boyar's purse.

You ask the toll-question. Few travelers know the road well enough to ask it. Sit. Mind the wind off the rocks - it carries every word said up here, and the pass remembers what the mouth forgets. What you are asking is not paid in coin, and what I give is not handed across a counter.
When the time comes, I bleed for the names already cut into the toll-stone above the switchback. That stone is small. My brother Caedric, who held the chain the night the Vlandian column tried to force it. Old Mara of the upper village, who fed my riders three winters before any of us could pay her back. The mule-boy Toren, who took an arrow meant for my throat. You have not yet been cut into that stone. Nor have you been struck from it.
Bring me a deed the pass cannot forget - a column turned back at the chain, a tax-wagon taken in MY name, a road kept open when the lowlands tried to choke it. Then the toll-stone learns a new mark. Until that day my chain is mine and my riders are mine, but you have already set foot on my road. Speak again when the rocks know your name.

Then the word is laid on the stone and the stone does not forget. Stand on the toll-step beside me. I take the chain from my own neck - the one the lowland sergeant put there in Jaculan before I broke his wrist for it - and I open the link with the cold pliers. Hold out your wrist. The link closes around it. Mine bears the matching kink where it was forced wide once and never sat flush again. Now we wear the same iron. Drink from the pass-horn. The water came down off the snow this morning. It tastes of slate and old smoke and the road we hold.
Brother on my road means this. The toll-stone reads two names from tonight. What climbs the pass climbs past you the same as past me. My switchbacks are your switchbacks. The men who tip their caps at the lower watch will tip them at you - and the ones who try the chain at the upper watch will pay you what they would have paid me, or they will pay in the same coin I take. My feud is your feud. The merchant-prince in Jaculan who put the price on my head - that price sits on yours now too, and I am glad of it.
Skarvac of the High Pass names you kin to the toll-stone, kin to the chain, kin to every switchback between here and the snowline. The Pass-Wardens will know your face by the iron. Jaculan will learn it the slow way. Brother - the road climbs, and we hold the high end of it together.

Then I have heard the answer in the only tongue the pass respects - the tongue of work already done. You did not climb up here to swear at me. You climbed up with the deed cooling on your hands and the word as the afterthought, the way a toll-stone is set before the road is named. Good. That is the order I trust. A man who comes with a speech first owes more than he brings. You came with the saddle full. Sit. Let the iron settle.
From this dusk on, the chain that lies across my pass lies across yours. When you raise your banner in the low country, my road empties of every other rider and fills with mine, and they come down the switchbacks at your call - not as men I have lent, but as men sworn. Your enemies are toll-evaders to me now. Mine you will ride against without asking the price. We do not pay each other in coin again. We pay in arms, in passage, in the dead we leave on the other man's ground. The toll-stone has both our marks cut into it.
The wind off the high passes carries names a long way, traveler. It will carry ours together now, lashed the way two horses are lashed across a saddle when one rider has fallen. My road is your road. The chain is the witness. This is not the hearth-bond - this is the colder one. The war-bond. It holds until the last of our enemies has been counted, and the high pass has not finished counting in my lifetime.

Done. Ten chain-men for seven days - I pick them off the toll-stone myself, the ones who have stood a full winter at the gate. My second is Brakka Cold-Hand, who keeps the count for me and knows which passes are mine and which are only borrowed. He rides at your stirrup. The other nine answer to him, and he answers to me.
Hear my terms, traveler. If a pass-warden of mine falls in your work, you carry his chain back to this stone - not his blade, the chain off his belt. That is how I know the man is done. If he lives, you send him home with the road-dust still on him; I want to see where he has been. My riders do not break shield for petty toll-skips or some lord's grudge. While the chain is on your shoulder, your road is my road - so do not spend them on small coin.
Seven days. The pass counts in sunsets, not in promises. When the eighth dawn breaks I expect Brakka at this gate with nine behind him, or a chain in your hand for every man I am short.

His name is {TARGET}. His banner flies over {HOME}, and his father's chain still hangs from the toll-stone above the High Pass - the chain my own father was throttled with, nine winters back, when he refused to bend knee and pay tariff on his own road. They left him swinging until the crows had his eyes. {TARGET} was a boy then. He has grown into the same chain, and he rides my road now as if the toll-stone forgot.
He moves with six lances and a Battanian forester who scouts ahead by half a league. The forester drinks at the waystation below Karakhergit on every third night - a flask of strong spirit loosens his tongue and his loyalty both. {TARGET} rests his column at the old shepherd ruins when the pass is choked with snow. Take him there. He sleeps with his sword across his knees, but he sleeps.
{REWARD} denars when the chain comes back to me with his hand still on it. The road remembers what the boy forgot. The pass remembers. Ride, traveler, and do not look back.

Skarvac of the High Pass has set the toll-stone against {TARGET} of {HOME}, and the chain on the road shall not lift until that name is struck from the pass. The grudge is cut into the lintel of his hold: nine summers past, a caravan of Skarvac's kin came down the switchbacks under safe-passage, eleven souls bound for the salt-fair at Pen Cannoc, and {TARGET}'s outriders cut the lead mule's traces above the Shrike-Drop ravine. Eleven went over. The salt was kept. No iron was paid, no name was spoken in answer. Skarvac offers {REWARD} and the weight of a road-debt finally closed. The pass remembers. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is dead, and {CHIEF} has been told. The toll-stone at the High Pass switchback bears a fresh notch cut beside the old one - the deeper gouge that has waited eleven winters since Brennic, {CHIEF}'s road-brother, was hauled off the pass in Lord Halric's chain-cart and never seen again past the Gilded Mile. The {REWARD} denars are weighed and pouched at the cairn-fire, and the road-baron's standing with the traveler-killer is set a degree firmer. The chain that took Brennic is answered with a chain of silver. The pass remembers, and the pass is paid.

Word climbed the switchbacks at first thaw - {TARGET} dead in a ditch beside the lowland road, ridden down by some Halric vassal's outriders over a quarrel that was never {CHIEF}'s. The chief took the news on the toll-stone, one thumb tracing the old notch he cut the day Brennic was hauled off the pass in a chain-cart, and said nothing for a long count. The grudge stood answered; the score had not been settled by the hand he sent. {CHIEF} weighed it cold. Quarter-pay was counted out onto the stone - {REDUCED_REWARD} denars, thin coin for a thin closure - and the bond between road-baron and hired blade was set a smaller notch firmer than before, honored but unwarmed, the kill owed but never owed back.

{VILLAGE} sits in the saddle of the lowland green, and {LORD} keeps it. A Vlandian baron-clan, that one - pretty banner, soft hands, harder pride. Three winters running they have refused my pass-toll. Three winters their wool has crossed the saddle-path at night, smuggled under straw, untaxed and unblessed. Last spring they took Brakka's nephew off the high road and worked him in their quarry until his lungs gave out. Brakka is my chain-warden. Brakka has not slept proper since. So {VILLAGE} owes me, and the boy owes a debt I mean to collect in stone and smoke.
Go down through the cleft after the morning mist lifts, not before - the lowland watch keeps a horn on the chapel roof and the mist hides their eyes, not yours. Burn the wool sheds first. Take the draft horses, the iron, the salt. Leave the chapel; I am not at war with their saints, only with their lord. Any quarry-warden you find, you put him on his knees and you ask him about a boy named Tavik. Then you do what your hand tells you.
For this work, {REWARD} when you ride back over the pass. {CHIEF} keeps his word. {LORD} does not. That is the whole of the lesson.

{CHIEF} names {VILLAGE} on the lowland side of the saddle-path and spits the name like a stone from his boot. The Vlandian holding of {LORD} has refused the pass-toll three winters running, run wool over Skarvac's road in moonless caravans, and last spring his chain-warden Brakka's sister-son was hooked off that road and worked dead in the village quarry. The boy is buried under their slag. The toll is unpaid. The chief wants the village broken to ash and the lord's wool burned where it lies. He sets the contract at {REWARD} denars, paid on the smoke.

{VILLAGE} burned to the stone-sills. {CHIEF} stood at the saddle-mouth and watched the smoke roll down the lowland road that had refused his toll three winters running. {LORD}'s wool-bales went up first, then the quarry sheds where Brakka's nephew had been worked under the lash until his back broke. The chain-warden himself walked the ash with a long iron and turned over what was left, looking for the boy's name cut into a beam. He did not find it, but he found enough. The pass-debt was closed. {CHIEF} counted out {REWARD} on a flat rock and pushed it across without a word.

Word reached the High Pass at first light: {VILLAGE} was ash before {CHIEF}'s axes ever crossed the saddle-path. Some other blade had drawn the lord {LORD}'s blood and burned the wool-sheds clean, leaving nothing for the chain-warden Brakka to settle in his nephew's name.
{CHIEF} took the news standing, said little, spat once at the snow. The toll was paid, in a manner of speaking - just not by his hand, and not in the coin his oath required. The quarry that broke Brakka's boy lies cold now, and that was the lion's share of the bargain.
He counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} on the trestle and pushed it across without meeting the eye. Half-debt for half-work. The road, he muttered, remembers who walked it first.

Cold. Real cold, not market-cold — the cold of a place that has no use for you.
Your breath whitens. The horse shifts its weight under you and you feel the slate slip beneath its hoof, hear the small bright clatter of it falling away into nothing, falling further than seems reasonable. You stop counting after the third bounce.
The trail tilts up and does not stop tilting. Loose scree. A switchback so narrow that one rider goes single-file and the other waits.
Look up.
A gate. Iron straps, oak gone grey from the weather, set between two raw walls of stone the mountain itself raised before any hands shaped them. Above the gate, a tower so narrow only one man can stand sentry there.
He is standing there.
He has been standing there since you came around the last bend, perhaps longer. His face is a smudge against the torch behind him. He does not call down. He does not lift the horn at his hip. He watches.
You watched him watching you for two long minutes. Then he turned aside, satisfied with something, and went back to his fire.
Inside the walls: smoke. A horse blanket drying on a line stretched between two boulders. Someone laughs once, low, and is hushed.
No banner flies above this place. No standard. None is needed.
The mountain is the banner.
You sit your horse below that iron gate and feel — for the first time on this errand, perhaps for the first time in a long while — that it may not be you who came here to take a measure.
It may be the other way around.
The horn on the tower lifts, finally. Not loud. Not a war-horn. The note of a man calling his lord to the gate to look at something interesting that has wandered up the road.
Pay for safe passage in the mountains. (500 denars)
Skarvac scribes a sigil on a strip of leather. "Wear this where my men can see."
"Our people held this pass before the empire had a name for it. We are older than any king."
"Mountain-spirits. Avalanche-mother. The cold star."
Skarvac chuckles. "This pass has eaten men with bigger swords than yours."
He inclines his head. "Strong walls. Strong men. Strong tolls."
Skarvac pours from an old cask of stolen Sturgian mead. "Tolls have to go somewhere. This is where most go. Drink, friend."
Your party gets bunks in the tower's lower hall. The walls are stone. The wind doesn't reach in. Your party rises strong.
Visit the cliff-forge.
A bearded man hammers iron into shape at a forge built into the rock. "Stolen ore, stolen tools, stolen apprentice. But the iron is good. The price is fair."
Browse the toll records. (100 denars)
Skarvac flips through a battered ledger. "We track every party that passes. One of them was another camp. Take it."
Visit the mountain-spirit shrine.
A tiny shrine of stacked stones at the cliff-edge. Old rags tied to it. Skarvac bows quickly. "We leave a coin. The mountain has been kind."
"Sturgian merchants started taking the western pass to avoid us."
"A noble's daughter eloped through here last week."
"There's a silver vein in the cliffs above us."
"A Vlandian heir was lost in an avalanche eight years ago."
"The empire's road tax goes through here. The collector pays us off."
"There's a hidden monastery somewhere on this peak."
"A caravan of pilgrims comes through every Saint's Day."
"Mountain Khergit clans are rising again on the eastern slopes."
"A dragon-bone, they call it — found in the highest pass."
"The pass freezes in deep winter. Whatever they were carrying is still up there."
"Twenty loads of iron ore. The mountain pays us in stone, but stone breaks. Bring iron and you've shown you understand the trade up here."
He breaks a chunk of ore in his hand and grunts. "Pure. Not the rust the southerners pass off. Trade with us, mountain-walker."
20 iron ore
"Thirty hardwood. The pass-fortifications need shoring up before the snows. Lumber's heavy, but we'll know who's serious."
He hefts a beam, tests its weight. "Good wood. Cut clean. The mountain remembers who carried for it."
30 hardwood
"Twenty-five pelts. The men who guard the high pass freeze if they don't lay thick under cloak. Bring fur or stay out of the snows."
He runs a thumb across the fur, grunts approval. "Heavy coats. The men will hold the high stones tonight."
25 fur
"Thirty ore and twenty hardwood. We're forging new pikes for the pass garrison. Bring both and you walk the high places with us."
He inspects a pike-shaft, nods. "Good iron. Good wood. The mountain is yours when you come up. Take what you need."
30 iron ore + 20 hardwood
"Forty iron and ten sets of tools. The smithy's running cold and the armorers need both. Heavy haul, mountain-walker — but it's how a man earns the high places."
He weighs the iron in one hand, tests a hammer-haft with the other. "Now we forge proper. The high stones know your name."
40 iron + 10 tools
"Two pack-mules and twenty-five iron. We move loads to the high pass that no horse can carry. You bring the beasts and the metal, you're one of us when the mountain calls."
He pats the lead mule's shoulder. "Good beasts. Steady. The pass is yours to walk now, like blood-kin."
2 mules + 25 iron
"Eighty iron and twenty wrought-iron ingots. The pass-armory will be the finest east of Pravend. Only a Reaver-friend brings this. Take your time, brother — but bring it all."
He runs a hand along the rack of finished pikes, then looks at you long. "You've done what no southerner does. The mountain calls you brother now. The high stones are yours."
80 iron + 20 wrought iron
"Fifteen refined-iron, fifty hardwood, thirty fur. The whole high garrison re-equips in one stroke. A blood-kin's task. You bring this, the mountain knows your name forever."
He stands silent a long moment, then claps your shoulder hard enough to bruise. "You re-armed our high pass. The Mountain Bandits will remember your blood and your name."
15 refined iron + 50 hardwood + 30 fur
"Twenty loads of iron ore. The mountain pays us in stone, but stone breaks. Bring iron and you've shown you understand the trade up here."
He breaks a chunk of ore in his hand and grunts. "Pure. Not the rust the southerners pass off. Trade with us, mountain-walker."
20 iron ore
"Thirty ore and twenty hardwood. We're forging new pikes for the pass garrison. Bring both and you walk the high places with us."
He inspects a pike-shaft, nods. "Good iron. Good wood. The mountain is yours when you come up. Take what you need."
30 iron ore + 20 hardwood
Repel the marked Vlandian probing force that approaches the High Pass within the next day — destroy the party where it climbs.
The Skarvac of the High Pass accepts your oath; the rite is sealed with a shallow palm-cut on the hereditary boundary stone of the pass.
Skarvac slams the boundary stone with the flat of his hand. "The pass is closed to you. Find a lower road, friend — this one ends here."
Ulan Twice-Banished
The Third Writ
You. Rider. The chief wants you at his fire. Some khan put his name on paper again — bounty, banishment, the whole song. Third time now. He laughed once when the scout told him. Just once. Go.

A khan's column crosses my grass this week, traveler. Guard riders, a polished emissary, satchels of sealed paper — tax-rolls, marriage-contracts, and one writ more. Banishment and bounty, renewed, my name under the seal. The third ever written against me. Twice a clan cast me out with words spoken at a fire. Now a khan does it with ink, from a hall I have never stood in. I want that writ. Not burned on the road — carried here, seal unbroken, into my hands. A man should own the paper that hunts him. Take it however the day allows. The wind will tell me how it went, so do not dress the story.
Good. Ride wide and read the dust — a column that heavy waters twice a day and hates every stop. Bring the seal unbroken, traveler. It has been years since anyone wrote to me.
As you like. But the writ still rides, and paper outlives riders. Once it reaches a wall-town, every bounty-man on the steppe learns my new price. Think again before the column finds a road.
The column still rides, traveler. Paper does not tire. Go and fetch my name back before some clerk in a wall-town files me away.
Khan's Emissary Column
The Khan's Emissary
Intercept the khan's emissary column on the steppe and secure the sealed writ of banishment and bounty written against Ulan Twice-Banished.
The writ has been taken from the emissary's column. Return to Ulan Twice-Banished at his camp and place the paper in his hands.

You are addressing an emissary of the khan's household. I do not treat with road-thieves. Whatever you imagine this column carries, it is worth less than what the khan pays for your kind by the head. Move aside.
Count my spears, then hand over the banishment writ.
Counted. Very well — the writ, seal unbroken, as it left the hall. A receipt is customary. I will not be asking for one.
Twelve hundred denars says that satchel rides lighter.
Documents are lost to weather all the time — the khan's clerks allow for it. Take it and ride. I was watching the horizon. I saw nothing.
The paper comes with me. Draw if you disagree.
Riders — earn your keep! Close the column! The satchels do not fall while one lance stands!
The khan's paper does not stop for beggars. Twenty lances ride behind me — petition them, if you must.

Give it here. Seal unbroken — you listened. Banishment renewed. Price raised. Good. A man should cost more at my age than he did at nineteen. No, it does not burn. The first two were written about me. This one is mine. It goes in the saddle-chest, with the things I keep.

Ash and crows two days before you reached it, my scouts say. Rain-soaked, seal crushed, half the ink run grey. Even my banishments reach me secondhand now. I keep it anyway. Half a writ, half a price, traveler — do not argue. I have been undercut before.
Twice-Banished Khan

Ulan was born to a steppe-clan that had ridden the western grass for nine generations, third son of a chief who had killed his own father to claim the herd-leadership. Ulan grew up in the ger-camps, learned bow and saddle by six, and rode his first cattle-raid at eleven. The first banishment came when he was nineteen — he killed an uncle who had insulted his mother, and his father (who had not loved his brother but loved tradition more) sentenced him to ride west alone. Ulan returned a year later with twenty followers, found his father had been killed by another rival in the meantime, and was promptly banished a second time by the rival who had killed his father — on the grounds that an exiled son should not return to claim a clan that did not exile him. Neither banishment took root. The rival who claimed the clan died in a hunting accident the following spring; Ulan's mother sent word that the herd-elders would accept him back, but by then he had built a band of his own and saw no reason to return. He rides the western steppe along a line that no major faction patrols, because no major faction owns it; his band raids what passes for trade-traffic out there, and he answers to no khan but the open sky.

The Steppe Bandits are not a clan and never were. They are the people no clan would keep — twice-exiled men, sons whose chiefs sentenced them to the long ride, daughters whose marriages dishonored a herd, oath-breakers whose oaths cost a herd to the wrong neighbor. Ulan was banished twice from his own family before he was thirty, and the band coalesced around his second exile. They keep three yurts and ride between them; they have never built a permanent camp and never will. They take from caravans crossing the steppe, from trade-trains foolish enough to ride without escort, from the rare imperial outpost stupid enough to be built where the grass grows tall. The signature of a Steppe Bandit raid is that there is no signature: they come, they take, the camp moves a week's ride before the news of the raid catches up. The Khanate has placed three separate bounties on Ulan and pulled all three back when the bounty-hunters returned with shaved heads and no horses. The eastern clans regard the Bandits as a dirty necessity — every chief who has ever needed a deniable rider on a deniable errand has known where the three yurts were that month.

The small, leathery rider dismounts without ceremony — a habit, perhaps, of a man banished from too many courts to bother with their forms. He leads his horse to meet you the way a host welcomes a traveler at the door of a gēr. His eyes do not match the welcome. "A guest. The gods send guests, even to Ulan Twice-Banished. You will eat with us, traveler. You will trade with us. Then you will leave alive — if the gods still send guests when we have spoken."

Ulan doesn't lead his horse out to meet you anymore — the courtesy is reserved for strangers. He stays at the gēr-flap, raises a cup, and waits for you to come in. "A guest twice over is no longer a guest, traveler. Eat. Drink. Trade. The gods who sent you the first time send you again, and Ulan listens this time without his hand on a knife."

A guest's name is wind under the gēr, traveler. The gods send guests; only deeds tell us which guests the gods meant. Ulan has a thing his men need done. Do it, and you become a guest the gods sent for a reason — not just one passing by.
The Steppe Bandits' camp is a tight cluster of three yurts, horses picketed in a ring around them. They keep moving — the camp will be gone in a week.

Ride west from the last watering-stand, two days hard across the open grass. You will find no road, no marker stone, no priest's cairn to count from - only the wind in the grass and the sun walking the sky. On the second evening look for three yurts pulled tight together like horses against a wolf, and a fire-pit dug shallow so the smoke does not climb. The felt door of the middle yurt is painted with a single sun. That is {HIDEOUT_NAME}, and that is my fire.
My riders watch the four horizons before you see the yurts. They will count your horses from a ridge you cannot find, and read your saddle-cloth before you read the grass. Come in slow and come in open-handed - reins loose, weapons sheathed, your banner showing high enough that the steppe knows your face. A rider will cross your path and turn his horse beside yours. That is the welcome. Follow him in.
Come fast, come hidden, come with an unmarked spear, and the first you will know of us is the arrow already in your throat. The steppe keeps no graves, traveler - the crows do that work. But ride to my fire the right way and you drink mare's milk under my roof, and what is mine is yours for the night. We will be gone from this ground in a week. The grass forgets us. Ride while the wind still knows the way.

The Khuzait khans send their riders into my watering-country like I am a stranger on my own grass. Twice now this season a noyan of the khan's household has crossed the salt-flats with his lancers, hunting me as a wolf hunts a lame mare. I know his banner. I rode under it once, before the council struck my name from the long-rolls and called me bandit. He drinks from cups my father gave him. Now he hunts me with them at his belt.
The Empire sends tax-wagons up the old caravan-road from the southern cities, and their cataphracts ride heavy enough that the steppe-grass remembers their weight for a week. I do not touch them often. Their commanders write down the names of every man they kill, and a written name is a curse that follows a clan three generations. The Aserai send no levies this far north, but their coin-traders ride with paid Vlandian sellswords - mercenaries, not vassals, and they ask no questions when a column goes missing.
The khan himself, the great khan, he has not spoken my name in seven winters. That is the deepest wound. If you ride khan's-country with his banner on your lance, traveler, my watchers will read you from three ridges away. Ride with no banner, or ride with one he hates. The steppe has long sight and a longer memory.

Borchu of the Wolf-Khans is a name I do not say twice. We grew up drinking the same milk, raided the same Khuzait outriders as boys, and when my own people cast me out he was the one who turned his horse and rode the other way. I owe him no blood. I owe him no fire. If our grass touches I ride wide, and he rides wider. That is the peace between Wolf-Khan and Twice-Banished, and it is colder than the deep winter.
Granny Hod's forest band sent a runner to my watering-stand last moon. She wants steppe-horses, fast ones, and she pays in Battanian silver that still has the boyar's mark on it. I will trade. She keeps her woods, I keep my open sky. Skarvac's pass-lords up in the mountains are another matter - they robbed two of my outriders on the Pravend road and left them for the crows. I have not forgotten. When the snow comes I will ride a hundred men up that pass and we will see how high his rocks make him.
The Slavers under Khalid have gone quiet. Three seasons no caravan, no chain-song on the dune road. That silence is not peace. That is a man counting his teeth before he bites.

A Khuzait silk-train rolls west from Makeb every ten days - eight wagons, twenty horse-guard, a captain called Tsegen who drinks airag from sundown to moonrise and trusts his outriders to do his looking. They water at the third stand past the broken kurgan, the one with the leaning stone where my grandfather pastured before the khan put a price on his shadow. The escort spreads thin at the watering because the horses must be unsaddled in turn. That is the hour. Three breaths of charge, no more, and the silk is yours.
The wagons carry Khuzait silk going to Vlandian factors at Pravend, and on the return-leg they carry silver going back to the khan's tax-riders. Either direction pays. The silver is heavier and slower-tracked - the khan does not count what bandits take, only what officials lose, and Tsegen will swear it was steppe-wolves to save his own neck.
If you ride, ride at second-watering, not first. Twenty horse will do it. Take the silk, leave the wagons burning, scatter the remounts toward Borchu's range so the trackers chase the Wolf-Khan's hoofprints and not yours. I take my own moon next quarter. There is steppe enough for two hunts. Do not be on this road when mine comes - I have been twice-banished and I do not share waterholes.

You ask the long-rolls question, rider, and you ask it on open ground where no walls can hide the answer. Sit. The wind is the only listener I trust, and it has heard worse from me. A khan who has been struck twice from the rolls does not give his name away again without weighing the giver to the half-ounce.
When I bled, I bled for a banner that is no longer flown. For the brother-khan who held my left when the rolls were first sealed against me. For the watering-stand widow who fed my horses the season after my own people spat my name into the dust. Twice my name was struck. Twice. And still I keep an oath-list of my own making, short as a winter shadow, and I add to it the way other men add a wife - rarely, and never twice the same way.
Ride with me where the grass goes thin. Cut a road open when the south thinks it closed. Stand beside a banner that no rolls will ever bless - mine, raised on steppe I claim by hoof and not by writ - and the long-rolls of my own keeping will learn another name. Ask again, traveler, when the wind knows you by something other than your face.

Then it is spoken, and the steppe hears it. Stand by the watering-stand. Drink from my horn first - I drink second tonight, as is right when a brother is made. Take my knife - the one I carried when they struck me from the rolls, when the khanate spat my name into the long grass. Open your palm where mine still bears the old white seam. Press them together. The blood runs into the earth and the earth remembers. The horses smell it. The wind carries it east to the camps that exiled me and west to the camps that never will. There. It is done. The mare-milk is poured. Your name is in my mouth now and it tastes like my own.
Brother in the steppe tongue is not a soft word. It means my saddle is your saddle. My yurt-pole holds your felt. The arrows in my quiver answer to your hand. When I was twice-banished I had no kin to ride for me - now I have you, and you have a khan who was a khan before they tore the title from him and is a khan again because he says so. Your mother is my mother. Your hunger is my hunger. My own banner, the one they tried to burn, flies for you now.
The open country knows your name. The watering-stand knows it. The lords who banished me twice will hear it on the wind and they will know a brother of Ulan rides the long grass. You are kin-by-blood to the Twice-Banished. Ride.

Then it is answered. I asked once if you would bleed for me, and you did not stand here and swear it with a smooth tongue - you went out and opened a vein in the world and brought me back the proof, dripping. The deed first, the word after. That is steppe-order. A lesser man would have galloped in with a speech long as a winter and a saddle light as a fledgling. You came in heavy and spoke last. Good. The Khan I was before they struck me from the rolls would have known you on sight.
Hear, then, the shape of what we are now. Not brothers - that is a hearth-word, and this is a saddle-word. From this hour my riders are your riders when the horn calls, and your feud is the feud of every man who eats from my pot. When the lowland lords ride to break you, they will find steppe-bows at their flanks and no clean road home. In return I take your sword-arm in mine when MY banner - my own banner, the one they tried to burn - rises against the kingdom that twice-banished me. Blood for blood. Saddle for saddle. Called once, answered always.
The wind carries this further than any herald. It will reach the watering-stands by dawn, the long-rolls by the next moon, and the men who exiled me before the snow is off the grass. Ride hard, ally. The steel is drawn. The bond is iron.

Done. Ten of my riders for seven days - I will cut them from the herd myself before the long-rolls are sung again. My second is Bayartu Iron-Stirrup, struck from the rolls beside me at Khuzait court and twice as patient with fools. He rides at your right hand. The banished know how to hold a line that is not their own. Seven days. I count them in moons, not coins.
Hear my terms, traveler. If a saddle-mate of mine falls under your banner, you bring me his bowstring and the name of the man who took him - I will ride out for that name myself when the loan is done. If he lives, you send him back with his horse and his honor in the same shape you found them. My riders do not draw bow for cattle-thieves or village quarrels. While they wear your dust, your war is mine - so spend them on work worth a Khan's sons.
The banished will know who borrowed them. See they have a story worth telling when the seven moons close.

His name is {TARGET}, and his banner hangs over {HOME} like it has a right to the sky. It does not. Nine summers ago his riders crossed the Bokai grass while my father was at the long-rolls naming the new foals, and they took my sister Altani off the colt-line for the bride-price of a Khuzait under-lord. She hanged herself in his hall before the second moon. The under-lord paid {TARGET} in salt and silver. {TARGET} kept both. I was struck from the rolls for failing to ride after her - my own banner burned by my uncles - and {TARGET} has slept easy under nine winters of stars that owed me her name.
He rides with twelve lances and a Khuzait herald who whispers his routes to anyone with a coin and a soft word. The herald waters his horse at the well outside {HOME} every third dawn. {TARGET} hunts cranes in the marsh-flats when the wind turns south - he goes light, four guards, no scout. Take him on the marsh road. He cannot run in mud.
{REWARD} denars when the herald brings me his ring, traveler. The silver is owed. The salt is owed. Altani is owed more than either, but the steppe keeps what coin cannot pay. Ride, and let the wind tell me when it is done.

{CHIEF} has named {TARGET} of {HOME} as the lord whose hide must answer for a banner cut down twice. The wound is old and exact - a winter raid on the Twice-Banished khan's own ger-camp on the Bokai flats, a wife and two sons dragged off in the dust, and {TARGET}'s outriders riding home with Ulan's own horsetail standard tied to a saddle-strap as trophy. The long-rolls of his fathers were struck through by men who served {TARGET}, and Ulan rides now with no clan-name behind his own. The Twice-Banished offers {REWARD} in caravan-silver for the deed. The steppe is wide. A banner waits to be answered. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is dead, and {CHIEF} has been told. The long-roll has been read aloud at the felt-wall, and the name that was scratched twice with a knife-tip - the name of the lord who set Ulan's banner in the dirt at Burkhan-Tal and laughed while the heralds struck him from the clan-rolls - is read no more. {REWARD} denars sit weighed at the chief's saddle, and the debt between khan-without-a-tent and the rider who answered for him is stamped a degree closer. Ulan rides under his own banner tonight. The two banishments are answered. The steppe keeps the rest, as the steppe keeps everything.

Word reached the ger-camp at dusk: {TARGET} was dead, run through by a rival lord's outriders on a frost-rutted road three valleys east. {CHIEF} heard it out twice, then went quiet. The long-rolls came down from the saddle-chest, and the knife-tip that had twice scratched the names of his wife and two sons - the ones dragged screaming from this very camp at Burkhan-Tal - now drew a thin third line beside them. The grudge stood answered. The killing had not been earned, though, and that mattered to a man whose pride had been banished twice already. The thin coin was counted out without ceremony: {REDUCED_REWARD} denars, quarter-pay for a quarter-debt. The bond sits a smaller notch firmer, no warmer.

{VILLAGE}. Say the name again so the wind hears it. That dung-heap pays its tribute in horses and felt to {LORD}, and {LORD} sat at the council fire two winters past and watched the elders strike my name from the long-rolls. Twice they have done this to me. Twice. Once when I was a boy of nineteen and my father's herds were still warm in the grass, and again when I came back grown and asked only for a tent and a name. They voted. They drank kumis while they voted. {LORD}'s own uncle raised the cup.
Ride at dawn when the felt-makers are at the racks and the horse-lines are loose. Take the herds first - every mare, every gelding, every yearling foal. Burn the felt only after you have driven the horses two valleys clear. Leave the old women. Leave the shrine-pole. I want {LORD} to find his village standing and empty, his wealth on four legs running east, and his name spoken in laughter from here to the Khuzait border.
When you bring me proof, {REWARD} is yours, weighed out in good silver and not the clipped coin the council uses. Ulan keeps his word. The council forgot that. {LORD} will remember.

{CHIEF} speaks the name {VILLAGE} as though spitting a stone from his teeth. It is a tributary of the Khuzait clan whose elders, sitting twice in council, voted to strike his name from the long-rolls - first when he was a boy, again when he was a man grown.
Their khan still drinks mare's milk paid in horses and felt sent up from {VILLAGE} each summer. {CHIEF} would see those tributes burned in the dust, the herds scattered, and a message carried back to that council: a name cut from the rolls is not a name silenced.
He offers {REWARD} for the village put to torch, and the silver-tongued {LORD} shamed before his elders.

{VILLAGE} burned through the night, and {CHIEF} watched the felt-roofs collapse without dismounting. The horse-tribute would not reach the council that struck his name twice from the long-rolls; the felt would not warm the elders who voted him gone. {LORD}'s house had paid in horses and felt for years, and now they paid in ash. {CHIEF} took the {REWARD} from a saddlebag of a rider sent to find him, weighed the coin once, and spat into the embers. Twice-banished, he said, and twice-remembered. Let the council count their losses in the morning.

Word reached {CHIEF} on the cold wind that {VILLAGE} was already smoke. Other riders, faster knives, had cut the throat of {LORD}'s tributary before his own hooves could mark the snow.
He sat long over the news, working a horse-hair plait between his fingers. The council that struck his name from the long-rolls a second time would hear of it by morning, and they would think their khan's felt and horse-tribute saved by some kinder hand. They would not know he had ridden against them at all.
"The mare is dead," he said at last, flat as old iron. "Another wolf ate her. The meat is gone." He counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} without looking up, and waved the matter from his tent.

The eye, out here, is a thing you stop trusting first.
By noon today you have unbelieved a lake — a real one, blue and calm, all the way to where the road met its shore and the shore became dust under your hooves. You have unbelieved a tree, twice; both trees were standing horsemen the wind had not yet reached. You have unbelieved a fire, which was nothing, a trick of sun on dry grass. The flat country owes you nothing and shows you everything, and the showing is mostly a lie.
So you do not, at first, believe the smoke.
It lifts off the rim of the world at the wrong hour for any honest fire, in the wrong colour for any kind of cookfire you have ridden up on, and you are tired enough that the eye has done worse to you before sundown. You ride toward it the way you have ridden toward every false promise the day has offered — without hope, only forward, because forward is the only direction the steppe gives you.
A mile.
Two.
The smoke holds.
A mile after that there are shapes under it. The shapes do not dissolve as you close on them. You have ridden close enough now that they should — the heat-haze should pull them apart into nothing, the way it has pulled every other dishonest shape apart today — and they do not. Three felt tents in a tight cluster. A picket-line of horses, some still saddled. Smoke that smells like real wood, not like the eye's idea of wood.
You sit your horse on the rise and you understand that the steppe has stopped lying for a moment, has held something up and let it stay solid in the heat, and that this is a courtesy the steppe pays only to the very few who live light enough to be allowed.
Below, an old man checks each picket-knot by feel. A woman packs a cook-pot away though the night is only half gone. A small girl sleeps in a saddle, certain it will carry her somewhere safer by morning.
Ulan Twice-Banished looks up from his picket-line and lifts a hand without surprise. He has been expecting somebody. He did not know it would be you.
You ride down before the steppe changes its mind.
Buy a steppe pony.
Ulan whistles. A boy brings forward three ponies. "Cheap because we steal them. Hardy because we ride them."
"Twice banished, twice free. The great khan called us small."
"Sky. Wind. Wolf."
Ulan whistles. Three riders appear over the ridge with bows drawn. "You are loud. Loud is bad here."
He gestures to a horse, almost smiling. "The horse is a friend. The friend is good."
The riders pass a skin of fermented mare's milk. Ulan drinks first. "Old way. Honors the guest. Refuse, you insult. Accept, you're brother for the night."
You sleep in the central yurt. The fire never goes out. Your party rises with the steppe-wind in their hair.
Trade with the yurt-maker.
A woman lays out felt panels, leather harness, simple tools. "Steppe goods. Light, strong, packs small. Travel-ready."
Hear the old khan's wisdom.
An ancient man, white-bearded, sits by the fire. He speaks slowly. "Listen. Once a khan thought he was the steppe. The steppe disagreed. Same steppe, no khan."
Hire a pony-breaker. (200 denars)
A grim-faced rider takes your horses and runs them through the steppe paces. "Now they ride sharper. Worth the coin." Morale rises.
"A khan's brother was assassinated last month."
"The great khanate is moving its herds west again."
"A Khuzait trader at Akakalat fences anything for half-price."
"A Vlandian noble pays in gold for steppe ponies."
"There's a buried camp on the steppe — Khuzait dead from a winter siege long ago."
"A wandering shaman lives north of here. He cures horse-sickness."
"The grass burns hot every year now."
"An imperial cartographer was captured by us last year."
"Someone in the great clans pays for stolen horses, no questions."
"There's a rumored treasure-mound from the old khanate."
"Ten horses. Sound legs, sound wind. We are nothing without mounts."
He claps a hand on the lead horse. "You ride well. The steppe knows you."
10 horses
"Thirty felt. Yurt-cloth, saddle-padding, men's coats. We can't camp without it."
He runs his hand over the bolts. "Properly pressed. The yurts will hold. Trade with us."
30 felt
"Five pack-camels. We range south sometimes — camels carry water where horses fail."
He pats the lead camel. "Strong-back beasts. The deep south is reachable now."
5 pack camels
"Twenty-five horses. A whole new herd. Bring them, and the open country is yours to ride."
He runs his hand through the lead mare's mane. "Magnificent stock. The steppe rides with you."
25 horses
"Fifteen horses and five camels. Mixed string for the long-range raid into the deep south."
He inspects the mixed string. "This rides as far as the spice country. Take what you need."
15 horses + 5 camels
"Fifty felt and ten horses. Full re-mount and re-yurt for the cold-camp shift."
He surveys the camp shrugging into new walls. "Now we overwinter strong. Take what you need."
50 felt + 10 horses
"Five Khuzait war-mounts and thirty pack-horses. The clan goes to war this spring. Only blood-kin help us mount the cohort."
He bows his head, the steppe-warrior's salute. "You have remounted us for war. Ride beside me, brother."
5 war horses + 30 horses
"A hundred felt, thirty horses, ten camels. We're moving the whole clan across the steppe to a new winter range."
He clasps your shoulder steppe-style. "The whole clan survives because of you. The steppe sings your name."
100 felt + 30 horses + 10 camels
Burn the standing-stone marker of the clan that exiled Ulan — destroy the small honor-guard patrolling the site.
The Ulan Twice-Banished accepts your oath; the rite is sealed solo, three arrows shot into the exile-marker on horseback alone, then once around the stone.
Ulan looses one arrow at the dust beside your foot. "The marker is yours and mine no longer. Ride. The next arrow finds higher."
Bjornulf Salt-Tongue
The Shore-Price

Oi — you the captain's landwalker? Good. He's in a black mood. Some harbor-rat impounded a beached keel and sold the crew's shares at auction. The silver's rolling inland on a wagon right now. Go hear him before he bites somebody.

You know what a share is, landwalker? It is not coin. It is the oath made countable. The Herring-Bane crew — nine oars, good men — beached on a storm-tide and walked to harbor for timber. The harbormaster impounded their keel and auctioned their shares off the quay like salvage. Like they were drowned already. Now a pay-wagon hauls that silver inland under guard, his factor at the head of it, counting what is not his. Bring the crew's silver home — every clipped coin. I keep maybe half my oaths, traveler. Ask anyone. But I swore on the salt that nine men get their cut, and this is the half I keep.
Good. The wagon rolls slow — silver is heavy and so is guilt. His factor holds the key and thinks paper is armor. Bring me the box whole. I weigh the shares out myself, on sail-cloth, the old way.
No? Then drink slower and think on it, traveler. A share stolen from one crew is stolen from every crew that ever pulled an oar for me. The wagon rolls while you chew.
One tide at a time, landwalker. You carry my errand already — finish it, then we talk shares.
Harbormaster's Pay-Wagon
Harbormaster's Factor
Intercept the harbormaster's pay-wagon on the inland road and recover the strongbox of auctioned crew shares. The column is led by the harbormaster's factor.
The strongbox is recovered. Return the silver to Bjornulf Salt-Tongue so the shares can be paid out to the beached crew.
This consignment travels under the harbor seal — lawful salvage, assessed and auctioned. If you have a grievance, the office hears petitions on quarter-days. Stand away from the wagon.
That silver is crew shares. Hand down the box and keep breathing.
I — yes. Under protest — recorded protest. Guards, ground your spears. The key is — here, the key, take it. I will enter it in the ledger as seized by force of arms. Which it is. Which it plainly is.
The salt does not file petitions. Draw.
Guards! Guards, to the wagon — spears, form on the — kill them, kill them now!
No. No, I think not. I have counted your riders and I have counted my escort, and mine is the longer column. The consignment proceeds. Go back to your beach.

Sail-cloth on the shingle, landwalker — nine piles, weighed twice against the mast-tally. Watch my hands, all of you. Watch that nothing sticks. A share is the oath made countable. The salt heard me swear it; now it hears it paid. Your cut pours last and pours full. Drink with us — the Herring-Bane crew owes you a song, and I intend to make them sing it badly and long.

An inland crew broke the box before you reached it, landwalker — what washed back is half, gathered coin by coin out of ditches and taverns. Nine thin piles tonight, weighed the same as fat ones. The sea robs clean. Only a landsman robs a robbed man twice. Half shares for you as well — the salt keeps its arithmetic even when thieves don't.
Salt-Tongue Captain

Bjornulf was a fjord-fisherman's son in a Sturgian coastal village so small the imperial maps did not record its name. He went to sea at eight as a netting-boy on his father's two-thwart skiff, and by fifteen he was crewing a longship out of a different fjord, having sworn off his father's business after his father drowned drunkenly in three feet of harbour-water. His first raid was with a Sturgian crown-licensed corsair against an imperial salt-shipment; his second was the same corsair, against the same crown, after the corsair stopped paying his shares. Bjornulf took the longship in the harbour with five other crewmen, sailed it south, and has been raiding ever since under no flag he did not paint himself. He speaks five languages badly and signs three of them properly; the sea is his only good language, and his crews speak it fluently regardless of where they were born. His longships have raided the imperial coast for so long the Sturgian crown stopped acknowledging he ever existed — easier than admitting they cannot catch him. The Empire makes no such pretense; they have placed a bounty of fifteen thousand denars on his head, twelve thousand on his Salt-Tongue cousin, and eight thousand on the longship that was once theirs.

The Sea Raiders are the oldest organized bandit-line in the modern kingdoms — a thread of fjord-raiders whose family-rolls run unbroken through six imperial reigns, four Sturgian crown-changes, and one full inter-kingdom war. Bjornulf's great-great-grandfather rowed the same coast Bjornulf rows now, and the longboat-keels he hauls onto the beach are built from the same stand of pine his ancestors timber-stamped a century and a half ago. Coastal fjord-villages supply the core of the band — second sons of fishing families with no boat to inherit, displaced shore-men whose harbors were taxed past sustainability, and the occasional Battanian fisher who could not abide a Vlandian harbor-master. They strike inland from the coast — never far, but far enough that the inland lords cannot quite credit what is happening. They do not raid villages they have raided in the same year; the Salt-Tongue Code, which Bjornulf inherited and his great-great-grandfather wrote, forbids it. The Sturgian crown has used them as auxiliaries in two coastal wars and disowned them in three. Among the coastal villages they are half-feared, half-counted-on — the way every coastal village half-counts on the sea itself.

The longhall falls silent when you push past the door-leather. The huge man at the high seat — beard bleached to driftwood-grey by salt and seasons — looks up from a horn of mead. His grin comes slow, the grin of a man amused that another fool has wandered into his hall. "A landwalker! And alive, even! Bjornulf has not seen one walk in unblooded since the snows came. Speak quick, traveler — my mead grows cold, and so does my mood."

The longhall does not fall silent for you anymore. Mead-horns tilt in your direction, a few crewmen call out names you haven't yet learned. Bjornulf himself rises this time, salt-bleached beard split by a grin that has actual amusement in it. "The landwalker returns! Twice past my door is a season's worth of luck, traveler. Sit, sit — Bjornulf pours for those his hall counts as half-friend now."

Bjornulf hears names every tide-fall, landwalker. Names wash up and wash out with the wrack. Crew-names — those carve into the longhall posts and stay. Earn yours. There's an errand my crew would have you run. Do it, and your name goes on Bjornulf's posts; not before.
The Sea Raiders' camp is on the beach — longboats hauled up on rollers, tents made of sail-cloth. The smell is fish, tar, and seaweed.

Follow the coast road north out of Varcheg until the shingle turns black under your boots and the gulls get loud enough to drown your own thinking. Half a tide on you'll smell us before you see us - fish-rack drying split cod on the wind, tar-smoke off the keels, the iron pot we keep wedged in the beach-stones never quite off the boil. Our hold lies at {HIDEOUT_NAME}, tucked behind a fold of cliff that the tide-charts pretend isn't there. Walk past the sail-cloth tents above the high-water line and you've already walked in.
My boys watch from the headland with the longboats hauled up on rollers behind them. They'll have your shape against the surf-line a good mile before you've smelled the cod. Come down the shingle slow, hands where a bowman can count your fingers, and shout my name into the wind - Bjornulf, loud, like you mean it. The gulls will carry it before you do.
Come creeping along the cliff-tops instead and the sea gets your bones before my lads do - we shove the wrong sort off the rocks and let the tide do the bookkeeping. Come the right way and there's a seat by the pot, salt-fish in your hand, and a story owed both directions. Sit. Drink. We'll talk.

Hah! The Sturgian boyars send their levy-boys down the coast road each spring, all wool cloaks and frozen toes, and we pluck them like cod from a weir. Prince Raganvad's vassals hold Varcheg above us - one of his housecarls, a thick-necked oaf calling himself Lord Stanimir, has sworn three times this year to burn my cove. Three times he marched. Three times he found nothing but gull-shit and a cold fire-pit. My boys row out the back channel before his boots crunch the shingle. The storm hides what the cliffs don't.
The Vlandians come too, by sea, the fool bastards. Some count's outriders sailing up from Ocs Hall thinking the northern fjords are open trade - we sank a cog of theirs last moon and her belly was full of southern wine. Drank it dry around this very fire. The Empire's tax-galleys stay south where the water is warm; they know better than to point a prow at our weather.
If you ride under a Sturgian banner, friend, the boyars will know your face from the ledgers before they know your name. Stanimir keeps a long memory and a longer rope. Sail under no banner at all and the coast is yours - the cod don't care whose coin you carry, and neither do I.

Hah! Sit closer, the wind off the cove will steal half my words and the cod-gulls the rest. You ask who I respect? Few. Vargolf Iron-eyed of the Frost Reavers - him I respect. He sent word last moon that my warbands crossed the Pravend road one too many times, and he is right, the bastard. I owe him a longboat of mead and a quiet talk before the thaw, or he rides north to my cove and we settle it in the old way, axe and oar. I would rather drink with him than bleed with him. Both end the same.
The Sky Raiders up in the crags - Aerlin's lot - they hunt the same Sturgian caravans I do, and that grates. We have not bled yet, but a season more of empty nets and we will. Granny Hod's forest band keeps to the deep timber west of here and stays clear of salt water, which is the only thing that keeps her old bones whole. The Highwaymen of the downs? I do not know their Reeve and I do not want to. Land-rats counting coppers.
What my scouts brought back is this - the Marsh Stalkers have gone quiet down south, and quiet Stalkers means a knife is being sharpened somewhere. Mark it.

Listen close, landsman, and hear how the cod swims. Every third week a Sturgian fur-train rolls down the coast road from Revyl bound for Varcheg - eight wagons heavy with sable and walrus-tusk, sixteen boyar-spears wrapped in wolf-cloak, and a captain who drinks more mead than a wedding-priest. They camp at the salt-marsh ford because the boyar-fool thinks the bog at his back is a wall. It is not a wall. It is my front door, and my boys swim it like otters in milk.
The trick, friend, is the dusk-hour. Their outriders ride wide at noon, tight at dawn, but at dusk they bunch by the fires because Sturgians fear the dark like children fear the cellar. Hit them then with thirty horse coming down the dune-spine and they break before the second wagon catches fire. The sable goes for a king's ransom in Pravend - Vlandian merchants pay double because they cannot trap the beasts themselves.
There is also a Khuzait silk-runner who threads the Varcheg quay every new moon, paying off the harbour-master in Aserai gold. Him you can BUY, not bleed. Slip him forty dinars and he tells you which hold carries the silk and which carries the salt-pork. Take the silk, leave the pork, and the longboats never even wet their oars. That is how cod swims, traveler. Mouth-first.

Ha! There it is - the oath-question, dropped at my fire like a stone in a still bay. You think I have not heard it before? I have. From men who choked on the asking and men who sang it drunk. The salt knows which is which, and the salt remembers longer than any of us. Sit. Drink. Let me weigh you the way the long-keel weighs a wave.
When Bjornulf bleeds, he bleeds for names cut into the mast of the Salt-Sister - my first keel, gone now to a southern reef. Eirik Broken-Tooth, my shield-brother since we were boys hauling nets at Varcheg. Old Hilde who pulled my mother screaming from the ice the winter I was born. Two oar-mates from the Pravend run who took spears that should have been mine. That is the oath-cup, friend. It is small. It is full. It does not pour easy.
You are not yet a name on my mast. But the timber has room. Bring me a deed the cove will sing about - a galley taken, a southern lord's gold pried loose, a wreckers' beacon doused before it killed kin of mine - and we will share mead-share proper. Until then, the long-keel runs and you run beside it. Ask me again when the salt has tasted your work.

Then by the salt and the storm, it is done. Stand up off that wet stone, brother, and drink - the oath-cup is full and the mead is mine and what is mine is yours from the keel up. Here - take my knife. Open your palm where mine bears the old grin from the night we burned the Varcheg pier and I swore on a dead man's mast I would never sail alone again. Press the cuts. Let the blood drip into the cup. Now we both drink - you first, then me - and the salt knows, brother, the salt knows. The long-keel under our feet just learned your name and the gulls overhead are already screaming it.
Shield-brother means this: my mead is your mead, my crew is your crew, my feud is your feud. When the Sturgian boyars send their riders south I row with you. When the lowland lords come hunting your hide the Salt-Tongue's oar-bench rows for you. We share the cup, we share the storm, we share the gallows if it comes to that - and laugh on the way up.
From this tide forward you are blood of Bjornulf, kin of the hidden cove, hearth-mate of every man on this long-keel. Varcheg will hear it. The boyar of Revyl will hear it and his bowels will turn. The salt knows, the storm knows, the dead at the pier know. Brother - drink deep. The sea has two of us now.

Hah! You answered with the deed first and the words after, the way a long-keel answers a storm - prow into the wave, mouth shut till the spray clears. I asked once if you would bleed for me, and you went off and bled before I had finished pouring the cup. The salt knows that order. The salt remembers when Old Hrothgar, my shield-brother, gave me a split lip and a longboat the same afternoon - deed first, jest after. You stand in his shadow now, and he was no small man.
So hear MY answer, loud, the way the cove hears the surf. From this tide forward, when you raise your banner, my long-keels put to oar. Not for coin. Not for a share of the hold. As blood-allies - your feud is my feud, your hunters are my hunters, and any lord who carves your name onto his blade carves mine beside it. You give me passage when the Sturgian shore turns cold against me, and a share of the salt when the season is fat. That is the bond. Mead-share, steel-share, grave-share if it comes to it.
The wind carries this oath now, shield-brother - down the coast, past Varcheg, into every cove that knows my flag. When steel is drawn, the storm-mouths will sing your name beside mine. Ride loud. The salt has heard us.

Aye, done and salted! Ten of my oar-men for seven tides of the sun - I will cull them off the strand myself before the gulls roost. My second is Hrolfi Brine-Beard, a shield-brother who has chewed more salt than you have drunk ale. He rides at your shoulder and speaks my mouth. If a cove-boy of mine drops in the muck of your fight, you bring his axe back wet or dry, I do not care which. If he lives, you bring him back hoarse and stinking of someone else's mead.
Hear me plain, traveler - my shield-brothers do not break the wall for coin or for whim. They break it because Salt-Tongue set them to it, and while they answer your horn your work is the cove's work. Do not piss them away on roadside scuffles and stray dogs. Seven days. I count tides, not promises.
The whole strand will know ten of mine rode out under your banner. The whole strand will be watching the horizon for their return.

Hark and drink slow, stranger, for the name is heavy. {TARGET}. He keeps his rotted banner over {HOME}, the same shore my long-keel beached at nine summers gone with my shield-brother Hrolf laid across the oar-bench, gut-split. {TARGET}'s coast-watchers met us in the surf with fire-arrows and a priest who blessed the burning. Hrolf and I had shared the oath-cup since we were boys cutting our first salt-teeth. That whoreson watched my brother cook in the wrack and laughed from his cliff. I have drunk to that laugh every winter since, and the mead has gone sour in my mouth.
He rides the coast road twice a moon to count his fishing rents, four lances and a turncoat Nord called Asbjorn who owes my cousin a debt the cousin will forgive for the right cup. Buy Asbjorn three horns of mead at the Tyal crossing and he will piss out his master's bed-hour. {TARGET} sleeps fat after the rent-counting. Take him then, before the cock sings.
{REWARD} denars when his head salts in my cellar, shield-brother. The mead-share waits, and so does Hrolf's shade. Ride hard, and the long-keel keeps the rest.

{CHIEF} has named {TARGET} of {HOME} as the man whose throat the long-keel was launched for. The grudge is salt-deep and specific - a shield-brother named Hrothgar drowned in a weighted net off the Skerry of Broken Oars, sunk on {TARGET}'s order after a tally-dispute over plundered grain that was never plunder at all but honest oath-coin. {CHIEF} swore at the oath-cup that day, mead spilled on the strake, that the man who weighted that net would be hauled up by his own ribs. The Storm-Mouth offers a heavy purse of {REWARD} and the closing of a debt the sea itself has been holding. The keel is wet. The oars are counted. The contract is open.

{TARGET} is dead, and {CHIEF} has heard it spoken across the oath-cup. The long-keel Saelvarg, burned to her waterline off the Pelegir skerries seven winters past, has been answered for - and Halvard Storm-foot, shield-brother dragged under by the chain-net that bloody dawn, can rest now that the noble who ordered the trap is meat for the gulls. {REWARD} denars sit heavy at the mead-share, counted twice by salt-stained fingers. The bond between Salt-Tongue and the traveler-killer is stamped a fathom deeper. The long-keel's name is sung whole again, and the tide takes the rest.

Word reached the salt-camp on a gull-bitten morning that {TARGET} was already cold meat - waylaid on some inland road by a rival lord's outriders, throat opened in a ditch far from any tide. {CHIEF} heard it out, then spat into the surf and stood a long while staring at the burnt ribs of the Saelvarg where she still lay rotting on the strand. Halvard Storm-foot was no closer to peace under the waves for a kill done by other hands. The grudge is technically answered - the bastard breathes no more - but the chief wanted the chain-net repaid by the one he'd sworn the iron to, not gifted by some stranger's blade. He counted out {REDUCED_REWARD} denars in thin coin, quarter-pay for a quarter-done thing, and clapped a shoulder without warmth. The bond stands a notch firmer, but cooler - salt without the fire.

By the brine in my beard and the salt in my teeth, you came at the right tide! {VILLAGE} - that's the grain-fat little hovel under {LORD}, a Sturgian fence-clan that twice now refused to launder my plundered cargo. Two seasons running, you hear? Two! And the second time, the swine tipped off a boyar's outriders who chased my long-keels halfway down the coast. I lost three good rowers and a chest of Aserai silks to those inland rats. They thought the sea wouldn't reach them. The sea reaches everywhere.
Here's the cut of it: ride at midnight, the village sits soft a half-day inland with no palisade worth the name and no watch worth the wages. Take the granary, take the smoked fish, take the iron tools. Leave the women and the wells - I'm a raider, not a butcher, and I want them rebuilding so I can come back and gut them again next harvest. Fire the headman's hall on your way out, that's the message.
Do this clean and {REWARD} denars sloshes into your purse, by the foam and the foul wind I swear it. Bring me ash on your boots and the smell of burning thatch in your cloak, and I'll pour the first horn myself. Now go, before the tide turns soft on us!

{CHIEF} spat the name {VILLAGE} across the longhouse board like a mouthful of bilge-water. Two seasons running, he roared, the fence-merchants of that inland Sturgian rat-warren had turned up their noses at honest plundered cargo, and worse, two seasons running they had whispered to a boyar's outriders the moment his keels touched silt. The grain-village under {LORD} sat soft and undefended a half-day inland, fat at midnight, and Bjornulf Salt-Tongue meant to see its thatch burn before the next tide.
He wanted a blade he had not already bought. {REWARD} in good silver if the torches went up before dawn.

{VILLAGE} burns behind the raiders, its grain-sheds gutted, its fences kindling, its midnight quiet broken into a long red howl that {CHIEF} drinks like ale. Two seasons of fence-merchants laughing at honest plunder, two seasons of {LORD}'s boyar-bought outriders sniffing the coast - the salt has its answer now, and the answer is ash. The Sea Raider spits over the smoking thatch, hauls the cargo none of those inland weasels would launder, and counts {REWARD} into the player's palm with a storm-mouthed laugh. Debt closed. Tongue salted. Tide paid.

Word washes up the coast that {VILLAGE} is a black smear in the dirt, torched by some other crew before {CHIEF} could put a keel to the river. Bjornulf Salt-Tongue spits, laughs the short laugh, and pours a horn anyway. Two seasons those inland weasels turned his cargo away at the fence-stalls and whispered the boyar's outriders onto his trail - now the gulls pick at their grain-pits and it was not his blade that did it. Cold comfort, he says, is still comfort. {LORD} is told the storm came without him; the purse is lighter for it.
{CHIEF} pays {REDUCED_REWARD} - a finder's cut for pointing the wind, not a raider's share.

The sea breathes in.
You hear it from the headland — the long whole rattle of stones turning over stones as the water draws back down the shingle, every pebble taking its small place in the count, the noise so old it has worn its own meaning out of the words men use for it. The sea breathes in. You stop your horse to let it.
Hold.
The sea breathes out. The swell rises and lays itself down on the strand and the same stones knock the other way. Salt mist comes off the break and rides up the headland and beads grey on your horse's mane. You take a breath without thinking. You take it on the sea's count.
The sea breathes in.
Out along the strand below — visible only because the moon has cleared a cloud, and only for as long as it stays cleared — a longship sits canted on the shingle, dragon-head black against the paler dark, strakes still wet from the work it was at an hour ago. A working ship. A ship come home tonight with the salt fresh on it. A cloud takes the moon back. The ship is dark again.
Hold.
The sea breathes out. The cloud thins. Now there are fires on the strand, low driftwood-fires sheltered in the lee of the hulls, and figures moving slow between them, and the smell of tar and brine and burning oak comes up the headland on the same breath. The sea will show you the camp at its own pace. It will not be hurried.
The sea breathes in.
You are breathing on the sea's count. You did not choose to. You realize, dimly, that you have been breathing on the sea's count since you stopped your horse. This is what the coast does to a man who does not belong to it. The coast does not ask you to belong. It only asks you to keep time.
Hold.
The sea breathes out. An old raider on the strand looks up from the fish-bone he is carving and meets your eye across the long fall of dune. He does not stand. He nods once. The nod is part of the breath — it falls on the exhale, the way the tide falls. He waits for the next in-breath to see what you will do.
The sea breathes in.
You go down to him.
Buy or sell with the smuggler.
Bjornulf claps a small ship-chest open. "What we don't want, we trade. What you don't want, we'll buy."
"A king's law ends at the shore. Past the shore is our law."
"Sea-fathers and storm-mothers. Old gods of the cold water."
Bjornulf laughs, big enough to scare gulls. "My grandfather killed a kraken with a knife! And you threaten ME?"
He spreads his arms. "It is good, yes? Sea, sand, sail."
Bjornulf cracks open a barrel of mead with his fist. "From the southern jarls' own brewery. We took the whole shipment. Drink, landwalker, drink!"
You sleep under sail-cloth, the surf hissing nearby. Your party wakes salt-touched and hungry for breakfast.
Listen to the storm-caller.
An old man with a beard like white kelp gestures you closer. "Storms speak. Most don't listen. I listen. The sea has news."
Trade with the sail-maker.
A woman with stained hands sews sail-cloth. "Sail, rope, hooks, salted fish. Sea goods. Cheap because we make our own."
Drink with the longboat crew. (100 denars)
The whole crew gathers around the fire. They sing the old songs — long, off-key, joyful. Your party joins in. They never sing the same song twice. Morale climbs.
"A Sturgian galley sank in the bay last month. Most cargo is still on the bottom."
"The imperial navy patrol changes every fortnight."
"A merchant prince in Quyaz wants ten chests of northern amber."
"A Battanian noble was lost overboard near here last winter."
"There's a smuggler's cave a day's sail north — used for two centuries."
"A Vlandian count's daughter was secretly shipped to Aserai."
"The old gods of the sea still take offerings."
"An imperial fleet captain is corrupt. We supply him."
"A drowned village lies a mile out — Sturgian, lost to a storm."
"The southern desert sultan has banned northern goods."
"Thirty fish. The sea provides, but our cellars run low between raids."
He sniffs a barrel. "Salt-cured well. You learned from real fishermen. Trade with us."
30 fish
"Twenty walrus-tusk. The carvers in the north pay handsomely, and we trade north as well as raid south."
He weighs a tusk. "Heavy ivory. The carvers will sing your praises. Trade."
20 walrus tusks
"Twenty-five whale-oil. The longships need it for caulking, the lamps need it for the dark months. Bring it."
He uncorks a flask, smells it. "Pure rendering. The hulls will hold another season."
25 whale oil
"A hundred fish and thirty hardwood. Fish for the winter store, wood for hull-patches."
He claps a fresh plank. "Boatbuilders' wood. Salt-fish for the dark months. You're a son of the cold sea."
100 fish + 30 hardwood
"Fifty walrus-tusk and thirty fish. The northern trade-run leaves on the new moon. Bring both for the run."
He nods at the loaded longship. "The northern carvers feast tonight. The cold-sea is open to you."
50 tusks + 30 fish
"Eighty fish and twenty whale-oil. We re-stock the cold-house and re-caulk the fleet before the autumn raid south. Bring both."
He surveys the fleet readying. "Sea-worthy. We raid south better-fed and tighter-hulled because of you."
80 fish + 20 whale oil
"Two hundred fish, fifty hardwood, thirty walrus-tusk. The full longship-fleet readies for the great raid down the imperial coast. Outfit us."
He stands at the prow of the lead-ship. "You launched the fleet that broke the empire's coast. The north sings your name."
200 fish + 50 hardwood + 30 tusks
"A hundred walrus-tusk, fifty whale-oil, thirty salt. The greatest northern trade-load this fjord has ever sent. Bring it all."
He claps your shoulder, an old sea-captain's blessing. "The cold-northern halls open to you. You walk in firelight wherever Sturgian iron rings."
100 tusks + 50 whale oil + 30 salt
Raid the marked coastal village's tribute caravan — take the salt and silver before the tide turns.
The Bjornulf Salt-Tongue accepts your oath; the rite is sealed in salt — a lick on the tongue, a swallow of cold seawater from the sealskin cup.
Bjornulf spits salt into the surf. "The sea drinks oath-breakers same as it drinks all the rest. Ride inland."
Hakkun the Sand-Reader
The Well-Killers
Dune-walker! The chief wants you. He's been crouched over his ash-bowl since first light, muttering about the deep wells. When the sand talks to him that long, somebody's about to bleed. Go on, move.

This morning I read the ash, and the ash was white as bone. Now I know why. A lord has cut himself a new trade road, and my people sit too near it, so he sends wagons south — quicklime, traveler. Lime for the deep wells. One sack and a well is dead for a generation. Ten wagons and the sand-clans die of thirst without a blade drawn. An engineer leads them, a man of measures and schedules, with outriders paid to keep the curious away. Stop the column. Turn it or break it — the wells do not care which. The sand has already shown me the wagons standing still. Go and make my reading true.
Good. The wind turned east last night — it knew your answer before your mouth did. Ride the new road south; the wagons raise white dust, not brown. Water is life, traveler. Bring mine home.
The sand shows me two readings, traveler. In one you ride, and the wells stay sweet. In the other, my people drink dust. Which one do you mean to make true?
The wagons still roll. Every sunrise I read the ash, and the ash is still white. Do not make me read it a third time.
Quicklime Column
Engineer Fazil
Hakkun the Sand-Reader has asked you to stop a lord's column carrying quicklime meant to foul the deep desert wells. Intercept the Quicklime Column and its engineer before the wells are poisoned.
The quicklime will not reach the wells. Return to Hakkun the Sand-Reader at his hideout to collect your reward.
You are standing on a surveyed road. I have eleven wagons, outriders, and a lord's seal that says this cargo moves. State your business quickly — I am due at the first well by dusk.
Ask your outriders my name — then turn these wagons around.
That name I have heard — from men who were still frightened when they said it. I build roads; I do not die on them. Turn the wagons! We go back. No blood over another man's road.
The wells stay sweet. Steel settles the rest.
Outriders — to me. Kill this one, and mind the barrels. Wages as agreed; double for whoever brings me the head.
Never heard of you. I have heard of my schedule — I keep it. Wagons, move on! If the name is worth anything, friend, now would be the time to show me.

Come to the well, traveler. Draw. Drink — cold and sweet, from the deep stone. I read the sand this morning. It showed me children at this well thirty years from now. You are in that reading, though they will never know your name. Here is your silver, counted slowly. Everything worth doing is done slowly. The dune holds its peace tonight, and so do I.

The wind did not wait for you, traveler. A khamsin came down on the column and buried half of it standing — the lime ruined, and the proof with it, under a dune that was not there at dawn. I read it, but I read it late. The wells are safe; the desert took the doing for itself. Half the silver. Not insult — arithmetic. The sand keeps its own ledger.

Hakkun was born into a desert-survey caste — a small Aserai sub-people whose ancestors served the early sultans as cartographers and well-finders, paid in silver and protected by royal warrant. The caste was disbanded a century ago when the sultanate reformed its tax-survey system; Hakkun's grandfather inherited the books, his father inherited the books, and Hakkun inherited a library of dune-charts more accurate than anything the current sultan possesses. He worked as a caravan-guide for fifteen years, the most expensive in the southern trade, and was never short of clients despite charging triple the going rate. The trouble began the year a corrupt sultanate official accused him of selling well-locations to bandits — a charge that was technically true insofar as the official had failed to pay him for the previous season's services and Hakkun had recovered his fee from a desert raid. The Sultan has tried three times to hire him as a guide and three times to hang him as a brigand; he has accepted neither offer with finality. The Desert Bandits are now a confederation of the dispossessed survey-caste families and a few hundred true desert-walkers who follow Hakkun for the same reason caravans used to: he knows where every well runs dry and which lord owns the men guarding it.

The Desert Bandits are the oldest survival of an Aserai survey-caste — a small sub-people whose ancestors served the early sultans as cartographers and well-finders, paid in royal silver and protected by royal warrant. The caste was disbanded six generations ago when the imperial-leaning sultans of the third Aserai dynasty replaced it with a court bureau of foreign mapmakers. The disbanded surveyors took their charts, their well-rods, and their sand-reading knowledge into the deep dunes and have lived there since. Hakkun is the eleventh chief by direct succession from the last royal-warrant survey-master. Admission is tightly controlled — descendants of the original caste, desert-village families with documented survey-bloodlines, and the rare outsider an elder vouches for after a year of testing. They take from caravans that cross the deep dunes without paying the customary water-tribute — a tribute the band considers payment for use of wells the caste's ancestors found. The Aserai sultanate has tried four times in three generations to extract a peace-deal that would re-recognize the caste in exchange for surrender of arms; Hakkun has refused all four because none of the offers came with a return of the original royal silver-stamp.

The Sand-Reader steps out of the shadow between two tents — robed, face-cloth wrapped against the wind, only the eyes visible. Those eyes find you and read you the way Hakkun reads dunes: slowly, patiently, complete. "You come to the dunes, traveler. The dunes know you now.
