Bandit Lieutenant

They say Garruk was a huntsman once, away in the cold marches where the forest grants no man an easy living. He kept the boar-runs and the deer-paths for a lesser lord, and there was no track laid in mud or frost or wet-rotted leaf that his eye could not read — a hoof half-filled with thaw-water, the white scar where a flank had brushed bark, the bruised stem that told him a beast had passed at dawn and not at dusk. The ruin of him came not by the sword but by debt and a burned steading: a winter that killed the seed corn, a master who hanged Garruk's brother from a roadside oak over a poached stag, and a grave they hacked from ground too frozen to take it, so that the stones had to be heaped on top against the foxes. After that the man went into the trees and did not come out the same. He had learned that what he had done to deer he could do to men, and that men, when they run, leave the richer spoor — they sweat, they weep, they grasp at branches, they look back.
He took the Bandit King's collar without ceremony and without love. Vaykos had no need to break him; he needed only to point. Where another captain swears for plunder or out of fear, Garruk swore because the King's banner gave his hunting a whole country to range across and a warrant no margrave's gallows could reach. The bargain was plain as a set snare. The King names the quarry; the Hound does not ask why, and the King does not ask how. It is the cleanest contract in all that outlaw host, and the most terrible, for there is no clause in it for mercy and no hour appointed for its ending.
It is the fleeing that he is given. When a debtor slips the King's reckoning, when a turncoat carries word down to the lowland lords, when a girl held for ransom climbs from a window and runs barefoot for the tree-line — these are not given to the host. They are handed to Garruk, and the men speak of that handing the way they speak of a door drawn shut in the dark. He goes out alone, or with two silent men who carry no torches, and he does not hurry, for he has learned that the hunted tire first and the hunted sleep worst. He reads the bent grass, the turned stone, the cold ash of a fire smothered too quick; he buries his face in a cloak thrown aside in panic and breathes the sour fear-sweat soaked into the wool until he knows the shape of the one who wore it. He has crossed three valleys and worn the soles from a season's boots after a single man, eating what the wood gave him, and at the end of it the man was found.
What sets the dread of him apart is that there is no hatred in it. A wolf does not hate the hare; it only closes the distance. Garruk will sit across a guttering fire from the one he means to take, break bread with him, speak low and almost kindly of the cold and the long road, and finish it in the grey hour before dawn with no more rancour than a man wringing the neck of a bird caught in a springe. The villages along the marches do not curse his name; they lower their voices when they speak it, as though a loud word might turn his ear toward them. Mothers along those frontiers tell their children that the worst thing in the wood is not the beast that roars and shows its teeth, but the thing that makes no sound and does not tire and is always, always nearer than it was.
Among Vaykos's captains he is the one the others will not cheat, for every man of them has done the cold arithmetic. A traitor may flee the King's wrath and win himself a head start of days, of weeks, of a whole frozen mountain range. It will never be enough. Somewhere far behind, unhurried and unhating, the Hound has already knelt to the first print and pressed two fingers to its cooling edge — and the Hound, in all the years men have feared him, has never once been called off.

Before the name went sour he was only Sevrin of the Ortwell shambles, a butcher's boy who knew the seams of a carcass before he knew his letters. He never did learn his letters. What he learned, hock-deep in offal and the cold copper stink of the killing-floor, was that a body keeps the same grammar whether it walks on two legs or four: the joint that wants to open, the soft place under the short ribs where the steel slides in without argument, the tendon that, parted, drops a thing where it stands. He might have grown old at the block, fat on lights and small thieving, had his fingers not strayed once into another man's purse and his luck not strayed with the magistrate's patience.
They did not hang him. Hanging is a kindness kept for men with kin to do the weeping. Instead the magistrate's man pressed Sevrin's left hand flat to the very block he had worked since he was a boy — the wood black and sweet with twenty years of blood — and took two fingers with a butcher's cleaver, slow, in two strokes, so the lesson would carry weight. The smallest, and the one that leaned against it. He was made to thank the court before they suffered him to crawl into the gutter and bleed.
He did not die of it, though the stumps wept and greened and a whole winter found him shivering in a doorway, teaching a ruined hand to break bread and open throats with three fingers and a thumb. That winter gave him the thing the magistrate had never thought to give: a whole hand, he came to understand, is a lazy hand. A man with all his fingers grips like a frightened fool, all knuckle and no thought, and shouts every stroke before it lands. Sevrin, robbed of the fist, had to keep the knife as a balanced thing and not a clenched one — held light, pinched between thumb and the two fingers the cleaver had spared, so the blade lay in his palm like a second tongue and spoke before the eye could read its lips. Come the thaw he killed three men. Not one of them saw the steel before it was already warm inside him.
Word of such a man runs the low roads faster than any herald's horn, and it was on the low roads that the Bandit King's reavers came upon him. They did not press him into Vaykos's host. They asked him, which is its own black species of dread. Sevrin took the collar gladly. A throne of mud is a throne still, and beneath the King a man of his peculiar craft need never again kneel snivelling before a magistrate. He had thanked the court once. Kneeling in the King's firelight he swore he would thank no man living ever again, and he keeps the oath by leaving the thanking to others.
In the host he breaches no wall, roars at the head of no charge. Sevrin is the quiet errand, the knife sent on ahead. Where the King would have a sentry gone, a tollman made reasonable, a rival lieutenant found cold in his blankets with no wound any surgeon can name, it is Sevrin who comes soft-shod through the dark and goes out the same way, the straw undisturbed behind him. The two taken fingers he kept; bone now, scraped and yellowed, strung on a cord at his throat. He is known to set them on the board during a parley, just so, where the other man's eye cannot leave them, and he says nothing of them at all. He has no need. The threat is the sum every captive works out alone in the dark: here is a man the law unmade and the cold did not finish, who came back from both the keener for it — and whatever the cleaver left undone, the three fingers it spared will see to themselves.

No man living recalls Maddoc young. The chroniclers of the river-towns set his name down two reigns past and already wrote it the way the marches say it now — Old Maddoc, as though he had come into the world grey and scarred and waiting. The truth, what little has survived the burying of it, is plainer and worse. He was a hearth-soldier once, swordhand to some thin-pursed lord of the marches whose name the dust has long since eaten, and when that house went down in a winter campaign no living tongue remembers, Maddoc walked out of the burning hall with embers in his beard and three other men at his back. He put all three in the cold ground before the thaw broke. He has been digging graves ever since. Not once has he been the man laid in one.
They reckon him sixty, and reckon like fools. No body carries the tally of hurts he carries on sixty winters alone; the count is written too deep, in too many hands. Every span of him is a ledger kept in scar. The white seam that splits brow from jaw where an axe swung a finger's width too wide. The two stiff fingers that will not close to a fist in any weather. The bitten notch in his ear, the puckered glaze of an old burn riding one forearm, the limp that wakes only when the frost comes down. He does not speak of them, nor finger them by the fire as lesser men finger their wounds for an audience. He stopped hating the men who dealt them long ago, for every last one of those men is under the sod, and Maddoc is not, and he holds that this settles the whole of the matter and wants no further word spent on it.
He took the King's collar the way a grey hound takes the warm side of the hearth — without illusion and without gratitude, for the shelter of it, because the road behind him ended in a ditch and Maddoc had decided, somewhere across the long years, that he would not die in one. Vaykos does not own Maddoc's love. Little reaches that far down in him now; the years have silted it over. But the King gives bread, and a fire that does not gutter, and a fresh crop of young men to outlive, and in return Maddoc gives the host the one thing a band of brigands most wants and least possesses — a memory. He knows which fords drown a man in the spring melt, which lords pay the agreed coin and which sell you to the gibbet, which ambush was sprung on this very hillside in a harder winter and whose blood it was that froze in the ruts come morning. He is the host's grey conscience, and the King prizes him above three captains who can swing a heavier arm.
He serves by waiting. While the hot-blooded ride whooping down into the killing, Old Maddoc holds the rear with a fist of the steadiest throat-cutters in the host, and it is from that patient back rank, and not from the screaming van, that the slaughter is truly governed — the line that does not buckle, the flankers ridden down in the wheatfield before ever they reach the road, the captive kept breathing because Maddoc, and no other eye among them, weighed what he was worth alive. Young raiders come to dread his silence sooner than another man's roaring. A captain who bellows can be read and got round. Maddoc only watches, slow and unblinking, and the watching speaks plain as a sentence read out: I have seen your kind a hundred times over, boy, and I have shovelled every one of them under the dirt. Do not make me dig the hundred-and-first.
That is the dread he throws — not the white heat of a killer in his prime, but the cold arithmetic of a man who has buried everyone. There is no proving yourself to him, no name loud enough to move him, no defiance he has not already stood over and outlasted. The marches whisper it low at the fireside: Old Maddoc does not kill in anger and does not kill in haste. He outlives. And the dying is left to come along behind, in its own time, as it always has, as it always will.

They named him Hagen at a font in the marches of Battania, a freeholder's son with three brothers and a strip of barley to his family's name. The Mappa Mundi remembers none of that. What it remembers is the year the levy came through and pressed the brothers into a border war no chronicle troubled to win, and left the boy to bury what the dogs and the ravens had not already taken. Nine days he laboured at it, they say. By the ninth he had set down the spade. He had learned the lesson no priest would teach him: that the earth is greedy and slow to close its mouth, but the birds are punctual, and they ask for nothing in return but patience.
Why he took the King's collar is told plainly enough. There is no acre left to a man who will not stoop his back, and Hagen would not stoop. He came to Vaykos already half a legend in the wrong fashion — a brigand who had fought the petty lords' bailiffs to a standstill in the Cuthrey thickets and burned the assize rolls in the ditch after, so that no parchment in the realm could any longer name him. The Bandit King keeps a use for the man other men will not stand shoulder to shoulder beside, and he gave Hagen a column and asked of it only two things: that it move, and that it be feared. Both Hagen has answered past the reckoning of any lieutenant under the black banner.
He serves by what he forbids. Where lesser captains strip the slain and leave the gleaning to the village widows, Hagen suffers no grave to be dug — not for the enemy, not for his own, for the crow draws no line between a kinsman and a foe, and neither, he says, should the living. A field he has crossed lies black by the second morning, the stubble crawling with wings, the wind off it gone thick and sweetish and loud with that wet tearing croak that does not cease from dawn to dark. And the host that feeds there does not scatter when he strikes his camp and marches on. It rises with him. It hangs above the column in a slow turning smoke of feathers, gorged and unhurried, and comes after. They have learned the tramp of his men the way a hound learns the note of its master's horn.
So the dread of him arrives before his vanguard, borne in on the wing. A watchman on a tower marks the crows kettling over the eastern road before ever he marks a single horse, and he understands, and the bell he hauls upon is less an alarm than a dirge. Towns have thrown open their gates to the rumour of feathers, the elders coming out grey and shaking with the keys before a spear was so much as levelled. He need not raise his standard; the sky raises it for him, restless and patient and black, wheeling above a man who has made of the battlefield's aftermath a thing as certain as the fall of night. Crowfeeder they call him, for the plain reason any child could give — and for a quieter one the old men only whisper: that the feeding was never the leavings of his war, but the whole purpose of it. The carrion is the one tithe Calradia ever paid him, and the one he means to go on collecting until there is no hand left to deny it.

They hanged him at the crossroads above Garios on a grey morning thick with wet rope and crow-dung, and by every law of God and gallows the drop should have ended the matter. He had been a debt-man once, a swineherd's son who put a billhook through a tax-reeve's eye over the price of a stolen sow, and the verdict took less time than the digging of the grave nobody troubled to dig. But the hemp was rotten and the knot was a coward's knot, tied loose by a hangman in a hurry to be out of the cold. When they hauled the cart from under him he swung, and kicked, and the rope groaned twice and parted at the third jolt, and dropped him choking into the churned black mud beneath his own dangling shadow. The reeve's men, who had laughed through the reading of the charge, did not laugh then. They saw a hanged man on his knees in the muck with his face gone purple-black and his tongue thick between his teeth and his eyes full of the long road that runs out past the edge of dying, and they dropped their pikes and ran. He knelt there while his heart remembered its work and the frost crept up through his knees, and then he stood, and then he walked, and he has been walking ever since with the rope's white kiss seared across his throat.
The scar never faded. It rides the column of his neck like a second mouth sewn shut, a pale rope-weal the breadth of a thumb, puckered and shining where the hemp burned through the skin, and he neither hides it beneath cloth nor boasts of it in his cups; he simply wears it, and lets men's eyes crawl to it the way eyes crawl to an open wound. Vaykos found him in a winter byre near the Heth marches, sitting alone among frozen cattle in the blue dark, too poor to be worth robbing and too strange to be worth the trouble of killing. The Bandit King asked him what he wanted of this world. Yorath answered, in the flat ruined whisper the rope had left him, that he wanted nothing at all — having already been stripped of the one thing a man clutches hardest, and found in the losing that it had cost him very little. Vaykos, who hoards the fearless the way a miser hoards clipped coin, gave him a fist of cutthroats and a black stretch of road, and asked no oath of him. A man who cannot be threatened cannot be bound, and so Yorath is held to the King by nothing in this world but his own dry, gallows humour.
He goes at the front of every storming, where the rope-shy and the praying hang back in the smoke. Yorath Gallows-Born walks into spear-hedges and burning doorways with the slow, unhurried gait of a man crossing his own yard at dusk, for the worst this world keeps in its cellar was already poured out over him on a wet morning above Garios, and the world has nothing left in its hands to show him. His own captains have watched him take a crossbow bolt through the meat of the shoulder and not so much as shorten his stride; watched him stand in a falling hail of arrows, head tipped back, laughing that cracked and breathless laugh, while better men clawed at the dirt for cover. They have stopped calling it courage. Courage is the mastering of fear, and there is no fear left in Yorath for the mastering — it died with him in the mud, and only the body climbed back out.
He keeps the frayed end of the hanging-rope coiled at his belt, blackened stiff with old Garios mud, and he lays it across the chest of any man who kneels and begs him for his life. To the doomed of three provinces that scrap of hemp is worse than any drawn blade, for the rope says plainly what his ruined voice will not: that he has knelt where they kneel now, that he has gone down the road they so fear to walk, and that it held nothing — nothing — he could not outlast. Mothers along the Hethrun hush their children with his name in the dark, and the hushing does no good, for a child may be frightened by a man who might yet be killed, and every soul on that river has come to know that this one already has been, and walked back, and is coming still.

Before the road from Pellamys to the river fords learned to dread his sign, Vess was no one — a thornland fowler's son, a netter of birds in the brackish marshes where the empire's writ frayed away to mud and reed. They say his father kept a shrike pinned in a willow cage and taught the boy its trade: how the butcher-bird, lacking the talons to hold what it slays, drives its prey down upon the blackthorn and the snapped branch — larder and gibbet in one — so the small dead hang in the cold to be eaten at the bird's leisure. The boy crouched in the frost-stiff sedge and watched the impaled voles go grey and rigid on the spines, and there he learned the lesson beneath the lesson: it is not the killing that masters a country, but the showing of it. A corpse seen is worth a hundred unseen.
His own ruin came in the year the tax-farmers fired the marsh villages for arrears no fowler's coin could ever cover. Vess walked out of the smoke with nothing left to him but the willow cage and a notched billhook, the reek of his burning home grey in his hair, and what the flames had stripped from him he swore to strip from every traveller still rich enough to lose it. For a season he hunted the roads alone, and the watch of three towns set a price upon a man none of them had ever glimpsed — only his handiwork, only the cold and careful things he left arranged behind him.
When Vaykos came east with his outlaw host, he did not trouble to break Vess to the collar; there was nothing in the man left to break. He had only to offer him the open road and a wider larder. The Bandit King gathers wolves and madmen and soldiers gone to rot, but in the Shrike he found a rarer creature — one who grasped that two hundred swords can hold a province of thousands, if the thousands are taught afresh each grey dawn what waits for the disobedient. So Vaykos gave him the toll-roads and the river crossings, and asked of him one thing only: that they stay quiet.
They stay quiet. Where Vess keeps the King's peace the caravans pay without a word of haggling and the headmen send their tithes unbidden, for the marches he holds are hedged about with his sign. A tax-collector lashed to a wayside oak, his ledgers stuffed sodden into his mouth, the ink run down his chin like black bile. A deserter set high in a leafless poplar, hung just so — within reach of the carrion crows, beyond the reach of any pity from the road below, which cannot raise its eyes to him and cannot look away. He does not hide his dead. He plants them. At the milestone, at the well, at the bend where the bride's cart must slow to pass — each one set with a fowler's unhurried patience, turned to the light so the living may read the warning whole and carry it home unbidden in their bellies. A village that has once seen the Shrike's hedge need never be raided twice.
Men say you come to know his country before you ever learn his name — by a sweetness on the wind that thickens as you ride, by the long silence of birds that will not nest where he has passed. He kills few, by the grim arithmetic of his trade; he has no need to kill many. One body, rightly hung, does the labour of a hundred blades. And Vess the Shrike keeps all the patience of the bird whose name he wears, content to wait still as deadwood in the thorn while a whole province, with no further teaching, learns of its own slow accord to be afraid.

BEGIN YOUR CHRONICLE
Walk away
Under the green roof a peace is sworn on the oldest oak, and every bow in the canopy is witness. The forest keeps no parchment; it keeps the shape of your word in the way the branches let you pass.
Honour it, and the woods open before you — no arrow notched, no snare set. Break it, and the trees themselves seem to remember which way you ran.
In the high passes an oath is spoken once and given to the echo. Stone does not bargain twice. The chief's word travels ridge to ridge faster than any rider, and so does yours.
Keep the peace and the passes stay open in any weather. Break it, and every goat-track grows a watcher, every scree-slope an ambush.
On the open steppe a peace is sworn to the sky, with a horse's breath for a seal. Nothing hides on the grass sea — not a rider, not a lie.
Hold to your word and the horizon stays empty where you ride. Break it, and the wind will carry your name to every saddle from here to the red dawn.
In the dunes a peace is a water-debt: sworn over the last cup, shared in the shade of one cloth. No oath binds tighter than thirst.
Honour it, and wells you never dug will be left unpoisoned for you. Break it, and the desert's patience becomes the chief's — endless, and always waiting.
A raider's peace is spat over the gunwale and sworn on the tide — salt takes the words down and does not give them back. The crews reckon a man by his wake, not his flag.
Keep faith and no longship shadows your sail. Break it, and every grey horizon hides a hull with your name carved in the oar-bench.
Even broken men keep one law: a peace bought is a night's sleep earned. They have nothing left but hunger and memory, and memory is the sharper of the two.
Feed the bargain and they scatter from your road like crows from a cart. Cheat it, and desperation makes them braver than any lord's guard.

There is no ink in a bandit's peace. It is sworn over a fire, witnessed by armed men, and remembered longer than any lord's treaty. Coin buys silence; blood buys respect. Either way the road behind you grows quieter, and the watchers in the rocks lower their bows.
But the wilds keep their ledgers too. A peace honoured carries your name to every campfire in the pass. A peace broken follows you further than any bounty.

THE JAILBREAK
The guard’s torch gutters against wet stone, and the reek of the pit clings to your throat. Somewhere far above — past the bars, past the long black stair — the night air is moving free.
Slip the lock while his back is turned. Keep to the shadows, count his rounds, and you may yet climb out of this hole.
— WHAT WAITS BELOW —
Fellow captives share the cells. Cut them loose as you go for renown, goodwill, and more hands to scatter the guards.
Locked chests hide coin and contraband in the dark — pick the locks one by one, or lift a guard’s key ring and open them all.
Your gear was stripped at the threshold. You’ll find your arms and armour again deeper in, not at the cell door.
Your cellmate goes with you — get him to open air and he swears his blade to you, but if he falls down here, he is gone for good.
The reward — your freedom, hard-won renown, and a sworn companion who will owe you his very life.
Fail, and they drag you back into the pit — bloodied, stripped again, and watched twice as close.

Halgar leans against a stack of crates and looks you over. "You want to know what I sell? First show me you can work. Kill three battanian patrol-leaders. Bring me eight prisoners. That's the easy one."
Halgar grunts and tosses you a purse. "You don't flinch. Good. We'll talk again."
Halgar drops a name and a number. "This time it's the lord himself. Alive. Five battanian heads to match. And bring me thirty hardwood — chains don't grow on trees."
Halgar nods. "You're a man worth knowing. Take your due."
Halgar looks at you a long time. "Last test. Kill ten of theirs. Take eighteen alive. Capture the lord. And fifty hardwood. After this, I'll show you what I really keep."
Halgar uncovers a hatch in the floor. "Down. You'll want to see her."
Once chained himself in a {CULTURE_BAT} noble's grain-cellar; got out the hard way and never let himself or anyone else forget what coin can do to a man.

Halgar opens the hatch. The smell rises first — damp earth, old straw, men. Five candles burn in clay holders, throwing the cage-shadows long. A {CULTURE_BAT} merchant in chains looks up; his eyes are tired in the way no rest can fix. A {CULTURE_VLA} sergeant's daughter sits on a pallet, knees pulled in. Halgar nods to a third cage at the back, hidden behind a hanging cloak. "That one I keep for paying customers," he says. "You're not there yet."

You asked. Most don't. Most look at the cages and decide the answer already, and walk off with their pity tucked under their arm like a loaf they paid for. Sit down. The trade pays a man what he was already owed, and I'll tell you how I came to collect. There was a noble in Battania once — fat in the belt, fat in the voice — who put me down a grain-cellar with a chain through my collarbone for the price of a stolen ox. Four months. You learn things down there. You learn that hunger is a kind of clock. You learn the shape of your own ribs through your shirt. You learn that a man with the key is just a man with the key, and keys can be taken if you're patient and the hinge is old enough. I got out the hard way. I left the noble in the cellar with my chain. After that I tried the honest roads. Smith's apprentice, drover, hauler for a {CULTURE_VLA} caravan. Coin came thin and went thinner, and every lord I bowed to had the same wet smile as the one in the cellar. So I stopped bowing. I cut a strap off a slaver's wagon outside Pen Cannoc and bought my first three souls with what was in the strongbox underneath. That was the ledger I started. I've been keeping it since. I don't tell myself I'm a kind man. Kindness is a coin I spent down in the dark and never got back. What I am is honest about the weight. A man in chains is a man in chains — I was one, I sell one, the iron doesn't care whose neck it sits on. The trade pays because the world is built on it, friend. Lords just hide their cellars better than I do. So that's what brought me. A cellar, a chain, a hinge that gave. Some men come out of the dark and swear it off. I came out of the dark and learned the price of it, and now I charge it. Don't look surprised. You asked.

The Brionne road runs fat right now. {CULTURE_VLA} wool carts move east with four guards, sometimes three, and the drivers drink at the last waystation before the woods. I had a man clear two of those carts last moon — kept the drivers, sold the outriders to a foundry-master in Galend who asks no questions about a missing tongue. That foundry buys steady. He pays in silver, not promises, and he likes his stock young enough to last the bellows ten winters. Lord Caladog of the Wolfskins is bleeding men. His warband took a mauling near Llugwy Ford and he's pulled his patrols north to lick the wound, so the southern trails between Pen Cannoc and the lowland villages sit open. A {CULTURE_BAT} girl alone on those paths is coin walking on two legs. I've taken three this season off that stretch and the chief still hasn't sent a single rider to ask after them. A lord who cannot count his own farmers is a lord I thank quietly. There's a {CULTURE_KHU} flesh-broker working out of Sanala calling himself Yerlan. He buys in lots of five or more, pays under-market, but he moves the stock east before any clan-rider can come looking. I dealt with him twice. The second time he tried to short me a denar a head and I broke his cousin's hand on the table — we settled fair after that. If you have bodies to move quick and don't care for top coin, he's the line. If you want full price, ride to Epicrotea instead; the arena-keepers there still pay in old gold and they don't haggle over teeth. Word is the {CULTURE_STU} timber-caravans running down from Varcheg are pulling thin escorts this season — the war up north ate their hired swords. Two wagons, six guards, mostly drunk boys with spears they don't know how to hold. A man with twenty blades and a quiet wood could clear one in an afternoon and walk away with three carpenters and a fletcher worth their weight. Carpenters fetch double from the {CULTURE_ASE} forts rebuilding their gates. I'd take that work myself if I weren't sitting on stock already. One last thing. There's a hedge-priest moving village to village in the {CULTURE_BAT} hills, buying chained folk and setting them loose — pays in coin he begs off {CULTURE_VLA} merchants. Sentimental fool, but his coin spends the same as any. I sold him an old man last week who wouldn't have lasted the road anyway. He thanked me. I took the silver. The trade doesn't care whose hand it passes through, only that the hand is open.
Skreg One-Ear
Was nobody's son; sold his own brother and never spoke of it again. Trades in the desperate.
Chief letting you in here? Bold. Try not to bleed on the floor.

Skreg leads you down a stair carved into raw dirt. Three pits, lids made of warped boards. Something moves in the second one. He doesn't say what. The fourth pit is empty — "That one's yours if you ever stop being useful," he says, and isn't joking.
What Skreg Says

You want the story? Cheap question. The answer is cheaper. I was nobody's son. My mother died on the road and the road did not stop for her. I learned early that a body is only worth what someone will hand you for it, and most days that is less than bread.
I had a brother once. Younger. He cried easier than me, which is to say he cried at all. A caravan came through with empty cages and a full purse, and I led him to the cage myself. I told him it was a game. I took the coin. I bought bread, and a knife, and a place by a fire where no one knew my face. I have never said his name out loud since. I will not say it for you either.
After that the trade was simple. The pit asked nothing I had not already given. I learned the marks — the ones who run, the ones who fight, the ones who go quiet and wait to die. The quiet ones sell best. {CULTURE_EMP}s especially. They were raised believing somebody would come for them, so they keep their teeth and their backs straight in the cage. A straight back is silver on the line.
I do not love it. I do not hate it. A man who hates his work drinks his coin and ends up in his own chains. I keep the ledger. I keep the cages. I keep the road from coming back for me the way it came for my mother. That is what pays a man into this trade — not greed, not cruelty. The road. The road is always behind you, and the only thing that puts distance between you and it is somebody else's neck under your hand.
So. You asked. Now stand off the floor and tell me what you came to buy.
Word from the Road

{CULTURE_EMP} caravans run the southern road from Amitatys these last weeks. Thin guards. The Senate pays in promises now, and a captain paid in promises hires fewer spears. I took three drovers off that road last moon. Two went to the pit. One I sold whole to a man who would not give his name. There is a noble out of Phycaon who lost his brother to bandits and has not slept since. He rides with six men and grief makes him stupid. Grief and a heavy purse — I have seen both on the same horse before. If a pit-master had ambition, that one rides alone past the broken mile-stone every third day at dusk. I am only saying what the road says. Razih buys quiet. The flesh-trade there moves through the back of a tanner's shop — you knock twice, you say the word *salt*, you do not look at the men in the corner. They pay in dirhems, weighed not counted. I will not name the tanner. A man who names tanners ends in a tannery. There is a new one working the eastern stretch. Calls himself Vellig, says he was a caravan-master once. He is not. He is some lord's bastard who learned the trade in a week and thinks chains are rope. He bought a {CULTURE_BAT} girl off me last month for half her worth and I let him, because a fool with coin is the best customer a pit-master can hope for. He will be dead by harvest. His coin will not. The {CULTURE_KHU} are moving south of Odokh and the steppes are emptying out — herder families on the road with no spear between them, only the old man and the boy. That is not trade, that is harvest. I take what the road gives. My brother taught me that, though he did not mean to.
Drust the Lung-Cut
Survived a hanging once and the rope marks never faded.
Three {CULTURE_EMP} dogs. Six prisoners. Easy work for a fresh hand.
Skreg counts your coin twice. Pays anyway.
This one's name is on the slip. Alive. Five more bodies. Twenty hardwood for the cages.
Skreg grunts approval.
Last one. Ten dead, fifteen alive, a lord captured, forty hardwood.
Skreg opens the cellar.
Volk Stone-Tongue
Once held a pass against three caravans alone; the survivors named him. He sells men because beasts are cheaper.
Hm. Chief's man. Down here we don't trust easy. Show me work.

The cellar is hewn from the mountain itself, cold even in summer. Volk's prisoners sit huddled in furs — he keeps them alive better than most, because frozen meat sells for less. A {CULTURE_STU} thane chained at the back recognizes you; nods once. He's been counting days. Volk pretends not to notice the count.
The Highrunner's Arithmetic

The pass took me first. Three caravans came up the road that winter, and I was the only blade on the rocks. I held the choke for two days. When the survivors crawled out, they gave me a name — Stone-Tongue — because I would not speak terms, only count the dead.
After that the work was simple. A man learns what his hands do best, and mine break the line where it bends. I tried beasts for a season — goats, a pair of mules — and the math was thin. Beasts eat through the snow and die on the slope. A chained man walks himself down to the buyer and carries his own weight in coin.
So I sell men. {CULTURE_STU} mostly. They come up these passes thinking the cold knows them. The cold knows nothing. I know the cold. I take them off the road before the road takes them, and I march them south to a ledger that pays in silver, not in stories.
You want the honest piece — there's no debt behind it. No brother lost, no woman buried. I looked at the trade and saw what it was. Cheaper than herding. Quieter than war. A mark on a wrist holds longer than a brand on a hide. That is what pays a man into this. Arithmetic, and a good pass to hold.
Now show me work, or take the road back down. I have caravans to count.
Word From The Pass

The Varnovapol road thins out past the second bend. {CULTURE_STU} wool-trains been running with four spears instead of eight — the boyar there lost men to the snow-fever and hasn't hired fresh. I held a pass alone against three caravans once. Four spears is not a guard. Four spears is a count of mouths to shut. There's a thane east of Revyl buying quiet. Won't say the name on open road. He takes the southern stock — {CULTURE_VLA}, {CULTURE_BAT}, anything that doesn't speak the tongue of his hall. Pays in old silver, the kind nobody asks about. I move two bodies a month his way and the ledger stays clean. A man calling himself Yarko works the Omor cut. Calls himself a trader. He's a fence with bad chains and worse prices. If you come down through the high pines, don't sell to him — he marks his stock with a brand on the wrist and the buyers know it and they pay him less for the trouble. Cleaner to bring them to me. Word is the prince's tax-rider rides north of Sibir next moon with a thin escort. Two retainers, a clerk, a strongbox. Strongbox is the smallest of the three. The clerk is the one worth chains — clerks read, and a reading man brings double in the southern markets where they need ledger-keepers and don't ask why his hands are scarred. I sell men because beasts are cheaper. That's still true. But the price on a {CULTURE_STU} smith just climbed a third since the empire started forging again, and the passes are full of smiths walking home from work they no longer have. Bring me one with strong wrists and we both eat well this winter.
Helka Ridge-Walker
Climbed out of a cliffside oubliette barefoot in snow.
Three {CULTURE_STU}s dead in the passes. Six prisoners. Off you go.
Volk slides a bag of coin across.
Marked {CULTURE_STU} lord. Alive. Five more dead. Twenty fur for the slings.
Volk smirks.
Twelve dead. Fifteen alive. The lord. Fifty fur.
Volk uncovers the deeper hold.
Bayan the Iron-Reins
Was a {CULTURE_KHU} horse-boy who watched his lord burn his village for grazing-land. Sells {CULTURE_KHU}s now.
Chief brought you here. Good. Ride hard, kill clean, bring what I ask. We talk.

There is no cellar — only a yurt pitched apart from the others, ringed with iron stakes. Inside, six prisoners tied wrist to wrist in a circle, the way wolves hobble their kills. A {CULTURE_KHU} noble's wife refuses to meet your eyes; her wedding-braids have been cut off and lie in a pile by the door. Bayan watches her watch the floor, and says nothing.
The Iron-Reins' Ledger

You ask what pays a man into the trade. Look at my hands. They were a horse-boy's hands once, soft on the bridle, hard on nothing. I brushed my lord's geldings before sunrise and slept in the straw with them after. That was a life. It was someone else's life.
The grass at our village ran thin one summer and my lord wanted it for his herds. He came down the slope with twelve riders and a torch. I watched my mother go into the smoke from behind a watering-trough. I watched my father go in after her. The lord saw me crouched there and rode past without a word — a horse-boy is not worth the turn of a head. That was the lesson. A {CULTURE_KHU} noble will burn you for grass and not remember your face by supper.
So I learned the reins he taught me and turned them. Every {CULTURE_KHU} caravan that crosses the steppe rim, every drover with a fat purse and a lord's seal on his belt — I cut them off the road and put them in the line. I sell them south, I sell them east, I sell them to anyone whose coin doesn't smell like home. The ones with noble cousins fetch best. I keep a ledger of their clan-marks and I have not forgotten a single one.
This is not vengeance. Vengeance is for men who think the ledger closes. Mine does not close. Every chain I lock around a {CULTURE_KHU} neck is grass paid back, one blade at a time. The trade pays well because the steppe is wide and the lords are many, and a man with iron reins can ride a long way before he runs out of throats to bind.
You came here for coin and a chief's nod. Good. Bring me {CULTURE_KHU}s — drovers, scouts, the soft-handed sons of the men who ride under banners — and we will talk longer. Bring me anything else and you waste my straw.
What Bayan Hears on the Wind

The trade-road south of Makeb runs fat this moon. {CULTURE_KHU} remount-strings move from the summer pasture to the winter camp, and the noyan who owns them sends only four lancers ahead, four behind. Four and four. I counted them myself from the long grass. A horse-boy learns to count men the way other boys learn to count stars, and I learned young. Lord Mesui rides drunk again. His own household whispers it at the well in Aksumel — two of his sons dead in the eastern raids, and now he drinks koumiss till noon before he mounts. His column drifts in single file along the river-bend. A man who cannot keep his line cannot keep his throat. Take him on the bend, take his retinue for the block. The buyers shift. Ortysia has gone shy — too many imperial eyes since the new garrison — but Quyaz takes anything with a pulse and asks no name. Their pit-master pays in old denars, clipped, but he pays the day you ride in. There is also a {CULTURE_STU} factor working out of a cellar in Revyl who buys {CULTURE_KHU} women only, no men, no children. I do not ask what he does with them. The ledger does not ask either. Word from the rim: a {CULTURE_VLA} called Halgar runs a cage in the western foothills and undercuts the rest of us by a third. Let him. His stock comes off the caravan-roads, soft hands, soft feet. Mine comes off the steppe. Different meat, different table. The {CULTURE_ASE} out of Quyaz pays steppe-price for steppe-flesh, and Halgar's western chain does not reach this far. One last thing, and hear me. A merchant caravan rode out of Chaikand three days back, light guard, heavy axles. Heavy axles mean coin, not grain. The driver is a cousin of the khan's tax-man, which means a ransom on top of the trade. Ride hard, kill the outriders clean, bring the cousin breathing. The rest you may sell or bury — I do not care which, only that the ledger closes.
Tarsa Blood-Mare
Rode a stolen {CULTURE_KHU} warhorse across two kingdoms to escape a lord she would not marry.
Three {CULTURE_KHU} horsemen down. Six prisoners. Plain work.
Bayan tosses the purse.
{CULTURE_KHU} lord, alive. Five dead. Twenty flax for binding.
Bayan nods grimly.
Twelve dead. Fifteen alive. The lord. Fifty flax.
Bayan stares east, then pays.
Hjalti Salt-Spine
Pulled an oar on three different crews. Started a fourth. Sells whoever crawls out of the surf.
Salt in your beard yet? Ha. Show me you can pull weight.

Hjalti's cellar is the bilge of a beached longship dragged up the strand. The hold smells of pitch and brine and human waste. Eight men chained to the keel-beam, all in stages of seasickness even on dry land. "Sea breaks them faster than chains," Hjalti says. "By the time the ship sells, they're glad to go anywhere with a floor that doesn't move."
What the Long-Boatswain Says

Three crews I pulled oar for before I was the one holding the rope. First crew, I was twelve, and the boatswain broke my nose for missing stroke. Second crew, the captain drowned a {CULTURE_STU} boy off the gunwale because the boy wept too loud. Third crew, I learned the trick of it — that a man pulling oar and a man in chains pull the same wood, only one of them gets paid in herring and the other in salt water up his nose. So I started the fourth crew myself. Bought the keel from a widow in Rivacheg who didn't ask where her husband went. Half my first take was {CULTURE_STU} fisher-boys, the other half was a Vaegir caravan that thought the coast road was safe in spring. The ledger keeps no opinion. The ledger only keeps weight. What pays a man into this trade. I'll tell you. The sea pays nothing — she takes. Raiding pays for one winter and a funeral. But the chain pays twice. Once when you put it on him, once when you take it off in a market square and somebody hands you silver for the trouble. Twice the work of an oar, and you stand dry. I sell whoever crawls out of the surf. Doesn't matter the cloak. {CULTURE_STU}, {CULTURE_BAT}, your cousin if your cousin is wet and breathing. The surf is honest — she sorts the strong from the weak before I ever lay a hand. I just wait on the beach with the rope and the count. You asked what pays a man in. Nothing pays you in. You wake up one morning at the oar and you understand the rope is in someone's hand, and it might as well be yours. Salt in your beard yet? Then you already know.
What Hjalti Hears on the Tide

{CULTURE_STU} coast road past Revyl is fat this season. The thaw came late and the fur-trains piled up at the crossings — twelve, fifteen wagons strung out with six guards apiece, and half those guards are drunk Vaegir boys hired in haste. I pulled a man off one such caravan last moon. Got eighty denars for him in Omor by sundown. No questions, no ledger. The buyer keeps a back door that opens onto the river. Lord Bakar's levy is south chasing a {CULTURE_KHU} raid that isn't there anymore. His northern villages stand thin — old men, fish-wives, the priest. I won't touch the priest. The rest go in the hold and nobody in Revyl counts the missing till the ice breaks again. A crew out of Tyal works that same stretch — Yngvarr Cold-Tongue, calls himself a captain now. He pays in salt and short weight. Steer wide of him or split your take before you sail with him, not after. The discreet buyers this month: a factor in Varnovapol who buys strong backs only, no women, no children, pays in {CULTURE_EMP} silver and asks if they can read. Don't lie to him; he checks. There's a quiet house in Pravend too, behind the tanner's yard — they take any flesh that breathes but they shave the price hard, claim the Empire's edicts have them nervous. Edicts. Ha. Coin still moves. It just moves slower and through more hands. Word from the gulls is that a {CULTURE_VLA} merchant convoy is putting in at Omor before the equinox — eight wagons, mercenary escort, fat with wool and a paymaster's strongbox. The escort captain is one Sir Roland, drinks too much and posts his sentries by the fire instead of away from it. I'd not take the wagons. I'd take the camp-followers and the boy who tends the horses. Less noise, same coin by the second town. Last thing. A {CULTURE_BAT} woman has been asking after me by name in Sibir. Sister to a man I sold three winters back, or wife, the messenger wasn't sure. I'd care more if she had coin. She doesn't. Tell her, if she finds your fire, that Hjalti is at sea and the sea keeps its ledger sealed.
Inga Wave-Cutter
Swam ashore from a wreck wearing a dead jarl's mail; kept it.
Three {CULTURE_STU} coast-lords. Six prisoners. Start there.
Hjalti spits and pays.
{CULTURE_STU} lord alive. Five dead. Twenty fur for the slaver-hold.
Hjalti grins through bad teeth.
Twelve dead. Fifteen alive. The lord. Fifty fur. After that — we sail.
Hjalti claps your shoulder hard.
Yusuf the Salt-Counter
Was sold once at the {CULTURE_ASE} pole-block at thirteen. Bought himself back by twenty-five. Counts every coin.
The chief's word carries weight — for him. Make yours worth something to me.

Yusuf's cellar is dug deep beneath the sand to keep the noon-heat out. The prisoners squat against the cool clay walls and rarely look up. He passes a waterskin around himself — "They sell for more if they don't dry," he explains. The far wall has a wooden post worn smooth by chained wrists. Yusuf touches it absently as he walks past. He doesn't say why.
What the Salt Taught Me

Thirteen. That was the price they wrote beside my name on the {CULTURE_ASE} pole-block. Not my age — the silver. A trader from Quyaz paid it without looking at my face. He looked at my teeth, my wrists, the length of my stride. The man who sold me was my uncle. He counted the coins twice before he walked away, and he never once turned his head. I stood on that block four hours in the salt-wind. Salt gets into the rope-burns and stays there. Years later, when a buyer haggles me down a dinar, I still feel it — that small white sting along the wrist, telling me what a man is worth when nobody speaks for him. So I learned to speak for myself. I learned to count. Every coin that crossed my palm I marked, and every coin I owed I marked twice. Twelve years it took. Twelve years of caravan work, of knife-work, of sitting at the fires of men who did not know my name and were better for it. At twenty-five I walked back to the same pole-block with a purse heavy enough to buy three of me, and I bought one. Myself. The clerk did not remember the boy. He wrote the sum down, took his cut, and asked if I wanted the receipt. I keep it folded in my belt to this day. After that, the trade was the only thing that made sense. A man who has been counted does not forget the counting. I do not hate the chains — chains are honest. The dinar is honest. What I hate is the uncle who looks away while the silver changes hands, and that one I cannot sell, because he is already in the desert somewhere, dead of his own thirst, I hope. So you ask what pays a man into this trade. I will tell you plain. The trade paid me back what was taken, dinar for dinar, and then it paid me a little more, and a man who has been counted will keep counting until the ledger runs out. Bring me a captive worth weighing, and we will talk. Bring me your purse light, and we will not.
What Yusuf Counts

The road from Quyaz to Iqbayl runs thin this moon. {CULTURE_ASE} caravans cut their guards from twelve spears to eight — the sultan's levy ate the rest, and the merchants pray to their stars instead. Stars don't stop a curved blade in dune-shadow. I take the third night out of the well at Bahyat; that's when the camel-drivers sleep heaviest and the moon is small. There's a buyer in Sanala wears clean linen and asks no names. Pays in silver, not gold — counts every coin twice before he lets you touch the purse. I like him. He took four girls off me last new-moon at forty-two dinars the head, and the ledger closed clean. Word is he ships them west by sea, but I don't ask. A man who asks too much gets sold cheap. Lord Unqid lost his second son to fever and three caravans to bandits in the same season, and his banner-men haven't been paid since the spring rains. His escorts walk slow now, look at the sand more than the horizon. A column of his moves through the Hubyar pass next dark moon. Twenty wagons. Six guards. You do the counting. Watch for a man called Khuzaim — calls himself a salt-trader, but he moves flesh out of Durrin by the back gate and pays his runners in promises. Two of mine went to him last winter and came back with nothing but bruises and a story. I do not deal with him now. If you see his caravan on the south track, take it. He won't report the loss; he can't. The {CULTURE_VLA} caravan-masters are the soft mark this season — they march through our sand like it's their father's pasture, and their sergeants drink at noon. One of them I sold at thirteen to the pole-block where I stood, and I remember his face. The desert keeps its ledger. I keep mine.
Layla Sand-Sworn
Walked seven days through the deep desert wearing only a stolen merchant's robe.
Three {CULTURE_ASE} dead. Six prisoners. The desert teaches you.
Yusuf weighs your purse, smiles.
{CULTURE_ASE} lord — alive. Five dead. Twenty salt for the brine-jars.
Yusuf nods slowly.
Twelve dead, fifteen alive, the lord. Fifty salt.
Yusuf draws back a curtain.
Brand the Frostbitten
Lost three fingers to a thrall-chain in a {CULTURE_STU} winter and never warmed since.
Chief warmed to you, did he? Cold doesn't. Prove yourself.

The cellar is a half-frozen ice-house, prisoners packed in straw so their breath doesn't waste heat. Brand walks among them counting fingers — "Lose two, price drops. Lose four, they go to the dogs." One of the prisoners, a {CULTURE_STU} boy of maybe sixteen, watches him with the dead calm of someone who has already stopped being a person.
What the Cold Bought

Three fingers. That's what the chain took from me, that first winter. I was fourteen, thrall-bound, and the iron froze to the bone before the {CULTURE_STU} master noticed his stock was rotting on the line. He cut them off himself, on a stump outside the longhouse, and threw them to the dogs. I watched the dogs eat my fingers in the snow. That's when the cold got in, and it's never gone out.
I worked the chain six more winters before I broke it. Killed the master with the same knife he'd carved me with. Walked north until the trees gave up. You ask what pays a man into this trade — I'll tell you. It wasn't coin. It was the ledger. Every {CULTURE_STU} throat I open now is a finger paid back. I'm not done counting.
The reavers found me half-dead on the ice, and they knew what I was the moment they saw the stumps. A man who's been on the line knows the line. I can read a thrall's price in his shoulders before he opens his mouth. I know which ones break in a week and which ones go three seasons. The buyers down south pay me well for that knowing.
Sometimes a young one asks me if I hate them — the {CULTURE_STU}s, the chained ones, the buyers who fondle the wrists before they pay. I tell him no. Hate warms a man. I haven't been warm since the dogs ate my fingers. This is just the work. Chain, mark, coin, next. The cold does the rest.
So when you ask what brought me here, friend, look at my hand. Two fingers gone on the left, one on the right. Each one bought by a {CULTURE_STU}, and each one I'm collecting back. Slow trade. Patient trade. The ledger keeps.
What Brand Hears on the Ice-Road

The road north of Varcheg runs thin this season. {CULTURE_STU} patrols have pulled inward to guard the Lord's hall, and the trade-track between two villages I won't name carries grain wagons with four guards where last winter it had ten. A man with cold hands and a quiet bow can take the drivers and leave the oxen — the oxen draw too much eye. I took six off that road already. Six pairs of hands that don't know the word for warm. Lord Bratomir lies abed with a wound that won't close. His housecarls drink in the longhouse and his daughter rides the timber roads with a sworn-sword and two girls. I won't say more on that. A man with my fingers does not boast before the take. But the ledger remembers, and someone will write that line before the thaw. Word from a tanner in Revyl — there's a buyer behind the back gate who pays in southern silver for women who can sew and men who can split wood. No questions on the mark. He sends his factor out at second moon, never the same alley. I sold him two last month. He pays slow but he pays, and he doesn't squint at the brand the way the legal markets do. A {CULTURE_BAT} crew works the western passes now. Calls himself Cuirig or some such — buys cheap, drives hard, loses one in three to the cold. Amateur. He'll cross my road before midwinter and we'll have a conversation about who pulls thralls out of MY snow. The Empire caravans coming up from Pravend run heavier guard than they did, but their scouts are southern boys. They don't know how the wind moves before a storm. Not enough to drown a dog. Enough for him. I left him there for the leeches and walked out wearing his coat. The chain I kept. It hangs by my hip still — same iron, same weight. I learned that day the mire takes what's owed it without asking twice, and a man who can't read the water is already a corpse that hasn't lain down. The trade found me after. {CULTURE_BAT} raiders came through the fen looking for tin and went home in my coffles instead, because they didn't know which tussock would hold them and which was a green lid over six feet of black. I sold the first three to a {CULTURE_STU} factor for forty denars and a salt block. Forty denars buys a lot of rope. Rope buys more men. Dry-land slavers haggle over teeth and shoulders. I haggle over lungs. A {CULTURE_BAT} who's spent a night chained to a stake with the tide rising will walk quiet to any buyer you put him in front of — the mud has done my breaking for me. That's what pays a man into this trade, friend. Finding the one thing the world gave you for free, and learning to sell it. You asked plain so I answered plain. Now show me you can stand where I stand without sinking, or take your boots back to the road.

Someone with twenty bows could take it without raising a voice. I'd take it myself, but I prefer the goods that walk and breathe.
The town of Llyngarth is buying quiet. Their reeve sent a man down to the fen-edge in plain wool, and he asked me about strong backs — no tattoos, no missing teeth, mouths that won't shout at market. He paid in good silver and bad lies. Their forge has more orders than free hands, and the guildmasters don't want it written in any ledger. I've sent three already. They'll take more.
Word is a {CULTURE_STU} called Yarvik is working the upper marshes, undercutting on women. He pays in furs, which means he's selling them east before the snow-roads close. Knew every channel between Pravend and the sea by sixteen.

The road taught me the rest — that a {CULTURE_VLA} merchant kneels the same as a {CULTURE_VLA} sergeant, that the silver weighs the same whether you cut it from a belt or buy it clean. I cut buckles for years before I understood the body inside the belt was worth more than the belt. Slow lesson. Expensive teacher. Now I sit at a toll-post my father would have hanged me for keeping. Took a horse and a sword from her own father at fifteen and ran.

The sand pays. That's the whole of it. You ask what pays a man into this. Hunger pays first. Then habit. Then the ledger — and the ledger is the worst of them, because once your name is in the southern books as a man who delivers, the dunes will keep handing you bodies whether you want them or not. Runaways. Debt-broke caravan guards. Whole villages the raiders couldn't be bothered to keep. The sand gives them up, I move them along. That's the trade.
I don't sell my own. The {CULTURE_ASE} I kill or chain, that's the line — they bled my first master's caravan, so they pay the toll forever. Everyone else, I weigh. Hessa down in the well-camp reads bones for me when the count gets thin; she told me once I'd die owing the desert more than it owes me. Maybe so. The ledger runs both ways out here, and the sand keeps better books than I do.
So you stand at my pole and ask the question men ask before they sign on. I'll tell you plain. There's no calling in it. There's no story worth the breath. A boy with empty hands took a dead man's rope, and the rope never let go. The chief vouches for you. The sand doesn't. Keep your count and keep your tongue, and we'll see what the dunes give back.

The south sand-routes are paying again. Two {CULTURE_ASE} grain caravans crossed my chain last moon with six guards apiece — six, where they used to ride twelve. The drought thinned their coffers, and thin coffers mean thin spears. I marked the routes in my ledger; the next wagon that runs that lean, I take whole. A {CULTURE_VLA} factor in Quyaz has been buying quiet. He won't say it at the block, but his man comes after dusk and pays in clipped denars for women who can stitch. Three I sold him last week, no questions on where they came from. The dunes gave them back; he asked only how strong their hands were. A man who knows the wadis could lift a string of their herders and be back in his cups before the dust settled. I'm not that man this season. The chief wants flesh, not feud. Was a merchant's wife who slit his throat and stole his caravan.

Decimus runs the cellar like a legionary holding-cell — six prisoners standing at parade rest, eyes forward, addressed by serial number rather than name. The cleanest cellar you've seen. "{CULTURE_EMP} discipline holds both ways," he says without smiling. The branded centurion on his cheek twitches as he speaks. None of the prisoners look at it.

I don't deny what they cashiered me for. I did it. Whether it was worth doing is a different ledger. The court took my sword, my pension, my name on the rolls. Two more brands on the back, for the discipline of it. Then they opened the gate and told me to walk.
A branded man doesn't get hired to guard a caravan. He doesn't get a plot of land. He gets one trade, and the trade is the one I knew already — moving men in a line, counting them, feeding them just enough. The only difference now is the chain instead of the marching order, and the buyer instead of the quartermaster.
I sell imperials. I sell the ones who used to stand a rank above me and look through me like I was air. Some of them I knew by name before the chains went on. I don't gloat. I weigh them, I price them, I move them on. The coin spends the same whether the neck under the iron is a farmer's or a tribune's, but I'll admit the tribune sits a little easier in the ledger.
That's what pays a man into this. Not greed, not appetite. A brand, a closed door, and the one skill the legion left him with. Discipline still matters in this work, more than people think. Show me you've got some, and we'll do business. Show me you haven't, and you'll learn what the line feels like from the inside.

His steward comes to the back of a wineshop near the south gate on the third evening of the week and pays in old denars for imperial-born only. He wants them literate. I sent him a clerk from Lageta last month — the man had cried himself hoarse before I marched him in, and the steward paid above the ledger without a word of haggle. They serve in cellars there, I think. They don't come back up. Olynia's caravan-master Kresos runs a thin guard on his copper string because he thinks his {CULTURE_ASE} paper protects him. There was a season I tried honest work. Guided a {CULTURE_VLA} merchant's son up to the standing stones for a fee. He paid in silver and looked at me like I was a dog that had performed a trick. That same week I roped a {CULTURE_BAT} woodcutter off a goat-track and a Sky-Raider quartermaster paid me three times the silver, and looked at me like a man. The ledger does its own arithmetic. I stopped pretending I hadn't read it.
Now I sit the crag and I watch. I see who's strayed from the village. I see who's bled their hunting-dog dry and gone deeper than they should. The highlands give them up to me one at a time, and I bring them down on a short rope. Some go quiet. Some go talking about their gods. The rock doesn't care which, and after twenty years up there, neither do I.
You asked what pays a man into this. Nothing pays him in. The hills push him to the edge of the trade, and one day he looks down and finds he's already standing in it. That's all. That's the whole story.

I started with one. A scout, separated from his patrol, his horse lamed in a drift. I took him at dusk and walked him sixty miles to a coast-trader who paid in silver and asked no questions. That coin bought me my first proper bow. The second {CULTURE_KHU} bought me a second man for the pack. The trade fed itself after that, the way a wolf-line feeds itself once it learns the shape of the deer.

A chained one pays in {CULTURE_ASE} ports, in coastal markets, in the hands of any man who has reason to want a steppe-rider broken. Killed three {CULTURE_KHU} nobles in a single winter and kept their daggers.

Has lived too long. Trades in souls — by which she means people. Her smile is colder than the chief's blade.

Hessa's cellar is round, walls painted with marks no living tongue still reads. The prisoners sit in a circle facing inward toward a brazier that never quite goes out. Each one wears a small bone token at their throat — Hessa's mark, she says. "Tells the dead which ones are mine." None of the prisoners speak. One of them is humming. Hessa hums along.

The bones taught me first. My mother threw them on a wolfskin when I was small, and the marks told her my brother would die before the snow. He did. She threw them again and they told her the price a {CULTURE_BAT} sword-merchant would pay for her second daughter. He paid it. That is the first thing I learned about the trade — the bones do not lie, and the buyers do not haggle when the marks are read true. I read them for the cult after she went into the grove and did not come back. Old women read bones; old women read men. There is little difference. A skull cracks the same way a purse does — a clean break along the seam, and out spills what was kept inside. I sat by the fire and I told the chiefs which captives would fetch coin in Pravend and which were only good for the altar. I was right more often than I was wrong. They began to bring me the live ones first, and the dead ones after. A soul has a weight, you see. I do not mean the priest's weight, the breath-and-light nonsense. I mean the weight in the hand when you grip a wrist and the pulse runs against your thumb. That weight is what I trade. I have held boys who weighed nothing and old men who weighed more than their chains. The bones tell me which is which before I ever lay a finger. I have lived too long for warmth. My husband is forty winters in the ground, my daughters scattered to four cultures, and the grove keeps the cold out of my hut better than any hearth. What is left for a woman like me but the ledger? I tally. I read. I sell. The coin goes to the cult and the cult feeds me, and when the bones finally say my own name I will lie down in the grove and stop counting. So that is what pays a man into this trade — or a woman, since you asked it of me. Hunger paid me first. The bones paid me after. And now habit pays me, which is the heaviest coin of the three.

The bones spoke last night. Three vertebrae fell toward the east road — {CULTURE_BAT} wool wagons crossing without enough spears. I read four guards, maybe five, and one of them limps in his left hip. The merchant who pays them is too thin in the purse to hire more. That road runs ripe for whoever has the stomach to cut the traces.
A lord south of here drinks himself stupid every third night. His hall is half-empty, his huscarls scattered chasing a feud he started drunk. I have heard his name twice in a week from travelers who didn't know they were telling me anything. A man like that loses daughters and stableboys before the harvest, and the bones don't lie about which way his hall is tipping.
The salt town down the coast — they buy quiet now. Their reeve has a back room and a coin scale, and he does not ask after the mark on a wrist or where the chain came from. Bring him strong arms and young backs. He pays in clipped silver, but the silver is real, which is more than I say of half the buyers between here and the river.
There is a {CULTURE_VLA} who calls himself a horse-dealer working two valleys west. He is no horse-dealer. He moves what I move, and he moves it cheap, which means he steals more than he buys. The bones say he will hang inside a year. Until then, do not undercut him on his own road — he keeps three killers and a dog that does not bark before it bites.
And the caravan out of the river-fort — the one that runs every new moon with the priests' tithe? Their captain was buried last week. The new one is a boy. The bones rattled when I asked after him. That is the sort of rattle that means a ledger waiting to be filled.
The Marked-Brother
Bears scars Hessa carved when he was a boy. He doesn't remember why.
Three of any blood. Six prisoners. The bones don't care.
Hessa cackles, pays in old coin.
A lord alive. Five dead. Twenty hardwood for the pyres.
Hessa smiles slowly.
Twelve dead, fifteen alive, the lord, fifty hardwood. The bones whisper.
Hessa opens the deep-stone door.
The field is yours. You take from the fallen:
Spoils of Victory
The chief expects something from you.

Sit close. Lean in. The smoke hides the words from ears that don't pay for them. You've earned a whisper, traveler — last moon a salt-runner from the eastern roads stopped here with a split lip and a thirst, and what he poured out with the ale was worth more than the coin he left. He said Lord Caladog is broke. Broke as a cracked crock. His steward has been buying barley on tally-stick from three different millers in Pen Cannoc, and none of them know about the others. When that house of straw falls, every grain-price from here to the coast jumps a quarter. Buy now, hoard, or sell early — your choice, but choose this week. The salt road through the gorge below Dunglanys is walking near-naked. Two escorts, both green, both drunk by midday — a goat-girl told a peddler told my smoke-boy. I don't tell you that so you'll rob it. I tell you so you'll know why salt prices here are about to climb to 14 denars a stone before harvest moon. The boys on the trees have already noticed. When the boys notice, the merchants stop coming, and when the merchants stop coming, even my pork goes hungry for brine. Now here's the bit that's worth your ear most. There's a fat little buyer up in Marunath — calls himself a quartermaster, dresses like a wedding — paying 42 denars a side for smoked pork. Forty-two. I sell the same side at the cookpot for sixteen. He's stockpiling for a march nobody's been told about yet, and he doesn't haggle. If you've a mule and three days, you can triple your purse and come back before the snow rots the last of the hams. One last thing, and then I'll let you go. Don't take the high pass next moon. A spice caravan came through last week with a crate of pepper they couldn't sell in Epicrotea because some new law about foreign goods — and they swore they'd seen a banner camped in the saddle of the pass that wasn't anyone's banner they knew. Forest's full of strangers wearing colors that don't match their faces. Eat. Drink. Then ride the river road. That's a smoke-master's tip, and it costs you nothing but a nod when you pass back through.

You want the secret? Come closer. Smell that smoke — that's not oak. Oak's what amateurs use, and amateurs in Pen Cannoc charge two denars a strip for pork that tastes like a tannery. Mine's beech, cut from the north slope where the lightning struck three summers back, dried two winters under tarp, and split thin as a blade's edge. Beech gives sweetness. But the trick — the real trick — is the apple wood I crumble in for the last six hours. Not chunks. Crumbs. Fine as snuff. The smoke goes from grey to gold and the fat on the pork turns the color of honey held to candle. The brine, now — that's where a Smoke-Master earns her name. Salt, yes, but coarse rock salt from the licks east of the brook, never sea-salt; sea-salt makes the meat weep too fast and the smoke can't catch hold. Juniper berries, crushed but not powdered — eight to a shoulder. Two heads of wild garlic. And here's what nobody knows: a single spoon of pine-tar honey, the dark kind the foresters scrape from hollow trees in late autumn. The honey draws the smoke INTO the meat. Without it you're flavoring the rind only. With it, the cure goes clear to the bone. My grandfather taught me this the winter I turned eleven. He was bleeding out in the snow — a forester's arrow, between the ribs — and he made me kneel and listen while he whispered the proportions. Said the smokehouse was older than our family and would outlast it, and somebody had to know. Said if I forgot the honey I'd be running a butcher-shed, not a smokehouse, and there's a difference. I have not forgotten the honey. Three winters past my death notice and I have not forgotten the honey. One last thing, since you've shown yourself useful. The hams I sell to the caravans bound for Marunath — I hang those a hand's-breadth higher than the rest. Cooler smoke, slower cure, twenty-eight days instead of twenty-one. They keep eight months on the road and the merchants pay me triple. If you ever pass that way and a fat man named Halmar of the Long Ledger tries to haggle you down on cured pork — tell him Old Brae says the price is the price, and the honey costs what the honey costs.
Dead Three Winters, Still Curing

Pays a man? Pays a woman, too, lad, and don't you forget it. I was born under the eaves of Pen Cannoc when it was still half a stockade, and my da kept the smokehouse for the timber-counts there. He died young of the coughing-sickness and left me the curing-shed, the salt-tubs, and a debt to a Battanian thane that I paid off in hams over six long winters. By the time I closed that ledger I knew the back of every alderwood fire and the front of every haggling jarl. Then the trouble came. A lord whose name I'll not speak — a southern man with a clean cloak and a dirty mouth — claimed my smokehouse stood on his cousin's grant. He sent men. I sent them back with knives in their belts and the wrong end of a hook through a thumb, and that night I walked out with what salt I could carry on a pony's back. The forest took me in because the forest takes everyone the towns spit out, and the chief here had a hundred raiders and not one soul who knew how to keep meat from going green by the third week. Three winters past my own death-notice, they tell me. Some clerk in Pravend wrote me down as drowned in the marsh-crossing — wrong river, wrong woman, but it suited me fine to be a ghost on the rolls. I built the curing-shed you see out yonder with my own hands and a borrowed adze. Salt I trade for in pinches off the Quyaz caravans when the boys bring me a wagon; alderwood I cut myself; the pork walks in on its own four feet from raids I do not ask after. Half this camp eats off my hooks. The chief knows it, the boys know it, and that is why no man here lifts a hand to Old Brae no matter how black my mood. I sell a leg of smoked shoulder for forty denars and a string of cured eels for fifteen, and if you think that's dear you can go gnaw a bowstring. The trade pays me in keeping warm, in being needed, in dying on my own schedule for a change. That's what pays a body into this trade, lad. Not coin — coin is just the tally. It's the want of a place where no clerk can write you dead twice.
What the Smoke Hears

Word on the deer-paths is Pen Cannoc burned through its winter salt stocks in a fortnight — some fool quartermaster up there is paying nine denars the pound for grey salt and not asking where it came from. If you've got a mule and a quiet road, that's coin sitting in a barrel waiting to be hauled. I'd go myself if my knees still bent. The Battanian drove a long herd of pigs east last moon toward Marunath, and half of them broke loose in the bracken north of here. Wether-Ban the Drover is offering finder's coin to any soul who pens the strays back — but between you and me, the boys upstream have been bringing me pork I didn't ask about, and I don't ask. Three winters I've been smoking that drove's loss into your suppers. Bad news for the porridge bowl. The grain wagons out of Dunglanys won't move this season — the miller's wife took ill and the wheel's been still since the equinox. That means Car Banseth will be buying oats off any caravan that can reach them by hard frost, and the price will double before the snow does. Stock now or starve clever. There's a sweetwine train coming up from Epicrotea under a Vlandian factor called Sir Aldrec of Hateng — three wagons, light guard, taking the southern track because the northern road washed out. Whether you mean to buy from him or relieve him of the burden is your business, but he'll be past the fording stones in eight days. The chief knows. The chief always knows. And one last thing, since you've stood here patient. A blight is creeping through the apple stands east of Hertogea — black-spot, the kind that ruins cider for three winters. If you've a friend with an orchard, tell them to burn the windfalls now. I lost my own grove to it once, long before this smokehouse. That's how I learned which trade keeps a body fed when the trees don't.
Old Brae of the Smokehouse
Cured venison for the Battanian wood-villages forty winters before a Vlandian tax-inspector burned his shed for "unlicensed barter." Came to Hod with three salt-barrels and a missing tooth.

Old Brae here, traveler. Hod's boys say you walked in alone, and the chief's word's good enough to keep your skin. But Brae's smokehouse is Brae's, and your boots haven't earned a rasher of it yet. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} — the wood-villages have been thin this winter — and I'll cut you the first slice off the rack.

Brae cures over alder-wood, traveler — not the green oak the lowland larders rush. Alder lets the salt walk in slow. Three weeks per haunch; the wood-villages knew the difference, before the lord forgot they existed.

Bring me three salt-sacks and a winter's notice, traveler — Brae'll cure you a haunch the Vlandian governor would have hanged his own steward for serving. A sample on the house. Walk back when you can.

Had a wife once — Mara of the upper birch-stand. Took the boys west when the gibbet-men came; never sent word after the first winter. Brae still sends a smoked haunch to the wood-villages every spring on her birth-month, in case the road runs both ways.

Aunt Lien runs a smokehouse-tavern at the Pravend crossroads — hidden under a butcher's awning. Tell her Old Brae cured the deer Hod's boys ate the night they hanged Brec. She'll seat you in the back room. Here's coin for the toll-clerk.

Lean in, friend. You've earned an ear, and I've got two of them full this week. A tinker out of Pen Cannoc rolled through three nights back, axle squealing fit to wake the dead, and over a cup of my worst he let slip that Lord Caradoc is in arrears to half the smiths in the western glens. Boy can't pay for the swords he ordered last harvest. His levy's marching with rust on the rims and the master-at-arms is quietly putting the good kit out to pasture in the back of the armory. If you've a spare blade and a soft tongue, you could fleece that household for a fortnight's denars easy. Now here's the prize cut. The Steelroad — the long stone track that runs from Marunath down toward the river fords — is carrying billet caravans this fortnight, and the escort has thinned to four lances on account of the muster up north. Four lances, friend. For wagons of half-finished steel. A smuggler I trust (and that's a short list) said the wheel-ruts are deep enough you can hear them coming from a ridge over. I'm not telling you to take it. I'm telling you what I heard. Do with it what your conscience can stomach. On the trade side — leather is glutted something fierce. Every tanner from here to Sanala is sitting on hides because the southern caravans came in two months late and three months heavy at once. Prices are on their backs and won't roll over till midwinter. Don't sell your tack now if you can help it. Conversely, iron stock's gone scarce in the hills — there's a fool of a merchant in Pravend who's paying near sixty denars the bar because his contracts run on and his suppliers walked. Sixty. For pig iron. I'd ride a week of bad weather for that ledger. That's the cream of it. Mend your straps before you go — I'll do the buckles cheap for the man who brought my coopering kit back to me. And keep what I've told you between the two of us. A barrel-mender hears things because nobody bothers to lower their voice around the fellow with the mallet, and I'd like to keep it that way.

You want to know why my barrel-staves hold a war-axe haft better than most smith's iron-bands? It is the soak. Green oak, split along the grain — never sawn, never. The blade splits where the wood wants to part; the saw lies to you, cuts across the fibres, and the haft breaks on the third swing.
