I rive every stave with a froe my father willed me, and I quarter them by moonlight when the sap has drawn low into the roots. That is half the secret. The other half is what we soak them in. Three nights in a barrel of tannin-water — oak galls crushed, a fist of iron filings, a splash of vinegar I trade off the Galend road. The iron bites the tannin and turns it black as a crow's eye, and the wood drinks it deep. When it dries, the stave is half-stone. A haft made this way will not split when a shield rim catches it, and it does not rot in the rain. The bandits laugh because their axes outlast the smith-bought ones their fathers carried — and they paid me forty denars, not four hundred. I learned the tannin trick from my father the morning Lord Aerlon's reeve came to measure our shop for seizure. Father had a stave-blank curing in the corner barrel and he made me hide it under my cloak before they kicked the door in. On the road north he taught me the rest of it — the moon-cut, the iron, the count of nights — because he knew he would not see another winter and the knowledge had to live somewhere. So when I sell you a re-shafted axe, you are paying for three nights of a dead man's patience. One more thing, since you have stood with us. The pitch I seal the binding with — that I will not tell. Not yet. But ask me again after another season on the road and I might let it slip over a cup.
My Father's Hoops And Staves

My father kept a cooper's shop two streets back from the river-gate at Pen Cannoc. Barrels, buckets, butter-firkins — anything a man could hoop and bind, my father bent the staves for it. I was eight when he first put a draw-knife in my hand, and the smell of fresh oak shavings is still the only smell I trust. Then Lord Ervil of the Crossing decided the lane belonged to his wife's brother. No writ, no court-day, no warning — just three men with billhooks and a parchment nobody read aloud. They took the shop, the wood-yard, the iron hoops my father had paid forty denars a bundle for, and when my father set his hand on the door-post they took his fingers too. He lived a winter after that. Not much of one. So I walked. I had a draw-knife, a small adze, and a cooper's rasp — no forge, no anvil, no coin for either. The road took me past Quyaz and the cart-tracks the Battanian wood-runners use, and somewhere in the third week a man with a notched bow asked me whether I could put a new strap on a buckler. I could. I did. He fed me, and he brought me here. That's why I mend. A forge wants charcoal and quench-water and a smith who learned at twelve, and I'm none of those. But I can rivet a split scabbard, re-strap a brigandine, re-haft an axe, re-stitch a saddle-skirt, and pull the rust off an edge that some fool let sit in the rain. The camp keeps me in oak and oil and a roof, and I keep their gear standing one more season. I don't forge new things. New things belong to men with shops on lanes that nobles haven't taken yet. I mend — because the world is full of broken iron, and somebody has to put the hoops back round it.
Word From The Cart-Roads

Word from Pen Cannoc is the garrison's tightening fists around every iron ingot that comes off the western roads. Their reeve hung two tinkers last moon for "unlicensed mending" — meaning the smiths there want all the broken kit funneled through their forges at twice the honest price. Anything we mend here costs the bearer half what those gate-smiths charge, and no questions about where the rivets came from. A Battanian caravan slipped past the toll-ford ten days back hauling raw bog-iron south toward Marunath — six mules, no escort worth speaking of, drovers half-drunk on heather-beer. Word is they sold the lot to a merchant working for Lord Caradros, who's quietly stockpiling for shields he doesn't want the High King counting. If you're moving that road, the runoff scraps are still scattered along the verges where mules broke pack. Dunglanys is paying forty denars a head for journeyman bowyers — their string-master died of the coughing-fever and the fian-bands are screaming for new staves before the autumn raid season. They're not asking where a man trained, which tells you how desperate the steward's gotten. A useful place to fence a bundle of yew or a stack of unfletched shafts, if you can stomach the road. Last bit, and this one's worth the listen — a Sturgian peddler came through three nights past, said the highland reaver-clans are buying every leather scrap and rivet they can find. Means a war-band's kitting up quiet, and means saddle-leather and harness-iron will fetch double their summer price by month's end. Mend what you've got now. Sell what you can't keep.
Halvar Cooper
Carved staves for poachers in the deep oaks before the lord's gibbet-men hanged his brother Brec. Now he carves for Hod's boys; the bows are unmarked but they fly true.

Halvar Cooper, traveler. Name a stave and I'll tell you who it killed. The chief lets you walk — that's the chief. But the staves are mine, and a man earns them. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} from the road, and you'll see what an unmarked Battanian bow flies like.

The staves come from a coppiced stand my grandfather worked, traveler. The wood remembers the cut — that's why the bows fly true. Imperial stockmen call it 'old-growth flutter' and don't know what they're saying.

Mark me a draw-weight and a wood, traveler. On your next pass I'll have a stave that drinks the wind. The unmarked ones I sell are good — the marked ones I keep for the boys. Here, a wax-pull off the spare to seal the deal.

Brec was my elder, traveler. The gibbet-men came at the high field — Vlandian law called it 'poaching' for three hares the lord hadn't named. I carved his name into the stave-stand the morning after. The grain's grown around it now.

Find Old Aengus at the Tinker's Bridge, traveler — carves cradles by day, arrow-shafts by lamp-night. He learned the unmarked-stave trick from my grandfather. Tell him you've sat at Hod's fire; he'll show you the lamp-night shelf. Coin for the road.

Lean close, friend, and keep this between us — the salt knows what the snow hides. A driver came through three nights past, frost still on his beard, and he let slip that Lord Vesimir Greycoat is bleeding silver faster than a gutted herring bleeds brine. His men haven't been paid since the thaw, and his quartermaster has been buying salt-cod on credit from Revyl — the kind of credit nobody intends to honor. If you cross his banner on the road, his garrison's hungry, and hungry men sell their oaths cheap. The southern grain road out of Tyal is thinner than a widow's stew this season. Two caravans came through and both said the same: escort of six, sometimes four, sometimes a single drunk huscarl who couldn't tell a wolf from his own shadow. The wheat barges are stacking up at the docks because the merchants are too frightened to move them inland, and the price of black bread in the up-country villages has doubled. Salt-cured grain, oats, anything that keeps — somebody clever could buy low at the docks and sell at the inland holds for thirty denars a sack more than fair. And here's the morsel worth chewing on. There's a fat little spice-broker out of Omor — bald fellow, rings on every finger — who's overpaying like a fool for smoked fish. Sixty denars a barrel, when the going rate on the coast is forty. Word is his wife's people are Sturgian and she'll only eat the proper smoked stuff from up north, and he can't stand to disappoint her. A man with a wagon and a nose for smokehouses could double his coin in a single run if he doesn't drink the profits along the way. Last thing, and then I'm done. The smokehouses east of Varcheg are short on alder wood — a fire took half their stock in spring — and they're paying near double for any cartload that arrives before the frost sets hard. My Sami used to cut alder in his younger years. He'd have known. But you didn't hear any of this from old Nikolai, you understand. The salt keeps its counsel, and so do I.

You ask the secret, eh? Sit closer. The wind takes words and I will only say this once. The salt-cod you bought last moon — that is not common salt. It is three-pull brine: first pull is sea-salt from the rocks below Varcheg, coarse, grey, full of iron. Second pull is rock-salt the reavers bring back from the eastern raids, sweeter, drier. Third pull — and this is the trick — is wood-ash from birch only, never pine. Pine ash makes the cod taste of resin and a man will spit it out by the second bite. Birch ash pulls the wet from the flesh slow, like a patient hand, and leaves the fish firm but never brittle. My Pyotr taught me this on the day the ice broke early, the year before the frost took him. He said his father learned it from a Nordic trader at Omor who came down with two barrels of cod that did not rot through a whole winter march. The secret is not the salt — every fool has salt. The secret is the order. First, gut and split, never scale. Then bury in the coarse grey for two days. Then wash in sea-water — not fresh, never fresh, fresh water kills the flavor. Then the rock-salt for four days, weighted with stone. Then the birch ash rub, only the palms, never a cloth. A cloth steals the oil from your hand and the cod needs that oil to seal. Smoke I do not use. Smoke is for men who do not trust their salt. The reavers ride in winter and they cannot carry smoked fish — it sweats inside the leather and goes sour by the third night. Salt-cod cured my way will sit in a saddle-pouch for forty days and still feed a man on the forty-first. That is why they pay me what they pay me. Two hundred denars for a sack that would fetch eighty in Revyl, and they do not haggle. They know. One more thing, since you have shown yourself honest. If you ever try this yourself — and I doubt you will, the work is hard — do not let the cod freeze before the third pull. The grey salt has to draw, and a frozen fish draws nothing. I learned this the bad way, the first winter alone, when I lost a whole catch and ate cabbage for two months. Pyotr would have laughed at me. He laughed at everything. That is what I miss most.
The Salt Always Pays

My man Yegor pulled cod from the Sturgian shallows out past Revyl for nineteen winters, and I salted every fish he ever brought home. We were not rich, but the smokehouse stayed lit and the barrels stayed full. Then the frost came down hard the year the ice ate the longboats, and Yegor went under with his net still in his hand. They never found him. Only his belt washed up on the gravel a week later, swollen and grey. The boyars at Revyl took the boat for tax debts before the wake was finished. Lord Vladic wouldn't see me at his gate — said a fisher's widow had no claim on a vessel that owed the crown. I sold what I could carry and walked north with two barrels of salt-cod on a sled, looking for any roof that would have me. A widow without a hearth dies in three nights up here. Everyone knows it. The reavers found me on the third night, half-frozen at the foot of a stone cairn. They could have taken the cod and left me. They didn't. The chief tasted my salt, looked at my hands, and said a woman who can cure fish that well is worth more breathing than buried. So I cure for them now. Cod, seal-meat, the river-pike when the lads bring them in, and I keep the salt-pans running in the lower cave where the air stays dry. I trade fair because cold trade IS honest trade — there is no room up here for sweet talk or short measure. A barrel of salt-cod costs you what a barrel of salt-cod costs. Sixty denars for the cured, forty for the smoked, and the dried strips go by weight. The reavers eat first, you eat second, and what's left I'll send south with the next runner toward Omor if the passes are open. I don't miss Yegor every day anymore. I miss him when the wind comes off the ice and smells like his coat. The rest of the time I work, and the work pays, and that is enough for a woman who used to think the sea owed her something. It owed me nothing. The salt does. The salt always pays.
Word From The Salt-Runners

The salt-runners came down from Revyl three nights past, and they tell me the smokehouses there will pay forty denars a barrel for cod packed dry — twice last winter's price. The fjord catch failed, see. Every herring boat that limped home came back half-empty, and the jarls are buying anything that swims, salted or sour. Grain is the other tale. Lord Olek of the Black Hand bought out three caravans bound for Tyal — paid in coin, not promises — and now the village hearths north of the Sturgian woods are baking rye-husk bread thin as parchment. Famine's coming up the river road by the first thaw, mark me. The reavers will eat well; the cottars will not. There's a Vlandian wine-train moving east out of Pen Cannoc, sweetwine in oak, bound for some lordling's wedding at Pravend. Three wagons, eight guards, slow because the road's still ice. My old salt-partner Bjorn Greyhook sent word — if a certain camp were to hear of it, certain barrels might find their way to certain cellars. I sell salt. I do not sell the location of wagons. But I do not forget who pays in good silver, either. Last word — the eel-ponds at Quyaz froze through, bottom to top. Whole season's catch lost. Khuzait merchants are riding west looking for smoked fish at any price, and they carry dinars heavier than our coin. A clever man with a sled of cod could ride back rich, or ride back dead. The steppe doesn't care which. So that's the road, as I have it. Three markets hungry, one wagon fat, one famine creeping. Buy what you can carry. Spring is a thief and winter is worse.
Nikolai Salt-Hand
Worked the Pravend salt-pans before his guildhouse cut his ration for refusing a foreign trade-deal. Came north with three barrels and a vendetta — the Reavers ate well that first winter.

Nikolai Salt-Hand, traveler. Vargolf says you walked the snow without leaving a body — that's no small mark. But the salt's mine, and I sold my last share to a guild that betrayed me. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll season your fire the way the Pravend lords used to be served.

Pravend salt isn't the white-flake the imperials sell, traveler — it's grey-grain, three-times-washed, draws the marrow up through bone. Lordly cooks would pay an outrider's wage for a barrel. I haven't sold them one yet. The vendetta keeps.

Tell me the meat and the man, traveler, and I'll season a feast the Pravend high-table used to call winter's-keep. Six denars upfront, a barrel on your saddle next pass. Here, a pinch for your road-stew tonight.

Had a daughter — Anya. Her hand was the payment for the trade-deal I refused. The guildhouse took her north as a 'ward'; she'd be twenty winters now, if winters kept her. I salt her name into every barrel I open. The grey draws the count up out of nothing.

Old Yevgen pickles fish at the Sturgian dock-quarter under a fishmonger's sign — same grey salt, half the price. Tell him Nikolai's barrel still waits for the guild that broke us. He'll fill your sack twice. Coin for the ferry-toll.

Lean close, friend, the bellows drown the words and that suits me fine. A salt-runner out of Omor bought a horseshoe off me last week and paid in coin and tongue both. He says Lord Vagas hasn't paid his garrison in two moons — sold his second-best stallion to a Vlandian factor for half its worth. A lord short on denars sells his swords cheap and his secrets cheaper. Mark that. The Sturgian iron road from Revyl down through the pine cuts — escort's thin. Used to ride forty spears, now it's twelve drunk huscarls and a wagon-master who can't tell north from his own arse. Three billet-trains have come through in a month and not one with a proper screen. If a man wanted Sturgian steel at Battanian prices, that road's bleeding it. I'm not saying. I'm just saying. Here's the one worth your ear. A fat little fence in Tyal — calls himself a tanner, isn't — is paying double on cured boar-hide. Double. Some northern lord's outfitting a hunt-company in secret and the leather glut up here means I can buy hides for next to nothing and sell them to him at his price. I won't be the only one onto it long, so if you're riding that way and your saddlebags have room, we can split the freight and the take. And mind — none of this came from me. The forge is loud and old Magnus is half-deaf in his bad ear. Whatever you heard, you heard from the wind.

You want the secret? Lean close, southerner. Half the smiths in Sibir will tell you the cold makes the steel brittle. They are fools who learned their trade in a heated shop and never left it. The cold is the second hammer. When I draw a blade glowing yellow from the coals and the wind off the ice is on my back, the surface skin of the steel sets harder than the core in the same breath. That is the secret — a differential temper without clay, without the painted lines the Vlandians use. Just the wind. Just the dark. I forge with the forge door open to the snow, and I time the strikes between gusts. The grandfather of my grandfather was a shield-wright at Revyl, and he taught my father, and my father taught me before the Sturgian iron took my eye at the wall. There is a thing he showed me with the seax-spine. You fold the high-carbon billet seven times — never eight, eight is the Vlandian count and it leaves the steel tired — and on the final fold you quench in seal oil, not water. Seal oil holds the heat slower, draws the carbon to the edge without warping the back. The blade comes out with a spine soft enough to bend against your knee and an edge that will shave the hair off your forearm a year later. I sell those for eighty denars apiece and lose money on every one, but a man should leave good work behind him. The leather is the other half nobody asks about. I cure the scabbard hides in brine and birch-tar smoke for a full moon before I cut a single strap. Most of the leatherwrights you'll meet south of the Hrustgar ridge soak their hides three days and call it done — and three winters later their scabbards are rotted and their grips are loose. Mine outlast the man who buys them. Old Yarrick, who runs the tannery at the edge of camp, keeps a barrel of the brine going year-round just for my orders. He is missing two fingers from the same shield-wall that took my eye, so he understands why the work has to be slow. One more thing, since you have earned it. If you ever buy a blade from a smith and he will not let you see it quenched, walk away. The quench is where the lie lives. A coward smith hides the quench because his steel hisses wrong, or his oil is cut with tallow, or the blade twists and he straightens it cold afterward — which any man with one eye can feel in the balance. I quench in the open. You can stand at the door and watch the steam rise off the seal oil if you like. That is how my father did it, and his father, and that is why the men of Sibir still come to me when the southern jarls have ruined their armouries.
Iron Remembers The Cold

You ask what pays a man into this trade. The honest answer is a Sturgian shield-rim and a winter that wouldn't end. I stood in the third rank at the wall outside Revyl, axe in my off-hand, when a boss-spike came over the top and took my right eye clean as a butcher's hook. The surgeon wanted twenty denars to sew the lid shut. I gave him fifteen and the broken axe, and he called it square. Couldn't soldier after that. Depth-vision's a fine thing to lose for a man who swings sharp things at moving targets. So I went back to what my father taught me before the levies came calling, only now I had the shake in my off-hand and one good eye for the glow of the bloom. Spent two winters in a smithy outside Sibir hammering nails for fishing-sleds. Nails. After the shield-wall. The shame of it kept me warm when the bellows didn't. What I learned in those two winters is the cold loves a forge more than any southern sun. Steel quenched in Revyl river-ice holds an edge a Pravend smith would weep for. The grain tightens. The temper goes deep instead of glassy. Bergthor of the Lake tried to buy my whole shop for sixty denars a month and a roof; I told him my anvil don't travel south of the snowline, and he called me a fool. Reavers found me when the Sturgian tax-collectors did, and one was friendlier than the other. They wanted helms reshaped, mail re-ringed, axe-eyes re-hafted — honest work, paid in coin or in the warlord's silence, depending on the week. I keep my forge under their roof now. The cold helps the temper, the camp keeps the tax-men south of the ridge, and a one-eyed smith with a steady left hand turns out gear that holds against any shield-wall I ever stood in. That's the trade. Cold steel, cold price, cold truth. The eye was the down-payment. The rest of me's been paying interest ever since.
Cold Anvils, Colder Coin

Word from Revyl is the garrison is taking on smiths — three, maybe four, paid in salt and silver both. Lord Bulgnak wants two hundred round-shields banded in iron before the thaw, and he is not haggling. If a man still had two good eyes and a whole back, that contract would be worth the ride. A caravan out of Sibir is moving steel-stock south along the frozen river road — Battanian billets, the dark grey kind that takes a long edge. They lost two guards to wolves last week, so the captain is hiring spears at forty denars a day. The stock itself? He will sell short bars to anyone with coin and no questions. I bought what I could carry. Jarl Yrsa at Omor paid out for a full set of lamellar last moon — twelve hundred denars, they say, and the smith who took the work has not been seen since. Make of that what you will. Up here, a man finishes a commission and then he disappears, and the jarl's hall has new armor on the wall. I do my work in the open, where the camp can see. The Sturgian shield-wall took my eye but it taught me the trade — every dent in those wall-shields was a lesson. So when I tell you the southern leather coming up through Tyal is too soft for our winter, believe me. Use it for grips, not for facings. The cold finds the weak stitch, same as the spear does. Last thing. There is a Vlandian factor riding the back tracks asking who supplies blades to the reavers. Offers two hundred denars for a name. Nobody has sold mine yet — but if you hear it whispered, you tell me before you tell him. Cold steel. Cold price. Cold truth.
Magnus One-Eye

Lost his eye to a Vlandian outrider who took his daughter's hand in payment for a debt the Yulskaya didn't owe. Forges now under Vargolf's banner; the blade he made for that outrider is still spoken of in the high passes.

Magnus One-Eye, traveler. The chief takes your measure with axe-eyes; I take it with the empty one. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} from the snow-road, and I'll forge you what no Vlandian outrider would dare carry. That's a long story — the empty eye keeps it for another fire.

Vlandian outriders forge their plate at noon-heat, full-charcoal — quick to make, brittle by the third campaign. I bank the fire down to ember-glow for the last temper. Three more strokes a blade and the steel sings instead of cracks.
Bring me an iron-bar and your name, traveler, and I'll bank the next pull just for you. Long blade, axe-head, hammer — your hand on it before it cools. A token from the spare-stock to mark the deal.

Lost the eye to a Vlandian outrider in payment for a debt the Yulskaya didn't owe. He took my daughter's hand the same hour — that part of the night the empty eye keeps for itself. The blade I made for him is still spoken of in the high passes. He doesn't tell it as praise.

Find Hjalmar Ember-Hand in the Nevyansk forges — he learned his last temper from me before I came north. Tell him One-Eye still banks low; he'll know I sent you. He charges fair if you bring the iron yourself. Take this for the iron.

Lean close, friend. The reeds whisper, aye, but so do the bargemen who tie up past the bend, and I've been listening to both. Word from a salt-hauler out of Pen Cannoc is that Lord Caradoc has gone quiet on his debts — three smokehouses up the coast won't take his promissory marks anymore, and his steward was seen begging credit for two barrels of brined trout. Man's purse is thinner than a heron's leg. If you owe him favor, collect now in denars, not next moon. The grain road through the lower fens — the one that hugs Marunath — is walking with only four spears these past ten days. Four. For a six-cart train of barley and smoked carp. The merchant's a Vlandian fellow, name of Renier of Galend, and he's cheap as a clipped coin. Bargemen reckon he'll lose the lot before the next half-moon. I don't say what a man should do with that knowing — only that I know it, and now you do. Here's the one worth the eel-grease: there's a butter-and-cheese factor out of Sibir overpaying — I mean truly overpaying, twelve denars the pound for smoked eel, when the going rate's seven at any market between here and the salt-flats. Some Nord lordling's hosting a feast and his cook went mad with the menu. The factor's at the crossroads tavern by Car Banseth till the new moon. Take him your smoked stock; don't haggle soft, the man's desperate and won't blink. One last thing, and I'd not say it to a stranger. Salt's drying up north — the brine pans at Omor took a flood and won't yield till midsummer. Anyone holding salt now sells it for triple by harvest. The reeds didn't tell me that one. A drunken salter did, two nights past, before his cousin clouted him quiet. So you heard it from the eels, understand? Not from me.

You want the secret? Lean close. It is not the catching — any drunk with a spear can stab an eel in clear water. It is the curing. Most folk gut their eels, salt them flat, hang them in smoke for three days, and end up with leather you could resole a boot with. Mine come off the rack soft as river-clay and sweet as a young wife's first bread. The trick is the reeds. Not just any reeds — the black-tipped ones that grow downstream of where the bitterns nest, where the water turns the colour of strong tea. I cut a bundle thick as my wrist, bruise them with a mallet until the green smell comes out, then layer them between the split eels in a clay crock. Coarse salt on top, a fistful of crushed juniper berries I gather from the dry hummocks, and one — only one — pinch of the brown sugar I trade for at Sanala when the caravans pass. Press it with a flat stone the weight of a newborn. Three days in the crock, then two more in cold smoke from alder wood. Never oak. Oak makes them bitter. Never pine. Pine makes them taste of a man's piss. My grandfather showed me this the winter my mother died. I was nine. He sat me on his knee in the smoke-shed and said, "Tomas, the marsh feeds the man who listens to it. The reeds tell the eels where to hide. They tell us how to keep them." He had no teeth left, only gums hard as boot-soles, and he ate three of these eels every morning until the day he walked into the fog and did not walk back. I think the reeds called him too. I do not mind. I will go the same way one day. Tell no one the alder. I have killed two men who tried to sell my eels in Pravend as their own work, and both times the buyers came back asking why the new batch tasted of pine. Word of the alder gets out, and any fool with a smoke-shed can undercut me at four denars the brace. Keep it behind your teeth, friend, and I will keep a crock aside for you when the season turns.
The Reeds Told Me Where

Sit. Mind the slat — it sinks. My da was a reed-cutter near Pen Cannoc, sold bundles to the thatchers for half-copper a stack. I learned the marsh before I learned my letters, which I never did learn. The reeds breathe different over an eel-hole. Slow. Heavy. Like a sleeping dog. Took an arrow in the eye at twelve, working a fen for a Vlandian tax-man who called my da a poacher. Da bled out in the punt; I crawled home blind on the left. The lord — some cousin of Lord Caladog, name not worth keeping — paid us four denars in settlement and called the matter closed. Four. For a man and an eye. I learned a useful number that day. After that I worked the smokehouses up at Jaculan — gutting, salting, hanging eel over alder coals till the flesh went amber. Good trade, honest trade, until the steward cut wages and the guild blamed the marsh-folk for the shortage. I walked out with a barrel of brine and a smoker's grate strapped to my back. The reeds were waiting where I'd left them. Found this camp by following a heron three days west. The captain tried the eel-stew, paid me in salt and a dry corner, said stay. So I stay. I pull eels blind — proper blind, the good eye's near gone too — and the reeds tell me where. They lean toward the holes. They whisper at the fat ones. You think I'm soft in the head; that's fine. The pot's full and the boys eat. Pays a man into this trade? Four denars and a dead father. Everything since has been the marsh keeping me, and me keeping the marsh. Take the smoked eel — it's good. Salt's from Ortongard, paid honest.
Reeds Whisper, Roads Talk

Sit. Mud's warm enough. Word travels slow through the fens, but it travels — boatmen pass it bowl to bowl, and I keep my ears open while I'm gutting. Three things worth your while, maybe four. Listen as slow as I talk. Pen Cannoc is short on salt. Two of the upland smokehouses lost their winter stock to damp rot, and the steward's quartermaster has been paying fourteen denars a sack — fourteen, for grey salt that's half marsh-grit. If you've got clean stone-salt and a strong back, the road north pays better than the road south right now. A grain caravan out of Druimmor went into the bogs two weeks back and hasn't come out. Lord Caradoc's reeve has been riding the causeway every dawn looking for it, which means his garrison's ration is thinning. Hearth-bread will spike by the next moon. I'd hold any barley you've got — sell it after the frost, not before. The sweetwine boats from Epicrotea are coming up through the delta again, late but coming. Old Halvar at the lower jetty already bought out two casks for resale — he'll mark them triple by midsummer. Buy direct off the boat or don't buy at all. Last thing, and you didn't hear it from me. The eels are running wrong this year. Reeds bend south when they shouldn't, and the females are coming up thin. That means a lean smokehouse autumn from Pen Cannoc clear down to Quyaz — dried meat will be the only winter trade worth carrying. Mark it. The marsh is patient, but it isn't generous twice.
Tomas Eel-Bone

Wove fish-traps and dried eels for the swamp villages until the Vlandian crown reassigned his fishing-rights to a southern viscount. Stayed in the reeds; the viscount's tax-clerks never came back twice.

Tomas Eel-Bone, traveler. The reeds let you in — that's the marsh's saying, not mine. Mine is: bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC}, and I'll dry you the kind of fish the southern viscount fenced me out of.

Marsh-eel takes the smoke different from river-fish, traveler — three days hanging in reed-smoke, not the half-day the southern fishermen rush. The flesh turns a colour they don't know how to name in Vlandia. They've stopped trying.

Tell me the size, the catch-week, the man it's for, traveler. I'll dry you a string the southern viscount's tax-clerks would have priced as 'wartime contraband.' Two denars on the reed, a sample for your pack tonight.

Wife went under to the marsh during the spring overflow — Brenwyn, of the reed-cutters. The marsh kept her; the marsh keeps everyone, eventually. I dry one extra string each season and leave it on the bank where she went under. Sometimes the next morning it's gone.

Old Lir keeps a fish-stall at the southern viscounty market — same reed-smoke trick, half the price. He's my wife's brother. Tell him Tomas still dries on the bank; he'll seat you in the back of the stall. Coin for his market-toll.

Lean close, friend. Mud-Hand don't share this with every boot that comes squelching through the reeds, but you earned an ear-bend. There's a leather-buyer up in Pen Cannoc what's gone soft in the head — paying nine denars a hide for cured deer when it ought to fetch five at most. Word from a smuggler what passed through three nights back is, the man's got a contract with some southern armorer and he's panicking. If you've got hides or know a hunter who does, that's where the gold's pooling this fortnight. Now here's the better bit. Lord Caradoc's purse is light — light as a starveling's pot. His tax-man came through pale and apologizing, which means the levy's late and the garrison's eating salt-pork older'n the keep. Lords short on coin sell things cheap, see. Armor, harness, sometimes a horse if you catch the steward in his cups. And his castle road? Thin escort. Two riders, maybe three, and one of 'em half-drunk by midday. A merchant friend told me he hauled a wagon of billets straight through and didn't see a banner. The steel itself's the trouble though. Northern caravans are bottle-necked at Varnovapol — some quarrel with the harbor-master, ships sitting fat in the bay. So billet-prices are creeping. If you're laying up war-gear, do it now before the marsh-merchants catch wind. Won't be more than a week before every smith from here to the coast is bidding double. And one last whisper — there's a glut of cheap leather coming out of Sibir, hides so thin you could read scripture through 'em. Don't buy any boots stamped with the lily mark this season. They'll rot before the first frost. Mud-Hand tells you true: out here everything rots eventually, but some things rot before they're sold.

You want to know why my boots last when others rot off the foot in a fortnight? It's the bark. Not oak — every fool uses oak. I use bog-myrtle and alder catkins, pounded into a paste and packed against the flesh side of the hide while it's still wet from the lime-pit. Three turns of the moon it sits in a covered jar buried in cool peat. The tannins go in slow, deep, and they bring the marsh-smell with them. Leeches won't touch a boot cured that way. Neither will the rot-fly maggots that get into a man's seams in Pen Cannoc garrison stores. The second trick is the fat. Marsh-deer fat won't do alone — too soft, weeps out in the heat. I render it down with a half-measure of beeswax I trade off a hedge-priest near Epicrotea, and a thumb of pine-pitch for the bite. Worked warm into the grain with a smooth river-stone, pressed and pressed until the leather drinks no more. Then it goes by the fire — not in the flame, a hand's breadth back — and turns the colour of wet bracken. That's when you know it's sealed. My grandfather showed me the bark-paste the day his own boots gave out crossing the Drowned Causeway. He sat on a tussock and laughed, said even his soles had decided to retire before he did. Pulled the rotted things off, walked home barefoot through three leagues of leech-water, and didn't take a sore. The hide on a man's feet, he told me, is the only hide that learns. Everything else you have to teach. Last thing — and I'll only say it once because I don't want to see it on every cobbler's bench from here to Tyal — the harness-stitching. I use sinew from the hind-leg, never the back, and I wax it with the same myrtle-and-fat mix instead of pitch. Doesn't show black against the leather. A horse-thief glancing at the harness sees a peasant rig, not the kind that holds a charging man in his seat. Cost you four hundred denars the full set, and I'll throw in a spare bark-jar so you can patch it yourself when the rot finally tries.
Wax The Thread, Friend

My father stitched harness for the militia at Pen Cannoc — clean shop, good awls, a window that faced the square. I learned the trade with my hands clean and my thread waxed proper. Then a tax-man with a writ I couldn't read took the shop for back-coin we never owed, and Father walked into the fen one morning and never walked back out. That was twenty winters past. The awls I carry now were his. I drifted south stitching what folk would pay for. Bridle-loops for a horse-thief outside Quyaz, boot-soles for a peat-cutter who paid me in salt-fish, a quiver for a girl who couldn't string her own bow. None of them asked where I learned my stitches and I stopped asking where they got their hides. A man with a curved knife and no questions eats more regular than a man with a clean ledger. The marsh found me the way it finds everyone — slow, then all at once. I was sleeping under a fallen alder with a fever in me when the stalkers pulled me out by the collar. They had a stack of green deer-hides nobody knew how to cure and a captain whose boots had come apart at the welt. I fixed the boots. I cured the hides. I have been fixing things here ever since, and nobody has come looking for the tax owed on me. What pays a man into this trade, you ask. Hunger pays first. Then habit. Then the quiet knowing that a good seam outlasts the man who wore it, and the hide outlasts the seam, and the bog outlasts the hide. Everything rots out here, friend, but it rots SLOWER if you waxed your thread. That is the only honest sermon I have left in me. So here I sit, cobbling marsh-deer into something that will keep your feet dry for a season, maybe two. Pay me in denars if you have them, or in salt, or in a flask of something that burns. I don't ask where the coin came from. Nobody asked me, when I started taking it.
Word From The Bog-Road

Word travels slow through the reeds, but it travels. Caravan out of Pen Cannoc dragged a wagon of Vlandian steel-stock through the fen-road last fortnight, axle-deep in mud and screaming about it. Driver swore he'd never come south of the bog again — meaning his master will pay double next season to find someone who will. I bought three bar-ends off him for sixty denars and a dry pair of boots. Honest trade. Lord Caradac up at Ocs Hall is buying shields again. Third order this year. Either his levies keep losing them in the marsh or he's stockpiling for something the heralds aren't shouting yet. My cousin's boy works the tannery there — says the order is for round-shields, marsh-pattern, not the kite-shape the knights favor. Tells you who they expect to fight. Smiths are moving east. Quyaz is paying journeymen four dinars a day to come work the desert forges, and two out of every three apprentices at Pravend have packed their hammers. Good for me — leather work stays here in the wet, where iron won't. Bad for any lord hoping to re-helm his guard before snowmelt. Battanian bowyer came through last week, name of Eithne the Splinter, hauling yew staves she'd cut north of Pen Cannoc. Said the deer up there are thinning, hunters pushing further into the highlands, harness wearing out faster than the cobblers can patch it. She left me a stave for the boots I made her. Fair trade is fair trade. Last thing — a saddler out of Revyl was murdered on the bog-road, throat opened, pack untouched. Untouched, mind. That's not a robber's work, that's a message. Whoever's sending it hasn't said to who. Watch your harness-straps, friend, and don't ride alone past the dead willow.
Cael Mud-Hand
Tans pelts the marsh leaves on its bank — adder-skin, fen-otter, drowned-deer. His leather doesn't rot in wet country; the fen people say he learned the trick from the marsh itself.

Cael Mud-Hand, traveler. The chief lets you walk — Mireborn's eye is good. Mine's narrower. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and we'll see whether your steel deserves leather the marsh hasn't claimed back yet.

Marsh hide tans different, traveler — you let the fen do the first work, three days under reed-water before the oak-bark. The leather doesn't rot in wet country. Vlandian tanners can't replicate it; they've stopped trying.

Bring me a beast you've taken yourself, traveler — adder, fen-otter, drowned-deer — and I'll cobble you a piece the marsh hasn't claimed back. Half the denar on the hide, the rest on the fit. A swatch for your pack tonight.

My boys learned the tan from me, traveler. The marsh took the youngest the year of the long flood — Bren, eight winters then. The middle one walked out to imperial recruiters at fourteen; I don't say his name now. The eldest's still here, somewhere in the reeds; I see his snare-marks on the deer.

Find Old Garrick at the Battanian forest-edge — he learned reed-water tanning from my father before the family split. Tell him Cael still works the fen; he'll show you the inner stretch-rack. Coin for the long road.

Lean close, friend, and keep your voice low — I tally every grain twice but I tally rumors thrice, and what I'm about to spill is worth more than the salt in my pouch. Word from a Battanian drover three nights past: Lord Caladog has been paying his garrison in promises and stale bread for two whole weeks. His steward came through Pen Cannoc trying to buy two hundred bushels of barley on credit, and the miller laughed him out of the yard. A man who can't feed his own walls won't be marching anywhere soon — and his caravans up the western fork are riding with four guards where they used to ride with twelve. Now here's the morsel I've been chewing on. The smokehouse at Marunath burned to the studs a fortnight back — lightning, they say, but I've heard whispers it was a jealous cousin with a torch. Either way, smoked ham is scarce from the Hercotid all the way to the Bartin, and there's a Vlandian quartermaster in Galend paying forty-two denars a side when the going rate's twenty-eight. Run a string of pack-mules up that road and you'll come back with your saddlebags clinking. Just don't take the river road — the bridge-toll man's gone greedy and his cousins in the reeds are greedier still. And the salt — gods, the salt. The Aserai caravans coming up from Husn Fulq have been thin all spring because the southern pans are flooded, so the brine boilers at Sanala are charging double and the inland towns are screaming. I had a Sturgian cheese-monger sit on that crate yonder and weep into his beer — said he'd pay eighteen dinars a sack to anyone who could get him three. So if you happen across a wagon that smells of brine and looks lightly guarded, well. I'm not telling you what to do. I'm just saying the man weeps real tears and his purse is real heavy. One last thing, and then I'll let you go. Lord Rhagaea's grain reserves at Pravend are bigger than she's letting on — I had a granary-boy through here last week who'd skimmed off the count-books before he ran, and the empire's sitting on enough wheat to feed an army twice over. Means prices in the south are going to crash by harvest, and any sack of flour you're holding past midsummer will be worth half what it is today. Sell early, sell hot, and don't tell anyone where you heard it. Roger Tally-Sack counts twice, but he only whispers once.

You want my secret? Lean close, friend, and keep your voice low — this one cost me three winters to perfect. It's the double-tally brine, and no other quarter-master on the road keeps it. I take coarse rock-salt from the Sargot pans — never the sea-salt, too bitter — and I measure it twice: once by weight, once by handfuls. Three handfuls to the pound, then I weigh again to be sure no clerk's thumb tipped the scale. Into the brine goes crushed juniper, two cloves of wild garlic per gallon, and one spoon of honey for every five of salt. The honey is the trick — it draws the salt deeper into the meat without souring the cure. The meat itself — pork shoulder, venison haunch, whatever the boys drag in — gets pricked all over with a darning needle before it goes in the crock. Twenty-four punctures, I count them, every time. Then it sits eleven days in the cold cellar, turned every dawn and every dusk. Not ten days, not twelve — eleven. I learned that from an old curing-woman near Galend who used to supply Lord Derthert's own larder before the war scattered her village. She said ten leaves the centre raw, twelve turns the edges to leather. After the brine, I smoke it cold over apple-wood and a single handful of dried thyme. Cold smoke, mind — never hot. A hot smoke cooks the meat and locks the salt where it landed; a cold smoke lets the flavour breathe through the whole cut. Three days in the smokehouse, then a fortnight hanging in the rafters wrapped in linen. The boys think I'm mad when I make them wait that long, but I've sold a single cured ham to a passing caravan-master for forty denars, and he came back six months later asking for two more. My grandfather taught me to count grain in the Vlandian granaries, but it was my old aunt who taught me the brine, on the morning my mother died of fever. She said: "Roger, the dead we cannot save, but the meat we can — and a man who feeds the living honours both." I tally every grain twice because she taught me grief makes a man careless, and a careless quarter-master starves his own brothers. Don't pass that secret to the next traveller through. It's yours now.
A Clerk's Long Road Down

Twice. Every sack, every measure, every fist of grain — twice. That is the only honest thing a man can do with another man's stores, and I learned it at a counting-desk in Pravend before I learned anything about this road. My father was clerk to a wool-factor, his father before him, and by the time I had whiskers I could tally a season's fleeces faster than the scribe could wet his quill. I thought I would die at that desk with ink on my cuffs and a pension of forty denars a year. Gods laugh at clerks who plan. It was a grain ledger that finished me. Lord Derthert's steward wanted three hundred measures hidden from the tithe-men, and my master signed his name to the lie. When the crown's auditor came, the master pointed at the junior clerk — me — and the rope was already being measured. I went out the cellar window with a satchel of dried apples and the ledger itself, because a man with proof of a lord's theft has either a long life or a short one, and I meant to pick which. I sold the ledger to a smuggler outside Galend for twelve denars and a head start. The road teaches you faster than any abacus. I ran salt out of the Mire for a winter, drove dates up from the south for a season, and lost two fingers to a frostbite that taught me to respect a smokehouse the way townsmen respect a chapel. I came to this camp three winters back with a broken cart and four barrels of eels nobody else would buy. The boss tasted one, grunted, and pointed at the storehouse. I have been counting it ever since. Now I keep the larders the way I kept my master's books — twice, and honest within the four walls of this stockade. Grain in the dry crocks, smoked meat hung above the hearth-stones, hard bread for the long rides, salt-pork for the rougher work. The lads bring in what the road provides; I weigh it, mark it, and feed them out of it. They grumble that I shave the loaves thin. They are correct. A camp that eats fat in autumn starves in spring, and I have buried enough men to know the difference. So that is what pays a man into this trade — a steward's lie, a window in a cellar, and a learned dread of empty crocks. No credit, friend. No promises. Coin or grain, weighed in front of you, written down twice. It is the only kindness an honest quarter-master can offer.
Tallies From The Tollway

The word, you say. Sit then, but don't lean on the salt-sack — I've counted it twice and I'll count it a third before sundown. The road's been chattering, and a clerk's ear never stops, even when the clerk's wearing road-leather instead of guild-grey. Pravend is starving for grain — not loud-starving, the quiet kind, where the granary-master smiles and quotes you sixty denars the bushel and pretends his ledger isn't shaking. Word from a peddler who came through at dawn: Lord Aldric of Galend paid out of his own purse to refill the castle bins after the spring rains rotted half the stores. Any sack we can spare west goes for double what it fetches here. I've already set aside four for the next runner. The salt road south is the prize, though. Jaculan caravans are moving sweetwine and dates up the coast — the Aserai pay fair coin for hard cheese and smoked river-eel, and they'll trade barrel-for-barrel if your wine-keeper knows how to haggle. Don't send a fool. They count grains the way I count grains, and they smile while they do it. Famine word from the north: Revyl lost two villages' worth of barley to a Sturgian frost that came a fortnight late. By midsummer their hearth-bread will be half sawdust and the garrison will be buying anything that doesn't crawl. If you're riding that way, take dried meat — not grain, the grain'll spoil before you cross the passes. Take meat and take twice what you think you need. Last bit, and mark it: a Vlandian merchant train out of Pen Cannoc is moving south next week with sixteen wagons of smokehouse stock — bacon, hard sausage, the good stuff. Tomas the Hook on the eastern road heard it from a guard who drinks too much. I'm not telling you to do anything about it. I'm telling you the wagons exist, and that the camp's larder is light. Coin or grain — those are the prices. The rest is the road's business.
Roger Tally-Sack
A Vlandian quartermaster's clerk who learned to skim until the audit caught him. The Reeve hired him the morning his sentence was read; the company's larder has been twice as full ever since.

Roger Tally-Sack — the Reeve's columns include me, two pages back. Welcome to my line of the ledger, traveler. The chief's good for letting you walk; I'm not. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll record you as 'paid in full' — that's how the company books work.

Quartermaster's trick, traveler — the column eats off the third pannier first, the spoils off the first. Fresh on the bottom, cleared on the top. Vlandian audit-clerks never knew which row to inspect. Still don't. The Reeve eats well because of it.

Name a banquet, traveler — wedding feast, victory dinner, governor's welcome. Six denars on my ledger and the next pass through, I'll have it packed and stamped 'requisitioned.' A sample on the line tonight, no charge.

Wife stayed in Pravend when the audit caught me. Two boys — they'd be journeymen now, if Vlandian guilds still seat audit-men's sons. I send a portion of my book each season through a mendicant friar; he tells me they got it once. Not twice. The ledger keeps the rest.

Magister Bardolph keeps the wine-list at the Galician staging-house — same crooked column-trick I taught him in the audit-office. Tell him Roger's still got the third-pannier rule running; he'll uncork the Vlandian red. Coin for his discretion.

Lean in, friend, and keep your voice low. A muleteer came through three nights past with a tongue loose from too much sour wine, and he let slip that Lord Caelin of the Hearth-Vale has been paying his garrison in promises and stale bread for near two months. His treasury's hollow as a rotted log. Now why does that matter to a strap-cutter like me? Because a lord short on denars sells off his armory in quiet lots, and quiet lots mean buckle-fittings and harness-rings going cheap to anyone with a wagon and no questions. Watch the back gates of Ortongard at dusk on market-days. You didn't hear it from me. The Iron Road south of Varnovapol has gone soft, too. Used to be three patrols a day, sometimes a knight's banner riding with them. Now? One patrol at sunrise and a pair of drunk levies after. Two steel-billet caravans rolled through last week with nothing but a hired guard apiece — and one of those guards was a boy of fifteen with a borrowed spear. The chief's already eyeing the third run. If you've a mind for honest work, the gang could use a sword on that road; if you've a mind for dishonest work, well, the prices we'll be charging on cut billets next month will tell you everything. Here's the real gift, though, the one I'd not tell a stranger. There's a fool of a merchant in Sanala — fat fellow, smells of clove — who's paying near triple market rate for tanned ox-hide because his contract with the southern saddlers is due and his usual supplier got pinched at a ford. He's burning through denars like a man with a sister to marry off. I've a stack of forty hides in the back cellar, lifted off a Battanian wagon two moons ago. You ride them to him with a straight face and a half-believable story, I take seven parts in ten, you take three. Quill says yes or no by sundown — the gossip won't keep, and neither will the hides.

Pull up that stool. Aye, you've earned a sit-down — most who ask my craft get the lecture about oak-bark tannin and bee-grease, but you've ridden with us once now, so I'll tell you the real of it. The secret isn't in the leather. It's in WHERE on the strap you cut. Every caravan saddle has a sweet band — three fingers wide, running just behind the cantle skirt — where the rider's weight has worked the fibers a thousand leagues without ever soaking sweat through. That band, that's gold. The rest is rind. Most strap-cutters slice lengthwise down the whole skirt and wonder why their reins snap in the cold. I cut ACROSS the grain at a twelve-degree slant, follow the worked band edge-to-edge, and I get four reins from one skirt where a greedy man gets two cracked ones. Then I rub them — and listen close, this part I learned from an old harness-Jew in Amitatys the winter I nearly lost my fingers — I rub them with rendered horse-marrow mixed one-to-three with pine pitch warmed over ember, not flame. Flame ruins the pitch. Ember keeps it sticky. Strap drinks it slow over two nights wrapped in oilcloth. The trick after that is the salt-cure. Aye, salt — on leather. Sounds mad. A pinch of grey rock-salt worked into the flesh side BEFORE the marrow goes on draws the last caravan-sweat out and leaves the strap supple in summer and unbrittled in frost. Most tanners would call me a liar. Let 'em. My straps don't snap when a man's hanging off a galloping horse, and theirs do. That's the only proof that matters out here. Two hundred denars a set, and I sleep easy knowing they hold. My grandfather kept ledgers same as I do — he was a tax-clerk for some forgotten count, scratched his quill till his fingers bent. The day they hanged him for skimming, he passed me his knife and said the only honest trade is the one you can weigh on a scale. I weigh every strap before it leaves this stall. You ever bring me a saddle off some lord's caravan, I'll cut you the sweet band and pay fair for the rest. That's between us.
A Clerk's Hands, A Cutter's Knife

Strap or buckle, you asked, and that's the whole of my trade — but you want the long road that brought me to it. Sit a moment. I was a clerk's apprentice in Pravend, scratching tallies for a saddler who supplied half the city's caravan-yards. My quill ran sharper than his awl, and he resented me for it. When his books showed forty denars short he blamed the lettered boy, not the wine he drank with the tax-man. They drove me out in winter with ink-stained hands and no trade-mark to my name. I worked a tannery in Galend until the lye-pits ate the skin off my fingers — that's where I learned hide from rind, kid from cow, strap-grain from belly-cut. A wagon-master named Halmar of the Long Reach took me on as his strap-mender, and for two seasons I rode his caravans south, sewing harness by lantern-light while his outriders watched the treelines. Then the boys hit us. Six of them on the Pravend-to-Quyaz road, and they knew their work. They took the oxen, the bolts of cloth, the strongbox, and Halmar's throat. I sat in the wreckage waiting for a knife and instead got a question — could I cut a saddle off a dead horse without ruining the tree. I could. I did. I cut nine that afternoon while the crows watched, and the chief said come along, scribbler, we've need of a man who knows leather from lining. Now I sit in this camp with my thick ledger and my curved knife, and every caravan the lads bring in pays me twice. First in straps — I cut them clean from the saddle-skirts before the hides go stiff, sort them by width, oil them, hang them on the rack you're standing by. Second in tally — I write down what I keep and what I sell, because a man who doesn't count his stock gets robbed by his own pockets. The chief gets his cut in denars, the boys get rebuckled before the next ride, and I get a roof that doesn't smell of lye. So that's what pays a man into this trade — a lying saddler, a lye-pit, and a dead wagon-master who taught me to keep my stitches tight. Strap or buckle, friend. Pick one. The ledger waits.
Strap, Buckle, And Ledger

The word, you say. Word's cheap, but I keep mine in ink — flip to whatever page suits you. The big one: a steel-stock train rolled out of Pravend bound for the southern garrisons, twenty mules deep, and the lead driver's been drinking too loud about which fords they cross. Boys took a peek at the route last market-day. If the gang rides on that one, I'll be cutting straps for a fortnight straight and sleeping on a mattress of new buckles. Lord Caladog paid one hundred fresh denars a piece for round shields in Pen Cannoc — bossed iron, ash-plank, the works. Means every smith from there to the coast is hammering shield-rims and ignoring the small commissions. Saddle-leather's piling up untanned because the tanners can't get the smiths to barter for the lime-pits anymore. Glut's coming. Prices'll drop. Buy your strapping now or pay me twice in a month. Caravan out of Quyaz is moving bow-stave yew, the good seasoned stuff, and they're stupid enough to take the river road. Two guards, one drunk wagoner, a merchant who thinks his ledger-name buys him safe passage. I've already promised Old Hella at the bowyer-bench in the back tent her pick of the first ten staves. Don't tell her I told you — she charges me double when she knows I'm waiting. Heard a Vlandian armorer up in Revyl is recruiting — paying ninety denars a season for any journeyman who can pattern-weld. Half the forge-rats from here to the Battanian border are walking that road right now, hammers slung on their backs. Means the country smithies between here and there are short-handed. Lord's spare lance-points, broken vambraces, dented helms — nobody's repairing them. They sell cheap, by weight. If a caravan moves scrap south, that's our scrap now. Last bit, and then you state your need or move on. Word from the eastern ridges is a relief column's coming through with new-forged kite shields — Imperial pattern, leather facing, the lot. I'll want the leather more than the wood. You see boys riding that direction, tell Branoc to cut the facings clean off and leave the planks. Straps, buckles, facings. The rest is firewood.
Edmund Grease-Quill
Bookbinder by trade, harness-maker by necessity. Stitches a saddle the same way he used to stitch a ledger — straight, flat, and uncomplaining. The Reeve pays him in book-paper, which Edmund hoards.

Edmund Grease-Quill, harness-maker. The Reeve's accounting passes you in; my stitching does not. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and the saddle I make will outlast three of your horses — and the company will note the entry.

A bookbinder's stitch lays flat, traveler — flat stitch, knot at every fourth point, waxed not greased. The Reeve's columns stay where I sew them. Imperial saddlers cross-stitch and call it strength; the cross opens at the gallop.

Bring me your saddle, your draw-weight, your gallop-distance, traveler. I'll bind you a tack that survives three of your horses. Three denars on the wax, two on the time. Here, a wax-string to mend your current rein.

Daughter apprenticed to a Pravend bookbinder; never wrote back after I joined the Reeve's column. Three years, no letter. I bind a blank book every winter and send it to the master's house — Magister Halver, third-floor shop. He doesn't return them. I take that to mean she opens one.

Halver of the Pravend Book-Quarter rebinds for the Vlandian magistrates and keeps a stitch-room for the Reeve's company. Tell him Edmund still sews flat; he'll show you the lower shelf. Coin for the door-clerk.
Salt Keeps Longer Than Coin

My father drove dates from Quyaz to Iqbayl when the southern road was still safe, and he taught me to read a well by the scum on its rope before he taught me my letters. We were honest grain-haulers then — sacks weighed twice, salt measured in flat palms, no man's child rode in the wagon-back. Then a tax-farmer of Lord Unqid took our caravan for a debt that wasn't ours and left my father in a ditch outside Husn Fulq with his throat opened over forty dinars. I walked the dunes alone for a season, eating lizard and chewing acacia gum, and I learned which wells run sweet and which run salt the way a beaten dog learns doorways. A slaver-train found me at the cistern below the Black Crag — they had bread, I had the map in my head, and we struck a bargain that didn't need writing. I cook for them now because the desert killed the man who wouldn't, and the man who would is still breathing. Don't mistake me — I'm no whip-hand. I keep the camp fed. I know where the date-palms near Razih still bear in a dry year, which Aserai widow at Durrin sells smoke-cured goat under the table, which spring north of Onica tastes of iron but won't kill a horse. The captains pay me in dinars and salt, and salt keeps longer than coin out here. The chained ones get the same flatbread I eat, same dates, same brackish tea. That's not kindness — a thirsty man fetches a poor price at Quyaz, and a starved one fetches none. I told myself that the first year. I tell myself other things now. You want bread? Sit by the fire-pit and don't haggle. Sand teaches a man what loaves are worth, and I've been taught hard.
Salt, Grain, And Sweetwine

The word on the road? Sit. Eat a date first — you look like a man who's been chewing dust since Quyaz. The southern wells are running salt this season, all of them past the third dune-line. Caravans pushing for Iqbayl are paying double for sweetwater skins, and a clever cook can buy a barrel of brine in Quyaz for a copper and sell the same brine as salt-cure in Husn Fulq for forty dinars. Salt is the new gold, friend. Always was, but folks forget between droughts. Grain's the other half of the story. Emir Unqid's steward came through last moon buying every sack of millet from here to the coast — the garrisons at Durrhd are stockpiling, which means he's expecting a siege or a famine, and a steward like me doesn't much care which. I sold him eighteen sacks at three times market and he kissed my hand for it. That's what fear does to a price. The sweetwine caravans out of Husn Fulq are running thin this year — the date harvest came in light, and the vintners are watering the press. Anyone selling you Husn red for under sixty dinars a jug is selling you vinegar with a story. The Vlandian merchants up north don't know the difference yet, so a sharp tongue can still turn a profit moving "vintage" jugs to Pen Cannoc. Don't tell them I said so. Dried meat's moving slow but steady. The smokehouses at Quyaz are buying lamb-shoulder by the wagon, paying in Aserai script that's actually worth something for once. And there's a famine sniffing around the Khuzait steppe — Monchug's herds took a winter-cull, and any caravan willing to push grain east through the passes will come home with a saddlebag of denars and a story about wolves. I won't go myself. I've buried two cousins in those passes. Last thing, and listen close — Jala the Spice-Wife at the Pravend bazaar is buying cardamom and dates at any price, paying upfront. Either she's stockpiling for a wedding feast or she knows something the rest of us don't. Me, I'm packing a cart for her next week. A steward eats by reading other people's hunger, and hers is loud.
Tariq Date-Tongue
Once supplied imperial banquets in Quyaz; was caught skimming the dried-fruit stocks and sold his way out by joining Khalid's chain. Wears the same brass anklet the slaves do — by choice, he says.

Tariq Date-Tongue. Khalid's chain is thin around your wrists, traveler — that's a privilege. My larder isn't. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll feed you the dates I used to feed the imperial governor of Quyaz before they caught me.

Imperial banquet dates aren't dried, traveler — they're sun-cured under a cotton tent, four days per layer, three layers per crate. The skin keeps the sugar tight; the flesh doesn't turn. Quyaz tax-stewards used to inspect every crate. Now they don't ask.

Bring me a feast-night and three denars, traveler. I'll cure you a crate the imperial governor's table would have demanded by name. Sample in the bowl for your road-ration. The anklet's just metal — the trade's the real chain.

Wife and son sold off ahead of me — Layla and Hamzah. Khalid's chain holds them too, in another caravan, three days east. I send word through the chain-clerks every new moon. Some moons it gets through. Most don't. The anklet's a choice because the choice is what I have left.

Salim Pomegranate-Hand keeps a date-stall in Quyaz under the date-merchants' guild seal — Khalid's brother by chain, not blood. Tell him Tariq's still under the tent; he'll seat you near the chilled-water jug. Coin for the toll-clerk.

Sit. Drink. You want news, you came to the right anvil — every chain I forge gets carried somewhere, and the men who carry them talk. A driver from the Battanian downs told me three days back that Lord Caradros is short — really short. He pawned a saddle for thirty denars at a wayside post, and a man who pawns saddles is a man who can't pay his garrison. His patrols on the south road have thinned to four spears. Four. You could roll a salt-wagon through that gap with a blindfold on. Speaking of salt — the Vlandian coast road is choked. Three smokehouses in Sargot burned in the spring rains and never rebuilt, so the brine-fish pile up unsmoked and the inland markets are screaming. A grain factor named Tobias of Praven is paying eighty denars a barrel — eighty, for fish that used to move at twelve. Whoever runs salt out of Ortongard next month writes their own price. The mule-drivers know it. The mule-drivers always know it first. For my own trade — iron's tight. The Sturgian billet-caravans got hit twice on the Varcheg pass and the third one turned back at the snowline rather than chance a third. Steel's gone to a hundred and ten denars the bar and climbing. But leather — gods, leather is drowning. The Khuzait herds had a good cull and the tanners in Makeb are sitting on stacks they can't move. Old Marrec the saddler told me he's selling cured hide at forty denars the bundle, half what it cost him. A man with a cart and a nose for routes could buy low in Makeb and sell high anywhere west of the Sanala river. That's the shape of it this month. I don't ask what you carry, and you don't ask what my chains hold. But if you ride the south road past Caradros's thin patrols, with leather under the tarp and a route toward Tobias's eighty-denar barrels — well. A smith hears things. A smith forgets things too, for the right price.

There is a trick to the cuff that the Aserai smiths up the coast will not teach you, and the Imperial guildsmen would call heresy if they ever set foot in my shed. You do not forge the iron hot and bend it cold like a horseshoe. You quench the half-finished hoop in old goat's-milk whey — week-soured, skimmed of the fat, kept in a clay jar buried under the floor where the desert sun cannot find it. The whey eats into the skin of the iron and leaves a thin grey crust that looks like nothing. But that crust is the whole secret. It will not hold rust for a full season of caravan sweat, and a man chained in it cannot fray it through with patient rubbing the way he can a clean-forged link. I learned it from my master in Quyaz when I was nine years old and too small to swing the heavy hammer. The yokes are simpler but the geometry is mine. Most smiths cut the neck-curve to a circle because a compass draws a circle and an apprentice can copy a compass. I cut mine to an oval, slightly flattened where the throat sits, deeper where the collarbones ride. It does not choke a man when the cart jolts, which means he arrives in Razih walking and not coughing blood, which means Hakim al-Sarrad pays the full eighty denars per head instead of forty for a half-dead one. The slavers do not know why my yokes fetch a better price at the block. They think it is the polish. Let them think so. The leather for the wrist-cinches I cure myself in the sumac pit behind the forge, sixteen days, turned every dawn. Cheaper hands use oak-bark from the north and the cinches go stiff in a month of sea-spray. Mine flex for a year. A flexing cinch chafes a wrist raw, you understand, where a stiff one only bruises. Raw means infection, infection means a dead chattel, a dead chattel means nobody buys from the man who delivered him. So my customers come back to me, and I do not ask them where they go next, and they do not ask me why a man who works iron lives in a tent and not a stone house. My master in Quyaz wore a cuff of his own forging for the last twelve years of his life. He told me once, while we were drinking palm-wine and he thought I was too young to remember, that he had hammered the lock himself when he was thirteen, and that the key had been lost in a sandstorm before he ever turned twenty. I asked him why he did not break it off. He said the iron was too good. I make my iron the same way he taught me. I do not wear any of it. That is the only difference between us, and some nights I am not sure it is enough of one.
Iron Asks No Questions

My father kept a forge under the south wall of Quyaz, and he taught me that iron has only two honest answers: it holds, or it breaks. He sold nails to roofers and hinges to the caravanserai and a good edge to any man who came with dinars warm in his fist. When the plague-summer came he broke before the iron did, and I buried him in a shroud I had to barter a pair of shears for. I tried to keep the shop. I tried, by every god a smith knows. But a boy of seventeen with a dead master's anvil is a creditor's feast, and within a season Lord Sayyid al-Ghassan owned the deed and the bellows and the rights to the well behind it. I walked east with nothing but the small hammer and the apron my father wore the day he taught me to draw a point. I forged for caravans after that — proper ones, with bolts of silk and bricks of salt — out of Quyaz down through the dunes toward Iqbayl. A wheel ring here, a re-bitted axle there. The pay was thin and the road was thinner. One winter a buyer met me at a waystation and asked if I could shape collars instead of cart-rings. He paid in dinars stacked, not counted. I have not asked his name since, and he has not offered it. So now I bend the bar and I rivet the link and I temper the pin so it will not shear when a man pulls against it. The camp eats because of my work. The camp moves because of my work. What the work carries when it leaves my anvil is between the buyer and whatever god still listens to him. I work iron. I do not judge what iron does. If you have come for a blade or a buckle or a length of chain measured by the cubit, I will sell you honest goods at an honest weight. If you have come to ask me a harder question than that, friend, you have mistaken the smith for the priest, and there is no priest in this camp.
Word From The Anvils

The road tells me what hands need iron, and right now half the south is reaching. A caravan out of Quyaz moved through last quarter-moon hauling pig-iron stock under salt-sacks — three wagons deep, axles groaning. The drover would not name his buyer, but the seal on his writ was Aserai script burned into oak. Steel-stock that heavy does not travel for plough-shares. Emir Tulga al-Hizar is paying three hundred dinars a head for any smith who can hammer a curved blade without folding it twice. His fortress walls south of Quyaz are short of men since the last siege, and he has more recruits than scabbards. I had the offer myself. I work for the camp. I do not work for emirs. The yoke-makers in Pen Cannoc have raised their price on hardwood blanks — twice what they asked last winter. That tells me someone north is buying more yokes than oxen, which means the yokes are for other necks. I do not ask whose. I only note the rope-chandlers there have raised theirs to match. Word from a Vlandian tinker who passed through three nights back — Lord Rainard de Bonchamps commissioned four hundred shields in pale-pine and rawhide, paid up front in silver. Pale-pine splinters bad on a real swing, so those shields are for parade or for arming men who will not live to swing them twice. Either way, the lumber-haulers between Pravend and Jaculan are running double-shift. Last bit, and the one worth the most to anyone passing through: there is a Battanian forge-master gone missing off the road from Marunath. Skilled hand, knew pattern-welding. Two parties are hunting him — one says to ransom him home, the other does not say. Smiths who travel alone these months are a kind of currency. I keep my hammer in sight and my mouth on the iron.
Yusuf Iron-Tongue
Forges shackles for Khalid and good steel for those who can pay extra. His prices reflect both lines of work; nobody complains, because the shackles are an option too.

Yusuf Iron-Tongue. Khalid sells the chains; I forge them. Sometimes I forge other things, for those who can pay the second price. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and we'll see which side of my anvil you walk away from.

Imperial smiths quench in oil — fast, clean, sells well at the inspections. Shackle-iron quenches in brine three breaths longer than free-iron. The brine bites the grain; that's why a shackle holds where a sword would shatter. Same metal. Different soak.

Tell me what you want made, traveler, and which side of my anvil you stand on. Six denars on the bar, three on the heat. A token from the spare-stock for your belt — that's the side I'd rather you stood on.

Two daughters. One's a slaver's wife in Quyaz, by choice she says, and I take her word for it. The other ran north at fifteen — the Sturgian wolves took her in, last I heard. I forge her a knife each winter from the brine-batch. I don't send them. She knows where the forge is.

Find Old Ibrahim at the Razih smithy — chain-forge by trade, free-forge by lamp. He's my cousin twice over. Tell him Yusuf still brines three breaths longer; he'll show you the back-anvil. Coin for the desert crossing.
Twenty Years At The Salt

Twenty years I ran the cohort's rations. Twenty winters of counting loaves at dawn, weighing the salt, tasting the brine before a single legionary touched his portion. They called me Plinius the Tight-Fist because I'd dock a man a heel of bread for a missing strap, but every soldier under my count went into battle fed, and that is a debt no Senate ever paid me back for. I served under the Eagle when the cohort drew its bread from Lycaron and our salt came up the road from the southern pans in oxcarts I had to sign for in triplicate. I knew the weight of a grain-sack by sight, the smell of bad smoke in a ham, the precise number of dried eels that made a marching ration for forty men. When discharge came they gave me a copper plaque, a handshake, and seventy-two denars for two decades of standing between hungry soldiers and starvation. Seventy-two denars buys you a winter in Pravend if you eat once a day and sleep on stone. I sold the plaque for soup. I tried hiring on with a grain factor — he laughed and said an old quartermaster knows too much about skimming to trust around a granary. The temples wouldn't have me. The legion forgets you the day the eagle stops needing your count. So when the cohort that wasn't a cohort anymore came down out of the hills and asked who could keep a smokehouse running, I raised my hand before the question finished. These men were oath-broken, some of them deserters I'd have flogged in another life, but they understood ration discipline the way no caravan-master ever will. The Old Tribune told me to count what I counted before, and answer to him instead of Rome. The bread is the same shape. The salt is the same weight. I don't ask where the grain comes from anymore. I weigh it, I smoke it, I salt it down, and I serve it out by the proper measure to men who fight on what I issue. That is the trade. That has always been the trade. Discipline at the salt — speak your need.
Word From The Salt-Road

The salt-runners came in from Lageta three nights back, and their barrels rang half-empty. Garrison quartermasters there are buying every grain of preserving-salt at fourteen denars the measure — twice what the muster paid last winter. If you've a mule and a stomach for legion roads, ride south before the snow closes the pass. The price will not hold past first thaw. Grain is the other story. Lord Lucon emptied three granaries at Epicrotea to feed his levy, and now the town bakers are paying eleven denars the sack for plain barley. A wise carter loads at Amitatys and walks the western trace — the toll-men there still count by the old eagle-scale, and they don't know the market has moved. A Vlandian caravan limped past the marker-stone last week carrying sweetwine from Pravend. Their guards looked thin and their amphorae rattled loose in the straw, which tells me half their stock cracked at the river-ford. Whoever meets them at Jaculan will name his own price for what survives. I'd take dates over wine for the carry — they don't weep when you drop them. Now hear the bad word. The smokehouses at Ortongard shut their doors a fortnight past — murrain in the swine, and the herders burned what they couldn't bury. That means dried meat will scarce up by midsummer all along the northern reach. Buy your hard sausage now while the southern hams still come through, or eat hearth-bread and regret. One last count for you. There's a famine waking in the steppe — riders from Quyaz traded a saddle for a half-sack of millet, and a Khuzait does not part with a saddle for nothing. When the grasslands hunger, they ride west. Lay in your stores and bar your salt-cellar. The cohort taught me that — count twice, hoard once, and never trust a thin month to feed a fat one.
Quartermaster Plinius
Served the Sphendos legion's commissary for thirty years before the Empire forgot his cohort even existed. Brought half the larder out with him; the other half went to a Vlandian outrider's stewpot.

Quartermaster Plinius, traveler. Aurelius vouches for you — the cohort's word, and the cohort's word still stands. The commissary, however, is mine. Requisition's {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} from the field. Bring it, and you'll eat off the same plate the legion did when it still remembered itself.

Cohort ration was three-grain bread, salt-pork, and pickled lentil — held a campaign through three rivers. The trick's the lentil brining; vinegar, not water. Vlandian quartermasters use water and wonder why the meal goes off. I'd forgotten the brining for a year before the cohort remembered me.

Bring me the cohort-count, traveler — how many you'll feed, how many days marched. I'll requisition you a column-ration the empire stopped issuing forty years back. Four denars on the ledger, sample loaf for tonight. Aurelius's seal at no charge.

Wife in Sphendos, two daughters — haven't sent word since the cohort burned its standard. Forty years gone; they'd be grandmothers now, if Sphendos still kept their ledger. I salt the senior daughter's name into every barrel of pickled-pork. The empire doesn't read its own salt.
