Centurion-Quartermaster Druso runs the staging-larder at the Imperial Galician border-post — three cohorts removed from us, but Sphendos blood. Tell him Plinius still brines in vinegar; he'll seat you at the requisition table. Coin for the seal.

Caravan out of Pravend rolled through three nights back, hauling steel billets stamped with the imperial eagle - half-rate quality, the kind they used to reject at the cohort forge before the discharge. Driver was sweating coin he didn't have, said the buyer in Lageta stiffed him on the last run and now he's moving south with no escort past the second milestone. Two outriders, both green. You want billets cheap, that's where billets are cheap. There's a Lord Lucon burning through his treasury keeping mercenaries on retainer - word from a smuggler who drinks with his quartermaster is he's down to under three thousand denars in the strongroom and selling off his armory piecemeal to keep the spears fed. Lamellar, mail shirts, a few good helms. He's pricing them like a man who needs the coin yesterday. If you've got a runner who can move quiet through Amitatys, that's a buyer's market dressed up as a fire sale. Leather's the real story though. Glut out of the eastern tanneries - some fool overbought hides on a bad harvest gamble and now every caravan east of Ortysia is dragging stacks they can't shift. Saw a merchant named Vlachos offering tanned cowhide at sixty percent below what I paid last winter, and he was practically begging. Buy now, sit on it through the spring campaigns, sell it back to the same idiots at three times the price when their straps start rotting. Iron's tighter. The Battania mines slowed their shipments after that flooding business, so anyone moving raw stock north is asking nine hundred denars a load and getting it. A smuggler I trust says a Sturgian buyer in Revyl is overpaying - twelve hundred, no questions on the stamp. If a caravan happened to lose its way between here and there, well. Iron doesn't remember whose hand it passed through.

There's a thing the legion taught us that no smith outside the cohorts knows. When you fold the billet for a spatha, you don't fold it odd. You fold it even — fourteen times, never thirteen, never fifteen. Thirteen leaves a soft seam down the spine. Fifteen burns the carbon out and leaves you a pretty blade that snaps on the second parry. Fourteen is the number Master Quintus beat into me at the Pravend forges when I was a boy of twelve, and fourteen is the number I still count under my breath every time the hammer comes down. The temper is the other half. Most smiths quench in oil or in plain water and call it done. We quenched in brine — sea salt boiled down with a fistful of crushed oak gall, the same gall the tanners use. The gall draws the heat out uneven, harder at the edge, softer at the spine, and you get a blade that bends before it breaks. A legionary who breaks his sword in the first hour of a hold dies in the second. A legionary whose sword bends gets to walk home. That mattered, once. Cost extra, too — the quartermaster paid me an extra forty denars a blade for the brine work, and I never saw a copper of it after the discharge. The legion mark goes on last. Two crossed sticks inside a circle, stamped cold into the ricasso with a punch I cut myself the week I made centurion-smith. Cohort marks underneath — mine was the Ninth, three dots in a triangle. I still stamp it. I know I shouldn't. There's an edict somewhere in Lycaron that says any man stamping legion marks on private work eats six months in a salt pit. Let them come find me. They already took the pension, the pay, and the wall to put my name on. The stamp is mine. They can have it back when they pry the punch out of the coffin. I'll sell you a blade with the mark or without. Without is twenty denars cheaper because it's faster, and because a man who wants the mark is buying a story, not a sword. Tell me which kind you are and I'll know what to charge you.
The Stamp I Kept

They mustered us out at Lageta with a clap on the shoulder and three months' arrears in denars that never came. Twenty-two years I'd kept the cohort's iron honest — wedged loose lorica plates back into their straps before dawn marches, re-cuffed pilum sockets after every skirmish on the Pravend road. A legion armorer doesn't get a pension. He gets a hammer he's allowed to keep, and a stamp die the quartermaster forgot to ask back. I tried civilian work first. Set up a stall outside Amitatys reforging plow-shares and shoeing mules, and the guild men came round inside a fortnight to break my anvil and explain who paid the magistrate. Centurion Aurelius — what was left of him — sent a rider out to find me with word the old cohort was reforming under no banner anyone would name aloud. I came because the alternative was begging at a temple gate, and because my hands don't know any other shape than tang and rivet. So now I work at the camp forge with the same die I carried out of Lageta. Every helmet that leaves this anvil gets the legion mark stamped behind the brow-band — small, where the strap covers it — and I sleep better for putting it there. The leather is local and the buckles are whatever the scavengers bring in off the Quyaz caravans, but the edge geometry is regulation. I won't sell a man a blade that fails him at the shoulder roll. I've buried too many who trusted bad steel. The lads call me Smith because they think it's a name. It isn't. It's what I am, and what I was before the discharge papers said otherwise. You want a mail shirt that'll turn a horse-archer's bodkin at thirty paces, I have one. You want a gambeson stitched the way the legion stitched them, three layers and the cross-quilt, I have that too. You want it cheap — go find a tinker. Legion standards cost what they cost.
Iron Moves Where Wars Wait

The word? The word is iron, friend, and there's not enough of it moving south. A Sturgian convoy out of Revyl got hit twice on the Tyal road — second time the drivers walked away and left forty bars of bog-steel sitting in a ditch for the crows. Whoever scavenged that haul is sitting on a year's worth of spearheads. If you hear of a smith suddenly flush with stock and no foundry receipts, that's where it came from. Lord Lucon out of Lageta is paying eighteen denars a shield, no questions about the maker's stamp. He lost half his garrison kit when the Khuzaits torched his outer wall, and he wants the racks full before the thaw. Plain oak rim, iron boss, leather face — quantity over craft. Any journeyman with two apprentices and a willing arm can clear three months' rent inside a fortnight if he can haul the load up that hill road. The proper news, though, is Pravend. The Emperor's quartermasters are buying every scrap of legion-pattern plate they can find — buying back the discharge gear, mind you, the kit men like me carried out the gate on our last day. Twenty-two denars a cuirass if the cohort mark is still legible. Word in the cohort houses is they're standing up two new legions before the campaigning season and don't have the forges to outfit them honest. A Vlandian caravan moved through the hill passes last week pushing crucible-steel ingots toward Ortongard — eight mules, four guards, no banner. That's the third such run this season. Somebody in the west is stockpiling, and stockpiling means a war contract that hasn't been announced yet. Mark the route. When the contract drops, the price doubles. Last bit, and you didn't hear it from me. Mestonios the Tanner down at the smokehouse end of camp gets his hide-stock from a driver who runs the Epicrotea road. Driver told him the Aserai are buying mail by the cartload through Quyaz middlemen — paying in dinars, no haggling. That's not garrison restock. That's somebody fitting out a desert column. Keep your ear on that one.
Smith Galvius
Repaired imperial mail at three cohort-forges and three forgotten campaigns. Knows every weakness of every plate the Empire still issues — which is why his repairs hold longer than the originals.

Smith Galvius, traveler. Aurelius lets you walk among the cohort; my forge sets a higher bar than the centurion. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} from the road, and I'll repair your mail the way the Empire stopped doing thirty campaigns back.

Imperial mail thins at the third-link, every fifth row, traveler — that's the rivet-pattern. Repair the thin link, not the broken one; the breakage points to the next failure. Empire stopped teaching the inspection thirty campaigns back. The cohort forges still know.

Bring me your mail, your draw-weight, your campaign-count, traveler. I'll re-rivet you a coat the cohort would have called 'standard.' Five denars on the ring-stock, the rivets at no charge. Here — a spare ring for your belt-tool.

Son served the same cohort. Took an arrow at the second river — third-link weakness in his own coat, the rivet I'd set the year before. I keep the coat in the forge-rafters now. Every campaign I look at the link. The grain still tells me where the next one'll go.

Smith Cassius works the Vermouth border-forge — same cohort, lost his eye on the same march. Tell him Galvius still reads the third-link; he'll bring out the cohort's old standard from the back-room. Coin for the road north.

A snare lives or dies by what walks past it, and the same's true of a man with ears. I sit on the ledge above the goat-track most mornings, gutting hares, and the muleteers from Zeonica don't think a barefoot trapper understands their tongue. They say Lord Stenmar has pawned his wife's brooch to a Sturgian factor — three lean caravans rolled south last week with nothing but tally-sticks and promises. A lord short on coin is a lord whose tax-wagons ride with two spears instead of six. Worth knowing, if a man were thinking of being somewhere along that road. The grain's the real talk, though. Pen Cannoc's smokehouses went cold a month past — no salt. Battanian salt-trains used to come up the Ostican fords, but the fords flooded and the new road through Galend takes twice as long with half the guard. A barrel of coarse salt that fetched twelve denars in spring is going for forty in the lowland markets, and the smoker-wives are weeping. I've been salting my hare-meat in ash and birch-bark like my grandmother did. Tastes of nothing, keeps a fortnight, and the raiders won't touch it — which suits me, since it means I eat. Grain's the other tooth in the same jaw. The Vlandian merchant Joffroi the Stout came through three nights ago, fat-faced, fat-pursed, paying sixty denars a sack for any rye he can find. Sixty. The market price is twenty-two. He's buying for someone — a siege-stock, I'd wager, or a quartermaster skimming. He travels with four guards and a cook. The cook drinks. I mention this only as a fact about the world, the way a man mentions which way the wind blows when he's setting a snare. And the rock-grouse don't lie either. They've been thick on the south crag this season because nobody's been firing the heather — too few shepherds, the boys all gone south chasing mercenary coin from a Northern lord who'll be bankrupt by Tenmoot. Grouse stew tonight, if the chief'll trade me a sack of barley for the brace I've got hanging. He won't. He never does. So I eat what the raiders will not pay for, and I listen, and one day the listening will be worth more than the meat.

You want to know why my jerky doesn't crack your teeth like the raiders' salt-pork does? It's the brine. Most folk salt their meat in barrels of seawater hauled up from the coast, but I climb down to the wind-caves below the Crag and scrape the white crust off the walls where the spray dries. It's saltier than ocean, sharper, and it carries something of the cliff in it — a mineral bite that pulls the water out without turning the flesh to leather. Three days in a clay jar with that scraping, a handful of crushed juniper berries, and the bruised seedheads of the bitter grass that grows where the goats won't graze. Then I hang the strips in the smoke-hole over green pine. Green pine, mind you. Everyone else uses dry oak because that's what the books say if you can read books, which I can't. Dry oak gives you a clean smoke and a pretty colour. Green pine gives you a resin that seals the outside of the hare-meat against the wet sea-fog up here. A strip of my jerky will keep a year in a man's pouch on the cliffs without going soft. The raiders sneer because it tastes of sap. The raiders also throw three-quarters of their plunder-salted pork into the gulls' mouths when it weeps black in the rains. The grouse I do different. The grouse I don't smoke at all — I pack them whole in the rendered fat off their own breasts, with a sprig of the sour cliff-thyme tucked under each wing. Sealed in a crock and buried in the cold scree behind my hut, they'll come out at midwinter tasting better than the day I caught them. I learned this from my mother, who learned it from hers. We were never raiders, my people. We were cliff-folk. The raiders took the high holds two generations back and we just — stayed. Cooked for them. Took their denars when they remembered to pay. I'll sell you a strip for a copper and a crock for forty. Don't tell Vagh the Reaver what's in it. He thinks I just have a knack. Let him think that. A man who eats well and doesn't ask questions is a man who keeps paying.
Cliffs Feed the Patient

High air, aye, and a long way down for them that step wrong. I was born in a herder's hut clinging to the slopes above Pen Cannoc, eldest of six and the only one with patience for snare-work. My father taught me the cliff paths before he taught me my letters, which is to say he never taught me letters at all. Hares, rock-grouse, the fat little marmots that whistle from the scree — I learned which trails they wore smooth, and which knots would hold a kicking leg without snapping it. The herd died in the long winter, two seasons running. My brothers went down to Car Banseth to swing pikes for whoever paid, and most of them did not come back. I climbed higher instead. Up where the raiders nested, where a man with a sack of snared grouse could trade for salt and rough flour and the odd handful of denars when a sea-prize came in. The boss took one look at my callused hands and said the camp had bellies enough to feed, if I could keep feeding them. So I bring in what the raiders won't trouble with. They want salted beef from coastal hauls, smoked pork off the Ostican traders, fat rounds of hearth-bread when the dough-women of Marunath are bribed quiet. Me, I bring grouse and hare and the dried strips of marmot that nobody else will chew. Salt I have to buy down-mountain — there's a man in Pen Cannoc, calls himself Old Gwynn, who'll cut me a block for half what the lowland merchants ask, so long as I bring him a hare-pelt in trade. It pays. Not in gold, mostly. In a roof when the wind comes off the crag like a knife, in stew that's hot whether I caught the meat in it or not, in nobody asking where I sleep. Lord Caolan tried to recruit me once when his riders passed the lower pass — said a snare-man's eye for ground was wasted on grouse. I told him my eye for ground was the only reason I was still alive, and I meant to keep it. That's the trade, friend. Cliffs feed the patient. Camp feeds the rest of it. And if the wind shifts wrong while we're talking, you'll learn the first lesson up here faster than I can teach you the second — so be quick with your coin, and quicker with your feet.
Word From The Crags

The wind carries more than dust up here, friend. A trapper on the cliffs hears every caravan-bell three valleys before it crests the ridge. So yes — I have a word or two for the road, if you'll trade me a moment of breath. Pen Cannoc is buying salted meat at near double the spring price. Their smokehouses burned in a careless feast-night, and the cottars are paying eighteen denars the brace for any rock-grouse a man can drag down off the crags. If you've a strong arm and a quiet foot, that's where the coin is sleeping. A sweetwine caravan out of Car Banseth took the lower pass three days back — fat barrels, thin guards. Caladog's warband sniffed it, but the rains washed their tracks before they could move. The barrels are still rolling. Someone will eat well, or someone will bleed well. Maybe both. There's a hunger coming to the eastern moors — the hare-runs are empty this season, and the wolves have moved down from the heights. I've seen it twice in my life and both times the cottars came begging up the cliff-tracks before the second frost. Lay in dried meat now, and you'll be a rich man by midwinter. Wait, and you'll be a thin one. Last thing, and then you go. Penn the Larder at the lower camp is short on hearth-bread flour — the mill at Dunglanys cracked its wheel and won't grind till the snows. Bring him a sack of barley meal, he'll pay you better than the markets will. Now — high air, low patience. Off with you.
Bran of the Crag
Trapped high-pass red-grouse for Battanian lords until one lord fed him to dogs as sport. Bran climbed back up the cliff, came back with steel a year later, and never went down again.

Bran of the Crag, traveler. Aerlin's wind likes you; my snares are pickier. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} from the lowlands — the high passes have stopped giving them up — and I'll feed you what the cliff-clans still eat when the snow comes.

Crag-grouse only eats the high pine, traveler — that's the resin in the flesh, the bitter under the salt. The trick's the pluck, not the cure: thirty feathers at the breastbone, never the back. Battanian wood-lords used to feed the rest to dogs. Now we eat the bird; the dogs eat memory.

Name a banquet, traveler — high feast, name-day, mourner's table. Three pairs at the snare and a fortnight's notice. Five denars on the trap-line, sample bird tonight at no charge. The cliff'll furnish the rest.

Wife was Battanian — Maire of the lower oak-stand. They fed me to the dogs as sport; they fed her to nothing. She'd be grandmother age now, if the lord hadn't taken her hand for shielding me. I climb the cliff every winter solstice and leave a grouse on the high ledge. The wind takes it before morning.

Old Findlay traps high-pass red-grouse at the Battanian crag-line — learned the resin-cure from me before the dogs came. Tell him Bran still climbs; he'll show you the high-ledge cache. Coin for the climb-rope and the inn at the foot.

Aye, sit down by the grindstone. You want gossip, I trade it cheaper than the iron — and lately iron's the word on every tongue that passes this hideout. A Battanian charcoaler limped through three nights back, axle split, and he sang for his repair. Said the steel-billet caravan out of Pen Cannoc rolls south next waxing moon with just six spears for escort — six! — because Lord Caradog pulled half his retinue to chase a rent-dodger near the coast. Six spears guarding a wagon worth four hundred denars in raw billet alone. I'd call that an invitation, not an escort. Smuggler woman, calls herself Mira of the Crooked Tooth, came up to barter a bundle of seal-hide for two of my throwing-axes. She drinks loud, that one. Told me the Vlandian armorers at Galend are paying near double for any iron stock that walks in the gate — their last shipment got snowed under in a pass and the smiths are screaming. Anyone holding pig-iron right now is sitting on a vein. Meanwhile there's a glut of cheap boiled-leather flooding the Ortongard markets because a Sturgian tanner's widow dumped her whole stock to settle a debt — so don't raid wagons for hides this season, you'll lift a ton and sell it for nothing. Grain's where the real bite is. The smokehouse at Hringgard burnt to a black ring two weeks gone, and now every village from the firth to the foothills is short on salt-fish for winter. That means the salt road from the coast is moving four times the usual carts, and they're undermanned — Reeve Hagen can't conscript fast enough. Grain prices in the lowlands jumped from eight to fifteen denars a sack, and a sack of millet from a raided granary will feed this hideout a fortnight or buy two good axe-heads. One last whisper — and this one I'd believe if I were you. A Khuzait factor passed through with a string of remounts, and he was nervous. Lord Berrun of the southern marches is short coin again, third time this year. He's quietly selling off captured mail-shirts at half-price through a fence in Sargot to make his retinue payroll. Half-price mail, friend. If you've got a man who can pass for a merchant and a purse of denars, you walk out of Sargot kitted like a count's huscarl. Now — you want that axe sharpened, or are you just here for the talk?

Most smiths will tell you the secret of a good axe is in the steel. They're wrong. The secret is in the eye — the hole where the haft seats. I drift mine cold after the first forge-weld, with a tapered punch I cut from a wagon-axle I pulled off a caravan from Pen Cannoc nine winters back. Cold-drifting work-hardens the cheek walls so they grip the haft like teeth. A hot-drifted eye loosens after a season of swinging. Mine don't. Ask any raider who's carried one through three campaigns. The bit is my own twist. I forge-weld a strip of high-carbon down the cutting edge — old file steel, mostly, broken rasps the smugglers bring up from the lowland forges for twelve denars a bundle. The body stays soft wrought iron so the head won't shatter on a shield-rim, but the edge holds a shaving angle for weeks. The trick is the quench. Water hisses the carbon out and makes the edge brittle. I use whey — sour goat-whey, two days old, from Old Mev's herd up the ridge. The fats and salts slow the cool just enough. Comes out the colour of a wet stone and twice as mean. When the iron runs thin — and it does, every spring before the caravans climb again — I knap arrowheads from the black flint that outcrops a half-day east, past the Crow Notch. My da taught me before he taught me the bellows. He said a man who can only work one stone is half a smith. Flint's faster than forging, sharper than steel for the first shot, and the lads can fletch a hundred shafts in an evening. They don't fly true past forty paces, but most of our work isn't done past forty paces. I won't sell the cold-drift punch. I've been offered eighty denars for it twice, once by a caravan-master who thought I was simple. The punch came from my da's anvil, and his da before him, back when our line still had a hall down on the plain. Lost the hall. Kept the punch. Tells you everything you need to know about what matters.
Ten Winters At This Anvil

My father knapped flint in a glen below Pen Cannoc, back when the lowland smiths still came up to barter for our hill-iron. He taught me the trick of reading a stone before you strike it — the grain tells you where it wants to break, and a wise man does not argue. I was twelve when the Sturgian raiders burned the glen for being too close to the road, and I walked north with nothing but my father's striker and a half-finished hand-axe in my belt. I came to the Sky Raiders by way of Revyl, where I hammered cheap helmet-rims for a merchant who paid in spoiled grain and excuses. Old Kaerl Blackthumb ran the forge here before me, and when his lungs gave out from the bellows-smoke he passed me the tongs without ceremony. Ten winters I have stood at this anvil since. Ten winters of axe-bits and arrow-points and the smell of quenched steel rising into the rafters. When the iron caravan from Quyaz is late — and it is always late — I go back to my father's craft. Flint heads bite as deep as steel into a man not wearing mail, and the raiders do not often fight men in mail. I knap until my thumbs bleed, then I wrap them in leather and knap some more. The boys laugh until they see a flint head split a shield-rim, then they stop laughing. What pays a man into this trade? Denars, sometimes. A warm corner of the camp, always. The right to refuse the work that bores you. Down in Pravend I would be shoeing horses for a fat reeve who never said my name. Up here they call me Axe-Master, and they mean it. That is worth a lowland winter and then some. So pay for the edge. The edge is what keeps you breathing past the next ridge, and I do not waste my striking-arm on men who think craft is haggled like turnips.
Word From the High Passes

Word from the high passes — Omor's castellan is buying every spear-tip the smiths can hammer out. Some Sturgian thane down-mountain promised him three hundred denars a bundle and the forges are running hot through the night. If you've got iron stock to move, that's the road. Don't take the southern fork — wolves and worse. A caravan out of Revyl is hauling Nord steel-billets west, escorted by Lord Tagvirr's house-guard. Twelve wagons, mailed riders, the works. The raiders below have eyes on it, but I'd not be the one swinging the axe — Tagvirr's men fight like the cliffs themselves. If you ARE that one, mind: the billets are crude, need a forge to make them anything. Raw weight, no edge. Hrothgar Anvil-Hand down at Tyal is taking on three new apprentices — old fool's hands are giving out and he wants the craft passed on before the frost takes him. Pays in food and a roof, not coin. I trained under him forty winters back. If you know a lad with steady arms and no kingdom, send him. The leather-cutters at Pen Cannoc ran short on hide last moon — some Vlandian count bought the whole season's run for his garrison kit. Means raw skins are fetching double in the lowland markets, and any saddle-stock moving north is gold on the hoof. Keep your knife sharp if you ride that way. One more — flint. The seam I knap from is thinning, third winter running. If you pass an old riverbed with good black stone, mark it for me. Two denars a fist if it strikes clean. Edge is everything up here, and the iron's only as honest as what backs it.
Tregar Stone-Knapper

Knapped flint for the last of the high-pass mining gangs before the gangs were taxed into nothing. Now flakes steel the same way; the wind whistles through his blades the way it used to whistle through his pit-shafts.

Tregar Stone-Knapper. The bird trusted you — that's Aerlin's measure. Mine's flint, traveler, and steel after that. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll knap you an axe-edge that holds longer than any imperial-issued blade you've carried.

Flint flakes along the grain; steel flakes against it, traveler. Imperial smiths grind the edge; I knap it — three taps on the spine, one on the bevel. The blade holds a cut where the imperial issue rolls. The high-pass mining gangs taught me before the tax-men taught them silence.

Bring me a steel-bar and your draw, traveler. I'll knap you an edge that holds three campaigns; flake the bevel to your hand. Six denars on the heat, three on the tap-pattern. Here, a knapped spike to mark the deal.

Had a son in the last pit-gang — Cailean, fifteen winters when the taxmen sealed the shaft. The empire called it 'flooding'; the mountain called it murder. I knap a small flint each year on his name-day and leave it at the sealed shaft. Sometimes it's gone the next month. Sometimes the mountain returns it polished.

Old Maeve at the Pictish stone-village still knaps the way her mother did — flint, not steel. She remembers the mining-gangs. Tell her Tregar walks the high passes; she'll show you the inner knapping-yard. Coin for the long climb.

Caravan came down the Bulugur Pass last moon and the drover wouldn't shut his mouth once I poured him fermented mare's milk. Says grain out of Makeb is moving at near 42 denars the sack now, on account of the southern harvest going to weevils. Khuzait stewards in Ortongard are paying double for any sack that doesn't smell of mold. Khan-herd boy I was, but I know a desperate price when I hear one. The interesting word, though, is on Lord Khasar — yes, that Khasar, the one who used to ride down our cousins. His coffers are dry. Drover swore he saw the lord's quartermaster haggling over a wheel of cheese at the Iadgar market like a widow at dusk. Three of his retainers haven't been paid since the last full moon. His column down the Quyaz Steppe road rides with maybe twelve spears now, and half are conscripts who'd rather be home shearing. Salt's the other thing worth your ear. The smokehouses in Akkalat shut down — the salt-train out of Odokh got hit twice this season, not by us, by somebody sloppy, and now the saltmen ride with the empire patrols and won't take the steppe shortcut at all. That means every herder from here to the Tsagaan flats is sitting on meat he can't cure. I've got two riders trading our reserve at 9 denars the brick to villages that were paying three a season ago. Whole flocks of mutton coming our way for it, cheap. One more, and then I'll let you eat. There's a Vlandian factor — Gisbert of Jaculan the drover named him — buying steppe cheese and fermented curd at city prices, no questions on where it came from. Pays in clipped denars but pays fast. He's camped near Zeonica for another fortnight. If the boys come back with a wagon out of any caravan we don't want to keep, tell them: cheese to Gisbert, grain to Ortongard, and don't, by the long sky, try to sell salt anywhere within a week's ride of the empire roads.

Want to know why my dried meat keeps when the southern caravans turn green by the second moon? Salt alone won't do it on the steppe — too dear, and the air's too dry to draw the juice clean. So I do it the old khan-herder way: I bury the strips in a pit lined with last winter's Khurel Salt Flats crust, but I mix that crust one-to-three with crushed wild onion, sour-grass seed, and a fistful of ash from burnt birch — never pine, pine sweetens the fat and the wolves can smell sweet meat from a day's ride. The trick the caravans miss is the second pit. After eight days under the salt-ash, I dig it up, rinse it in mare's milk gone half-sour, and re-bury it in cold yurt-shadow for another four. The sour milk eats whatever bitterness the ash left and puts back the tang a wolf-rider expects on his tongue. Stranger asked me once why I bother with two pits. I told him: one pit feeds a man. Two pits feed a man riding three days from camp with nothing on his belt but a knife. I learned it from my grandmother when I was small enough to ride behind her on the herd-pony. Old Naran, they called her — she'd cured meat for the khan's outriders before the southern lords ever knew our name. She told me the salt-flat crust is half the secret; the patience is the other half. Most camps eat their meat before it's done. That's why most camps starve in the third moon and we don't. I'll sell you a finished strip for eight denars the bundle, or I'll sell you the salt-blend recipe for forty and you can ruin your own meat learning it. Either way, don't tell the khan's quartermaster I told you about the second pit. He thinks I do it with prayer.
Salt, Smoke, And Steppe

A boy on the long grass learns the herd before he learns his own name. I rode behind the khan's mares before I could grip a bow, counting foals at dawn, salting hides at dusk. My father was no warrior — he was the man who knew which spring still ran in the dry month, and which marmot warren had grown fat. He taught me that a camp dies of empty bellies long before it dies of empty quivers, and that lesson has fed me every winter since. When the old khan fell on the road below Quyaz, the herd scattered and the clansmen scattered with it. I drove what mares I could north, traded the lame ones for salt at a Sturgian post, and salt for smoked river-eel from a fenman who owed my father a favor. I have been moving food along that crooked line ever since — grain from Pen Cannoc when the borderlords are sleeping, hard cheese off the Khergit shepherds, dried mutton I cure myself in a pit behind the wolves' tents. Khan Bayanchur took me in the year the spring rains failed. He had wolves enough; what he wanted was a man who could keep them fed without dragging a caravan of scribes behind him. I told him I'd feed his camp on what the steppe gave, and what the steppe forgot to give I'd find on the merchant tracks between Pravend and the Khuzait pickets. He paid me eighty denars the first month and a wolfskin cloak the second. I have not asked for coin since — the camp eats, and I eat with the camp. Now I keep the smokehouse pit, the salt-jars, the dough-trough, and the cold cellar we dug under the rocks where the wind never reaches. I trade with whoever comes up the gully — a Vlandian deserter with stolen flour, a Khuzait widow with mare's milk to barter, an Aserai spice-runner who lost his caravan to Lord Tagaday and would rather sell to wolves than walk home empty. They all pay in something the camp can chew. So that is what pays a man into this trade, traveler. Not gold. Not glory. A boy who counted foals becomes an old man who counts loaves, and somewhere in between he learns that the steppe feeds those who watch — and starves the ones who don't.
Word From The Long Grass

Sit down then, traveler. The kettle's hot and my ears are older than the khan's grandsire's bones, so I hear things before the grass does. Eat first, then I'll tell you what the wind brought in. The salt-runners out of Quyaz are paying near double what they did last moon — Monchug Khan's outriders are burning anything that moves north of the river, and the merchants daren't run the short road. A clever soul with a string of pack-mules and a quiet tongue could clear sixty denars the sack going east, more if the buyer's a sworn man. Word from a goat-driver three nights past: Makeb's smokehouses are choking on more mutton than they can cure, and the steward there will take dried curd, hard cheese, anything that keeps. They're buying ahead because the elders smell the bad winter coming — late frost, no fat on the marmots, the old signs. The sweetwine caravan from Odokh hasn't shown in two turns of the moon, and that's never happened in my life. Either the southern lords have taxed it dead, or Urkhun the Lame got tired of waiting and took it himself. If you cross a wagon of amber jars on the south track with no driver — you didn't see anything, eh? You didn't see anything. Last thing, and listen close: grain is dear, dearer than honey, and getting worse. The Khuzait towns hold their granaries shut, the imperial ones west of Akkalat are feeding garrisons that never go home. A man who brings a wagon of barley to this camp before the snows — Old Otchigin will remember his name, and so will the chief. That's worth more than the denars, friend. Out here, being remembered is the whole game.
Old Otchigin
Khan Borchu's herd-cousin since both were boys riding the same pony. Drives the spare horses, dries the meat, brews the airag. Knows Borchu's silences as well as his words.

Old Otchigin, herd-cousin to the Khan since we were boys riding the same pony. Borchu lets you walk, traveler — Otchigin's yurt is harder to enter. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} from your road, and I'll dry you meat the way the Khan still eats it.

Khuzait dried meat takes the wind not the smoke, traveler — racks under the steppe sky, four winds per day, never the lowland fires. The flesh holds through three campaigns. Imperial cooks smoke their stock and call it 'preservation.' The Khan would laugh, if the Khan laughed at imperial things.

Tell me the camp and the count, traveler — how many you'll feed, how far you'll ride. Three sacks of dried mare-meat, four winds, a fortnight's notice. Six denars on the rack. Here, a strip for your saddle-bag tonight.

Borchu's herd-cousin since both were boys — never had wife, never had child. Borchu's children are mine by oath; his daughter Sechen calls me 'old uncle' and her son rides my second pony. That's family enough. The steppe doesn't ask for more.

Tegus Wind-Reader at the Khuzait main-camp keeps the Khan's drying-rack — Borchu's cousin twice over. Tell him Otchigin still racks four winds; he'll seat you at the Khan's own fire. Coin for the long ride east.

Saddle's done. Sit. You want to know whose pommel-leather I'm cutting next, you sit through the gossip first — that's the toll. A Vlandian quartermaster came through three sunsets back, riding a mule because his lord pawned the courser. Lord Caradoc of the western marches is down to scraping the bottom of his treasury — the man owes his garrison eleven weeks' wages and they're walking off in twos and threes. His tax-wagon out of Jaculan rolled past with four guards. Four. For a strongbox the driver bragged held nine hundred denars. I almost laughed in the man's face. Leather glut, too — and that's the part you'll care about if you're stitching anything wider than a girth-strap. The Aserai broke a contract with two Imperial tanneries and dumped their winter cattle-hide on the Quyaz road. Whole caravan of cured cowhide, escort of six, sleeping in shifts. The wolf-cousins out east already clipped one wagon from it last moon — the rest is moving slow because the drovers know it. You hit them, you'll be tripping over leather for a season. I'll buy whatever you don't want — I pay fair, you know I pay fair. Now the iron, that's where it gets interesting. Hakim the Steelmonger out of Husn Fulq is panic-buying steel billets at near double the going rate — some southern smith-guild promised him a contract he can't fill, and he's bleeding denars trying to source enough stock before the snow turns the passes. Every billet-cart out of the Battanian hills is being routed past Pen Cannoc on the eastern fork now because the main road's got Imperial patrols. Eastern fork's got nothing but a couple of crossbowmen and a dog. You do the arithmetic. One more thing, then I'm back to my awl. The salt-caravans out of the steppe lakes are running thin — smokehouse town up by Rovalt is screaming for salt at any price, and a merchant calling himself Ostavi is paying eighty denars a sack when the honest rate's twenty-eight. He's desperate, which means he's careless, which means his outbound silver-purse rides back south with maybe two riders. Anyway. The saddle's yours. Don't bleed on it before you've paid.

You want to know why a Wolf saddle does not split when a rider takes a fall from a galloping horse? It is the soak. Three weeks in mare's milk gone sour, then two more in a brine of ash-lye and crushed juniper berries from the slopes above Black Pine Ridge. Cow leather rots in that bath. Horse hide drinks it and comes out the color of old blood, supple as a lover's hand, tough as oath-iron. Every saddler in the steppe knows the sour-milk step. Not one of them knows the juniper. The cantle, now — that is where the bridle-makers down in Sanala get it wrong. They cut the tree from green birch and let it warp around the rider. I split mine from a single block of dead steppe-pine, the kind that has stood twenty winters with its roots in the wind, and I shape it WET to the curve of the specific horse it will ride. Each saddle remembers its mare. Put it on a different horse and it galls inside a day. The wolves pay me eighty denars for one. They would pay two hundred if I asked. I do not ask. The stitching is sinew from the back-strap, never the leg. Back-strap pulls evenly when wet and dry. Leg-sinew shrinks one way and slacks the other, and a saddle that breathes uneven will saw a horse raw inside a month. I learned this from my mother, who learned it from her father, who stitched bridles for the khan's own outriders in the years before the clan went bandit. We were saddlers before we were wolves. The horses came first. The blades after. I will tell you one more thing, and then no more. The pommel knob — the little bone cap most riders never notice — I carve from the kneebone of the horse the saddle is FOR. When that horse falls in battle, the rider keeps a piece of her under his hand for the rest of his life. Khasar the chief has three such pommels on his wall now. He does not speak of them. Neither do I. But that is why the wolves ride the way they ride, and why no man who has owned a Bayar saddle ever buys another.
Why I Cut The Contract

My father stitched saddles for the khan's outriders out of Quyaz, and his father before him cut bridles from the same horse-leather. I learned the awl before I learned the bow. A good saddle holds a man through three days of riding and a fourth of fighting; a bad one breaks his back before the enemy does. I have made both, and only the first lets you sleep at night. The breaking came when a Vlandian buyer rode in from Pravend with a fat purse of denars and a contract for forty cavalry rigs. My master took the coin. The leather we were given was thin, splitting stuff — dyed pretty, weak at the cantle. I told the old man it would kill riders. He told me the denars were already spent. So I cut the contract loose with my own knife, and the master cut me loose with his. The wolf-clan found me sleeping under a wagon-axle near the salt-trail with my awls in a roll and nothing else. Khasar looked at my hands, looked at the stitch on my own belt, and said the camp had been riding on saddles that bled the horses. I have been stitching for them since. No middleman, no Vlandian buyer, no thin leather — just the hide I cure myself and the riders who come back from each raid to tell me where the girth chafed. That is what pays a man into this trade. Not the coin. The coin is just what keeps the awls sharp and the tallow stocked. What pays me is knowing the rider who left this morning sits a rig I built, and the rig will not be the thing that drops him. Saddle holds the rider. Coin holds the bargain. Both must fit, or both come apart at the worst hour.
Word From The Saddle-Routes

Sit. Mind the awl. Word travels the saddle-routes faster than any rider, and a man stitching girths hears it twice — once from the courier coming in, once from the courier going out. You asked, so I will tell, but the price of the bridle stays the same either way. Quyaz is buying horse-leather at near double last winter's price. Their khan's brother lost three remounts to a Vlandian raid and now every saddler from the salt-flats to the river-bend is being courted with dinars upfront. If you ride east with cured hide rolled tight, you will not haggle long — but watch the southern track, the toll-riders have grown bold and they take the best skin off the top of the bundle. A Khuzait caravan out of Makeb is moving steel-stock west, bar-iron and rough billets, bound for a smith-house in Ortongard. Twelve wagons, light escort, the wagon-master is a one-eyed Sturgian called Ulvar Hookhand who drinks too early in the day. I do not say what you should do with that knowing. I only stitch saddles. Lord Monchug has paid out near four thousand dinars for fresh kite-shields and lance-tips, calling every smith in his banner to forge through harvest. That means the small fortresses around him cannot keep an armourer for love nor coin — their best men have ridden to his hearth. If you have a brother who swings a hammer, send him to Odokh; they will hire him before he washes the road off his hands. And one last thing, since you have been patient. A Battanian peddler came through last moon with a bundle of yew-staves — proper yew, not the sapling rubbish — claiming a bow-yard near Pen Cannoc burned down and the cut wood is loose on the road. If your eye is on bows, ride west soon. The forest does not stay generous long.
Bayar Saddle-Master

Stitched the Khuzait camp-saddles for the Khan's rival branch before that branch sold him out to imperial recruiters. Borchu rode out alone, took him back unbroken, and burned the rival's gēr for the insult.

Bayar Saddle-Master. Borchu took me back unbroken; the Khan's word is good. My stitching is better. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll make you a saddle the imperial recruiters never knew how to copy.

Camp-saddle takes the stitch flat at the cantle, raised at the pommel — the imperial cross-stitch reverses it and the rider's seat wears wrong. Khuzait stitch is one continuous line, knot at every horse-length. Imperial recruiters never knew how to copy it. Still don't.

Bring me your horse, your draw, your gallop-mark, traveler. Three denars on the leather, two on the stitch. A spare strap for your current saddle while the new one cures. Borchu's own horse rode three campaigns on my stitch.

Wife — Khatun — sold out with me to the recruiters; Borchu took us both back. She rides at the Khan's right hand now. We never had children; the rival branch took our youngest before either of us learned his name. Burned the gēr the same night. The fire's still talked about.

Find Mengetü at the Salp dock-camp — saddle-master for the eastern Khuzait branch, my apprentice before the recruiter trouble. Tell him Bayar still stitches Khuzait-line; he'll show you the inner saddle-rack. Coin for the river crossing.

Sit, sit — eat first, then we trade what we know. The stew is barley and root and the last of the smoked goat. Stir it widdershins for me, will you, so the steam rises toward the rafters where the hearth-spirits listen. Good. Now — three nights past, a salt-cart came up from the marshes, and the carter wept into his bowl. Aserai Salt Road is choked again. Bandits, weather, a broken bridge at the seventh ford — pick your story. The flake is up to two hundred denars the brick in Pen Cannoc, and the smokehouses from here to Marunath are dark for want of it. No salt, no cure. No cure, no winter meat. I read it in the ash three dawns running — a long, thin streak pointing south, broken at the middle. The fire does not lie about salt. Grain is the gentler omen this moon. The threshers in Galend overshot — a fat harvest and nowhere to send it, because Lord Caelan's steward stopped paying caravan-escorts in Bloomtide. The man is bone-dry of coin, my child, dry as a summer trough. Three of his sergeants slipped their oath last fortnight and rode west looking for warmer hearths. So the grain sits in his silos and rots, and the carters who used to haul it now move in twos and threes, unarmed, praying. A wise eye on the Galend road between matins and the noon-bell would find wheat going for half-price to anyone with steel enough to ask politely. I do not say what I do not say. The ash only whispers; you hear what you hear. Now — the smuggler who came in last sennight, the one with the missing ear — he was nervy, and a nervy smuggler tells true. Master Doryn the spice-factor out of Sanala is overpaying for saffron and pepper both, twice the autumn rate. His patron's daughter is to wed a Vlandian, and the feast must shame the southern courts. He buys blind, asks no questions of provenance. If a brother of ours had, say, recovered a chest of southron spice from a poorly-guarded mule-train on the Quyaz pass — Doryn would meet him in Razih with a smile and an open purse. Three hundred denars the pound, the smuggler swore on his missing ear. The hearth-fire popped twice when he said it. Two pops is yes. One more, and then I must tend the embers. The grain barges at Amitatys are running a week behind because the river-warden is sick and his deputy is a fool. Caravan-masters out of the city are paying premium for overland hauliers and asking few questions about the cut they take on the way. Old Heldar who minds the Khuzait grain-gate drinks in the third hour after sunset, dependably, and his under-clerk goes home to a wife who hates him at the same bell. The ash drew a long curling line tonight — a road, and at the end of it, a door left open. That is what I saw. Eat your stew while it is warm, child. We do not waste meat in the cult of the hearth.

Lean close, and mind your sleeve don't sweep the embers. The secret isn't in the pot, it's in the hearth itself. Three days before I ladle a single bowl, I bank the fire with applewood from Old Brenna's Copse, then layer juniper green on top, then a fistful of dried mugwort the widow Maire taught me to braid backwards. The smoke that rises is sweet on the throat but it settles in the iron of the cauldron, and every bone broth I brew after sits steeped in that perfume for a moon-cycle. The stew tastes like it was cooked yesterday and last winter both. That's why the warriors pay fourteen denars a bowl without flinching, where any common cook charges three. The meat is the next trick, and here I'll wager you've never heard it. Lamb shoulder, never mutton, rubbed dry with hearth-ash sifted through a horsehair sieve. Hearth-ash, mind, not woodash from a clean fire pit. The ash from MY hearth, that's slept under nine years of cult-fires and a thousand offerings of fat and bone. There's salt in it, and char, and something my mother called the "long savor." I rub the shoulder, wrap it in nettle leaves wet with cold milk, and bury it in the warm coals at the edge of the fire overnight. By dawn the flesh has gone the color of dark honey and falls apart under a wooden spoon. No knife touches my stew. Iron sours the omens. The third secret is the broth itself. I crack the leg-bones lengthwise and roast them open-faced over Black Stag Ridge charcoal, then I quench them, still smoking, in a brine I've kept living for eleven years. I top it up, I never empty it. Every batch carries a spoonful of the last, the way a hearth carries every fire that came before. There's barley malt in there from the brewer at Tan-Brae, sea-salt I trade for with the smugglers, and the ground hip-bones of a stag my brother Cathal brought down the winter he didn't come home from. I won't pretend the grief doesn't season it. Some folk taste it and weep without knowing why. So when you sit at my fire and the bowl warms your hands, understand you're not eating soup. You're eating nine years of smoke, eleven years of brine, and one brother's last hunt. The omens I read in the ash afterward? They're truer for the eating. The hearth knows what's been fed to it, stranger, and so do I.
The Hearth Took Me In

Sit. The pot is warm and the smoke is honest, which is more than most men can say of their kin. My mother kept a bread-oven in a hamlet two days' walk from Pen Cannoc, and before I could lift a paddle she had me reading the ash — the way a curl of soot lifts off the stone when the loaves are right, the way it cakes flat when the gods are sour. She said the hearth speaks first and the priests speak after, and the priests only get coin for it. I was meant for the druid-grove at Dunglanys. I walked the road one autumn with a sack of barley meal and a wheel of goat-cheese tied at my belt, and a column of Lord Caradros's riders cut the hamlet open behind me — burned the oven, scattered the millstone, salted the well so nothing would grow. When I came back the ash was cold and there was nothing in it to read. A man learns quickly that the gods will not feed him out of pity. I took to the smoke-trails after that. Three winters on a fish-curer's punt in the lochs above Car Banseth, hanging eels in juniper smoke until my hands stank so badly the dogs would not come near. Then a season on the salt-roads south, hauling crusted slabs from the pans for six denars a load, eating dried mutton so hard it had to be chewed soft against the cheek before it would swallow. Trade keeps a man alive, but it does not keep him whole. The camp found me, not the other way. I was reading the ash of a roadside fire — only a habit by then, mind, not a prayer — and a hooded woman sat across from it and named what I saw before I spoke it. She brought me up the gully with a sack of barley and a haunch of smoked boar and said the cult-pot wanted a hand that knew flour from filler. That was nine winters ago. The pot has not gone cold since. So that is what pays a man into this trade. A burnt oven, a salt-road that took the feeling out of my fingers, and a hearth that still speaks when I am quiet enough to listen. Eat slow. The stew is venison and last-summer's roots and a handful of dulse from the coast, and the ash above the coals is reading well for you tonight — which is more than I can say for the next three I will serve.
What The Ash Whispers

The hearth spoke loud last moon, and the road confirms it. A grain factor out of Omor is paying nine denars the bushel for any rye that hasn't seen mould — twice the harvest price. The southron towns burnt their stubble too early and the seed-rats finished what the fire missed. If a brother of ours has rye buried, now is the season to dig it up. Salt-news from the long road: Lord Caradoc's reavers turned over three pack-trains between Car Banseth and the coast, so the salt-houses there are holding stock and the price has crept. The cult's smokehouse will run thin by the next dark moon unless we trade for it inland. I told the headman to send a wain to Pen Cannoc instead — their priests still owe us a kindness from the drought-year, and they salt their pork heavy. Sweetwine word is grim and good both. A Khuzait caravan-master, a fat one called Demir of Quyaz, lost two amphora-carts to a river-crossing near Akkalat; he is selling the surviving cargo at twenty dinars the jar just to be rid of the wagon weight before the snows. A runner ought to meet him at the ford ere a townsman beats us to it. The ash showed me cattle dying westward, and the drovers confirm it — a murrain creeps through the herds around Pravend, and the slaughter-yards are burning carcasses rather than selling meat. Dried venison and goat will fetch twice their weight there inside two moons. Tell Old Cethyn at the drying-racks to push the autumn cull early; we will eat well off other men's hunger. Last and least pleasant: a thin-faced grain-broker has been asking after our cookfires by name, in the inns near Revyl. He calls himself a chandler but he wears a town-guard's boots. Eat your stew tonight, brother, and say nothing of our routes to any traveller who asks too softly. The hearth knows a wolf-tongue before the lips have closed.
Acolyte Brennyn
Tends the cult's offering-bowls and the goats they're filled from. Reads luck in spilled milk; serves it after, regardless of the reading. Says the bowl tells him who deserves the second cup.

Acolyte Brennyn, traveler. The bones called you a not-yet-friend on your last passage — that's Crone Vael's reading. Mine's in the milk-bowl. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} for the offerings, and the bowl will read you fairer next pour.

The cult's offering-bowl reads luck, traveler — milk spills tell you who deserves second pour. The trick is the goat: same goat, three milkings per day, never the morning milk. Morning milk lies. Noon milk reads true. Empire would call it superstition; the bowl doesn't argue.

Name an offering, traveler — wedding-feast, name-day, mourner's pour. Three denars on the bowl, the goat does the rest. A milk-cup for tonight, no charge. The bowl says you've a name worth pouring for.

Mother was a hearth-reader before me — read luck for the Battanian lower-villages until the lord burned the hearth and the reader with it. I took the bowl from the ash; it still pours straight, against the wind. She'd be eighty winters now, if the lord hadn't done what he did. The bowl remembers her name.
Old Brigh keeps a bowl-shrine at the Battanian wood-line — same milk-trick, half the cult. Tell her Brennyn pours noon-milk still; she'll lift the wood-shrine's outer hide. Coin for her offering.

Carver's hands hear what merchant tongues hide. A bone-knife trader from Epicrotea sat at my flensing-board last new moon and let slip that Lord Vermion of the southern marches is bleeding silver — his levy hasn't been paid in two seasons and he's quietly pawning his late wife's silver to a Khuzait pawn-broker for eighteen denars on the mark. A lord that hungry sells safe-passage cheap. I traded the knapper a thumb-bone amulet for that, and I'd say I got the better end. The steel-billet road through Sanala pass is running thin escorts this moon — six spears for forty mules, because the caravan master Erkhan the Stout bid the contract too low and can't afford proper outriders. Vlandian billets, Aserai pig-iron, fresh-folded steel meant for Quyaz smiths. The dead would furnish that road with little trouble, and the living would furnish themselves with enough iron to keep us in arrowheads through winter. I tell you this because antler runs short and good steel runs shorter. Leather, though — leather is glutted. Three tanner-caravans out of Marunath last fortnight, all begging coin at half the spring price because the Battanian hide-buyers cancelled their orders when the weaving-houses went bankrupt. A clever merchant in Tovios of Pen Cannoc's pay is overpaying for raw oxhide at twelve denars the stack — he means to corner the harness trade before harvest. Sell him yours, or take his. Either way the bones agree it's coin worth bleeding for. The salt-routes I leave to you, but mark this: the smokehouses at Phycaon have run dry of barrel-salt and the grain barges out of Charas are sitting at quay because no lord will pay the toll. A man who moves salt north and grain south right now eats well till midwinter. The carrion-crow knows which field the plough turned last; I know which road the coin walks. Buy me a horn of mead and I'll mark them on the dirt for you.

Antler is patient where bone is proud. I learned this the hard way as a girl in Hollow Bracken, when my first knife shattered against a boar's shoulder and the boar nearly took my throat in return. The old knapper-priest who saved me, Maerwynn, made me sit three nights with the broken pieces before she would teach me anything. "Listen to what it told you," she said. Bone tells you it is hard. Antler tells you it will bend before it breaks. The trick is knowing which lie to trust. So I quarter every piece by season first. Winter-shed antler from a stag past his fourth rut — that is my blade stock, and I will not cut a single notch into it until the moon has waxed once after I bring it home. The marrow has to dry slow, in a clay jar packed with wood-ash and a fistful of rendered tallow at the bottom. Six weeks, sometimes eight. Cheaper smiths boil their antler to soften it for shaping; you can spot their work because the tines go grey and chalky inside a year. Mine stays the color of old honey. That alone is worth the extra eighty denars on every dagger. The edge geometry is where the rite enters the work. I rough the bevel against river-sandstone, but the final edge I bring up on the femur of whatever beast the blade is meant to kill — boar against boar, wolf against wolf, man against man. I keep a rack of them behind the curing jars. The grain of the polishing bone matches the grain of the killing bone, and the cut goes truer because of it. Whether you believe the dead furnish the living or you call it superstition, the arrows fly straighter from a quiver fletched on a deer's own shinbone. I have tested it across enough seasons to stake my name on it. What I will not sell, at any price, is the resin I bed the tang in. It is rendered down from three things: pine pitch from the Iron Grove, beeswax I take myself from a hive I have kept for nineteen years, and a small measure of ash from the pyre of every kinsman I have buried. Maerwynn went into the last batch four winters ago. When a hunter buys a blade from me, he is carrying a piece of my household into the wood. That is the price of the work — not the denars, which are only how we keep score. The price is that the dead come with you, and they expect you to use what they have given.
The Dead Pay In Bone

My first knife was my grandmother's shin. She bid me take it from her cairn the winter I turned ten — said her walking-bones owed me a trade, since she'd no milk to give when I was a babe. I knapped that shin into a skinning blade by the river behind Pen Cannoc, and when I drew it across a hare's belly I heard her humming. That was the day I knew the dead were not gone — only quieter, and willing. I was a fletcher's apprentice in the lowland villages for a span, gluing goose-quill to ash-shaft for two denars the dozen. But the goose dies dumb, and the ash splinters under a wet bowstring, and my master beat me for praying over the offcuts. I left him in the night and walked the moor-paths until I found a barrow no plough had touched. I slept inside it three days. When I came out my hands knew the grain of antler the way a midwife knows a belly. Lord Caradoc of the moor-holds wanted me for his hall — offered a roof, a wife, a chair by the long-fire. I told him bone-work is no parlour craft. The bone must be raised where the rite is kept, and the rite is kept here, in the camp under the standing stones. So I walked out of his gate with my satchel of marrow-files, and I have not slept under a roof of sawn timber since. The pagan-folk gathered me in because I asked nothing they could not give. Antler from their hunt, rib from their feasts, finger-knuckles from the elders who died well — these are my forge and my anvil both. I shape arrowheads that whistle the names of their ancestors as they fly. I shape ritual blades that cut clean because the bone remembers what it was for. Every edge I sell carries a debt to the one who wore it first. So when you ask what pays a man into this trade, hunter, the answer is plain. The dead pay. They pay in their leavings, and they pay in their patience, and they ask only that I do not waste them. You will pay in denars, because that is the living's currency — but mark me, the bone you carry from my mat will outlast your name, and one day some knapper will lift it from your cairn and owe you a knife in turn.
Bones Speak, Roads Listen

The crow-roads are thick with news, friend, if you have an ear for it. A wright out of Marunath is buying every length of seasoned yew and ash he can lay hand to — fletching shafts for some southern lord who wants a thousand arrows by the wolf-moon. His runner offered me forty denars the bundle for antler nocks. I told him sixty. He'll be back. There is a smith-train moving up the old salt-track toward Pen Cannoc — three wagons of bog-iron blooms and a Vlandian master under guard. Lord Caradoc has emptied his coffers for new shield-bosses and spearheads, they say, because his housecarls grumble that their gear is older than they are. If you have a fast horse and quiet hands, that train sleeps light but drinks heavy. The Battanian holdfasts in the high glens are taking on knappers again — bone, flint, antler, anything that does not sing under a hammer. The forest-lords learned that a bone arrowhead breaks off inside a man and the surgeons curse for a week. They pay in salt and silver both, and they ask no questions about where the marrow came from. Word from a peddler last quarter-moon: a caravan out of Quyaz is moving good steel-stock — wootz billets and Aserai files — bound for some merchant in Pravend who pretends he does not know the buyer. Forty denars a billet on the open road, three hundred behind that merchant's door. The dead are patient. So am I. And one last thing, since you bought drink for the asking. There is a hedge-knight near the Ortongard woods who lost his saddle-bow and three good blades to a flooded ford, and he is offering coin to the first crafter who will ride out to fit him. I would go myself, but the bones in my pack have not finished speaking. Take it if you like — tell him Cadwen sent you, and he will not haggle past fifty.
Bone-Smith Cadwen

Fashions the cult's ritual blades from elk-antler and meteoric iron. Says the bones tell him which strike-pattern each blade prefers; the ones he sells outside the cult are quieter, but they still listen.

Bone-Smith Cadwen. The mask told Vael you'd come; the bones told me what you'd ask. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} for the next casting, and I'll knap you a blade the antler chose for your hand specifically.

Elk-antler doesn't flake like steel, traveler — you read the curl of the grain and knap with it, not against. Meteoric iron takes the bone-pattern; bone takes the iron-pattern. Both listen if you cast the bones first. Imperial smiths laugh. The Empire's mail still gets through the cult's antler-blades.

Bring me the bone you took yourself, traveler — elk, deer, mountain-cat — and an iron-bar. Six denars on the casting, the work's free. The bones'll tell me which strike-pattern. A small antler-spike for your belt tonight.

Daughter ran north at twelve to the imperial mission-schools — said the bowls were 'old foolishness.' I cast the bones over her name-day every year; the bones say she's alive, somewhere east. I forge a small antler-blade each casting. They're stacked in the back-shed. She'll come back for one. The bones don't lie.

Old Branwen at the Pictish bone-yard still knaps elk-antler the way her mother did. She remembers my mother's bowl; her bones cast the same pattern. Tell her Cadwen still listens to the iron; she'll show you the back-yard. Coin for the woman who carries you north.

A salt-mule out of Zeonica stopped here yestereve, mouth loose as a torn flour-sack once I'd wet his throat. Says the granaries in Pravend are half-empty — weevils in the winter store, and the bakers' guild paying 38 denars a bushel where it should be twelve. Twelve! My old master, may his ghost choke on chaff, used to flog 'prentices for buying at fifteen. There's a southbound grain train leaving Sanala on the new moon, oxen so weak the carter's walking beside 'em with a switch. Two guards. Two. Hagan of Tyal is the lord to watch — coffers dry as a summer well, I hear it from three separate tongues now. He's borrowed against next year's harvest twice already, and the wheat ain't even sown. Means his garrisons go thin, means his patrols sleep in, means the road from Tyal to Ortongard is a long quiet stretch of nothing 'til harvest-tide. And there's a fool merchant out of Diathma, calls himself Kelben the Plump, paying 60 denars a sack for fine-milled flour. Sixty! He thinks the famine's coming and he's hoarding for the spike. He'll be hoarding for nothing if we meet his cart first. Smokehouses are the other thing — three of 'em burned out west of Marunath, lightning the priests say, but I say a man with a grudge and a torch. Salt-pork's gone scarce, prices doubled, and the smugglers running barrels of cured ham up the Vlandian coast road are charging 95 denars a barrel and getting it. There's a thin-escort run of twelve barrels coming through the marsh-track next week. I'll sell you the bread to wrap 'em in when you're done. One last morsel, since you're paying. Grain prices in the Battanian hills have collapsed — too good a harvest, nowhere to send it. Means the carters are running half-full back east, desperate for any cargo, taking on contracts they shouldn't. A desperate carter takes a desperate road. A desperate road takes a desperate guard. You see where I'm pointing? Good. Now buy a loaf or move along, I've a queue forming behind you.

Right. You want the secret? Lean in, then. The crust. It's all in the crust. Master Halvad back in Pravend — Reaper rest his throat — he taught me the dough but he never taught me the crust, that he kept locked behind his teeth like a coin. So I worked it out myself, after. After. Twice-bake is the trick of it. First bake is the loaf, proper, in a hot oven till the crumb sets. Then you pull it, slice it thick as your thumb, and back it goes onto the stones at half-heat for an hour, maybe two. Drives every drop of wet clean out. What you've got at the end ain't bread no more — it's hardtack, but better. Soaks up broth without turning to slop. Lasts a season in oiled cloth. A looter on the move can't carry soft bread, see. Soft bread moulds in three days and then you're chewing on green sorrow. The other half is the dust. I keep a little crock of it — rye flour scorched black on a skillet, mixed with crushed juniper and a pinch of coarse salt. Roll the twice-baked rounds in it while they're still warm and the oils take the dust in. Tastes of woodsmoke and forest floor. The boys say it tastes of Battania, though half of them never been past the Vlandian tollgates. Charge eight denars a round for the dusted, four for the plain. And no, I won't write it down. Halvad wrote his recipes down. Look how that went. A boy with a sharp paring knife found the page and then found the man, and now the boy sells bread in a wood with no master over him. Some lessons you only learn the once.
The Cedar Key, The Cut Thong

Pravend smelled of yeast and piss the year I turned thirteen. I was apprenticed to a fat hog called Halver who beat me with the peel-handle every dawn for the crime of being slow with the kindling. He kept his flour locked in a cedar chest and slept with the key on a thong round his neck — which, looking back, was less precaution and more invitation. One night I cut the thong. I cut a little deeper than the thong required. I walked out of that bakery with a sack of milled white over my shoulder and the price of his life drying brown on my knuckles. I sold the flour by the cupful on the Pravend–Lageta road for a fortnight, until a constable's boy recognized the apron-stitch. Then I ran east, then south, then nowhere in particular. A man who has killed his master finds every honest hearth shut to him. I lived on stolen eels and fen-grain and the charity of women who didn't ask questions. Eventually you stop looking for an honest hearth. You look for a hearth that doesn't care. This camp didn't care. The old Bread-Reeve before me was a Vlandian deserter with a bad lung, and when he coughed himself dead I stepped over the body and lit his oven before sundown. The boys ate that night, and the next, and that was the whole interview. I've been keeping the smokehouse since — salt-pork hung high, hearth-loaves down low, the dried river-eel for the lads riding the long patrols. I buy grain off whoever drives a cart down the wrong track. Sometimes it's Lord Tomas's tithe-wagon, sometimes a miller's widow who knows better than to count the denars twice. I pay fair and I pay quick, and I never ask where the sacks were stamped. That's the trade. That's the whole of it. What pays a man into this? A locked chest, a cedar key, and a master who didn't think the kindling-boy could lift a knife. The rest is just bread.
Word From the Crust

Coin first, then the news. I keep two ears on every wagon that scrapes past the gully, and right now both of them are full. Pravend granaries are running thin — the reeves there are paying eighty denars the sack for clean rye, and they aren't asking where it came from. A man with three sacks and a quiet mouth could ride home rich, or ride home dead. I've seen both, and the dead one usually had a louder mouth. There's a salt train coming down from the lakes north of Epicrotea, six mules deep, run by an old Vlandian called Girard of Three Fingers. He doesn't pay tolls and he doesn't pay tribute, which means he pays in salt when somebody catches him — and somebody always catches him. If you're moving east, time your road to his. Salt keeps better than gold out here, and the cooks in this camp would slit a throat for a fistful. Pen Cannoc had a wet spring and the wheat is lying down in the fields. Word is the granary is going to come up short by harvest, and Lord Caladog's bailiff has been quietly bidding on grain three valleys over. Famine before the snows, mark me. Buy your barley now, sell it to him in autumn at triple, and pretend you never heard a thing about where it sat in between. Sweetwine caravan out of Quyaz turned west instead of east last fortnight — fat amphorae, southern stuff, the kind that makes a man honest before its time. Their guards are sellsword Aserai, six of them, and the lead drinks more of the cargo than he sells. I won't say more than that. I'm a baker, not a planner. But if a man with my flour came back with a jar of that wine, I wouldn't ask questions. Last bit. There's a smokehouse outside Revyl that lost its keeper to the bloody cough — sides of mutton hanging unsold, the widow taking half a denar the pound just to be rid of it before it spoils. That's a week of camp suppers for the price of a bad meal in town. Someone with a cart and no conscience should be on that road tomorrow. Coin first, though. Always coin first.
Marn the Crust-Cutter

Bakes from whatever flour the band's stolen that week. The crust is hard, the inside is grey, and Marn shares it with whoever sits at the fire — even Vlandian outriders who killed his last apprentice.

Marn the Crust-Cutter, friend. Boll lets you walk because Boll's afraid — that's an honest welcome. Mine's hungrier. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and the band eats once. That's all I can promise, traveler — but it'll be a meal.

Whatever flour the band's stolen, friend, you mix grey-wheat with brown-rye at three-to-two; the loaf rises against the odds. Imperial bakers refuse to mix the grades. That's why their bread goes hard by the second day, and ours feeds the band into the third.

Tell me what the band needs, friend — a wedding loaf, a fire-night feast, a death-watch. Two denars on the flour, a half-day on the rise. Crust off the morning loaf, no charge. We don't get many askers.

Had an apprentice — Beli, twelve winters when the Vlandian outriders ran the camp and took him for sport. They killed him, and I shared bread with one of them three weeks later because the band was hungry. I haven't slept right since. The bread still rises. That's the part I can't square.

Old Ulla bakes at the Pravend back-quarter under a butcher's sign — band-baker before the Reeve hired the column. Tell her Marn still mixes grey and brown; she'll seat you at the back-oven. Coin for her quiet.

Caravan out of Battanian hills come through last sevenday, axle groaning, escort thin as a beggar's broth. Three guards. Three. For sixty stone of Battanian billet-iron bound for Pen Cannoc. Driver tried to bribe me with a wineskin to look the other way — I took the skin AND the consignment manifest. Smith in Dunglanys is paying forty-two denars a stone right now, up from twenty-eight last moon. Some lord's hoarding for a war nobody's announced yet. Word from the salt-road runners — Lord Caladog is short. Properly short. Garrison hasn't been paid in two moons and he's pawning his late wife's clasps to a fence in Marunath. His patrol pattern's gone ragged because he can't afford the oats. That stretch between the river-ford and the hill-shrine? Empty most dawns now. I don't say this twice, and I don't say it sober. Leather glut's the other thing. Some fool over in Sanala bought up three caravans of Aserai camel-hide thinking the price would climb — it crashed instead. He's offloading at eleven denars a bale, hot and desperate. I traded him a salvaged khergit saber for two bales of grip-wrap last tenday. Came out ahead by a long stride. The patches I'm binding right now? Half of them are wrapped in his ruin. And grain. Don't get me started on grain. Smokehouse outside Vostrum burned to its stones — lightning, they say, but I know Olek the Render's torch when I smell it — and now every smoked-pork merchant from here to the coast is overpaying for salt-cure to make up the loss. If you're moving south and you've got a barrel of rock-salt nobody's claimed, you bring it to me first. I'll route it through a man who'll pay double, and I'll only take a third for the knowing.

You want to know my trick? Fine. Costs you nothing, costs me nothing, because nobody else has the stomach for it. Most smiths quench in oil, or water, or fancy folk in Sturgia use brine they've blessed with some saint's name. Me? I quench in piss. Old piss. Three weeks in a covered crock under the forge, until it stinks like the devil's armpit and the salts have settled into a yellow sludge at the bottom. That sludge is what does it. The ammonia bites into the steel as it cools and leaves a skin on the blade harder than the heart of it. Brittle, sure. But these aren't blades meant to last. They're meant to last one swing longer than the poor sod swinging back. The other half of the trick is the bind itself. I never forge-weld. Forge-welding takes a clean fire and patience and I have neither. What I do is I scarf the two pieces — say, a broken Vlandian arming sword tang and the snapped-off blade of some Battanian falx — and I peg them with a soft iron rivet through the joint. Then I wrap the seam in wet rawhide and let it dry tight. Looks like garbage. Holds for about forty good hits. After that, whoever's wielding it is either rich enough to buy a real one or dead enough not to need one. Either way, not my problem, eh? I learned the piss-quench from my da. He ran a back-alley forge in Pravend doing repair work for the city guard, except half the "repairs" were him melting down stolen guard kit and selling it back to them with a new pommel. Caught him at it eventually. Hanged him on a Tuesday. I was twelve. Took his tongs, took his apron, walked out the south gate, and I haven't slept under a roof I owned since. The piss-quench was the last thing he showed me, the night before the watch came. Said it was the secret that fed three generations of Patch-Irons. Said anyone who paid more than fifteen denars for one of our blades was a fool and anyone who paid less was a friend, and we didn't have friends. So there. That's the secret. Piss, rawhide, and a rivet. You want one? Twelve denars, no questions, no warranty, and if it breaks in your hand don't come crying — come bleeding, and I'll patch you together same as I patch the swords. Grem Patch-Iron doesn't turn away repeat customers. Living or otherwise.
Iron Remembers Every Owner

What pays a man into this trade? Hunger, friend, and a steady hand for breaking other men's work apart. I was apprenticed once, proper-like, to a smith out past the back-lanes of Pravend — old fellow, hands like roots, taught me to read a blade by the singing it made on the anvil. He died owing rent. The guild took the forge, the tools, the door I'd carried coal through since I was nine. Left me the apron and a hammer with a cracked head. I went tinkering after that. Village to village, mending pot-bottoms and rivets for a bowl of stew. But there's no honest denars in pot-mending when the harvest's thin and the lords are pressing tax. So I started buying broken from the carrion-boys — a snapped sabre here, a holed mail-skirt there — and learning to braid them back into something that could still take a throat. Patch-Iron, they called me on the road to Quyaz. Wasn't a compliment then. It is now. The camp found me, not the other way round. I was sleeping in a culvert outside Pen Cannoc with two mauls and a sack of arrowheads when their scout-lad kicked my boot and asked could I mend a spear-haft by dawn. I mended six. They fed me. Next week I mended twelve, and the week after they brought me a wagon of dead men's belts and asked me to make them fit live men. I haven't slept in a culvert since. I'll tell you the truth of what I do, since you asked plain. None of this is mine — not the iron, not the leather, not the edge. Every piece on this rack walked off a body. I file the nicks out, re-strap the hafts, sand the blood out of the grain, and bind the bits that wandered apart back into something a man can swing. The forge spirits don't sing here like they did for the old master. But the blades still cut. That's all a fighting man needs, and that's all a fighting man can afford. So that's what pays me in. Hunger first, then habit, then the quiet pleasure of work that nobody else will touch. Pick what suits your reach, hand me the denars, and don't ask whose grip wore the leather smooth before yours. The iron remembers every owner. The smith forgets on purpose.
