Word From The Ditches

Word travels slow when you live in a ditch, but it travels. A pack-train rolled out of Pravend three nights back hauling bar-iron south — proper stock, not the rust I usually rivet. Outriders were thin. The lads who saw it counted six guards for twelve mules. Somebody is going to eat that caravan, and somebody after that is going to sell me the cut-offs for forty denars a bundle. Lord Galosh out near Car Banseth paid a forge full of coin for new kite-shields last moon — boiled hide over green pine, painted before the glue set. Half of them will split by harvest. His sergeants already started buying replacements quiet-like, off-roster, off-ledger. That means battered shields walking back through the hills with no paperwork on them, and battered shields are my bread. The Quyaz bowyers are short on horn again. Some southern war ate their supply, and now every steppe rider west of the river is paying double for a half-decent recurve. If you've got a stave that isn't cracked through the belly, drag it here before the next snow — I'll pay you better than a clan trader and ask half the questions. A scrap-runner came through yesterday whispering that Revyl is recruiting smiths. Real smiths, with their own tongs, for the lord's own armoury. Old Hessa the file-cutter packed up and went. Good for her. Bad for me — she was the only one nearby who could re-temper a sword spring without snapping it, and now every busted longblade in three valleys ends up on my anvil instead of hers. Last bit. There's a thief-camp two ridges east trying to move a crate of Pen Cannoc mail — proper riveted, lord's-mark stamped right on the collar. They want eighty denars a shirt and they're nervous about it. Nervous sellers drop their price by sundown. If you're buying mail this season, wait two days and walk east. Tell them Grem sent you and they'll knock ten off just to be rid of the smell.
Grem Patch-Iron

Hammers broken farm-tools into knife-shapes by a fire that's barely a fire. His blades chip on the second cut, but they'll get you through the first — and Grem says that's all most fights need anyway.
Grem Patch-Iron, blade-bender. Boll's mercy got you in; my anvil's slower. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC}, and I'll bind you a blade that holds the first cut and prays through the second.

Farm-iron's brittle past the second cut, friend — the smelt was cold, the temper was a hope. I draw the blade thin at the spine, thick at the cutting-edge: the spine flexes instead of breaking. Holds the first cut. The second's a prayer. Most fights are first-cut anyway.

Bring me a broken plough-share or a snapped scythe, friend, and a name. I'll patch you a knife by next pass. One denar on the heat, nothing on the iron — you're bringing it. Here's a spare patch-blade for the road.

Wife and boy went into a Vlandian outrider's pyre — winter raid, the band scattered, they didn't run fast enough. I forge knives now and the knives know it. Each blade I bend bends a little for them. The band eats once. That's all I can promise. It used to be everything.

Old Hroth bends iron at the Pravend low-quarter back-alley — apprentice of mine before the band scattered. Tell him Grem still draws thin at the spine; he'll set up his anvil for you. Coin for his hammer.

Aye, sit down on that barrel — careful, it leaks brine. The cellar's cool, the hams are hanging, and old Pavlos has a tongue loosened by his own smoke. You want gossip? I've got gossip salted and stacked like cordwood. A grain factor out of Epicrotea came through last sevenday, mule-thin and twitchy, paying me three times the going rate for a side of smoked pork because his master's larders are bare. Bare, mind you — in harvest month. That tells you the lord up there has spent his coin on something he shouldn't have, and the steward's covering with caravan-purchases at any price. If you've a wagon of barley sitting idle, point it at Epicrotea before the month turns. They'll pay eighty denars a sack and not blink. Salt's the other story, and a worse one. The pans down at Pen Cannoc have been short three caravans running — bandits, weather, who knows, but the smokehouses from here to Marunath are sweating. I've had two cellar-masters write me begging for the rind-cuts I usually toss to the dogs. Yorek of the Northvale, the one with the cleft lip, told me over a cup that he paid forty denars a measure for grey table-salt — grey, mind, the cheap stuff — and counted himself lucky. If a wagon of clean white salt rolled through the pass right now, the driver could name his price and three towns would fight him for it. Which means, of course, somebody's going to try moving one. And somebody else is going to try meeting that somebody on a quiet stretch of road. Speaking of quiet stretches — the river-track between Zeonica and the lowland ferries is running with two guards per wagon. Two. I had it from a caravan-cook who shared my fire and my wine and didn't ask why I was asking. Their factor cut the escort because the season's been peaceful and the men cost twelve denars a day. Smoked hams, oil, jarred fish, and — this is the part — a strongbox of trade silver for the lowland buyers. Two guards. Against whatever the woods decide to send. I'm not telling you what to do with that, friend. I'm a cellar-master. I smoke meat. But if a man wanted to know which road was thin this season, that'd be the road. Last thing, and then I'll let you eat. Athas the Pedlar — fat man, bad teeth, drives a green wagon — has been overpaying for any smoked goods he can find, and he's working a circuit through the high villages. He's got a contract with someone in the south, I'd wager a tournament-town caterer, and he's desperate enough that he doesn't haggle. If you bring me a clean piglet by week's end I'll smoke it for shares, and we'll sell it to Athas at his asking price, and he'll thank us with that ugly smile of his. The rock makes the meat better, I always say. The rock, and a cellar-master who keeps his ears open.

My grandfather dug this cellar with his own hands, you know. Forty paces into the limestone, where the Spine breathes cold even in high summer. The rock here — it sweats. Not water, exactly. Something else. A mineral breath that settles on the hams and pulls the moisture out slow, slow, the way a patient man pulls a secret from his wife. The trick is the salt-pack, three layers. First, coarse rock-salt from the Karod Pans — the gray kind, never the white, never. Then crushed juniper berry and a fistful of dried bilberry leaf, which is my own addition; my grandfather used only juniper, but I caught a Battanian girl chewing the leaves once for her belly and thought, why not the meat? Then a second coat of salt, fine this time, ground in a hand-quern I keep oiled with sheep tallow. Forty days the ham sleeps in that pack. Not thirty-eight. Not forty-two. Forty. The cellar tells me when. After the salt, the smoke. Beech for the first three days — sweet, almost like honey at the back of your throat. Then I switch to mountain pine, but only the heartwood, never the resinous outer rings or the ham will taste like a torch. Six days of pine. Then one final day with a handful of dried mountain thyme thrown on the embers, which my mother taught me before the fever took her. That thyme day is what makes a buyer pay forty-two denars for a hock when the lowlanders sell theirs for twelve. People ask me why I do not move down to Ortongard where the markets are richer. I tell them: the rock makes the meat. You cannot carry the rock. Pavlos stays where the cellar is, and the cellar stays where my grandfather put it, and that is the end of that conversation.
The Rock Remembers Salt

My grandfather was a charcoal-burner above the pass at Tyal, and when the lowlanders burned his kiln he dug a cellar instead. Said the mountain owed him a roof if it would not give him trees. I was a boy with a clay lamp and a hand axe, and I helped him scrape the chamber wide enough to hang four hams from the rock. The salt came up from Pen Cannoc by mule, twelve denars a sack when I was small, thirty now if the trader is honest, sixty if he's not. I learned to read a ham the way a scribe reads a seal — by smell, by weight, by the way the rind hardens against the thumb. Mountain stone keeps the cold in summer and the damp out in winter, and that is half of curing. The other half is patience, which the lowlands do not teach. I came down once. Took service in a kitchen at Ortongard under a steward named Cuno of the Three Knives, who paid in coppers and beatings. When his lord lost a feud, the household scattered, and I walked back up the old goat-path with a sack of juniper berries and a head full of grudges. The cellar was still there. The rock remembers what men forget. These boys here — they ride down, they ride up, sometimes they come back lighter than they went. They want meat that travels. I give them ham wrapped in birch-bark, hard cheese rolled in ash, a flask of pine spirit for the cold nights. They pay in denars when they have them and in promises when they don't, and the promises mostly hold because a man who lies to the cellar-master eats badly all winter. So sit. The grandfather's stone is under your boots and the hams are over your head, and that is what pays a man into this trade — a hole in the mountain, and the sense not to leave it twice.
Word From The High Passes

Word on the road? Aye, sit closer — the wind eats half a man's voice up here. The mountain caravans out of Epicrotea have been hauling rock-salt south again, two wagons a fortnight, and the merchants there are paying near forty denars a sack to anyone who can get it past the slopes. If you've got mules and a quiet route, that's silver waiting on a hook. The hill-folk around Pen Cannoc are buying smoked mutton like a famine's coming — and one is, mark me. Lord Caladog's levy stripped three valleys of breeding ewes for his winter march, and the shepherds left behind have nothing to lamb come spring. Grain'll spike by harvest-end, and the man with a full cellar will be a small king. There's a Vlandian sweetwine train moving up through Jaculan — barrels marked with the Hawcaster seal, bound for some inland keep that pays in foreign coin. I've a cousin who watches that pass for the toll, and he says the guard is thin after the third bridge. A thirsty cellar-master would pay eighty dinars a cask, no questions, no seal-marks read. And listen — the eel-smokers down at Ortongard have lost their hearth-master to the bloody flux, and their stock is rotting on the racks. Anyone who can ride down with cold-cured salt before the autumn fairs will buy three winters of meat for the price of one. My grandfather dug this cellar through living rock so the hams would hang sweet — I know spoilage when I smell it on the wind. That's the word. Drink your cup, friend. The mountain keeps its own time, and the roads will still be there when you've eaten.
Pavlos Mountain-Tongue

Salts the venison the Pass-Lord's hunters bring in. Knows which slope yields the saltiest deer. Has never come down from the pass; says the mountain feeds him better than the lowland did when he was a boy.

Pavlos Mountain-Tongue. Skarvac took your toll-discount, traveler — the Pass-Lord's mood was generous today. The cellar's mood isn't. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll salt you a haunch the imperial governor's table never tasted.

Mountain venison salts different than lowland, traveler — the salt sets in three days where the lowland needs five. The trick's the slope: north-face deer, never south. South-face flesh holds the heat too long; the salt walks the wrong way. The pass-lord eats only north-face.

Tell me the feast-night and the count, traveler — pass-toll wedding, name-day, governor's table. Three denars on the cellar-stock, sample haunch for tonight. The mountain doesn't furnish small quantities.

Came up from the lowland fifty winters back as a boy — left a younger sister at the foot of the pass, never went down for her. She'd be sixty now, if winters keep her. The mountain feeds me better than the lowland did. I tell myself she'd say the same. The cellar doesn't argue.

Old Spyros runs the foot-of-pass inn — keeps the mountain-salt trick for travelers willing to coin twice. He's my sister's son, by what the inn-folk say. Tell him Pavlos still salts north-face; he'll seat you at the back-table. Coin for the climb back up.

Caravan out of Epicrotea rolled through last week with three mules of half-finished steel billets bound for the lowland forges — escort? Four boys with spears and one drunk sergeant. I traded a sack of horseshoe nails for a sniff of what they carried, and let me tell you, the man fronting that shipment, a Vlandian factor named Geirhard the Stout, is overpaying by near forty percent. Word is he lost his last two convoys on the Battanian foothills road and now he panics, pays whatever the smelters ask. Anyone with a mule and a hammer could undercut him. Iron stock is thin everywhere south of the pass — the Sturgian mines at Revyl sent only one wagon down this season instead of the usual three, and a smuggler called Kettil Squint told me it's because the local lord's debt collectors seized the ore-carts to settle a gambling marker. So if you're sitting on rough pig-iron, hold it. Price will double before the first thaw. The leather, though — gods, the leather. Every tanner from Pen Cannoc to the coast is choking on hides after that cattle-plague culled the herds early, and they're dumping cured calfskin for forty denars a bundle. There's a lord — won't say the name out loud, but he wears Aserai silks and rides a Vlandian charger, you'll work it out — who's so short on coin his armorer is melting down old tournament prizes to pay the smiths. His paychest is empty by the third week of every month, and his caravans run the Onica-to-Hubyar road with one outrider and a prayer. Three of my regulars have already worked out where to sit and wait. I don't ask what they bring back, I just ask what cut of the steel they want forged into billhooks. Last thing, and this is the one worth a flagon of arak: a Khuzait merchant named Bayan Tsetseg is buying salt at twice the going rate out of Akkalat — twice, friend — because the smokehouses east of the steppe lost their grain stores to mildew and now they're racing to cure meat before the cold sets in. He pays in raw silver, no haggling, no questions. If you can move salt and you don't mind a long ride, that's the easiest two hundred denars a load you'll ever earn. Tell him Pass-Smith sent you and he might even throw in a flask of the good stuff.

Most smiths along the lowlands will tell you a blade wants slow heat and slower cooling. They are fools who have never worked above the snowline. Up here at the Stone Shed the air itself drinks the warmth out of the steel before you can blink, and if you temper by the colour of the metal the way the manuals say, you'll pull a brittle stick out of the slack-tub every time. So I read the smoke instead. Pine resin smoke off the forge throat — when it curls left and clings to the rafters, the steel is ready. When it goes straight up, the heart of the iron is still cold and you've got another two breaths to wait. The trick I sell my edges on, though, is the quench. I keep two barrels under the bench. One is brine — coarse salt scraped off the goat-hide racks, dissolved in meltwater from the pass. The other is rendered mutton tallow with a fistful of crushed juniper berries stirred through it warm. A bandit blade gets the brine first for three heartbeats, then straight into the tallow until it stops singing. The brine sets the edge hard as glass, the tallow softens the spine just enough that it bends instead of snapping when you hook a shield rim. Old Vasily, my master down in Rovalt, would have called it heresy. He died of a snapped sword in his own hand, so I think I'll keep being a heretic. The geometry I grind is my own as well. Most armourers put a convex bevel on a chopper for strength. Mine are hollow-ground a finger's width back from the edge and then convex behind that — a sort of hidden waist. It bites deeper into a gambeson because the hollow lets the wedge of the blade pass through the cut instead of getting pinched. Costs me an extra hour at the wheel per blade, which is why I charge what I charge. Eighty denars for a hand-axe is highway robbery in Epicrotea, but up here a man pays it because the alternative is dying with a dull edge. I'll tell you the last secret for free, since you've stood through the whole sermon. The iron I use isn't bought. The caravans that come over the pass shed nails, hoop-bands, broken bridle-bits, the occasional snapped sword some fool didn't bother to pick up. My boys scrape the trail every spring melt and bring me the gleanings. I forge-weld it cold-shut in a billet of nine layers, fold it twice, and that's what becomes your axe. So when you swing it, remember — half a hundred merchants and dead men went into that edge before you did. Treat it like it has a memory, because it does.
What The Road Sheds

My da was a wheelwright in a village two passes south of here, and he taught me the truth of iron before he taught me my letters — that a strap pulled cold cracks at the third bend, that a nail set wet rusts the wood around it, that an edge ground thin sings but does not bite. We worked the wagons coming down from the high country, and when the merchants of the lower towns paid us in coppers thinner than birch-bark, my da would smile and say the road still owed us. He died still owed. I went up to the pass-towns then, looking for honest forge-work, and I found it for a while under a master in a shuttered yard near the market road — a quiet man who let me hammer out the rough billets while he did the finish-edges. When the levies came through and took him for a kingdom-debt I could not name, I took his anvil on my own back down the goat-tracks and kept walking. An anvil weighs what a man weighs. I know, because I carried mine the same distance my master carried his name. The camp found me before I found it. I was sleeping in a stone shed where the snow gathers thin, and a rider came up at first light with a broken cheek-strap and a horse going lame, and he asked what I wanted for the fix. I said pass-iron — whatever scrap the caravans had dropped on the switchbacks below, brought up to me by the basket. He laughed, and the next morning there was a basket. The morning after, two. So that is the bargain, friend. The riders bring me what the road sheds — broken pot-iron, snapped saddle-buckles, a cracked sword-tang from some boy who thought he was a swordsman down by Pravend — and I give them edges that hold and straps that do not crack at the third bend. Coin moves through here too, sure, denars when a man has them, but iron is the older currency and I trust it further. I am not proud of every blade I have set a handle to. But I am proud of the work. A strap pulled warm, a nail set dry, an edge ground to bite — that much I still owe my da, and I pay it every morning I light the forge.
Word From The High Pass

Caravan-talk drifts up the switchbacks before the snow does, traveller. Word is the garrison at Chaikand is buying every shield-blank a smith can hammer flat — Lord Ürkhün lost half his round-targes to a steppe skirmish and his armourers can't keep the rivet-line moving. If you've a wagon of poplar boards and rim-iron, that's eighty denars a shield, no questions about where the steel came from. There's a steel-stock train climbing the Onika road right now, six mules deep, bound for the foundries at Quyaz. Imperial ingot, the heavy grey kind that rings clean off the anvil. They march light because the snow's late this year and they think the high passes are quiet. They are wrong about that, but I did not say so. Down on the lowland circuit, Lord Pelle paid out for two hundred kite-shields and a fresh stand of spear-heads — coin came from selling off his late brother's racing string, they say. His smiths at Pen Cannoc are turning away apprentices, so any journeyman wandering this way has nowhere honest left to go. Some of them end up at my shed. Some of them end up worse. A Vlandian buyer was through here a fortnight back hunting for blackened mail and helms of any cut, paying sixty dinars a coat and not haggling. He never said which border lord he served, and I never asked. If you've war-spoil rusting in a saddlebag, you bring it to me before the snow closes the gap — I'll move it down the chain and we both eat. Last thing, and mark it. The forge-town at Revyl is short on charcoal and shorter on hands — old Master Hjalmar died at his bellows last month and no one's stepped to the hammer. Anvil-iron's gone scarce all the way to the coast because of it. Pass-iron, pass-price. Both fair. Bring me scrap and I'll cut you a piece worth carrying.
Kostas Anvil-Hand

Repairs imperial mail with mountain-iron — the kind that takes three more strokes to set right but holds three more strokes longer. His repairs outlast the originals, which Skarvac says is why the imperial patrols keep losing.

Kostas Anvil-Hand, Pass-Smith. The Pass-Lord lets you walk; the anvil decides whether you carry. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} from the lowland forges, and I'll repair you mountain-mail that holds against three more strokes than imperial issue.

Mountain-iron takes three more strokes to set than imperial issue, traveler — the ore's tighter, the grain runs wrong, you fight it for the first half-hour. After that it holds three more strokes longer than anything Aserai-side. The patrols keep losing. They don't know the count of strokes.

Bring me a broken pass-blade, traveler, and a draw — I'll re-temper you mountain-iron the lowland forges don't know how to copy. Six denars on the heat, the iron's already paid. Here, a spare wedge for your belt.

Father worked the same anvil; grandfather, the same again. Three brothers — two went down for the imperial recruiters' bounty, one stayed. The two never came back; the third drinks too hard now. The anvil's mine because the anvil chose. The lowland chose the others.
Find Old Theodoros at the Aserai dye-quarter forges — apprentice of mine before the southern war. Tell him Kostas still strikes the mountain-count; he'll show you the back-anvil. Coin for the desert.

A caravan limped in past dusk with their axles squealing fit to wake the wolves, and the headman, one Tariq of the Soft Hands, paid eighteen denars a sack for the mouldy barley I had been feeding the goats. Eighteen! The smokehouses out by Quyaz have all gone cold, you see, on account of the salt-train from the southern flats never showing its face this moon. No salt, no smoked mutton; no smoked mutton, and every cook from here to the coast is buying grain like the locusts are due tomorrow. Now I sat that soft-handed fool down with a bowl of mare's milk and let him talk himself dry. Says the road from Sanala to the eastern fords has but four spearmen and a one-eyed crossbowman guarding three wagons of hard cheese and pressed curd. Four! In my grandfather's day you would not move a basket of dung past the cairns with fewer than twenty. And he says Lord Vlachus is so short on coin he sold his wife's silver to pay his garrison last fortnight, which means his patrols on the western salt-road will be thin as broth for the next two moons. The boy who tends his ponies let slip something even tastier while pretending to admire my cheese-press. A grain factor out of Onira, a fat one called Eshmun the Weigher, is paying twenty-six denars the bushel for any oats he can get his pudgy fingers on, because his contract with the city watch comes due before the snows. Twenty-six! You could load a string of mules with mouldy fodder from the floor of any abandoned barn and ride home a rich man, if you had the stones to brave the road and the wits not to talk about it in the wrong ger. So when you ride out, ride east before the cheese-wagons get to safer country, and ride hard. And mind, when you come back, the salt-prices will only have climbed higher, so save me three handfuls from whatever you cut loose. A man my age cannot eat unsalted curd forever, the steppe was greener once and the cheeses were softer, and Old Ozcin remembers.

The secret, child? It is the bag. Not the milk, not the mare, not even the season — the bag. Mine is mare-stomach, scraped with a flint not a knife, never washed with water from a running stream. Running water carries spirits that sour the starter. I rinse it only with the rain I catch in Sharir's Hollow after the first hard frost. That rain is sweet. River rain is jealous. For the kurut — the hard cheese the riders take into the long grass — I press it in a sling of horsehair, not cloth. The hair lets out the whey but keeps the salt-skin tight. I salt twice: once with the rough grey crystal we pick from the lick-stones near Tulga's Bend, then again three days later with crushed wild garlic-root burnt black on a flat stone. The second salting is what makes my cheese keep for a year on the saddle. Other women salt once and weep when it moulds by midsummer. I do not weep. The mare-milk drink — the koumiss the boys swagger over — I do not stir with wood. Wood drinks the sour. I stir with a horse's rib, dried two winters in the smoke-hole. My mother stirred with her mother's rib for forty years; when she passed, I burned hers proper and started mine fresh from a grey mare I rode as a girl. The rib remembers the rhythm. The bag, the salt, the rib — these are the three things. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling you a flat sour drink for the price of a fat one. I will sell you a skin of koumiss for thirty denars and a wedge of kurut for fifteen, and I will not tell Bayan-Khor you asked about the rib. He thinks I learned it from a Khuzait trader and it pleases him to think so. Let him think so. The steppe was greener then, and a woman could keep her own secrets without a chief deciding they were his to know.
Mare-Milk and Long Memory

A boy on the long grass learns the herd before he learns his own name. I rode behind the khan's mares before I could grip a bow, counting foals at dawn, salting hides at dusk. My father was no warrior — he was the man who knew which spring still ran in the dry month, and which marmot warren had grown fat. He taught me that a camp dies of empty bellies long before it dies of empty quivers, and that lesson has fed me every winter since. When the old khan fell on the road below Quyaz, the herd scattered and the clansmen scattered with it. I drove what mares I could north, traded the lame ones for salt at a Sturgian post, and salt for smoked river-eel from a fenman who owed my father a favor. I have been moving food along that crooked line ever since — grain from Pen Cannoc when the borderlords are sleeping, hard cheese off the Khergit shepherds, dried mutton I cure myself in a pit behind the wolves' tents. This camp took me in because I knew the old way of the kumis — three days of beating, the right cradle of felt to keep the skin warm, the trick of the second souring that turns mare-milk to a drink that lasts a campaign. I keep the hard cheeses too, pressed between river-stones and salted from the lick-flats out past Iuteus. A raider can ride a week on a fistful of that cheese and a strip of dried horse — and the boys here ride hard. I do not ride out with them. My knees gave up that road long winters ago. But every man in the camp eats from my hand once a day, and pays me in coin or in trade-skins, and that is exchange enough. Steppe gives, steppe takes — and Old Ozcin stands at the gēr-door with a ladle, keeping the balance.
Word From The Long Grass

Sit. The kumis is in the skin by your knee — pour your own, I'm too old to lean. You ask for the word on the road, and the road has been talking. Riders came through three nights back, hooves still hot, and they paid for cheese in dinars minted in Quyaz. That tells me the southern khans are flush again, and flush khans buy salt before they buy swords. Speaking of salt — Odokh market is paying double the spring rate. Their smokehouses ran dry curing horseflesh for the warband Urkhun Khergit is pulling together east of the river. If you've got brick-salt to move, take it there before the moon turns, not after. After, every petty trader on the steppe will have heard, and the price will fall like a stone in a well. A sweetwine caravan out of Pravend is wandering the trade-track to Pen Cannoc — three wagons, two guards too drunk to count their fingers. The drover is a fat southerner called Astrades, and he overpaid for his hires. He'll be on the bend past the salt lake in maybe ten days. I am only telling you what I heard. What you do with hearing is your own steppe. Now the bad word. Grain is going to bite hard come the cold moons. The Quyaz harvest was thin — the millet went brown on the stalk, and the river ran low for the second year. I have seen this before, boy. When the granaries up there start hoarding, the villages down here start eating their seed-stock, and then come spring there is nothing planted and the children start dying. Buy your grain now. Buy more than you think. I am stacking sacks behind the gēr-wall and I do not care who calls me a miser. Last thing. There is a Vlandian wine-merchant asking after dried mare-meat in Onira — he wants it for some lord's hunting feast, will pay in silver and ask no questions about where the horse came from. If you have a string of poor ponies you would rather not explain, that is your road. I'll trade you a wedge of hard cheese for the news of how it goes. Steppe gives, steppe takes. So does Old Ozcin.
Old Ozcin
Gēr-Steward

Pitches Ulan's tents, dries his meat, brews his kumis. Has followed Ulan through both banishments and the one return that didn't take. Says the gods sent guests for a reason, and Ozcin has fed every one of them.

Old Ozcin, gēr-steward to Twice-Banished Ulan since the first banishment. Ulan's hand is open to you, traveler — the gods sent you. The cookpot's fussier. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and you'll eat at our fire the same as the Khan's branch used to.

Khuzait kumis ferments three days in the gēr-leather, never the wood barrel, traveler — wood spoils the bite. The leather breathes; the leather knows. Imperial vintners try wood and call it 'kumis-equivalent.' The Khan would spit. Has, twice.
Tell me the camp-count and the rite, traveler — name-day kumis, wedding-stand, mourner's pour. Three denars on the leather, a fortnight on the ferment. A horn-cup for your road-stew tonight.

Sons both ride with Ulan — the eldest at the right hand, the youngest at the second-pony. Wife died at the second banishment; the cold took her. The gods sent us guests to feed, so we kept feeding. The hand grew strong from the pour. That's how it goes.
Khentii Wind-Stand keeps the Khan's-branch yurts — knew Ulan before the striking-off. Tell him Old Ozcin still ferments in leather; he'll set the gēr-flap aside for you. Coin for the long ride.

A trader out of Makeb wintered with us last moon, his cart axle split, his tongue loose from too much fermented mare's milk. He let slip that Khuzait noyan Urkhun is hauling a steel-billet caravan up the Amitatys trail with only six horse-archers riding flank. Six. For nine hundred weight of Sturgian billet bound for the Ortongard smithies. The man practically drew me a map between belches, and I drew my own conclusions while he slept it off. The leather glut out west is the other piece worth knowing. Tanner Bayazid at Quyaz overbought hides after the Aserai cull and now he's dumping cured cow at twelve denars the bundle when last spring it was thirty. Smugglers running south through the Dirigh Aboard dunes pay near nothing for it. Means every bow-grip I wrap costs me half what it did, and I'm passing none of that to you, friend. A man has to eat. Better piece yet, Lord Monchug's bannermen haven't been paid in two market-rounds. Heard it from a salt-runner whose cousin rides with their levy. They're selling sinew and horn off their own remounts to make ends meet, which is how I got my last three bundles of bull-horn for forty denars the lot. If you're hunting a lord who can't keep his retinue's loyalty come winter, that's your man. Grain's the only sour note. Smokehouse at Chaikand burned to the foundation last waning moon, and the caravans that used to glaze their meat there are now overpaying Salt-Captain Nogai for preserves out of Dunglanys. Grain followed the salt — both up by a third. Tells me the bow trade is steady but I'd not buy bread on credit this season. Now. You want the recurve, or the long-draw?

Hai, you ask the old bow-wright his secret? Sit. The horn is the bone. The sinew is the muscle. The wood is just the spine that holds them quiet between shots. Most fools in the lowlands glue all three with hide-cement and call it done in a moon. The bow splits in a hard winter and they curse the steppe. I cure mine eighteen months, sometimes twenty. Belly of mountain-sheep horn, scraped down with a goat-tooth scraper until it sings flat against my thumb. Back of sinew from the back-strap of a long-running mare, never a stall-fattened beast — a mare who has run knows how to spring back. Core of mulberry from the South Bend only. Birch breaks. Maple lies. Mulberry remembers. The trick that no Imperial fletcher will ever copy: I boil my fish-glue with crushed millet husk and a pinch of the white salt from Lake Vagosh. The husk gives it tooth, the salt keeps it from going soft in summer rain. When I lay the sinew, I chew each strand first — yes, chew — until my own spit softens the bundle. Then it lays flat on the back and dries into the wood like it grew there. The Khergit master who taught me, Old Boroldai, said a bow that has not tasted its maker's mouth is just a stick. I was nine years old and I thought he was being cruel. Now I am fifty and three, and I have not made a bow any other way. The last secret is the binding. After the sinew sets I wrap the grip in horse-tail wound against the lay of the hair, never with it. Goes on dry, tightens as it cools. Foreign buyers ask why my bows cost three hundred denars when the Vlandian crossbowyer down the road sells for ninety. I tell them: his bow will kill a deer at fifty paces this autumn. Mine will kill a deer at a hundred paces, every autumn, for the next forty winters. My father's bow still hangs in my brother's ger. He died with it across his back at Two-Rivers Pass when I was twelve. The horn is yellow now and the sinew has darkened like old honey, but the draw is still thirty-eight pounds at twenty-eight inches. Test it yourself when you ride east. Tell my brother Tergel sent you. He will not weep, but he will pour you the good kumis. So. You still want to buy one, or did you only come to learn?
Horn, Sinew, Honest Hands

What pays a man into this trade? The bow does, friend. My grandfather bent his first stave when he had no beard, and I bent mine before I had teeth enough to chew dried curd. We are bow-wrights of the eastern grass — no forge, no anvil, no clatter of hammers. A length of mountain-goat horn, the back-strap sinew of an old gelding, a slab of birch for the core, and patience enough to wait through a winter while the glue cures. That is all a man needs to put death at three hundred paces. I learned the craft in my father's ger, west of Quyaz. We rode for old Urkhun Khan in those years, and his archers carried our staves into every skirmish along the river road. A good composite takes two summers to finish — horn glued in spring, sinew laid in autumn, the whole thing tillered slow through the cold so the layers learn to breathe as one. Rush it, and the bow blows apart on the third draw and takes a man's eye with it. I have seen that. I do not rush. The trade brought me here through a poor bargain. A Vlandian factor out of Pravend paid me sixty denars for a dozen finished bows and then sold them on for six hundred to his own knights. I rode after him with a half-strung stave across my saddle. I did not catch him. What I caught was a writ on my head and a long ride east into country where writs do not travel. The chiefs here took me in because every camp needs a man who can fit a string and cut a nock straight. So now I bend horn for the riders who shelter under this ridge. I take the sinew they bring me off the steppe ponies, I take the goat-horn from the mountain hunters, and I make bows that throw a heavy arrow through mail at sixty paces. The price is fair if the buyer is fair. I have no use for a man who haggles by lamplight and then says my draw weight is light at noon. Bow shoots true if the buyer is true. Be honest, and you will leave my stall with a stave that outlives your sons.
Word From The Long Tracks

Word came down the Volga track last moon — Khuzait Khan Monchug's outriders are buying every horn bow they can find for the Quyaz levies. Pays in fresh denars, not shaved coppers, and asks no questions about the maker's mark. I've sent two dozen east already, and the courier swore the khan's quartermasters wanted twice as many. The Pen Cannoc woodyard is short on yew this season — frost split half their winter cull, and the Battanian fletchers are sniffing around steppe traders for laminated horn-and-sinew instead. Won't last; their pride won't let them buy "easterner sticks" for long. But while the desperation holds, a clever runner moves stock north and comes back with denars heavy enough to drag the saddle down. A Khergit caravan out of Tulga dragged itself in three nights past, all dust and broken axles. They had sinew — good sinew, ox-back, the long stuff — and traded it cheap for water and a dry place to sleep. I bought the lot. So if you're after a stave that won't crack come dry season, you came to the right tent at the right moon. Hear this too — Lord Urkhun in the south steppes lost his master bowyer to a cough, and the man's apprentice is too green to draw a war-weight stave. Word is the lord's offering forty denars a day plus quarters for any wright who can fit out his druzhina before the spring raid. I won't go — I've ridden enough lords' camps to know how those tales end — but a younger pair of hands might do well there. Last bit, no charge: don't take steel-tipped shafts west through the Pravend highway. Imperial customs hanged two arrowmongers last month, called them munitions-runners. Take the goat tracks south of the river. Slower, but the buyer is true at the other end.
Tergel Bow-Wright

Strung horsebows for the Khan's branch before the branch struck Ulan's name from its rolls. Strings them now for whoever pays. Khuzait still — you can hear it in the way he flexes the staves before sale.
Tergel Bow-Wright. Ulan's word is good; my horn-glue is better. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll string you a bow that makes the imperial recruiter's stomach turn at fifty paces.

Khuzait horsebow takes the horn-glue at three layers, not the imperial-issue two, traveler — that's why a Khuzait bow holds the draw through a campaign's worth of weather. Imperial recruiters can copy the curve. They can't copy the glue. They've stopped trying.

Bring me a draw-weight and a horse-height, traveler — I'll string you a bow that turns the imperial recruiter's stomach at fifty paces. Four denars on the horn, a fortnight on the glue. Spare string for your current bow, no charge.

Father was a bow-wright in the Khan's branch; his name was struck from the rolls the same day Ulan's was. He drank himself into the steppe at sixty-three. I keep his glue-pot on the bench. I haven't used it in twenty winters. I open it once a year on the name-day to check the smell. It still holds.
Old Erdene strings bows at the Salp river-camp — apprentice of mine before the strikings. Tell her Tergel still lays three layers; she'll show you her glue-stock. Coin for the ferry.

Sit, sit — mind the net, I'm halfway through this knot. You want gossip? I salt fish for a living, friend, and salt is half the news of the coast. Every smuggler what beaches a skiff to refill brine barrels leaves me three rumours for one barrel, and lately the barrels have been thin. Word off a Vlandian runner two tides back — grain out of Pravend is fetching near forty denars the sack inland, on account of the smokehouses at Jaculan shutting down. Three of 'em, all at once. Cooper's son took ill, the brine-pits soured, who knows. Point is — no smoked herring moving north, which means salt-pork's gone scarce, which means any caravan dragging barrels of cured anything is worth twice what its escort's paid to guard it. And the escorts? Thin. Lord Derthert's pulled half his hearthmen east for the border, so the coast road between Sargot and the bay's running with four spears where it used to run with twelve. There's a fat grain-factor named Olbas overpaying for anything salt-cured — paid sixty the sack last fortnight, paid eighty this one. He's contracted to feed a garrison and the garrison won't wait. Smugglers say he's holed up at Rhotae sweating into his ledger. And — this one's gold — Count Laudavix is short on coin. Pawned his wife's gulls-eye brooch, the runner swore on his mother. Means his patrols ain't getting paid, means his patrols ain't patrolling. So here's the sea's verdict, friend, and I trust the sea more than I trust any man on it: somewhere between Sargot and the smokehouse-empty north, a brine-barrel caravan is rolling toward Olbas's purse with four tired spears around it. I'd not say where exactly. I just knot nets. But the tide goes out tomorrow at the third bell, and a small boat could be at the coast road by dusk.

The brine I cure my hold-fish in is no secret to any sea-wife who's salted her man's catch — but the second wash is mine, and I'll thank the sea I learned it. After the first three days in heavy salt, I pull the fillets, rinse them in cold seawater drawn three leagues out from any river-mouth, then lay them back in a fresh barrel with the salt cut by a fifth and a fistful of crushed juniper-berry mixed in. The juniper kills the rot that creeps in past day twelve, and it leaves a sharp green smell on the fish that the crew swears keeps the gulls off the rigging when they eat on deck. The trick — and this is the part I don't say aloud at Sargot market when the fishmongers come sniffing — is that the second-wash brine must sit one full tide-cycle in a copper-bottomed cask before the fish goes back in. Copper, not iron, not wood-lined. The brine goes faintly blue and tastes wrong on the tongue, but it kills whatever sickness the gut-strings leave behind, and a barrel cured that way will feed a long-ship six weeks past landfall without a man taking the shivers. I trade a finished cask for forty denars and the buyers think they're robbing me. I learned the copper-cask from an old steward called Eystein who served three chiefs before mine and lost his right hand to a hauling-rope off the cliffs near Omor. He used to say the sea decides who eats and who feeds the gulls, and a steward's only job is to make sure the answer comes out right for his own crew. He showed me the trick the winter before he died — one-handed, mind you, scooping juniper from a clay pot while I stirred — and made me promise I'd never sell the method to a shore-man. I haven't. Not in eleven seasons. The nets I knot are a separate matter and any rope-hand can copy them, but the cure goes with me to whatever cold strand the sea picks. If a man asks me sweetly and pays for two casks at once I might let slip that copper matters, but I won't say why, and I won't say how long. Eystein's ghost can keep that much for himself.
Knots, Salt, and Debt

A man pays himself into this trade with cold hands and colder patience. I learned the knots on my father's smack out of Rivacheg, mending herring-nets by lamp-oil before I could swing an oar. When the ice-wind took him over the gunwale one black October, the boat went to his brother and the debt came to me — eight denars a week to a salt-factor who smiled like a gutted cod. I tried the honest run for three winters. Hauled barreled cod down to Revyl, sold smoked eel at the quay-markets, kissed the boots of every customs-clerk who'd take a bribe in fish instead of coin. Then Lord Hrothgyr raised his levy-tax on small craft and the salt-factor doubled his cut, and one morning I stood on my own dock owing more than the timbers were worth. The longships came through in spring. Their steersman wanted a man who could read a net's bellyful at a glance, salt a hold so the catch held three months, and keep his mouth stitched about where the cargo came from. I weighed honest starvation against dishonest supper and chose the supper. Been salting their hold-fish ever since. I don't ask whose village the grain came from. I count barrels, I rub salt into the cracks, I knot the boarding-nets so they don't fray when a man's life hangs in them. The sea decides who eats out there — I just make sure the eating lasts till the next landing. Pay fair and you'll get a fair weight; cheat the scale and you'll find a hook in your bread.
Word From The Tides

The fjord-towns of Omor and Rissun are paying double for salt-pork this season — the herring runs failed twice off the cold shoals, and the smokehouses sit empty. A barrel that fetched eighty denars last winter moves for one-sixty at the wharf, no haggle, no questions asked of the seller. If you've a hold of cured meat and a stomach for the run past Revyl, that's coin worth wetting your boots for. Word came down from a gull-eyed runner two tides back — Raganvad's steward is buying every grain-sack between here and the Sturgian shore. They mean to victual a long campaign, or feed a fleet, or both. He pays in struck silver, not promises, which is more than I can say for the southern lords. The price won't hold past midsummer, mind. Sweetwine's gone scarce as a calm sea. The Vlandian galley that used to call at Pen Cannoc with casks from Sargot hasn't shown her sail in three turnings — coast watchers say she was taken near the Battanian rocks, hull and all. What stock remains, the Quyaz caravans are running overland through Khuzait country, and they ask their weight in dinars for it. There's a famine coming to the eastern villages, mark me. The locusts hit the rye-fields outside Pravend, and the river barges aren't moving relief fast enough. Dried eel and twice-baked ship-bread will trade for amber, for iron, for whatever a desperate man has left to give. Mira Salt-Hand at the Vlandian harbor told me as much when she ran a load past us last fortnight, and she's never wrong about a hungry market. Last bit — the smokehouse at Omor burned. Cooking-grease fire, the whole rig down to char and nails. Any cured fish you can put on the dock there before the lord rebuilds, you'll be the only seller standing. The sea decides who eats, aye, but a man with salt and a fast keel decides who eats *well*.
Holvar Net-Master

Mended longship sails for two captains who drowned and one who didn't. Now mends Bjornulf's. Doesn't speak much about the drowned ones — though the third's hall sits just up the coast and Holvar knows the way.

Holvar Net-Master, traveler. Bjornulf shouts you in; the longhall's another matter. The captain's mead is his to pour; my cured fish is mine to grant. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll fill your sack from Bjornulf's own stores.

Cure fish in three rinses of saltwater, not the river-rinse the southerners use, traveler — saltwater bites the rot before it sets. The third rinse is the slow one; one breath per fish, no more. Bjornulf's hall eats through the winter on the third rinse. The southern halls don't get past the second.

Tell me the longship and the crew-count, traveler — fortnight at sea, full ration. Two denars on the salt, a sample on the saddle tonight. The cured fish'll hold to the third coast if the bag's tight.

First captain drowned with my brother aboard — Ari, eighteen winters at the oar. Second captain drowned with Bjornulf's father. The third's still going. Brother was the better fisherman. The sea takes the wrong ones first; that's the cure I learned. I rinse three times now, every fish, no exception.

Yngvar Cold-Hand keeps a longhall up the coast under the third captain's old banner — knew my brother. Tell him Holvar still rinses three; he'll seat you at the back-fire. Coin for the longship passage.

Crew rowed in last sundown with a strake full of bent anchor-iron and a story worth more than the metal. Says they shadowed a billet-caravan three days out of Pravend, plate-stock bound for some hungry lord's smith. Six guards. Six. For a wagon worth eighteen thousand denars if the steel grades clean. Whoever hired that escort is pinching coppers, and pinched coppers make a forge-smith like me very interested in where his road bends next. The talkative one was a tin-peddler we let drink instead of drown. He swears Lord Unwalin is two months behind on his garrison's iron account and paying his armourer in promises and salt-cod. Salt-cod, brother. A vassal that can't settle a smith-bill won't settle a ransom either, so if his outriders come sniffing the cove, we hold him cheap and let the crew vote. I'd take half-price in good billet over full-price in his rusty denars. Smugglers out of Ortongard told the cook there's a leather glut south — three tanneries dumped hides at four denars the bundle because a southern army cancelled its order. Means scabbards and grips cost me nothing this season. Means I can wrap every axe-haft in doubled hide and still undercut the inland forges. Means, also, that anybody trying to sell us leather at the old price is robbing us, and I'll know the face when I see it. And one last thing the tide brought in — a grain-hoy out of Epicrotea is overpaying for pig-iron, twenty over market, because their own foundry cracked its bloomery wall. Halvar heard it twice in two different taverns, so it's true enough to act on. Bring me scrap. Bring me wrecked plate, broken cleavers, snapped anchor-flukes — anything ferrous, I'll forge it into trade-billets and we'll sail them north before their masons finish the patch. The sea gives the metal, the gossip tells us where to spend it.

Anchor-iron. That's the secret nobody west of Jaculan wants to hear, but it's the truth of every axe I hang on this rack. The crew drags up flukes and shanks from wrecks off the skerries — old Vlandian patrol-galley anchors mostly, the four-armed kind with the crown forge-welded thick — and I cut them down at the throat. The iron's been soaking brine for forty, sixty, a hundred winters. It comes out of the salt slow and stubborn and a little bit angry, and that anger is what I want in a war-axe. The trick is the fold. Bog-iron a smith will fold seven times, eight, to chase the slag out. Anchor-iron I fold only three. Any more and you cook the sea out of it. You want to leave the salt-ghosts trapped in the grain — little black streaks you can see on the etch if you polish it right. That's where the edge lives. When you hew a shield-rim, the ghosts catch and tear instead of skidding off clean. Old Hroar Two-Tongues down at Omor calls it dirty work and charges three hundred denars for a smooth blade. Mine go for one-twenty and bite twice as deep. Let him keep his clean steel. I quench in seawater too, not the rain barrel. Has to be drawn fresh that morning, west side of the headland where the current pulls strong — I won't use harbor water, harbor water's tired. The hiss when I drop a hot blade in is different. Sharper. My father taught me to listen for it. He was anchorsmith on a Sturgian longship before the wreck at Sigil Reef, and when they hauled him out of the surf three days later the only thing still on him was the hammer at his belt. That hammer's the one I'm holding now. He used to say all metal comes from the sea anyway — ore was just sea that forgot how to flow. I didn't understand him till I started forging from anchors. Now I think he might have been the only honest smith I ever knew. So when you swing one of mine, you're swinging something that already drowned once and came back meaner. Keep it oiled with seal-fat, not olive — olive goes rancid and the ghosts hate the smell. And if she ever sings to you in a storm, don't be frightened. That's just the salt remembering.
Sea-Iron Paid Me In

My da' was a wrecker on the cliffs north of Rhotae, and the sea paid him in iron more often than fish. Every storm scattered Imperial galleys on his rocks, and every dawn we'd walk the shingle pulling anchors, chain, sword-shards, broken cleats — anything the salt hadn't eaten through. He taught me to read a beach the way a townsmith reads a billet, and he taught me the only honest creed I've kept: all metal comes from the sea anyway, boy. The mines just borrowed it first. I served my apprentice years under a Vlandian smith in Sargot, hammering horseshoes for Lord Tythos's riders until the man caught me filing down a captured corsair-axe for a dock-hand who'd paid me three denars in copper. He called it theft of forge-time. I called it side-trade. The magistrate sided with him, and I lost the right hand at the wrist for it — not the whole hand, mind, just the four fingers and a thumb that mattered. Anchor-Hand they call me now, because what they fit me with after is a bent iron hook a Nord smith brazed onto the stump in Omor, and it grips a tong-handle better than the meat ever did. The crew picked me up off a beached longship two winters back, half-starved and bartering my hammer for hardtack. The boys had hauled a whole Imperial bow-anchor up the strand and didn't know what to do with three hundred-weight of soft iron. I showed them. One anchor becomes eleven axes, fourteen sax-knives, and enough nails to re-strake a hull, if you know the heats. They've kept me in coal and quenching-oil ever since, and I've kept their edges honest. I don't forge for kings here, and I don't forge pretty. What I make has to bite through mail in one swing and not snap when it hits a shield-rim, because if a brother goes down for a bad weld, that's my name on the cairn. So when you bring me denars, I weigh them against the iron the same way the sea weighs everything — slow, fair, and without flattery. Sea-iron, sea-price. That's the trade that paid me into this camp, and it's the trade that'll bury me out of it.
Sea-Iron, Sea-Word

Word came down from Rissal last fortnight — the lord there is paying double for arrowheads, three hundred per gross. Some Vlandian dog kicked over a hornet's nest on his eastern march and now he wants every smith from here to Ortongard bent over an anvil. Won't pay sea-rates, mind. Inland coin always smells of fear and tries to haggle. There's a steel-stock caravan coming down the coast from Omor, heading for the Vlandian markets. Three wagons, Battanian guards, moves slow on the headland road past the white cliffs. I'm not telling you what to do with that. I'm telling you what's on the road. Eirik Stormcrow over in the next bay already knows. He pays his crew in denars now, not shares — make of that what you will. Lord Caladog commissioned a hundred shields out of Pen Cannoc — limewood, iron rims, his clan-knot pressed in the leather. The smiths there are turning away apprentices and the price of rivet-stock has gone stupid. If you've got a sack of bog-iron lying somewhere you forgot about, take it inland. You'll come back rich enough to drink for a season. Saddle-trade is dying on the steppe road. Khuzait riders aren't buying — something's stirring out past Quyaz and they're making their own gear, fast and rough. The leather-cutter in Revyl told me he hasn't sold a war-saddle in two moons. Bad sign for him. Good sign for whoever buys his stock cheap before he packs it in. Last word — and this one's worth the listening. A Sturgian smith called Vasili Greybeard died at his forge last month, left a workshop full of half-finished pattern-welded blades and nobody to claim them. His widow's selling the lot for under two thousand denars just to clear the floor. That's anchor-iron prices for sword-steel. Somebody's going to walk into Revyl and walk out a rich man. Might as well be someone who knows how to listen.
Snorri Anchor-Hand

Forged longship anchors and sword-edges for three crews before settling under Bjornulf's hall. Salt-bleached like everything else here. Says the salt makes his steel sing different — "Sturgian-deep," he calls it.

Snorri Anchor-Hand, salt-smith. Bjornulf laughs you in — that's the captain. The forge takes its measure slower. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll edge you a blade the longhall posts will remember the day you walked out with it.

Salt-bleached steel sings different, traveler — the brine bites the grain, the edge takes the bite. Imperial smiths fresh-water their tempers and wonder why their blades chip on the third strike. Sturgian-deep, I call it. The longhall posts still bear my anchor-marks where they bit on the first cut.
Bring me a steel-bar and a longship-deck, traveler — I'll edge you a blade the longhall'll remember. Five denars on the heat, the brine's already drawn. Here, a wedge for your belt while it cools.

Wife drowned at the first cure — Helga, twenty winters at the smithy. She'd boil the brine while I struck. The longhall keeps her name in the rafter beam, third post from the door. I run the blade across the post every new moon, just to listen. The wood still answers.

Old Sigurd forges at the Sturgian dock-quarter under the old longhall's stamp — Helga's brother by oath. Tell him Snorri still brines deep; he'll show you the anchor-mark anvil. Coin for the longship passage.

Sit, sit. The clay pot does not boil faster for staring at it, and old Kareem has tongues to wag while the dates soften. You smell that? Cardamom from a caravan that limped through here three sunrises ago, paid me in spice because their coin-purse was already light. They came down from Husn Fulan talking like men who had seen ghosts. Said the granaries up that way are half-empty, that the steward there is buying wheat at near a denar a measure when last moon it was selling for sixty. Someone, somewhere, has held back his harvest, and the price climbs each week the wind blows wrong. Now, here is the meat in the broth. The salt road that bends past the dry wadis, the one the caravan-masters call the Long Tongue, it carries only six spears with it now. Six. For wagons hauling rock-salt and dried fish out toward Quyaz. The merchant Habib al-Mu'allim is the one paying for the escort, and his guards grumble he has stopped buying them new boots. A man who saves on his guards' boots saves on his guards' loyalty, you understand me? Six spears, fat sacks, and a master whose purse-strings are knotted twice. I do not say it is an invitation, brother. I only say the soup notices when meat falls in. The cook before me, may his soul digest gently, told me always: listen for which lord borrows from which merchant. Word from the cousin of my brother-in-law, a fig-hauler, is that the lord at Bilghar is so short on denars he sold his own wife's cookware to settle a debt with the spice guild. When a noble pawns the pots, he soon pawns the patrols. Mark which villages near his lands lose their riders first. That is where the smokehouses will go quiet, that is where the salted goat will stop reaching market, and that is where a hungry caravan will pay double for what we can supply. One more thing, then I must turn the dates before they weep. There is a fool of a grain-buyer working the eastern oases, a fat-faced southerner named Yusuf bin Tareeq, who pays seventy denars the measure for barley he could get for forty if he only haggled. The boys say he is buying for some northern lord's army and does not care what it costs, only that the sacks arrive. If you happen to come into barley, by whatever wind blows it your way, ride east, find the fat-face, and let him empty his purse into yours. Now go. The dates are calling, and old Kareem does not let dates wait on gossip.

Most folk think a date is a date. Squeeze it, sniff it, pop it in the mouth — sweet is sweet, yes? No. A date sings, friend. Press your thumb against the skin and listen with your fingers. The Nahasa khalas hums low and oily, made for slow stewing. The amber ajwa from the high palms snaps like dry parchment — that one you crush into the salt jar, never the pot. I learned this from my mother in a caravanserai outside Quyaz, before the soldiers came and the well went bitter. She would not let me touch the cooking fire until I could tell her, blindfolded, which of seven dates came from which oasis. Took me until I was eleven summers. So here is the secret of my pot, and I tell it because you have paid in good denars and because old men grow tired of hoarding. I cook lamb in three layers. The bottom: green dates, the under-ripe ones the merchants throw out — these I pound with cumin seed and the rendered tail-fat of the fat-tailed sheep, and I press it into the clay before any meat touches it. This is the foundation. The middle: the meat itself, rubbed only with sour camel-yogurt and a black salt I cure myself from the flats near Husn Fulq. No spice. Spice in the middle is a coward's trick. The top: a crown of fully-ripe medjool, split and seeded, laid skin-down like little boats. Sealed with a paste of flour and water around the lid. Six hours in the coals. The green ones below give the bite, the medjool above weep their honey down through the meat. By the time you break the seal, the lamb has eaten the dates and the dates have eaten the lamb, and you cannot tell where one ends. The trick, the real trick — lean closer, I will not shout it — is the black salt. Every cook claims a salt blend. Mine is roasted in a sealed pot with a single handful of dried pomegranate skin and three locust husks. Yes, locusts. The husks burn to a bitter ash that pulls the sweetness of the date sideways into something the tongue cannot name. Yusuf the Lame tried to steal the recipe by watching me through a tent-slit in Iqbayl; he got the pomegranate but missed the locusts, and now his stew tastes like a sad woman's apology. I do not laugh at him. Much. I have not cooked at a proper hearth in eleven years. The caravan moves, the pots travel rolled in felt, and I read the dates by torchlight while younger men watch the dunes for riders. Sometimes I think of my mother's kitchen, the blue tiles, the smell of cardamom at dawn. Then I taste a khalas, and I know which oasis it grew in, and I know I am still her son. Eat slowly, friend. A date that took seven months to ripen deserves more than two bites.
A Pot, A Palm, A Patience

My father kept a date-grove outside Quyaz, and before I could lift a basket he taught me to listen to the fruit. A date talks, friend — the thin-skinned ones whisper of too much sun, the heavy ones grunt of a slow autumn, and the sweet-bellied khalas hum like a woman who knows she is loved. I read them the way the qadi reads scripture, and by my twelfth season my father charged the caravans an extra dinar a sack because the boy could pick out the bitter ones blind. Then came the tax-year Emir Unqid doubled the salt levy, and the grove went to his bailiff for a debt my father did not owe. I walked west with a clay pot, a handful of pits, and the clothes the bailiff did not bother to take. For a long season I cooked for a spice train running between Iqbayl and the southern wells — millet porridge in the mornings, mutton and dates stewed slow at night, the kind of food that keeps a man upright in a saddle for sixteen hours. A raid finished the spice train south of the salt pans. The drivers ran, the camels scattered, and I sat down beside my pot because a man my age does not outrun horses. The chief of that raiding band lifted the lid, tasted the stew, and laughed — said any cook who could keep a stew sweet through a fight was worth more than the silver in the saddlebags. So he kept me, the pot, and the last of my dates, and rode me here. That was eleven seasons ago. The boys bring me grain stolen off the Pravend road, salt prised from southern flats, smoked goat from the high pens, and I turn it into something that tastes like a man still has a home. I keep my own date-palms now, in pots beside the cistern — three of them, grown from the pits I carried out of Quyaz. They fruit thin and bitter, but they fruit. So that is what pays a man into this trade — a stolen grove, a slow kettle, and the simple truth that hungry men do not care whose flag flies over the cook. Patience opens the date. Coin opens the pot. Sit, and I will open both.
Word From The Dune-Tracks

Sit, sit. The clay pot keeps its heat better than my old bones, so lean close. Word came in two nights past with the salt-runners out of Quyaz — the granaries there have cracked open at last, and the steward is paying eighty dinars the sack for any clean barley that still smells of the field. If you carry grain south, do not waste it on the coastal towns. Quyaz hungers louder. There is a sweetwine caravan crawling up from Iyakis — six camels, two of them limping, and the master is a Vlandian called Tomas of the Vine who tips his guards in copper and his cook in nothing at all. They take the long western track to avoid the toll-fort. If you have honey or pressed dates to trade, his hands are loose by the third cup of his own cargo. I would know. I taught the boy who pours for him. Bad news rides faster than good. The southern oases between Ar-Razir and the salt-flats have gone bitter — three wells in a row, all fouled, and the goat-herds are already burning their dead kids. A thin year is coming for that whole stretch. Buy your dried meat now, before the harvest-towns hear and the price jumps. Salt too. Always salt. A merchant out of Husn Fulq rode through yesterday looking for cinnamon and saffron at any price — some Aserai emir is marrying his third daughter and the kitchens are panicking. Spice that cost you forty dinars last moon will fetch a hundred and twenty if you reach the wedding gate before the feast. Ride hard, or do not bother. And one whisper, friend, because you bought the date and not just the talk. Sister Halima who keeps the smokehouse at the second waterhole has begun salting twice what she sold last season. She does not salt for nothing. Either she knows a famine I have only smelled, or a war-band is paying her in advance. Either way — fill your saddlebags with hearth-bread and dried lamb before you ride west. The pots here will still be warm when you return. If you return.
Old Kareem Date-Reader

Read sand for caravans before the dunes claimed his last wife. Now reads it for Hakkun's fires; the cookpot fills the same. Says the sand told him three winters back that you'd come — but the sand says that to everyone.

Old Kareem Date-Reader. The sand spoke your name three days running, traveler — Hakkun's reading. The cookpot heard it once. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} from the road, and the dunes will speak it fairer come morning.

Sand-cured dates take the four-day tent, not the three the Quyaz merchants rush, traveler. Fourth day's the bite — the sun pulls the last water and leaves the sugar in long strands. The dunes know the count. The merchants don't ask the dunes.
Tell me the caravan and the rite, traveler — wedding-night, name-day, mourner's pour. Three denars on the tent, a fortnight on the cure. A date for tonight's road-ration.

Wife went under to the dunes — sand-storm, the long crossing, the third caravan I lost. The sand said her name back to me the next dawn; said it three days running. I read sand for Hakkun's fires now and the sand still says her name some nights. I keep listening because she's still saying it.
Old Yusra reads sand at the Quyaz market-edge under a date-stall awning — knew my wife. Tell her Kareem still cures four days; she'll show you the back-tent. Coin for the desert crossing.

Sit. The coals are hot and so is the tongue today. A salt-trader out of Quyaz staggered in at dawn looking for a re-shod camel and a man to listen, and I am both. He says Emir Unqid is bleeding silver — three caravans gone to our cousins this season, and his clan-coffers down to whispers. The emir's quartermaster was at Iqbayl last week offering 240 denars a head for any veteran who could ride a sand-mare. That is the price of a desperate man, friend. A lord who pays 240 today pays nothing next month, because his caravans will be lighter still. Now lean closer — this is the part worth the visit. The Husn Fulq road, the long crooked one that hugs the dry wadi, is running with two-spear escorts. Two. For caravans hauling steel billets out of the northern foundries. I have seen the wagons myself, axles dragging, and the guards are boys with their fathers' helmets sliding into their eyes. Whoever owns those billets — and a smuggler hinted it is a factor working for Hakim al-Sarraj — has bet on speed over swords. Steel-billet caravans, my friend. The kind a forge would weep for. The kind a clever cousin would meet at the third bend past the dry well, where the cliffs throw a shadow at second prayer. The grain news is uglier and that is why I am pricing scimitars at a discount this fortnight. Razih's smokehouses burned in the dry-wind storms — three of them, the big ones — so cured meat is gone from every market between here and the coast and salt has tripled. The caravans coming up from the southern salt-pans are guarded like queens. Do not touch them. But the GRAIN going DOWN to feed those same salt-pans is barely watched, because nobody guards what nobody robs. Merchant Yusra bint Tahir is overpaying — 85 denars a sack at Mughar, which is twice the honest price — because her ovens go cold without it. A wagon of her grain re-sold to her own factor at a different gate would be tidy work. One last thing, and then I want to see coin on the anvil. There is a leather glut. A tannery upriver miscounted its herds and the hides are piling up — three caravans came through last week with bundled hides nobody wants, sold at thirty a stack and the owners glad to be rid of them. I bought what I could for grips and scabbards, which is why these curved blades on the rack are cheaper than last moon. The desert heat does half the work; a cousin's whisper does the other half. So — are you buying a sword, or buying a map? I sell both, and the second one costs more.

The desert is half the work. People hear me say it and laugh, but I mean it the way a man means his own name. The forge gives me the first heat — the sand gives me the second. When I draw a blade from the coals and lay it on the long iron tray sunk into the floor, the sand under it is already eighty degrees from noon. It does not steal the warmth back the way a stone slab would. The steel cools the way a man falls asleep in shade — slow, even, no flinch in the grain. That is half my temper, and I never paid a copper for it. The other half is the curve. Every Sand-Smith out here forges curved, and every fool thinks the curve is for looking pretty on a hip. It is not. A curve cuts longer because the edge meets the meat at a slipping angle, the way a reed knife peels a date. I draw mine with a fuller no thicker than a thumb-bone, set high on the spine, and I never grind the belly symmetrical — the underside of the curve gets a finer bevel than the top, because the underside is what does the work in the downstroke from a camel. A straight-ground blade chips on the third fight. Mine come back to me after twenty, and the owners want them re-polished, not re-edged. That is the difference, and I charge eight hundred denars for it without blinking. The quench is where I lose apprentices. I do not use water and I do not use oil — I use brine drawn from the salt-pans south of Quyaz, three jugs a season, hauled in by a cousin who owes me his teeth. The salt bites the surface faster than oil and leaves a skin on the steel that takes rust the way a tortoise takes rain — it just shrugs. You can leave one of my blades on a saddle for a week of sandstorm and the edge will still shave. Try that with a Sturgian longsword and you will be filing red dust off it by the second night. I learned all of this from my father, who learned it from his, and his hammer is the one on the second peg — the short one with the cracked haft I will not replace. He worked this same floor when the gang here was only six men and a goat, and when Sariq's grandfather was still raiding caravans on foot. I tell the young ones who come to buy that they are not paying for the steel. They are paying for four generations of men who learned that the desert is a partner, not an enemy, and that a smith who fights his climate dies poor. I have never been poor. Look at the rings.
Heat, Hammer, And A Debt

My father was a knife-grinder in Quyaz, and his father a horseshoer before him. I learned the bellows before I learned my letters. By twelve I could draw a tang true; by sixteen I could fold a billet seven times without a single grey seam. The trade was honest then, and the sand was just sand. I set up my own forge along the caravan road south of Iqbayl. Curved blades, mostly — a desert man wants a sword that draws clean from the saddle and clears the scabbard before his horse takes a second step. Emir Unqid's outriders bought from me, and so did the spice-guards bound for Pen Cannoc. Three hundred dinars for a good shamshir, more if the customer wanted gold wire down the fuller. I was not rich, but I slept on a proper rope-bed. The debt is what brought me here. A caravan-master fronted me ore from Husn Fulq on credit, and his caravan never came back from the dunes. His brother wanted blood or coin, and I had neither in the quantity he preferred. The camp's quartermaster heard of my trouble and made me an offer — work the forge here, the debt becomes his problem, and a man stops looking over his shoulder for the brother's knife. So now I forge in a sand-floored shop with the desert pressing against my back. The heat is half the work, you understand — the sun softens the steel before the coals ever touch it, and a smith who knows the trick saves a third of his charcoal. My blades go out on the saddles of men who do not always come back, but the steel does not care who carries it. Steel only cares that it was made true. I do not call this a fall. I call it a season. The forge is hot, the coin is honest, and the brother of that caravan-master is two provinces away. A man can live a long while on less.
Words From the Bellows

Aye, sit close to the bellows — the wind eats words out there. The road's been busy this moon, and a man who hammers steel hears more than a man who carries it. Caravans stop here for water, and water loosens tongues better than wine. Listen. A long string of Aserai pack-camels is creeping up from the southern wastes toward Quyaz, hauling Khuzait raw iron through a back-trail their guides swear no patrol uses. Twenty bars per beast, near forty beasts. If it arrives, every smith from here to the dune-line drops their price on billet. If it doesn't arrive — well, then I get rich, and somebody's bones bleach a little whiter. Emir Tamar is paying real coin at Sanala for any smith who can hammer mamluke sabres to the old curve — eight dinars a blade, lodging thrown in, and he asks no questions about the man's last forge. Half the journeymen out of Iqbayl have already walked there. I'd go myself if I hadn't sworn off cities that hang their smiths when the war turns. A noble's quartermaster came through three nights past, looking to buy four hundred leather-faced shields before the dry season breaks. He flashed a purse of dinars stamped with the Banu Hilal seal, which means somebody in the deep south is preparing to march and doesn't want it known yet. Watch the southern trade roads close — when shields move in bulk, blood follows within two moons. Last bit, friend, and worth the listening. The old salt-and-iron caravan that links Bilegan to Quyaz has lost two runs in a row to no bandit I know of — clean ambushes, no bodies, just empty wagons. Somebody's hoarding steel-stock and doesn't want the market to figure it out. If you've a strong arm and a quiet horse, there's coin to be made escorting the next run. Or taking it.
Zafir of the Forge
Forges in the dunes the way other smiths forge in towns — slower, by sun-heat as much as charcoal. The blades he tempers cool blue under the desert moon, which Hakkun says is the dunes' approval.

Zafir of the Forge. Hakkun reads sand; I read steel. The Sand-Reader's word is good. Mine's slower — sun-heat takes its time. Bring me {BP_VENDOR_QUEST_DESC} and I'll cool you a blade as blue as the noon sky over the dunes.

Sun-heat tempers different than charcoal, traveler — slower bite, longer hold. The blade cools blue under the desert moon, not the imperial grey. Hakkun says it's the dunes' approval. I think it's the patience. Either way the blade holds three campaigns where the Quyaz issue gives up at one.
Bring me a steel-bar, a draw-weight, and a noon-time, traveler. I'll temper you a blade the dunes've signed. Six denars on the sun-heat, the brine's the desert's. A small spike for your belt tonight.

Son apprenticed under me — twelve summers at the bellows. The desert took him at the fifth crossing; not the sand, the heat. Stuck at the high noon when I told him to rest. The forge was his first word. He'd be twenty-five now. I temper at noon still, the way he wanted.
Old Hassan forges at the Quyaz inner-quarter — sun-heat trade by the same dunes. Tell him Zafir still cools blue; he'll show you the back-anvil. Coin for the desert crossing.

You were born far from here, in a house of small people — the kind kings never meet and tax collectors never forget. Then came the year it all broke, and what you lost is your business; that you lost it is written all over you, plain as a brand.
On the road inland, a one-eyed peddler pressed this book into your hands and would take no coin for it. "The kings will tell you what Calradia is. The road will tell you the truth."

— AND THE ROADS KEPT WRITING —

◆ The First Parley — {CTX} raised the white flag, and {HERO} rode in under it without drawing steel. The chronicle marks the day; the roads marked the precedent. A stranger who sits at a chief's fire does not leave one.
◆ Kin & Oath — the {CTX} spoke for {HERO} at last. A company that answers to no crown now answers, in some measure, to one name. Sworn kin cost more than hired swords, and are worth the difference.
◆ The Open Camp — the watch at {CTX} stood aside and let {HERO} walk in past the stakes. A camp that opens its gate has decided something about {HERO} no lord ever will.
◆ The Horn Answered — {CTX} burned to {HERO}'s horn, and the tithe it owed some distant lord it paid, that season, to the road instead. The chronicle does not moralize. It only tallies.

◆ Blood for Blood — {CTX} changed hands at the point of {HERO}'s siege, and a banner the heralds had no entry for flew above a wall that had only ever known a king's. The clerks will want a fresh page.
